Spatial Jurisdiction: The UNFCCC Secretariat operates globally, supporting the implementation of the UNFCCC and its related agreements across all countries. Its jurisdiction covers the entire atmosphere, as well as the land and ocean surfaces that are affected by or influence climate change.
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: The UNFCCC Secretariat is responsible for facilitating international cooperation on climate action, supporting the development and implementation of the UNFCCC and its related agreements, and providing technical and logistical assistance to the parties and stakeholders (https://unfccc.int/about-us/about-the-secretariat). This includes organizing and servicing the sessions of the Conference of the Parties (COP), the subsidiary bodies and other constituted bodies, maintaining the official records and documents of the convention and its protocols, and coordinating with other relevant international and regional organizations and processes (https://unfccc.int/process-and-meetings/what-are-governing-process-management-subsidiary-constituted-and-concluded-bodies).
Source of Jurisdiction: The UNFCCC Secretariat derives its mandate from the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) (https://unfccc.int/resource/docs/convkp/conveng.pdf). Additionally, the UNFCCC Secretariat's jurisdiction is influenced by the Kyoto Protocol , and the Paris Agreement. These agreements, particularly Articles 2-7 of the Kyoto Protocol  ((https://unfccc.int/resource/docs/convkp/kpeng.pdf)) and Articles 2-15 of the Paris Agreement (https://unfccc.int/files/meetings/paris_nov_2015/application/pdf/paris_agreement_english_.pdf?gclid=CjwKCAiA98WrBhAYEiwA2WvhOmz_K80dVb1ZLjpfckneL_gnl1kyg-FWmkaJwOJ86ZhIyhM-JyjQjBoCAJIQAvD_BwE), outline the areas of cooperation, communication, and compliance between the UNFCCC Secretariat and the parties and stakeholders of the convention and its protocols
Defined Objectives: The secretariat's duties under the Convention include organizing and servicing sessions of the Conference of the Parties and its subsidiary bodies (Article 8, paragraph 2 (a)); compiling and transmitting reports from Parties and other sources, and supporting technical and financial assistance to Parties, particularly developing countries, for Convention compliance (Article 8, paragraphs 2 (b), (c), and 7); preparing and presenting activity reports to the Conference of the Parties and coordinating with relevant international organizations (Article 8, paragraphs 2 (d) and (e)); handling administrative and contractual arrangements as directed by the Conference of the Parties for effective functioning (Article 8, paragraph 2 (f)); and executing other specified secretariat roles in the Convention, its protocols, and tasks assigned by the Conference of the Parties (Article 8, paragraph 2 (g)). These responsibilities are key to ensuring effective implementation and coordination within the Convention's framework. (https://unfccc.int/resource/docs/convkp/conveng.pdf)
Strategies: The UNFCCC Secretariat executes its objectives via several strategies: firstly, a six-year Strategic Plan, revised biennially by the Conference of the Parties, which establishes the secretariat's vision, mission, strategic goals, core functions, and targets. This plan, applicable for 2020-2025, aligns with the Paris Agreement and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, detailed in decision 18/CP.25. Secondly, a biennial programme budget and workplan, devised by the secretariat and ratified by the Conference of the Parties, detail activities, outputs, indicators, and resources corresponding to each strategic objective (https://unfccc.int/sites/default/files/resource/sbi2021_04E.pdf). The current budget and workplan for 2022-2023 are tailored to the Parties' needs and stakeholders' priorities, as outlined in decision FCCC/SBI/2021/4/Add (https://unfccc.int/sites/default/files/resource/sbi2022_inf03.pdf). It also maintains the registry for Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC) established under the Paris Agreement, a key aspect of the implementation of the Paris Agreement (https://www4.unfccc.int/sites/ndcstaging/Pages/Home.aspx?_gl=1*ewhacw*_ga*MjAxOTI0NTk2NC4xNzAxOTkxOTI3*_ga_7ZZWT14N79*MTcwMTk5MTkyOC4xLjEuMTcwMTk5ODIxNC4wLjAuMA..). Finally, various agreements, mechanisms, platforms, and initiatives provide an operational framework for implementing the Convention, the Kyoto Protocol, and the Paris Agreement, addressing adaptation, mitigation, finance, technology, transparency, and capacity-building, with key instruments listed here (https://sdg.iisd.org/news/unfccc-closes-2020-with-28-long-term-low-emission-development-strategies/).
Inter-Institutional Relationship: The UNFCCC Secretariat maintains collaborative relationships with various UN agencies and international organizations to advance climate action and sustainable development (https://unfccc.int/sites/default/files/resource/sbsta2022_inf01pdf.pdf). This collaboration includes working with the UN Development Programme (UNDP) on implementing NDCs under the Paris Agreement, with UNESCO to promote climate change education and research, and with the WHO and WMO to address health risks and improve climate data related to climate change (https://unfccc.int/documents/628347). Additionally, the Secretariat aligns with the UN Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD) and the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) as part of the Rio Conventions from the 1992 Earth Summit. They focus on tackling climate change, desertification, and biodiversity loss through initiatives like land degradation neutrality and sustainable management. Strengthened by a 2023 memorandum of understanding, their cooperation is guided by the Joint Liaison Group (JLG), established to enhance synergy and coordination among the Rio Conventions (https://unfccc.int/resource/docs/publications/adaptation_eng.pdf).
Vertical Coordination: Vertical coordination within UNFCCC involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other specialized agencies, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and local authorities. This is structured under the Relationship with Other Bodies section of the Convention, specifically in Articles 7, 8, 11, and 16. The UNFCCC operates through a Conference of the Parties (COP) of all the members, a Bureau of 11 members, and a secretariat headed by an Executive Secretary (Articles 7 and 8). The UNFCCC also has two subsidiary bodies for scientific and technological advice (SBSTA) and for implementation (SBI), as well as other subsidiary bodies and mechanisms as needed (Articles 9 and 10). The UNFCCC facilitates the provision of financial resources and the transfer of technology to developing country Parties, through a financial mechanism operated by an entity or entities designated by the COP (Article 11). The UNFCCC also adopts and amends annexes to the Convention, which may include lists of Parties with different commitments or responsibilities in accordance with the rules of procedure and the principles of the Convention (Article 16). (https://unfccc.int/resource/docs/convkp/conveng.pdf)
Horizontal Coordination: Horizontal coordination within the UNFCCC involves collaboration across various sectors and stakeholders in the climate change arena, including governments, institutions, civil society, the private sector, and the scientific community. This coordination is structured under the Institutional and Financial Arrangements section of the Convention, specifically outlined in Articles 7-11 (https://unfccc.int/resource/docs/convkp/conveng.pdf). The UNFCCC has established the Conference of the Parties (COP) as its supreme decision-making body, which adopts decisions and protocols for implementing the Convention's objectives and principles. It also has set up two subsidiary bodies: the Subsidiary Body for Scientific and Technological Advice (SBSTA) and the Subsidiary Body for Implementation (SBI), to support the COP (https://unfccc.int/resource/docs/convkp/conveng.pdf). Furthermore, the UNFCCC defines a financial mechanism to aid developing countries and a mechanism for resolving questions about Convention implementation (https://unfccc.int/resource/docs/convkp/conveng.pdf). It also collaborates with the IPCC to ensure scientific coherence, with the GEF (https://ccsr.aori.u-tokyo.ac.jp/old/unfccc4/pdfs/unfccc.int/resource/docs/cop2/15a01.pdf) and GCF (https://www.ciesin.columbia.edu/repository/entri/docs/cop/FCCC_COP17_dec03.pdf) for financial resources and with the Technology Mechanism for climate technology development and transfer, as detailed in various decisions decision 1/CP.16 (https://unfccc.int/resource/docs/2010/cop16/eng/07a01.pdf). This structure facilitates information exchange and communication on actions addressing climate change and its impacts.

Institution: Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), and the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR)
Spatial Jurisdiction: OHCHR's authority is global, encompassing the human rights of all people in all countries and territories.  OHCHR's authority is not limited by any specific distance or boundary, but by the principles and standards of international human rights law (https://www.ohchr.org/en/about-us/high-commissioner).
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: The OHCHR is responsible for protecting and promoting the human rights of all people in all countries and territories, regardless of their legal status, nationality, or any other distinction. This includes addressing human rights issues, such as discrimination, violence, torture, arbitrary detention, enforced disappearances, and freedom of expression (https://www.ohchr.org/sites/default/files/Documents/Publications/FactSheet26en.pdf). OHCHR also provides technical assistance, monitoring and reporting, advocacy and awareness-raising, and capacity-building for human rights, as well as supporting the implementation of the UN's human rights mechanisms and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (https://www.ohchr.org/en/countries/technical-cooperation).
Source of Jurisdiction: OHCHR derives its mandate from the Charter of the United Nations, which establishes the promotion and protection of human rights as one of the purposes and principles of the UN, particularly chapter 1 (article 1), chapter 3 (article 13), chapter 9 (article 53),  chapter 10 (article 62 & 68), chapter 12 (article 76) (https://treaties.un.org/doc/publication/ctc/uncharter.pdf). Resolution A/RES/48/141 adopted by the UN General Assembly established the post of High Commissioner for the promotion and protection of all human rights and outlined the mandate, functions, and responsibilities of the High Commissioner, as well as the location and resources of the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (https://www.securitycouncilreport.org/atf/cf/%7B65BFCF9B-6D27-4E9C-8CD3-CF6E4FF96FF9%7D/a_res_48_141.pdf). Additionally, OHCHR's jurisdiction is influenced by the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (https://www.un.org/sites/un2.un.org/files/2021/03/udhr.pdf) and the international human rights treaties (https://www.un.org/en/global-issues/human-rights), which confer legal form on inherent human rights and develop the body of international human rights law. The treaties, particularly the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (https://www.ohchr.org/sites/default/files/ccpr.pdf) and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (https://www.ohchr.org/sites/default/files/cescr.pdf), outline the obligations and duties of States to respect, protect and fulfil human rights. OHCHR also supports the implementation of the UN's human rights mechanisms and procedures, such as the Human Rights Council, the treaty bodies, the special procedures, and the Universal Periodic Review, which provide further legal frameworks for OHCHR's jurisdiction over specific human rights issues and situations (https://www.ohchr.org/en/instruments-and-mechanisms/international-human-rights-law).
Defined Objectives: OHCHR, as mandated by General Assembly Resolution 48/141, aims to promote and protect all human rights. Its objectives include promoting all civil, cultural, economic, political, and social rights (paragraph 4 a), carrying out tasks assigned by UN bodies in human rights and making recommendations (paragraph 4 b), promoting the right to development and enhancing support from UN bodies (paragraph 4 c), providing advisory services and technical and financial assistance to support human rights actions and programs (paragraph 4 d), coordinating UN education and public information programmes in human rights (paragraph 4 e), actively working to remove obstacles and prevent human rights violations (paragraph 4 f), engaging in dialogue with governments for human rights implementation (paragraph 4 g), enhancing international cooperation for human rights promotion and protection (paragraph 4 h), coordinating human rights activities across the UN system (paragraph 4 i), streamlining the UN human rights machinery for improved efficiency (paragraph 4 j), and overseeing the Centre for Human Rights (paragraph 4 k). These roles establish the OHCHR as the key UN entity responsible for human rights activities under the Secretary-General's direction. (https://www.securitycouncilreport.org/atf/cf/%7B65BFCF9B-6D27-4E9C-8CD3-CF6E4FF96FF9%7D/a_res_48_141.pdf)
Strategies: The OHCHR executes its objectives via several strategies: firstly, a four-year Management Plan, revised biennially by the High Commissioner, which establishes the OHCHR's vision, mission, priorities, results and strategies (https://www2.ohchr.org/english/OMP_22_23/documents/OMP-2022-2023.pdf). This plan, applicable for 2022-2023, aligns with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the international human rights treaties, as well as the UN's 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://www.ohchr.org/en/about-us). It also maintains the Universal Human Rights Index, a database of the recommendations and observations issued by the human rights mechanisms, a key aspect of the implementation of the human rights standards (https://www2.ohchr.org/english/OMP_22_23/documents/The-pillars-of-our-programme.pdf). Finally, various agreements, mechanisms, platforms, and initiatives provide an operational framework for implementing the OHCHR's mandate, addressing civil, political, economic, social and cultural rights, as well as the right to development, with key instruments listed here (https://www.ohchr.org/sites/default/files/Documents/Publications/OMP_II.pdf).
Inter-Institutional Relationship: OHCHR collaborates with various organizations to promote and protect human rights (https://www.ohchr.org/en/about-us/what-we-do). It works with the Human Rights Council (HRC), established in 2006 by resolution 60/251, serving as the main intergovernmental body responsible for human rights issues (https://www.dfat.gov.au/sites/default/files/ohchr-assessment.pdf) (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N05/502/66/PDF/N0550266.pdf?OpenElement). As the secretariat of the HRC, OHCHR's relationship with the Council is based on resolution 48/141, paragraph 4 (b), which entrusts the High Commissioner with the task of making recommendations to the competent bodies of the UN system in the field of human rights (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N94/012/56/PDF/N9401256.pdf?OpenElement). Additionally, OHCHR supports the treaty bodies and special procedures, providing substantive and technical assistance for the monitoring and implementation of international human rights instruments and standards, as mandated by resolution 48/141, paragraph 4 (a) and (d) (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N94/012/56/PDF/N9401256.pdf?OpenElement). It also cooperates with UN agencies, funds and programmes, as well as regional and national human rights institutions, civil society organizations, and other actors, to enhance coordination and effectiveness of human rights activities throughout the UN system, as stipulated by resolution 48/141, paragraph 4 (h) and (i) (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N94/012/56/PDF/N9401256.pdf?OpenElement). Moreover, OHCHR participates in the Universal Periodic Review (UPR), offering technical and logistical support for the peer review mechanism of the human rights situation of all UN Member States, as established by resolution 60/251, paragraph 5 (e) (https://www2.ohchr.org/english/bodies/hrcouncil/docs/a.res.60.251_en.pdf).
Vertical Coordination: Vertical coordination within OHCHR involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other specialized agencies, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and local authorities. This is achieved through dialogue, cooperation, and assistance (https://www.ohchr.org/sites/default/files/english/planaction.pdf). This is structured under the Establishment of the post of High Commissioner for the promotion and protection of all human rights section of the General Assembly Resolution 48/141, specifically in paragraphs 2-5 (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N94/012/56/PDF/N9401256.pdf?OpenElement). The OHCHR operates under the direction and authority of the Secretary-General, and reports annually to the General Assembly and the Economic and Social Council (paragraph 2). The OHCHR also works with the Human Rights Council, the treaty bodies, and the special procedures, providing substantive and technical support for the monitoring and implementation of international human rights standards (paragraph 4 a and d). The OHCHR cooperates with UN agencies, funds and programmes, as well as regional and national human rights institutions, civil society organizations, and other actors, to enhance coordination and effectiveness of human rights activities throughout the UN system (paragraph 4 h and i). OHCHR's work is organized around seven regions, each overseen by a Regional Representative who works closely with the High Commissioner to implement strategies and programmes across all levels of the Office (https://www.ohchr.org/en/about-us/where-we-work). There is also the Senior Management Team (consisting of the High Commissioner, Deputy High Commissioner, Assistant Secretary-General, and Directors of the thematic and geographic divisions) providing strategic and operational guidance to the High Commissioner on matters related to the programmatic and managerial work of OHCHR; and ensuring coherence and alignment between the three levels of the Office and the governing bodies (https://www2.ohchr.org/english/OHCHRreport2021/documents/OHCHR_AR-2021_Management.pdf). Also, a network of country offices and human rights advisers supports the OHCHR's work in promoting and protecting human rights as an integral part of regional and national development policies (https://www.ohchr.org/EN/Countries/Pages/WorkInField.aspx). Additionally, OHCHR participates in the Universal Periodic Review, offering technical and logistical support for the peer review mechanism of the human rights situation of all UN Member States, as established by resolution 60/251, paragraph 5 (e) (https://www2.ohchr.org/english/bodies/hrcouncil/docs/a.res.60.251_en.pdf).
Horizontal Coordination: Horizontal coordination within OHCHR involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the human rights domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, academic community, and other UN agencies to ensure that human rights are respected, protected, and fulfilled in all policies and that human rights policies are consistent with other sectoral policies. This coordination is guided by the mandate of the High Commissioner for Human Rights, as established in the General Assembly resolution 48/141 (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N94/012/56/PDF/N9401256.pdf?OpenElement). For example, OHCHR works with the justice sector to promote the rule of law and access to justice for all (https://unsceb.org/sites/default/files/imported_files/Annex2Activitiesfinal7June_0.pdf), with the development sector to integrate human rights into the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://www.ohchr.org/en/sdgs/ohchrs-work-2030-agenda-sustainable-developmentx), or with the peace and security sector to prevent and respond to human rights violations in conflict and post-conflict situations (https://peacemaker.un.org/sites/peacemaker.un.org/files/DPPA-OHCHR-Joint-Practice-Note.pdf). Horizontal coordination within OHCHR can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the UN Common Country Analysis (https://procurement-notices.undp.org/view_file.cfm?doc_id=194928) and the UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework with UNCTs (https://unsdg.un.org/2030-agenda/cooperation-framework), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral mechanisms, networks, and platforms, such as the Human Rights Council or the UN Human Rights Treaty Bodies (https://www.ohchr.org/EN/HRBodies/Pages/HumanRightsBodies.aspx), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for human rights mainstreaming and engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Human Rights Indicators (https://www.ohchr.org/EN/Issues/Indicators/Pages/HRIndicatorsIndex.aspx) or the Human Rights Based Approach to Development Cooperation (https://www.ohchr.org/Documents/Publications/FAQen.pdf), (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for human rights issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Human Rights Day (https://www.ohchr.org/en/about-us/human-rights-day) or the Annual Report of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (https://www.ohchr.org/sites/default/files/documents/publications/ohchr-reports/ohchr-report-2022.pdf). The OHCHR provides leadership and coordination on matters related to human rights, supports the development and implementation of human rights norms and standards, provides technical assistance and capacity-building to States and other actors, and monitors and reports on human rights situations (https://www.ohchr.org/EN/AboutUs/Pages/WhatWeDo.aspx). OHCHR facilitates the participation of various actors in the human rights sector and enhances cooperation and coordination within the UN system on human rights matters (https://www2.ohchr.org/english/OHCHRreport2022/documents/UN-Human-Rights-at-headquarters-.pdf).

Institution: Convention on the Intergovernmental Maritime Consultative Organization (IMO) Secretariat
Spatial Jurisdiction: The IMO’s authority spans a global geographical area, facilitating maritime cooperation and development across diverse regions. Its mandate covers member states’ territorial waters, extending to their exclusive economic zones (EEZs), typically up to 200 nautical miles from the baseline (https://www.imo.org/en/OurWork/TechnicalCooperation/Pages/Geo-Coverage.aspx#:~:text=Africa,Western%20Asia%20and%20Eastern%20Europe)
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: The IMO's jurisdiction encompasses a comprehensive framework for the safety, security, and environmental performance of international shipping. It is responsible for setting global maritime regulations, ensuring fair and effective implementation, and promoting maritime safety and environmental protection (https://www.imo.org/en/About/Pages/Default.aspx). This includes overseeing maritime security, technical cooperation, environmental concerns, and legal matters related to shipping activities (https://www.imo.org/en/OurWork/Security/Pages/GuideMaritimeSecurityDefault.aspx). The IMO also focuses on energy efficiency, new technology, and innovation within the maritime sector, contributing to sustainable economic growth and supporting the UN SDGs (https://www.imo.org/en/About/Pages/Default.aspx). It provides leadership in developing standards and policies, offering technical support to countries, and monitoring global maritime trends (https://www.imo.org/en/OurWork/TechnicalCooperation/Pages/Default.aspx)
Source of Jurisdiction: The IMO's jurisdiction is established by the Convention for the creation of the International Maritime Organization (IMO), adopted at a diplomatic conference held in Geneva in 1948 under the auspices of the United Nations Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC) (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%201276/volume-1276-I-4214-English.pdf). The Convention, which entered into force on 17 March 1958, defines the IMO's mandate, particularly in Article 1, which outlines its purposes, including cooperation among governments in the field of governmental regulation and practices relating to technical matters of all kinds affecting shipping engaged in international trade (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%201276/volume-1276-I-4214-English.pdf). Furthermore, the IMO's role in implementing regulations is reinforced by the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), specifically Article 94, which mandates states to effectively exercise jurisdiction and control over ships flying their flag (https://www.un.org/depts/los/convention_agreements/texts/unclos/unclos_e.pdf). This includes the duty of the flag State to implement regulations recognized as IMO shipping rules and standards (https://www.un.org/depts/los/convention_agreements/texts/unclos/unclos_e.pdf). Furthermore, various IMO conventions such as SOLAS 1974, MARPOL, STCW 1978, and others influences IMO's mandate, under which administrations are responsible for implementing laws and regulations to ensure maritime safety and environmental protection (https://www.imo.org/en/OurWork/IIIS/Pages/default.aspx). In addtion several Protocols, Amendments, Recommendations, codes and roslutios of the IMOenabling it to function as a global standard-setter for maritime safety, security, and environmental performance. (https://www.imo.org/en/OurWork/Environment/Pages/International-Conventions,-Protocols-and-Codes.aspx)
Defined Objectives: According to Part I, Article 1 of the International Maritime Organization (IMO) Convention, the IMO’s objectives include several key objectives: providing machinery for cooperation among governments in the field of governmental regulation and practices relating to technical matters of all kinds affecting shipping engaged in international trade (Article 1a); encouraging the removal of discriminatory action and unnecessary restrictions by governments affecting shipping engaged in international trade (Article 1b); considering matters concerning unfair restrictive practices by shipping concerns (Article 1c); considering any matters concerning shipping and the effect of shipping on the marine environment that may be referred to it by any organ or specialized agency of the United Nations (Article 1d); and providing for the exchange of information among governments on matters under consideration by the organization (Article 1e);  consideration of any matters that may affect the freedom of shipping of all flags to take part in international trade (Article 2b); and the consideration of any matters concerning shipping and the effect of shipping on the marine environment (Article 2c). (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%201276/volume-1276-I-4214-English.pdf)
Strategies: IMO implements its objectives and mandates through various strategies, such as a six-year Strategic Plan adopted by the IMO Assembly every two years that defines the mission, vision, principles, directions, indicators, and outputs of the Organization. The current plan for the six-year period 2024 to 2029 is aligned with the UN Sustainable Development Goals and detailed in [resolution A.1149 (32)] (https://www.imo.org/en/MediaCentre/PressBriefings/pages/IMO-Assembly-adopts-budget,-strategic-plan.aspx). Another strategy is a biennial budget and work program which is prepared by the IMO Council and approved by the IMO Assembly, and outlines the resources, accomplishments, and achievements for each output of the Strategic Plan (https://www.imo.org/en/MediaCentre/PressBriefings/pages/IMO-Assembly-adopts-budget,-strategic-plan.aspx). The current program reflects the needs and priorities of the members and the industry and detailed in [resolution A.1150 (32)]. Thirdly, the 2023 IMO Strategy on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships sets a vision to reduce GHG emissions from international shipping and phase them out as soon as possible, with specific targets for carbon intensity reduction and the uptake of zero or near-zero GHG emission technologies (https://wwwcdn.imo.org/localresources/en/OurWork/Environment/Documents/annex/MEPC%2080/Annex%2015.pdf). Additionally, the IMO maintains various regulatory frameworks, such as the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea (SOLAS) and the International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships (MARPOL), which are periodically updated to meet new challenges and technologies in maritime transport (https://www.un.org/depts/los/consultative_process/mar_sec_submissions/imo.pdf).
Inter-Institutional Relationship: The IMO collaborates with a diverse array of organizations to support its maritime governance objectives. It maintains formal relations with 66 intergovernmental organizations, as governed by Articles 25 and 66 of the Convention on the International Maritime Organization (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%201276/volume-1276-I-4214-English.pdf), and detailed in resolution A.1168(32) adopted by the IMO Assembly on 15 December 20211 (https://wwwcdn.imo.org/localresources/en/KnowledgeCentre/IndexofIMOResolutions/AssemblyDocuments/A.1168(32).pdf). This includes cooperation with the United Nations (UN), with the relationship between the IMO and the UN outlined in Part XV of the IMO Convention, specifically Article 592 (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%201276/volume-1276-I-4214-English.pdf). The IMO also engages with non-governmental international organizations that contribute expert advice to IMO Member States on their respective areas of work, with formal relations established as per the provisions contained in the Rules and Guidelines for Consultative Status (https://wwwcdn.imo.org/localresources/en/OurWork/ERO/Documents/RULES%20AND%20GUIDELINES%20FOR%20CONSULTATIVE%20STATUS%20-%20December%202019.pdf). Additionally, the IMO supports the implementation of the UN Decade of Ocean Science for Sustainable Development, collaborating with various stakeholders to enhance ocean governance3. These relationships enable the IMO to fulfill its mandate, ensuring the safety, security, and environmental performance of international shipping, and facilitating global maritime cooperation1. The IMO collborates with the  IOC inl research efforts to understand and address human impacts on the ocean’s ecosystems (The IOC coordinates global research efforts to understand and address human impacts on the ocean’s ecosystems, where the IMO contributes with its expertise on maritime aspects1.),  including the  Global Ocean Oxygen Decade  (GOOD) (https://www.ioc.unesco.org/en/global-ocean-oxygen-decade). IMO collabortes with the IOC, IAEA, UNEP, WMO, and others on the  GESAMP Working Group 45 on Climate Change and Greenhouse Gas Related Impacts on Contaminants in the Ocean (http://www.gesamp.org/work/groups/wg-45-ghg-impacts-on-contaminants-in-the-ocean). IMO als collaboration with GEF and UNDP to protect marine biodiversity by preventing the transfer of invasive aquatic species through the GloFouling Partnership project (https://www.google.com/search?client=safari&rls=en&q=GloFouling+Partnerships&ie=UTF-8&oe=UTF-8) .
Vertical Coordination: Vertical coordination within IMO involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other specialized agencies, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and local authorities. This is structured under the Relationship with Other Organizations section of the IMCO Convention, specifically in Articles 45-48. The IMO operates through an Assembly of all the members, a Council of 40 members, and a Secretary-General (Articles 12-18 of the Convention) The IMO operates through its Assembly, Council, and a series of committees and sub-committees, Legal Committee, Technical Cooperation Committe, Facilitation Committee and the Secretariat that address various aspects of maritime safety, security, and environmental protection (https://www.imo.org/en/About/Pages/Structure.aspx). It also works closely with Member States to implement and enforce international maritime conventions and standards (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%201276/volume-1276-I-4214-English.pdf).  . The IMO also has committees, sub-committees, and other subsidiary bodies (Articles 19-24). The IMO assists members in the implementation of its conventions, codes, standards, and guidelines, and provides technical assistance and capacity building upon request (Articles 25-26).  This coordination is also structured under the IMO’s framework for cooperation with intergovernmental organizations, as established in resolution A.1168(32) adopted by the IMO Assembly (https://wwwcdn.imo.org/localresources/en/KnowledgeCentre/IndexofIMOResolutions/AssemblyDocuments/A.1168(32).pdf).  The World Maritime University (WMU) and the IMO International Maritime Law Institute (IMLI) are key educational pillars of the IMO, fostering expertise and knowledge in maritime law and policy (https://www.imo.org/en/About/Pages/WMUandIMLI.aspx). There are also some affliated bodies to the IMO including  the Global MTCC Network (GMN)  focusing on improving energy efficiency in the maritime sector and supports developing regions in moving towards maritime decarbonization (https://www.imo.org/en/OurWork/PartnershipsProjects/Pages/IMO-EuropeanUnionProject.aspx) . IMO has regional coordinators/advisors for technical cooperation activities, in Cote d'Ivoire, Ghana, Kenya, Philippines and Trinidad and Tobago (https://www.imo.org/en/about/pages/structure.aspx#9). The IMO operates a network of regional centers, including NOWPAP MERRAC, REMPEITC-Caribe, MEMAC, ROPME, REMPEC, PEMSEA, and PERSGA, which play crucial roles in regional maritime safety, security, and environmental protection efforts
Horizontal Coordination: Horizontal coordination within the IMO involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the maritime domain, such as governments, the shipping industry, port authorities, maritime training institutions, and other UN agencies to ensure that maritime safety, security, and environmental protection are integrated into all policies (https://www.un.org/en/chronicle/article/role-international-maritime-organization-preventing-pollution-worlds-oceans-ships-and-shipping). This coordination is guided by Articles 25 and 66 of the Convention on the International Maritime Organization (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%201276/volume-1276-I-4214-English.pdf). For example, the IMO works with the education sector to promote maritime training and capacity building through institutions like the World Maritime University (WMU) and the International Maritime Law Institute (IMLI) (https://www.imo.org/en/About/Pages/WMUandIMLI.aspx), with the environmental sector to address issues like biofouling and greenhouse gas emissions through initiatives like the GloFouling Partnerships project (https://www.imo.org/en/OurWork/PartnershipsProjects/Pages/GloFouling-Project.aspx), or with the development sector to enhance maritime capabilities in regions like Africa, Asia, and the Caribbean through its Integrated Technical Cooperation Programme (https://www.imo.org/en/OurWork/TechnicalCooperation/Pages/ITCP.aspx). Horizontal coordination within the IMO can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Global SAR Plan (https://www.imo.org/en/OurWork/Safety/Pages/GlobalSARPlan.aspx), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the Global Integrated Shipping Information System (https://gisis.imo.org/Public/Default.aspx), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for maritime sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the International Ship and Port Facility Security (ISPS) COde (https://www.imo.org/en/OurWork/Security/Pages/SOLAS-XI-2%20ISPS%20Code.aspx) , (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for maritime issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Day of the Seafarer (https://www.imo.org/en/About/Events/Pages/Day-of-the-Seafarer-2024.aspx). The IMO provides leadership and direction on matters critical to maritime safety and security, shapes the maritime research agenda, sets norms and standards, articulates evidence-based policy options, provides technical support to countries, and monitors and assesses maritime trends (https://www.imo.org/en/OurWork/TechnicalCooperation/Pages/Geo-Coverage.aspx). The IMO facilitates the participation of various actors in the maritime sector and enhances cooperation and coordination within the UN system on maritime matters (https://www.imo.org/en/OurWork/TechnicalCooperation/Pages/Geo-Coverage.aspx)

Institution: Division for Ocean Affairs and the Law of the Sea (UN DOALOS)
Spatial Jurisdiction: UN DALOS does not have authority over any specific ocean space. Rather, it provides legal and technical assistance to States and intergovernmental organizations on matters relating to ocean affairs and the law of the sea, and also supports the Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf, which examines submissions by coastal States on the outer limits of their continental shelf beyond 200 nautical miles from the baselines.
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: The UN DOALOS's mandate includes providing information, advice and assistance on ocean affairs and the law of the sea, services on conservation and sustainable use of marine biological diversity of areas beyond national jurisdiction development, and protection of the marine environment​​, as well as technical and legal assistance to States on the delimitation of maritime zones and the settlement of maritime disputes.
Source of Jurisdiction: DOALOS derives its mandate from the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS). Additionally, DOALOS’s jurisdiction is influenced by the agreements relating to the implementation of Part XI of UNCLOS (https://www.un.org/depts/los/convention_agreements/texts/unclos/unclos_e.pdf)) and the United Nations Fish Stocks Agreement (https://www.un.org/oceancapacity/sites/www.un.org.oceancapacity/files/files/Projects/UNFSA/docs/unfsa_text-eng.pdf). The agreements, particularly Articles 2-4 of the 1994 Agreement and Articles 5-8 of the UNFSA, outline the areas of collaboration, consultation, and information exchange between DOALOS and the International Seabed Authority and the regional fisheries management organizations.
Defined Objectives: According to the Secretary-General’s bulletin ST/SGB/2015/3, DOALOS's objectives encompass several key functions: promoting understanding of the UNCLOS and related Agreements, as well as aiding in their uniform application (Section 9.2 a); providing extensive support to meetings concerning the Convention, focusing on sustainable management of marine resources and dispute resolution (Section 9.2 c); assisting the Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf with technical aid for delineating continental shelf boundaries (Section 9.2 e); and supporting the General Assembly in matters of ocean and maritime law, including policy guidance and reporting on developments (Section 9.2 g) (https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/798635/files/ST_SGB_2015_3-EN.pdf?ln=en). Additionally, DOALOS offers substantial support to the Review Conference on the UNFSA and consultations of States parties to that Agreement, and provides policy recommendations to support General Assembly resolutions on ocean affairs and sustainable fisheries ((https://www.un.org/oceancapacity/sites/www.un.org.oceancapacity/files/files/Projects/UNFSA/docs/unfsa_text-eng.pdf). This multifaceted role ensures the effective implementation of legal frameworks pertaining to ocean governance.
Strategies: . DOALOS) executes its objectives through a multifaceted strategy: primarily, a continuous programme of assistance to States and intergovernmental organizations in the field of oceans and the law of the sea, which includes the uniform and consistent application of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea and related Agreements (https://www.un.org/ola/en/content/div-doalos). This assistance is tailored based on the needs of beneficiaries and is aligned with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and its Sustainable Development Goals (https://www.un.org/oceancapacity/). Additionally, DOALOS administers several Trust Funds established by the General Assembly to support States, particularly developing States, in implementing the Convention and participating in ocean-related work of the General Assembly (https://www.un.org/oceancapacity/tf). Furthermore, DOALOS provides advisory services, reference collections, databases, studies, and guidelines on ocean affairs and the law of the sea (https://www.un.org/oceancapacity/). It also plays a pivotal role in the Regular Process for Global Reporting and Assessment of the State of the Marine Environment, including Socioeconomic Aspects¹. These strategies and mechanisms collectively form the operational framework for DOALOS to fulfill its mandate and contribute to global ocean governance and sustainable development.
Inter-Institutional Relationship: DOALOS collaborates with key organizations to support ocean governance. It liaises with the International Seabed Authority (ISA), implementing a relationship agreement effective since 25 July 1996, as per UNCLOS Annex III Article 4 and the 1994 Agreement Article 177, detailed in resolution 48/263 (https://documents.un.org/doc/undoc/gen/n94/332/98/pdf/n9433298.pdf?token=YhD8GNV5K9pWhEpVuW&fe=true). Similarly, DOALOS maintains a relationship with the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS), providing administrative support based on an agreement aligned with the Tribunal's Statute Article 5 (https://www.itlos.org/fileadmin/itlos/documents/basic_texts/statute_en.pdf) and the 1994 Agreement Article 178, detailed in resolution 51/204 (https://documents.un.org/doc/undoc/gen/n97/769/51/pdf/n9776951.pdf?token=FFhG7JOPZn4wAkSphS&fe=true). Additionally, DOALOS supports the Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf (CLCS) by providing technical assistance and facilities, aiding developing states in their submissions, with its functions detailed in CLCS Rules of Procedure and Annex II of UNCLOS (https://documents.un.org/doc/undoc/gen/n08/309/23/pdf/n0830923.pdf?token=KvJ2MrzDVqwVV4OiQU&fe=true). It also services the Informal Consultative Process (ICP) on Oceans and the Law of the Sea, preparing related reports, with its mandate in resolution 54/33 (http://www.worldlii.org/int/other/UNGA/1999/71.pdf). Moreover, DOALOS facilitates the Regular Process for Global Reporting and Assessment of the Marine Environment, established in 2002, to enhance scientific understanding and decision-making, involving a Group of Experts and a Working Group, with terms detailed in resolution 57/141 (https://www.un.org/en/development/desa/population/migration/generalassembly/docs/globalcompact/A_RES_57_141.pdf). Moreover, DOALOS provides capacity-building assistance to developing countries in the field of ocean affairs and the law of the sea, through training, fellowships, technical assistance, and financial support (https://www.un.org/ola/en/content/div-doalos).
Vertical Coordination: DOALOS engages in vertical coordination with various levels of institutions, including the United Nations, specialized agencies, regional bodies, national governments, and local authorities, as outlined in section 9.2 of its governing document.  The structure of this coordination is outlined in the Secretary-General's Bulletin ST/SGB/2021/1, which organizes the Office of Legal Affairs and details the functions of DOALOS (https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/798635/files/ST_SGB_2015_3-EN.pdf?ln=en). It operates under the guidance of the Under-Secretary-General for Legal Affairs and the Director of the Division, with specialized sections and units handling distinct functions (section 9.3). DOALOS aids in implementing the Convention and related Agreements, offering technical cooperation and capacity building (section 9.4). It maintains liaison with entities like the International Seabed Authority and the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea, and provides support to the Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf, the General Assembly, and the Regular Process for Global Reporting and Assessment of the Marine Environment, incuding Socioeconomic Aspects (section 9.5) (https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/798635/files/ST_SGB_2015_3-EN.pdf?ln=en).  DOALOS operates through the Meeting of States Parties to the Convention, providing substantive servicing to this and other related bodies². It also assists members in implementing the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea and related agreements, offering training, fellowships, and technical assistance (https://www.un.org/depts/los/doalos_activities/about_doalos.htm). DOALOS's work is structured to ensure the consistent application of the Convention across various levels of governance, supporting the development of maritime policies that align with international law (https://www.un.org/depts/los/doalos_activities/about_doalos.htm). The Division also engages with the International Seabed Authority and the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea, maintaining liaison and providing administrative support as necessary¹. Additionally, DOALOS supports the Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf and facilitates the Regular Process for Global Reporting and Assessment of the State of the Marine Environment (https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/798635/files/ST_SGB_2015_3-EN.pdf?ln=en).
Horizontal Coordination: Horizontal coordination within DOALOS involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the ocean domain, such as fisheries, environment, security, trade, science, private sector, civil society, and other UN agencies to ensure that ocean affairs and the law of the sea are integrated into all policies (https://www.un.org/ola/en/content/div-doalos). This is structured under the section 9.5 of the document, which outlines the inter-agency cooperation and coordination of the Division (https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/798635/files/ST_SGB_2015_3-EN.pdf?ln=en).  This coordination is guided by the mandate of DOALOS to promote the uniform and consistent application of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) and related agreements (https://www.un.org/ola/en/content/div-doalos). The DOALOS participates in the inter-agency mechanism UN-Oceans, which seeks to enhance the coordination, coherence and effectiveness of competent organizations of the United Nations system and the International Seabed Authority on ocean issues (https://www.un.org/depts/los/coop_coor/un_oceans.htm). The DOALOS also liaises with other specialized agencies, regional and sub-regional organizations, non-governmental organizations, and academic institutions on matters related to ocean affairs and the law of the sea (https://www.un.org/oceancapacity/). DOALOS conducts consultations with regional intergovernmental organizations and others in Africa, Asia-Pacific, and Latin America/Caribben to gain insight in ongoing regional programmes and activities on ocean governance and to identify capacity-building needs and priorities in the region (https://www.un.org/oceancapacity/consultations).  The DOALOS facilitates the exchange of information and best practices among governments and other interested parties on issues under its consideration. For example, DOALOS works with the scientific community to support marine scientific research and with environmental sectors to address marine biodiversity conservation (https://www.un.org/depts/los/general_assembly/general_assembly.htm). Horizontal coordination within DOALOS can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders (https://www.un.org/depts/los/biodiversity/prepcom.htm), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as UN-Oceans, the inter-agency coordination mechanism on ocean and coastal issues (https://www.un.org/depts/los/consultative_process/consultative_process.htm), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for engagement with other sectors and stakeholders (https://www.un.org/depts/los/), (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for ocean issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders (https://sustainabledevelopment.un.org/content/documents/5214236EGM%20Report%20on%20Oceans.pdf). DOALOS provides leadership and direction on matters critical to oceans and the law of the sea, shapes the ocean governance research agenda, sets norms and standards, articulates evidence-based policy options, provides technical support to countries, and monitors and assesses trends related to oceans and maritime affairs (https://www.un.org/ola/en/content/div-doalos). DOALOS facilitates the participation of various actors in the ocean sector and enhances cooperation and coordination within the UN system on ocean matters (https://www.un.org/ola/en/content/div-doalos).

Institution: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO)
Spatial Jurisdiction: The FAO’s jurisdiction spans a vast array of marine and inland waters, delineated by the boundaries of member states’ exclusive economic zones (EEZs), territorial seas, and inland waters. This includes all ocean spaces and maritime zones under the purview of each member state, extending to the limits of their recognized jurisdiction, whether it be 200 nautical miles for EEZs or other specified distances for territorial seas and inland waters (https://www.fao.org/cwp-on-fishery-statistics/handbook/general-concepts/main-water-areas/en/)
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: FAO’s remit includes nutrition, food and agriculture, which cover fisheries, marine products, forestry and primary forestry products. Its programs aim to raise levels of nutrition and standards of living, secure improvements in food and agricultural production and distribution, better the condition of rural populations, and contribute to an expanding world economy and ensuring humanity’s freedom from hunger (https://www.fao.org/3/ac621e/ac621e03.htm)
Source of Jurisdiction: The FAO’s jurisdiction is established through a variety of international agreements and legal frameworks. Specifically, the FAO’s mandate is outlined in its own founding document, the FAO Constitution (https://www.fao.org/3/k8024e/k8024e.pdf). Additionally, the FAO operates within the scope of various international treaties and agreements that relate to food and agriculture. For example, the Agreement on Port State Measures to Prevent, Deter and Eliminate Illegal, Unreported and Unregulated Fishing (PSMA) is an important instrument that falls under the FAO’s purview (https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/rulesneg_e/fish_e/2009_psma.pdf). Furthermore, the FAO is also influenced by  the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), which provides a legal framework for the conservation and sustainable use of oceans and their resources (https://www.un.org/depts/los/convention_agreements/texts/unclos/unclos_e.pdf) and the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) to support the sustainable use of biodiversity in agriculture, forestry, and fisheries (https://www.cbd.int/doc/legal/cbd-en.pdf)
Strategies:
The FAO executes its objectives through a series of strategic measures: initially, the FAO Strategic Framework 2022-31, endorsed by the FAO Conference (https://www.fao.org/3/cb7099en/cb7099en.pdf). This framework is aligned with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and emphasizes the 'four betters': better production, better nutrition, a better environment, and a better life (https://www.fao.org/strategic-framework/en).
Additionally, the FAO develops a biennial programme budget and workplan, approved by the Council (https://www.fao.org/3/nn539en/nn539en.pdf). Also, the FAO Science and Innovation Strategy Action Plan (2022-25) provides a common framework for FAO action at the country, sub-regional, regional and global levels (https://www.fao.org/documents/card/en?details=CC7559EN). in addtion, there is the FAO National Framework for One Health framework to implement the One Health approach at the national level  and assist national authorities in (i) enhancing national capacity for zoonotic diseases and AMR for prevention, detection and response; and (ii) improving joint coordination and collaboration between major stakeholders (https://www.fao.org/3/cb4072en/cb4072en.pdf).  There is also the The Director-General’s Medium Term Plan 2022-25 and Programme of Work and Budget
2022-23 which  sets out the Strategic Objectives and Outcomes for
achievement by Members and the international community with support from FAO, in accordance with the Strategic Framework 2022-31 (https://www.fao.org/3/ne576en/ne576en.pdf). Regulatory mechanisms such as the Codex Alimentarius provide standards to ensure food safety and trade (https://www.fao.org/fao-who-codexalimentarius/codex-texts/list-standards/en/).
Inter-Institutional Relationship:
As stated in its constitution, the FAO maintains relations with the United Nations as a specialized agency (Article XII), and with other international, regional, and national organizations and authorities related to food and agriculture (Article XIII). The FAO may also enter into agreements with Member Nations for the establishment of international institutions dealing with food and agriculture (Article XV) (https://www.fao.org/3/k8024e/k8024e.pdf). The FAO engages with a diverse array of institutions to advance its mission. It partners with Member States and various stakeholders, including civil society, the private sector, academia, and research centers, to combat food insecurity and malnutrition (https://www.fao.org/partnerships/en/). The FAO’s collaboration with academia and research institutions is crucial for mobilizing knowledge and innovations, as well as for providing evidence-based solutions to policy processes (https://www.fao.org/partnerships/academia/en/). 
Furthermore, the FAO works closely with international organizations to facilitate partnerships for food and nutrition security, agriculture, and rural development3. For instance, the FAO’s Strategy for Private Sector Engagement aims to strengthen strategic engagement with the private sector towards achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) (https://doi.org/10.4060/cb3352en). In addition, the FAO is involved in South-South Cooperation, which is a key instrument for delivering on its mandate and achieving the SDGs (https://www.fao.org/3/i5163e/i5163e.pdf). This cooperation is facilitated through the FAO’s Partnerships and UN Collaboration Division, which develops strategic cooperation with non-state actors (https://www.fao.org/3/cc7997en/cc7997en.pdf).
Vertical Coordination:
The FAO’s vertical coordination involves collaboration with various levels of governance and institutions, including the United Nations, specialized agencies, regional and intergovernmental organizations, national governments, and local authorities. The FAO operates through the Conference of all the members, the Council, and a secretariat headed by a Director-General  (Articles III, IV, V, and VII). It also has committees, commissions, and other subsidiary bodies that assist members in implementing standards, policies, and programmes, providing technical cooperation and assistance upon request (https://www.fao.org/3/k8024e/k8024e.pdf)
The FAO’s work is organized around five major programme areas, each overseen by a Deputy Director-General who works closely with the Director-General to implement strategies and programmes across all levels of the Organization (https://www.fao.org/3/ne576en/ne576en.pdf). The Senior Management Team, consisting of the Director-General and Deputy Directors-General, provides strategic and operational guidance to ensure coherence and alignment between the different departments and divisions of the Organization and the governing bodies https://www.fao.org/about/org-chart/en/). Furthermore, the FAO’s structure includes Regional, Liaison, and Country Offices, Subregional Offices, and Partnership and Liaison Offices, which facilitate the FAO’s work on the ground, ensuring that its global mandates are translated into local action (https://www.fao.org/about/who-we-are/worldwide-offices/en/). The Governing Bodies, such as the Conference, Council, Regional Conferences, Committee on World Food Security, Council Committees, and Technical Committees (https://www.fao.org/unfao/govbodies/home/en/) and the Statutory Bodies (https://www.fao.org/unfao/govbodies/gsb-subject-matter/subject-matter/en/) , play a pivotal role in decision-making and oversight. The Oversight Advisory Committee further supports this structure by providing independent advice on issues related to governance, risk management, and internal control https://www.fao.org/about/oversight-advisory-committee/en/). In alignment with the UN Development System reform, the FAO leverages the UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework and UN Common Country Analysis to integrate food security and agrifood systems transformation within the broader UN support to national governments (https://www.fao.org/partnerships/fao-un-system/en). This approach ensures that the FAO’s efforts are harmonized with the UN’s overarching goals and contribute effectively to sustainable development initiatives globally.
Horizontal Coordination:
Horizontal coordination within the FAO involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the food and agriculture domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, scientific community, and other UN agencies to ensure that food security and nutrition are considered in all policies and that agricultural policies are aligned with other sectoral policies (https://www.fao.org/partnerships/en/). This coordination is guided by Article 1 of the Constitution of the FAO (https://www.fao.org/3/k8024e/k8024e.pdf). For example, FAO works with the environmental sector to address climate change impacts on food security (https://www.fao.org/3/i5188e/I5188E.pdf), or with the economic sector to enhance rural development and livelihoods (https://www.fao.org/agrifood-economics/areas-of-work/en/), and with the ocean sector  to enhance underwater food systems and ensure sustainable aquatic food production for the growing global population (https://news.un.org/en/story/2022/06/1121602). Horizontal coordination within FAO can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Global Action Programme on Food Security and Nutrition in Small Island States (https://www.fao.org/3/i7297e/i7297e.pdf), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, such as the Committee on World Food Security (https://www.fao.org/sustainable-development-goals-helpdesk/champion/article-detail/committee-on-world-food-security/en), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, such as the Voluntary Guidelines on Food Systems and Nutrition (https://www.fao.org/cfs/vgfsn/en/),
(4) Advocacy campaigns like World Food Day (https://www.fao.org/newsroom/detail/world-food-day--global-ceremony-highlights-water-s-role-against-troubled-backdrop/en) or The State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World report (https://www.fao.org/publications/home/fao-flagship-publications/the-state-of-food-security-and-nutrition-in-the-world/en). The FAO provides leadership on global food security, shapes the agricultural research agenda, sets standards, offers evidence-based policy options, provides technical support, and monitors food and nutrition trends (https://www.fao.org/3/cb7099en/cb7099en.pdf). It facilitates the participation of diverse actors in the agricultural sector and enhances cooperation within the UN system on food and agriculture matters (https://www.fao.org/partnerships/en/)

Spatial Jurisdiction: The IPCC's authority is global, covering all regions of the world and their climate systems (https://www.ipcc.ch/about/). This includes the atmosphere, the oceans, the cryosphere, the land surface and the biosphere. The IPCC does not have any legal or political jurisdiction over any specific area, but rather provides scientific assessments and guidance for governments and other stakeholders. The IPCC divides the world into 10 regions for its interactive atlas (https://interactive-atlas.ipcc.ch/regional-information/guidance), which shows the projected changes and impacts of climate change for each region based on different scenarios and models. The regions are: Africa, Asia, Australasia, Central and South America, Europe, Mountains, North and Central America, Polar Regions, Small Islands and Oceans.
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: The IPCC is responsible for assessing the science related to climate change and its impacts, and for putting forward possible solutions (https://www.ipcc.ch/about/). This includes reviewing and summarizing the best information on climate change from various sources, such as peer-reviewed literature, government reports, and non-governmental organizations (https://www.ipcc.ch/about/). The IPCC also provides policy-relevant, but not policy-prescriptive, guidance for decision-makers, as well as projections and scenarios for different levels of greenhouse gas emissions and adaptation measures (https://www.ipcc.ch/about/structure/). The IPCC works with three Working Groups and a Task Force, each dealing with a specific aspect of climate change, such as the physical science basis, the impacts and adaptation, the mitigation options, and the inventory of greenhouse gas sources and sinks (https://www.ipcc.ch/about/structure/).
Source of Jurisdiction: The IPCC derives its mandate from the Decisions and Resolutions of its parent organisations, WMO and UNEP, which established the IPCC in 1988 as an intergovernmental body to assess the scientific information on climate change and its impacts, and to formulate response strategies for the management of the climate change issue. Specifically, the WMO Executive Council Resolution 4 (EC-XL) (https://archive.ipcc.ch/docs/WMO_resolution4_on_IPCC_1988.pdf) defined the initial terms of reference and objectives of the IPCC. The IPCC's mandate was subsequently updated and refined by various resolutions and decisions of the governing bodies of WMO and UNEP, as well as by the IPCC itself, to reflect the evolving needs and challenges of the climate change issue. Over the years, key resolutions and decisions have shaped the IPCC's mandate including the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) (https://unfccc.int/files/essential_background/background_publications_htmlpdf/application/pdf/conveng.pdf); the IPCC Principles Governing IPCC Work (https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/09/ipcc-principles.pdf), which were adopted by the IPCC at its 14th Session in 1988 and approved by the WMO Executive Council and the UNEP Governing Council, and which define the IPCC's organisation, procedures, functions, and products; and the IPCC Procedures (https://www.ipcc.ch/documentation/procedures/), which were adopted by the IPCC at various sessions and approved by the WMO Executive Council and the UNEP Governing Council, and which provide detailed rules and guidelines for the IPCC's work, such as the preparation, review, approval, and publication of its reports, the election of its bureau and chair, and the participation of experts and observers. The IPCC's jurisdiction is also influenced by the requests and guidance received from the UNFCCC and other relevant bodies, which provide the policy context and demand for the IPCC's assessments and products (https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2021/07/AR6_FS_What_is_IPCC.pdf). The IPCC's mandate is also supported by the scientific community and the public, which provide the knowledge base and the legitimacy for the IPCC's work (https://www.ipcc.ch/about/).
Defined Objectives:
As defined in Paragraph 2 of Resolution 4 (EC-XL) of the WMO Executive Council (https://archive.ipcc.ch/docs/WMO_resolution4_on_IPCC_1988.pdf), the IPCC's objectives include the following main tasks:
(1) Assessing the scientific information that is related to the various components of the climate change issue, such as emissions of major greenhouse gases and modification of the Earth's radiation balance resulting therefrom, and the environmental and socio-economic consequences of climate change; (2) Formulating realistic response strategies for the management of the climate change issue; (3) Providing scientific and socio-economic information and advice, initially for the development and negotiations of a UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) and after its entry into force, to continue to work closely with the UNFCCC and provide scientific, technical and socio-economic information and advice; and (4) Reporting on its activities to the governing bodies of WMO and UNEP and communicating the results of the assessments broadly. These tasks enable the IPCC to fulfil its role as an intergovernmental panel on climate change that provides authoritative and comprehensive assessments of the current state of knowledge on climate change and its potential impacts.
Strategies: The IPCC executes its objectives via several strategies. The IPCC operates through three Working Groups (WGs) and a Task Force on National Greenhouse Gas Inventories (TFI), each supported by a Technical Support Unit (TSU) (https://www.ipcc.ch/working-groups/). The WGs assess the scientific literature on the physical science basis of climate change (WG I), the impacts, adaptation and vulnerability (WG II), and the mitigation of climate change (WG III). The TFI develops and refines methodologies for the estimation and reporting of greenhouse gas emissions and removals. The IPCC also produces reports (https://www.ipcc.ch/reports/) in forms of Special Reports, Methodology Reports, Technical Papers and Synthesis Reports like AR6 reports (https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/syr/downloads/report/IPCC_AR6_SYR_SPM.pdf) on cross-cutting topics. The IPCC develops its work programme based on the requests and guidance from its member governments and observer organizations and the work programme is reviewed and approved by the IPCC Plenary, which is the main decision-making body of the IPCC (https://www.ipcc.ch/about/structure/). The IPCC budget is funded by voluntary contributions from its member governments and other organizations. The budget covers the operational costs of the IPCC Secretariat, the Technical Support Units, and the travel and meeting expenses of the IPCC Bureau members, authors, reviewers, and other experts involved in the IPCC work. The budget is prepared by the IPCC Secretariat in consultation with the IPCC Bureau and the Technical Support Units, and is submitted to the IPCC Plenary for approval for each assessment cycle, which typically lasts six to seven years. The budget is subject to an annual audit by an external auditor. The budget cycle is also aligned with the calendar year (https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/decision_p35_budget.pdf). In addition, the IPCC Scholarship Programme provides funding for young scientists from developing countries to pursue studies on climate change (https://www.ipcc.ch/about/scholarship/).
Inter-Institutional Relationship: The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) collaborates with key organizations to support climate change governance. It liaises with the United Nations (UN), implementing a relationship agreement effective since its establishment in 1988 (https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2021/07/AR6_FS_What_is_IPCC.pdf), as per the UN's mandate to provide policymakers with regular assessments of the scientific basis of climate change, its impacts, future risks, and adaptation and mitigation options. Similarly, IPCC maintains a relationship with the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), providing vital scientific information to limit climate change and establish a strong link between sustainable economic development, climate change, and vulnerability (https://www.undp.org/blog/five-key-takeaways-latest-ipcc-report). Additionally, IPCC supports the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) and the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) by assessing the scientific literature and providing vital scientific information to the climate change process (https://unfccc.int/topics/science/workstreams/cooperation-with-the-ipcc/background-cooperation-with-the-ipcc). It also services the Conference of the Parties (COP) and the Subsidiary Body for Scientific and Technological Advice (SBSTA) (https://unfccc.int/process/bodies/subsidiary-bodies/sbsta), by preparing related reports within its mandate. Moreover, IPCC facilitates the assessment process through its Task Force on Greenhouse Gas Inventories, carrying out important work on methodologies for estimating and reporting GHG emissions (https://www.ipcc.ch/working-group/tfi/).
Vertical Coordination: Vertical coordination within the IPCC involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other intergovernmental and nongovernmental organizations, national governments, and scientific bodies. This is achieved through the IPCC’s mandate, principles, procedures, and structure, which are guided by the IPCC’s founding resolutions and decisions of the IPCC as structured under the Organization and Governance section of the IPCC Principles (https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/09/ipcc-principles.pdf). The IPCC operates through the IPCC Plenary of all the members, the IPCC Bureau of 34 members, and a secretariat headed by a Secretary (https://www.ipcc.ch/about/structure/). The IPCC also has Working Groups, Task Forces, and other subsidiary bodies (https://www.ipcc.ch/working-groups/). The IPCC’s work is organised around six regions, each represented by a Vice-Chair and other Bureau members who work closely with the IPCC Chair and the Co-Chairs of the Working Groups and Task Forces to oversee the preparation and approval of the IPCC reports and products (https://www.ipcc.ch/bureau/). There is also the IPCC Executive Committee (consisting of the IPCC Chair, the IPCC Vice-Chairs, the Co-Chairs of the Working Groups and Task Forces, and the Secretary) providing guidance to the IPCC Chair on strategic and administrative matters, and ensuring coordination and consistency across the activities of the IPCC (https://www.ipcc.ch/executive-committee/). Additionally, the IPCC has four Technical Support Units (TSUs) that provide scientific, technical, and operational support to the IPCC Chair, the Working Groups, and the Task Force on National Greenhouse Gas Inventories (https://www.ipcc.ch/technical-support-units/). Besides the IPCC Chair, at the IPCC headquarters, there is a clear line of responsibility within the secretariat staff comprising of a Deputy Secretary, a Head of Science, a Senior Communications Manager, and other administrative and technical officers (https://www.ipcc.ch/secretariat/). In addition, the IPCC engages with various partner organizations and observers, such as the Global Climate Observing System (GCOS), the Group on Earth Observations (GEO), and the Future Earth initiative, to enhance the availability and quality of data and information for its assessments (https://www.ipcc.ch/about/observer-organizations/).
Horizontal Coordination: Horizontal coordination within IPCC involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the climate change domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, the scientific community, and other UN agencies to provide the world with a clear scientific view on the current state of knowledge in climate change and its potential environmental and socio-economic impacts. This coordination is guided by the Principles Governing IPCC Work (https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/09/ipcc-principles.pdf). For example, IPCC works with the energy sector to assess the mitigation potential and costs of different energy sources and technologies (https://www.ipcc.ch/report/renewable-energy-sources-and-climate-change-mitigation/), with the agriculture sector to evaluate the impacts of climate change on food security and land use (https://www.ipcc.ch/srccl/), the ocean sector to examine the changes in the ocean and cryosphere and their implications for ecosystems and human well-being (https://www.ipcc.ch/srocc/), or with the health sector to analyse the risks and opportunities for health adaptation and mitigation (https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg2/chapter/chapter-7/). Horizontal coordination within IPCC can take various forms, such as (1) Joint preparation and approval of assessment reports and special reports with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Sixth Assessment Report (https://www.ipcc.ch/assessment-report/ar6/) or the Special Report on Global Warming of 1.5°C (https://www.ipcc.ch/sr15/), (2) Participation in intergovernmental and multisectoral panels, working groups, and task forces, such as the IPCC Bureau (https://www.ipcc.ch/bureau/) or the Task Force on National Greenhouse Gas Inventories (https://www.ipcc-nggip.iges.or.jp/), (3)Development and dissemination of guidelines, methodologies, and data for climate change research and policy, such as the 2006 IPCC Guidelines for National Greenhouse Gas Inventories (https://www.ipcc-nggip.iges.or.jp/public/2006gl/) or the IPCC Data Distribution Centre (https://www.ipcc-data.org/), and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for climate change issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the IPCC Outreach Programme (https://www.ipcc.ch/outreach/) and IPCC Communication Strategy (https://archive.ipcc.ch/meetings/session35/IAC_CommunicationStrategy.pdf). In addition, the IPCC provides scientific assessments of the state of knowledge on climate change, its causes, potential impacts and response options, informs the negotiations under the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), engages with a wide range of interested parties at various levels, and ensures the quality and transparency of its work (https://www.ipcc.ch/about/).

Spatial Jurisdiction: IOC jurisdiction is global delineated by the boundaries of member states’ exclusive economic zones (EEZs), territorial seas, and  extending to the limits of their recognized jurisdiction, whether it be 200 nautical miles for EEZs  (https://www.ioc.unesco.org/en).
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: The IOC's subject matter jurisdiction encompasses global ocean observation and data exchange, marine scientific research, and capacity development to improve management, decision-making, and sustainability of the marine environment. This includes overseeing the implementation of international programs like the Global Ocean Observing System, promoting marine spatial planning, and supporting the application of oceanographic data and services for societal benefits. The IOC also addresses marine pollution, climate change impacts on oceans, and fosters international cooperation for the conservation and sustainable use of ocean resources (https://www.ioc.unesco.org/en).
Source of Jurisdiction: The IOC’s authority is derived from its statutes, particularly Articles 1 to 6, which outline its establishment, purpose, functions, membership, organizational structure, and relation to other organizations​​. The IOC derives its authority from the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO)'s constitution (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%204/volume-4-I-52-English.pdf) . Specifically, the IOC was established by Resolution 2.31 of the UNESCO General Conference at its fifth session in 1960 (https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000114583). The IOC’s jurisdiction is further defined by its own statutes and the rules of procedure adopted by its Assembly (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%204/volume-4-I-52-English.pdf). . The IOC operates within the framework of international law, particularly the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), which provides the legal basis for its activities related to the oceans and coastal areas ((https://www.un.org/depts/los/convention_agreements/texts/unclos/unclos_e.pdf) ). The IOC’s mandate is also supported by the UN General Assembly resolution A/RES/72/73 proclaiing the United Nations Decade of Ocean Science for Sustainable Development 2021–2030 (https://documents.un.org/doc/undoc/gen/n17/421/90/pdf/n1742190.pdf?token=kneHbLVHaUpcHqGOQg&fe=trueby).
Strategies: IOC implements its objectives through series of strategic measues including, the  Medium-Term Strategy 2022-2029 approved by the b IOC Assembly and Executive Council meetings  (https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000381388.locale=en),  providing a roadmap for its goals and activities. Secondly, the IOC’s actions are guided by decisions made during the annual Assembly, which sets the direction for the organization’s work and strategic focus. The current focus includes the Ocean Decade Implementation Plan (https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000377082), which aims to generate the science needed for a sustainable ocean. Additionally, key strategic decisions are made biennially at IOC Assembly meetings and annually at Executive Council meetings, including the IOC develops biennial budgets and work plans that detail activities, outputs, indicators, and resources for each strategic objective (https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000375020). These are tailored to the needs of the Member States and the priorities of the global oceanographic community. Significantly, the IOC is tasked by the United Nations General Assembly with leading the implementation of the UN Decade of Ocean Science for Sustainable Development. At the regional level, the IOC’s regional sub-commissions, such as WESTPAC and IOCAFRICA, IOCCARRIBE, IOCINDO also have corresponding Implemetation plans and Ocean decade roadmaps focused on regional engagement and address specific challenges relevant to their areas (https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000381488).
Inter-Institutional Relationship:
IOC collaborates with UN specialized agencies and international organizations related to marine sciences. It acts as a joint mechanism for UN organizations in marine science fields, fostering cooperation and ensuring that its requirements are considered in their programs​​. 
The IIOC fosters relationships with various institutions to support its mission.
