It collaborates closely with the UNESCO, as the IOC functions as a specialized agency within UNESCO, detailed in Article 1-10 of the IOC’s statutes ((https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%204/volume-4-I-52-English.pdf)). The IOC also partners with the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) to advance global oceanographic and atmospheric research, as outlined in the collaborative agreement between the two entities (https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000369984). Furthermore, the IOC works in conjunction with the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) to address marine environmental issues, with cooperation terms specified in the agreement between IOC and UNEP (https://wedocs.unep.org/bitstream/handle/20.500.11822/21052/UNEP(DEPI)_EAF_CP6_BUR.DOC_6%20MOU%20between%20IOC%20&%20UNEP.pdf?sequence=1&amp%3BisAllowed=). The IOC’s engagement with FAO, IAEA) and the  World Health Organization, through the MOU on ciguatera poisoning (https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000369940). 
Additionally, the IOC maintains a relationship IMO, FAO, WMO, IAEA, and UNEP on the Joint Group of Experts on the Scientific Aspects of Marine Environmental Protection (GESAMP) (https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000104624). The IOC also contributes to the Global Ocean Observing System (GOOS), which is an international collaborative effort to observe the ocean and provide data for scientific research and policy-making (https://www.ioc.unesco.org/en/global-ocean-observing-system). IOC has also built relationship with NGOs and private sectors, including A partnership agreement with the International Monohull Open Class Association (https://www.sail-world.com/news/226163/?source=email), World Ocean Council (https://www.oceancouncil.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/12/b4f999d04e84ded11337cc3c8c17a9b2.pdf), and Fugro (https://oceandecade.org/news/fugro-and-ioc-unesco-launch-working-group-to-unlock-private-sector-ocean-data/).
Vertical Coordination: Vertical coordination within the IOC involves collaboration with various levels of institutions and authorities. The IOC, under UNESCO, engages with Member States, United Nations bodies, and other international organizations to achieve its objectives. This coordination is structured under the IOC’s statutes and strategic plans, which outline the framework for cooperation with entities at different levels. The IOC operates through its Assembly, Executive Council, and Secretariat, which are responsible for implementing the decisions and strategies of the organization. The IOC also has subsidiary bodies, such as regional sub-commissions and working groups, that address specific regional and thematic areas. Within the OCean Decasde Framework, IOC coordinate with the Decade Coordination Unit (DCU) which is  the central hub that manages the day-to-day operations and implementation of the Ocean Decade, Decade Advisory Board, composed of fifteen members, provides strategic technical advice on implementation of the Ocean Decade (https://www.oceandecade.org/decade-advisory-board/), Ocean Decade Alliance an high-level group of eminent partners which aim to catalyze large-scale resource commitments towards the Decade through networking, resource mobilization and influence (https://www.oceandecade.org/ocean-decade-alliance/), .Decade Collaborative Centres and Decade Coordination Offices to provide targeted support to the Ocean Decade through a coordination and catalysis role for Decade Actions at the regional or thematic level (https://oceandecade.org/decade-collaborative-centres/), Decade Implementing Partners including non-UN regional or international stakeholder organizations that sit outside formal governance and coordination structures of the Ocean Decade (https://oceandecade.org/decade-implementing-partners/) and Informal Working Groups.  The IOC’s work is organized around six major programme areas (Understand, Measure, Alert, Evaluate   Manage, and Enable) each overseen by a Head of Sections ( (Science, Ocean Observation and services, Tsunami, Marine Policy, Ocean Literacy)) who works closely with the Executive Generall to implement strategies and programmes across all levels of the (https://www.ioc.unesco.org/en/enable)Within its Secretariate,  IOC operates the IOC Science and Communication Centre on Harmful Algae, Intergovernmental Coordination Group for the Indian Ocean Tsunami Warning and Mitigation System, Indian Ocean Tsunami Information Centre, Caribbean Tsunami Information Center, and the IOC/WMO Joint Centre for Oceanography and Marine Meteorology in situ Observations Programmes Support. The IOC’s efforts are further supported by a network of national focal persons (http://itic.ioc-unesco.org/index.php?option=com_oe&task=viewDocumentRecord&docID=17716) ), and also the National UNESCO Commissions offices (https://pax.unesco.org/countries/NationalCommissions.html) who promote the safe and sustainable use of ocean resources. Also through its  International Oceanographic Data and Information Exchange (IODE), IOC coordinates a global network of more than 100 National Oceanographic Data Centres (NODCs), Associate Data Units (ADUs) and Associate Information Units (AIUs) to manage and make available millions of ocean observations that contribute to ocean data products and services developed and used by other IOC programmes (https://www.ioc.unesco.org/en/data-information).  There is also the IOC Project Office in Venice  dedicated to o Ocean Literacy programs regarding marine science education and communication https://oceanliteracy.unesco.org/intergovernmental-oceanographic-commission-of-unesco-ioc-unesco/).
Horizontal Coordination:
Horizontal coordination within the IOC encompasses collaboration across various sectors and stakeholders, including governments, scientific communities, and international institutions, to ensure ocean policies are integrated and aligned with broader governmental objectives (https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000381388.locale=en). This approach is underpinned by the IOC's mandate to promote international cooperation and coordinate research and capacity-building programs for ocean and coastal areas, as outlined in the IOC Medium-Term Strategy 2022–2029 (https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000381388.locale=en). Forms of horizontal coordination within the IOC include:
1. Joint planning and execution of initiatives, such as the Tsunami Ready programme (https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000385113.),
2. Participation in intergovernmental committees and global partnerships, like those fostering the UN Decade of Ocean Science for Sustainable Development (https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000385113.),
3. Development and dissemination of guidelines and frameworks for ocean policy engagement, exemplified by the IOC Strategic Plan for Ocean Data and Information Management (https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000385113),
4. Advocacy and communication efforts to promote ocean science and sustainability, as seen in the State of ocean  report (https://www.ioc.unesco.org/en/state-ocean-report#:~:text=The%20State%20of%20the%20Ocean%20Report%20is%20the%20first%20such,ocean%20protection%20and%20sustainable%20planning.), and  Advocacy campaigns like World Ocean Day (https://www.unesco.org/en/days/oceans)

Spatial Jurisdiction: The IAEA's authority is global, encompassing the nuclear activities and facilities of its member states (https://www.iaea.org/about/governance/list-of-member-states). This includes a focus on states that have signed the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT), with authority extending to all peaceful and military nuclear activities, materials, and equipment within these states, covering key nuclear safety and security issues (https://treaties.unoda.org/t/npt/participants).
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: The IAEA is responsible for ensuring the safe, secure and peaceful use of nuclear energy and technology, especially among countries that have committed to non-proliferation and disarmament obligations (https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/18/03/competency-framework.pdf). This includes addressing nuclear safety and security issues, such as safeguards, emergency preparedness, radiation protection, nuclear waste management, and nuclear security (https://www.iaea.org/topics/safeguards-agreements). The IAEA also provides technical cooperation, scientific research, education and training, legal assistance, and policy guidance for peaceful nuclear development, as well as supporting the implementation of the IAEA's Statute and the UN's development goals (https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/18/03/competency-framework.pdf).
Source of Jurisdiction: The IAEA derives its mandate from the Statute of the IAEA, which was approved by the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in 1956 and entered into force in 1957 (https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/statute.pdf). The Statute provides the legal basis for the IAEA's jurisdiction over the promotion and control of the peaceful uses of nuclear energy and technology, as well as the verification of compliance with non-proliferation and disarmament obligations (https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/statute.pdf). Additionally, the IAEA's jurisdiction is influenced by the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT), particularly Article III, which entrusts the IAEA with the responsibility of applying safeguards to all non-nuclear-weapon states parties to the treaty, as well as other states that have concluded safeguards agreements with the IAEA (https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/publications/documents/infcircs/1970/infcirc140.pdf). The IAEA also finds its mandate from the implementation of other international legal instruments related to nuclear safety, security, and cooperation, such as Article 5, 18 and 23 of the Convention on the Physical Protection of Nuclear Material (https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/infcirc274r1.pdf), and Article 8 and 18 of the International Convention for the Suppression of Acts of Nuclear Terrorism (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Treaties/2005/04/20050413%2004-02%20PM/Ch_XVIII_15p.pdf). These instruments and initiatives provide further legal frameworks and mechanisms for the IAEA's jurisdiction over specific nuclear issues and challenges.
Defined Objectives: The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), as stated in Article II of its Statute (https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/statute.pdf), aims to accelerate and enlarge atomic energy's contribution to peace, health, and prosperity worldwide while ensuring no assistance is used for military purposes. Its key functions include encouraging research and practical application of atomic energy for peaceful uses (Article III, paragraph A 1), providing materials, services, and facilities for atomic energy development and application, focusing on under-developed areas (Article III, paragraph A 2), fostering the exchange of scientific information and training in peaceful atomic energy uses (Article III, paragraphs A 3 and 4), establishing safeguards against atomic energy's use for military purposes (Article III, paragraph A 5), setting safety standards for health protection and danger minimization (Article III, paragraph A 6), and acquiring facilities for carrying out its functions (Article III, paragraph A 7). These roles establish the IAEA as a key international organization promoting peaceful nuclear energy use and preventing its militarization (https://www.iaea.org/about/overview).
Strategies: The IAEA executes its objectives via several strategies: firstly, a six-year Medium Term Strategy, prepared through a joint consultation process among Member States and the Secretariat, which establishes the Agency's strategic direction and roadmap for the preparation of its programme and budget, by identifying priorities among and within its programmes for the achievement of its statutory objectives in an evolving international environment (https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/23/02/mts2024_2029.pdf). This strategy, applicable for 2024-2029, draws upon the previous Medium Term Strategy 2018-2023 and may be updated, if deemed necessary by the Board of Governors, adapting to new developments and evolving needs and priorities of Member States (https://www.iaea.org/about/overview/medium-term-strategy). Secondly, a biennial programme and budget, approved by the General Conference, which details the expected results, performance indicators, and resources corresponding to each major programme area. The current programme and budget for 2022-2023 are aligned with the Medium Term Strategy 2018-2023 and reflect the Agency's response to the COVID-19 pandemic, as well as its support to the implementation of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/gc/gc67-5.pdf). It also maintains the safeguards system, which verifies the compliance of States with their non-proliferation and disarmament obligations, as well as the technical cooperation programme, which assists Member States in the peaceful application of nuclear science and technology (https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/safeguards_web_june_2015_1.pdf). Finally, various legal instruments, initiatives, platforms, and networks provide an operational framework for implementing the Agency's mandate, addressing nuclear safety, security, and cooperation (https://www.iaea.org/topics/nuclear-knowledge-management).
Inter-Institutional Relationship: The IAEA collaborates with various organizations to achieve its objectives. It engages with 178 Member States and various stakeholders through the General Conference, which is the highest policy-making body of the Agency and meets annually to approve the programme and budget, as well as the Board of Governors, which consists of 35 Member States and meets five times a year to examine and make recommendations to the General Conference on the IAEA's accounts, programme and budget, and to consider applications for membership (https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/18/08/the-iaea-policy-making-organs-providing-guidance-for-the-agencys-work.pdf). As an autonomous organization within the UN system, the IAEA's relationship with the UN is guided by an agreement signed in 1957, which stipulates that the Agency shall report annually to the General Assembly and, when appropriate, to the Security Council, and shall cooperate with the Economic and Social Council and other specialized agencies (https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/207456/files/A_RES_1145%28XII%29-EN.pdf?ln=en). Additionally, the IAEA supports the implementation of the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT) and other international legal instruments and initiatives related to nuclear safety, security, and cooperation, providing verification and inspection services, technical assistance, and policy guidance for Member States, as detailed in the IAEA Statute, Article III (https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/statute.pdf). It also cooperates with other UN agencies and organizations, such as WHO, FAO, UNEP, and OECD/NEA, as well as regional and intergovernmental organizations, such as the European Union, the African Union, and the Organization of American States, addressing common nuclear issues and challenges, as recognized in various resolutions and agreements (https://www.iaea.org/about/partnerships), (https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/publications/magazines/bulletin/bull29-3/29301081418.pdf), (https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/publications/magazines/bulletin/bull37-3/37305381015.pdf).
Vertical Coordination: Vertical coordination within the IAEA involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other specialized agencies, regional and intergovernmental organizations, national governments, and local authorities. This is achieved through reporting, cooperation, and assistance (https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/publications/magazines/bulletin/bull37-3/37305381015.pdf). This is structured under the Relationship with the United Nations section of the IAEA Statute, specifically in Articles XI-XIV (https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/statute.pdf). The IAEA operates through the General Conference of all the members, the Board of Governors of 35 members, and a secretariat headed by a Director General (Articles VI-VIII) (https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/statute.pdf). The IAEA also has committees, commissions, and other subsidiary bodies (Article IX). The IAEA assists members in the implementation of its standards, policies, and programmes, and provides technical cooperation and assistance upon request (Article III) (https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/statute.pdf). The IAEA's work is organized around six major programme areas, each overseen by a Deputy Director General who works closely with the Director General to implement strategies and programmes across all levels of the Agency (https://www.iaea.org/about/organizational-structure). There is also the Senior Management Team  (consisting of the Director General and Deputy Directors General) providing strategic and operational guidance to the Director General on matters related to the programmatic and managerial work of the IAEA; and ensuring coherence and alignment between the different departments and divisions of the Agency and the governing bodies (https://www.iaea.org/about). Also, a network of regional and liaison offices and technical experts supports the IAEA's work in promoting the safe, secure and peaceful use of nuclear energy and technology as an integral part of regional and national development policies (https://www.iaea.org/contact). Additionally, the IAEA operates 8 nuclear applications laboratories in Seibersdorf today represent a dynamic hub, where scientists, technicians, fellows, interns and students from all over the world work and collaborate to apply the benefits of nucler technology in solving day-to-day social and economic problems (https://www.iaea.org/newscenter/multimedia/photoessays/eight-laboratories-eight-stories-success-development),  and 3 safeguards offices, and Environment Laboratories Monaco, and  3 Laboratories & Research Centres (https://www.iaea.org/about/organizational-structure/department-of-nuclear-sciences-and-applications/nuclear-applications-laboratories), and four  designated International Centre based on Research Reactors (ICERRs) that make their research reactors and ancillary facilities available to other IAEA Member States for capacity building and R&D objectives (https://www.iaea.org/about/partnerships/international-centres-based-on-research-reactors-icerrs). Besides the Director General, at the IAEA headquarters, there is a clear line of duty within the leadership team comprising of a Deputy Director General and 6 Directors with portfolios focusing on different aspects in accordance with the IAEA's mandate (https://www.iaea.org/about/organizational-structure/department-of-management). In addition, the IAEA promotes partnerships among nuclear education and training institutions across the globe through several agreement (https://www.iaea.org/newscenter/news/iaea-fosters-collaboration-agreement-among-regional-nuclear-education-networks).
Horizontal Coordination: Horizontal coordination within IAEA involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the nuclear domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, scientific community, and other UN agencies to ensure that nuclear energy is used for peaceful purposes and that nuclear safety and security are maintained in all activities and policies. This coordination is guided by Article III of the Statute of the International Atomic Energy Agency (https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/statute.pdf). For example, IAEA works with the energy sector to promote the use of nuclear power as a low-carbon energy source (https://www.iaea.org/topics/nuclear-power-and-climate-change), with the agriculture sector to enhance food security and sustainable development (https://www.iaea.org/topics/food-and-agriculture), the ocean sector to develop a science-based understanding of changes in the ocean and support climate change monitoring and adaptation activities (https://www.iaea.org/newscenter/multimedia/videos/nuclear-science-for-ocean-health) or with the environment sector to monitor and protect the environment from radiation and pollution (https://www.iaea.org/topics/radiation-protection/environment). Horizontal coordination within IAEA can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Technical Cooperation Programme (https://www.iaea.org/services/technical-cooperation-programme) or the Nuclear Security Plan (2022 - 2025) with UNODC, INTERPOL and WCO (https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/gc/gc65-24.pdf), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the Committee on the Safety of Nuclear Installations (https://www.oecd-nea.org/jcms/pl_24829/committee-on-the-safety-of-nuclear-installations-csni) or the UN Scientific Committee on the Effects of Atomic Radiation (https://www.unscear.org/unscear/en/about-us/index.html, (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for nuclear sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the International Basic Safety Standards (https://www-pub.iaea.org/MTCD/Publications/PDF/Pub1578_web-57265295.pdf) or the Integrated Nuclear Infrastructure Review (https://www.iaea.org/services/review-missions/integrated-nuclear-infrastructure-review-inir), (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for nuclear issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the International Conference on Nuclear Security (https://www.iaea.org/events/icons2024) or the Nuclear Technology Review (https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/gc/gc67-inf4.pdf). The IAEA provides leadership and direction on matters related to nuclear energy, science and technology, shapes the nuclear research agenda, sets norms and standards, articulates evidence-based policy options, provides technical support to countries, and monitors and assesses nuclear trends (https://www.iaea.org/about/overview).

Institution: International Council for the Exploration of the Sea (ICES)
Spatial Jurisdiction: The International Council for the Exploration of the Sea (ICES) has a broad area of competence, primarily focusing on the Atlantic Ocean and its adjacent seas, with an emphasis on the North Atlantic (https://www.ices.dk/about-ICES/who-we-are/Documents/ICES_Convention_1964.pdf). While the exact delimitation of this area is not precisely defined, ICES's work has great relevance to all oceans, including areas beyond national jurisdiction (ABNJ) (https://www.un.org/bbnj/sites/www.un.org.bbnj/files/ices3.pdf). This suggests that ICES's authority may extend to the exclusive economic zones (EEZs) and territorial waters of its 20 member countries (https://meetings.pices.int/Publications/Presentations/PICES-2021/ICES-2021.pdf), covering key marine habitats and migratory routes.
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: ICES is committed to advancing and sharing scientific understanding of marine ecosystems and the services they provide (https://www.ices.dk/news-and-events/news-archive/news/Pages/A-year-of-advancing-and-sharing-marine-science.aspx). This knowledge is used to generate state-of-the-art advice for meeting conservation, management, and sustainability goals (https://www.ices.dk/about-ICES/Pages/default.aspx). ICES also addresses challenges in energy transformation and publishes a roadmap for offshore renewable energy (https://www.ices.dk/news-and-events/news-archive/news/Pages/OREroadmap.aspx). Furthermore, ICES is involved in the modelling and assessment of fishery resources (https://www.ices.dk/news-and-events/news-archive/news/Pages/TS_fisheries_modelling.aspx).
Source of Jurisdiction: ICES derives its mandate from the 1964 Convention for The International Council for the Exploration of the Sea (https://www.ices.dk/about-ICES/who-we-are/Documents/ICES_Convention_1964.pdf). This Convention established ICES as a leading multidisciplinary scientific forum for the exchange of information and ideas on all aspects of marine sciences pertaining to the North Atlantic, including the adjacent Baltic Sea and North Sea. Specifically, Article 1 of the Convention defines the duty of ICES, which includes promoting and encouraging research and investigations for the study of the sea, particularly those related to the living resources thereof while Article 2 outlines that the Council shall be concerned with the Atlantic Ocean and its adjacent seas, and primarily concerned with the North Atlantic. Additionally, ICES's jurisdiction is influenced by the decisions adopted by its principal decision and policy-making body, the Council (https://www.ices.dk/community/groups/Pages/COUNCIL.aspx). The Council comprises a President and two delegates appointed by each of the 20 Member Countries. ICES's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international cooperation agreements (https://www.ices.dk/about-ICES/global-cooperation/Pages/Cooperation-agreements.aspx). These agreements provide further legal frameworks for ICES's jurisdiction over specific marine issues and domains.
Defined Objectives: According to the Convention for the ICES (https://www.ices.dk/about-ICES/who-we-are/Documents/ICES_Convention_1964.pdf), the Council's objectives encompass three main duties: promoting and encouraging research and investigations for the study of the sea particularly those related to the living resources thereof (Article 1 a); drawing up programmes required for this purpose and organising, in agreement with the Contracting Parties, such research and investigation as may appear necessary (Article 1 b); and publishing or otherwise disseminating the results of research and investigations carried out under its auspices or to encourage the publication thereof (Article 1 c). These duties enable the Council to fulfil its role as the organisation responsible for carrying out a programme of international investigation of the sea, especially in the Atlantic Ocean and its adjacent seas, and primarily in the North Atlantic (Preamble; Article 2).
Strategies: ICES executes its objectives via several strategies. Firstly, ICES has a Strategic Plan (https://www.ices.dk/about-ICES/strategicplan/Pages/default.aspx) that defines its direction and priorities relating to science, data, and advice, and to develop the capacity needed to fulfill this commitment. This plan is supported by a Science Plan and an Advisory Plan (https://www.ices.dk/about-ICES/how-we-work/Pages/Our-strategy.aspx). The Science Plan highlights seven interrelated scientific priorities and how ICES network will address them. Secondly, ICES is a leading multidisciplinary scientific forum for the exchange of information and ideas on all aspects of marine sciences. It promotes, encourages, develops, and coordinates marine research through data sharing (https://www.ices.dk/data/dataset-collections/Pages/default.aspx). It also publishes and disseminates results of research and provides non-biased, non-political scientific advice to member nation governments and international regulatory commissions (https://www.ices.dk/Science/publications/Pages/Home.aspx). Thirdly, ICES has a collection of helpful guides and policies that help understand how to work with data, and how ICES receives and outputs data (https://www.ices.dk/data/guidelines-and-policy/Pages/default.aspx). It also has a system of committees, more than 100 working groups, symposia, and an Annual Science Conference (https://ices-library.figshare.com/ndownloader/files/33403040). Finally, ICES is committed to building a foundation of science around one key challenge: integrated ecosystem understanding of marine ecosystems. ICES advances this through the coordination of oceanic and coastal monitoring and research, and advises international commissions and governments on marine policy and management issues (https://www.ices.dk/sites/pub/CM%20Doccuments/2001/GEN/gen0201.pdf).
Inter-Institutional Relationship: ICES collaborates with various organizations, partners and stakeholders to achieve its defined objectives. ICES has established formal cooperation agreements with the Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission of UNESCO (IOC/UNESCO) and the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) (https://www.un.org/depts/los/convention_agreements/ICSP13/ICSP13_Contributions/ICES.pdf). As an observer to the UN General Assembly, ICES contributes and engages actively in relevant work, such as working towards the Sustainable Development Goals (https://sdgs.un.org/statements/international-council-exploration-sea-ices-15934.); contributing to the UN Decade of Ocean Science for Sustainable Development (UNESCO/IOC); the Informal Consultations of States Parties to the United Nations Fish Stocks Agreement; and the UN Open-ended Informal Consultative Process in Oceans and the Law of the Sea (https://www.un.org/depts/los/convention_agreements/ICSP13/ICSP13_Contributions/ICES.pdf). ICES also expands its human capacity building services thematically and geographically by organizing a series of training courses for the Large Marine Ecosystem practitioners under the GEF/UNDP ‘Strengthening Global Governance of Large Marine Ecosystems and Their Coasts through Enhanced Sharing and Application of LME/ICM/MPA Knowledge and Information Tools’ LME-LEARN project (https://www.un.org/regularprocess/content/international-council-exploration-sea-ices).
Vertical Coordination: Vertical coordination within ICES involves cooperation with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other international organisations, regional fishery advisory bodies, and Member states. This is achieved through working arrangements, scientific advice, and data sharing. This is structured under Article 4 of the ICES Convention (https://www.ices.dk/about-ICES/who-we-are/Documents/ICES_Convention_1964.pdf), which states that the Council shall seek to establish and maintain working arrangements with other international organisations which have related objectives and cooperate, as far as possible, with them, in particular in the supply of scientific information requested. ICES operates through the Council of all the members, the Bureau of the Council as the executive committee, the General Secretary and other staff as the secretariat, and various committees and working groups for different scientific and administrative functions (Articles 6-13). ICES also provides non-biased, non-political scientific advice to member nation governments and international regulatory commissions on marine policy and management issues (Article 1). ICES's work is organised around six regions, each with a regional coordinator who facilitates the communication and collaboration between the ICES secretariat, the national delegates, and the scientific community (https://www.ices.dk/community/Pages/Regional-coordinators.aspx). There is also the Science Committee (SCICOM) and the Advisory Committee (ACOM), which oversee the scientific and advisory activities of the ICES, respectively, and report to the Council (https://www.ices.dk/community/groups/Pages/default.aspx). Additionally, ICES has over 150 expert groups, workshops, and strategic initiatives that conduct and coordinate marine research and provide scientific outputs and advice to the ICES and its clients (https://www.ices.dk/community/groups/Pages/default.aspx).
Horizontal Coordination: Horizontal coordination within ICES involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the marine sciences domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, the scientific community, and other international organizations to ensure that marine research is promoted, developed, and coordinated. ICES publishes roadmaps for offshore renewable energy and provides advice on marine species like the Northern shrimp in Division 4.a West (northern North Sea, Fladen Ground) and Anchovy in Subarea 8 (Bay of Biscay) (https://ices-library.figshare.com/ndownloader/files/43537026). Horizontal coordination within ICES can take various forms, such as (1) joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, like the Working Group on SmartDots Governance and the Working Group on Integrated Assessment (https://www.ices.dk/data/tools/Pages/smartdots.aspx), (2) participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the Working Group on Zooplankton Ecology and the Working Group on Marine Mammal Ecology (https://ices-library.figshare.com/ndownloader/files/41451087), (3) development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for marine sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Second Workshop on Stock Identification and Allocation of Catches of Herring to Stocks (WKSIDAC2) (https://www.ices.dk/about-ICES/Documents/Resolutions/2022%20Resolutions/FRSG%20Resolutions%202022.pdf), and advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for marine issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the ICES Annual Science Conference (https://ices-library.figshare.com/ndownloader/files/43418841). The ICES provides leadership and direction on matters related to marine sciences, shapes the marine research agenda, sets norms and standards, articulates evidence-based policy options, provides technical support to countries, and monitors and assesses marine trends (https://www.ices.dk/news-and-events/Documents/Press%20Room/ICES%20general.pdf).

Spatial Jurisdiction: IFAD's jurisdiction is not limited to any specific geographical or political, or economic zones, but rather covers the rural areas of its 177 member states, which include developing, middle and high-income countries from all regions of the world (https://www.ifad.org/en/web/operations/regions). IFAD does not have a specific mandate or jurisdiction on oceans and maritime zones, but it does support projects that involve coastal communities, fisheries and aquaculture in some countries.
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: The IFAD Secretariat is responsible for investing in rural people, empowering them to increase their food security, improve the nutrition of their families and increase their incomes (https://www.ifad.org/en/about). This includes supporting initiatives that improve land and water management, develop rural infrastructure, train and educate farmers in more efficient technologies, build up resilience against climate change, and enhance market accessibility. IFAD also provides grants and low-interest loans, strengthens policies and promotes innovation, in order to achieve sustainable benefits for the poor at scale and support all countries to achieve lasting, systemic change (https://www.ifad.org/en/vision).
Source of Jurisdiction: IFAD derives its mandate from the Agreement Establishing the International Fund for Agricultural Development, which established IFAD as an international financial institution and a specialized agency of the United Nations (https://www.ifad.org/documents/38711624/39421015/agree_e.pdf/b06d3b8f-6fb5-4db1-8054-b1ef21d746a5). Specifically, Article 2 of the Agreement defines the objectives and functions of IFAD; Article 3 outlines the membership and voting rights of IFAD; Article 6 describes the organization and management of IFAD; Article 7 specifies the use of resources and conditions of financing by IFAD; Article 8 establishes the relations of IFAD with the United Nations and other organizations, institutions and agencies; Article 9 regulates the withdrawal, suspension of membership, and termination of operations of IFAD; and Article 10 of the Agreement grants the legal status, privileges and immunities of IFAD. Additionally, the By-laws for the Conduct of the Business of IFAD (https://www.ifad.org/documents/38711624/39421006/bylaw_e.pdf/d96589cb-8970-4862-af2e-c7fb4ed03c72?t=1651150969488) states that the by-laws shall govern the conduct of the business of IFAD, and that the by-laws may be amended by the Governing Council or the Executive Board (Preamble). IFAD's jurisdiction is also influenced by the policies and criteria for IFAD financing 9https://www.ifad.org/documents/38711624/39421030/ifad_financing_e.pdf/46846eb9-1053-4bcc-acf1-1e8756831fbb?t=1653556237925), which provide the general principles and operational guidelines for IFAD's lending and grant activities. These policies and criteria are periodically reviewed and updated by the Executive Board to reflect the changing needs and priorities of IFAD's target groups and member states. IFAD's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, the Paris Agreement on Climate Change, and the Addis Ababa Action Agenda on Financing for Development, which provide further legal frameworks for IFAD's jurisdiction over specific rural development issues and domains (https://www.ifad.org/documents/38714170/40237917/IFAD+Strategic+Framework+2016-2025/d43eed79-c827-4ae8-b043-09e65977e22d).
Defined Objectives: According to Article 2 of the Agreement Establishing the International Fund for Agricultural Development (https://www.ifad.org/documents/38711624/39421015/agree_e.pdf/b06d3b8f-6fb5-4db1-8054-b1ef21d746a5), IFAD's objectives encompass several key functions: mobilizing additional resources to be made available on concessional terms for agricultural development in developing Member States (Article 2, paragraph 1); providing financing primarily for projects and programmes specifically designed to introduce, expand or improve food production systems and to strengthen related policies and institutions within the framework of national priorities and strategies (Article 2, paragraph 2); furnishing technical assistance and policy advice, as well as facilitating the access of developing Member States to technology and information, in support of the above-mentioned activities (Article 2, paragraph 3); and promoting and facilitating the participation of the rural poor, particularly women and youth, in the decisions and activities affecting their living conditions and well-being (Article 2, paragraph 4). These functions enable the Fund to fulfil its role as an international financial institution and a specialized agency of the United Nations dedicated to eradicating rural poverty in developing countries (https://www.ifad.org/en/vision).
Strategies: IFAD executes its objectives via several strategies: firstly, a ten-year Strategic Framework (https://www.ifad.org/documents/38714170/40237917/IFAD+Strategic+Framework+2016-2025/d43eed79-c827-4ae8-b043-09e65977e22d), revised every four years by the Governing Council, establishes the IFAD's vision, mission, strategic objectives, outcomes and pillars of results delivery that will guide its operations over the 2016-2025 period. This framework aligns with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://www.ifad.org/en/strategic-framework) and responds to the commitments of the Thirteenth Replenishment of IFAD's Resources (https://webapps.ifad.org/members/repl/13/1/docs/IFAD13-1-R-7-PPT-on-Workplan-and-Sessions.pdf). Secondly, an annual Result-Based Programme of Work and Budget, devised by the IFAD and approved by the Executive Board, details the activities, outputs, indicators and resources corresponding to each strategic objective. The Indicative Programme of Work and Budget for 2024 is based on the principles of efficiency, effectiveness and value for money, as outlined in document GC 47/L.8 (https://webapps.ifad.org/members/gc/47/docs/GC-47-L-8.pdf). It also supports the implementation of the Environment and Climate Change Strategy, which consolidates and updates IFAD's strategy and policy frameworks on environment and climate change for the 2019-2025 period (https://webapps.ifad.org/members/eb/125/docs/EB-2018-125-R-12.pdf). IFAD's budgeting process is based on a results-based approach that aligns the Fund's resources with its strategic objectives and operational priorities. IFAD reports periodically on its budget performance and achievements to its Executive Board. IFAD has four major funding sources: (1) contributions from its members, (2) investment income, (3) loan repayments by recipient countries, and (4) borrowing from its member states. These resources feed its work program, and are supplemented by co-financing from beneficiary countries and other donors. Contributions are voluntary and multi-year in nature. Every three years, IFAD organizes a replenishment conference, corresponding to a work program. it also receives supplementary funds from various sources, such as climate financing and bilateral grants (https://www.ifad.org/en/finance). Finally, various agreements, mechanisms, platforms and initiatives provide an operational framework for implementing the Strategic Framework, addressing rural poverty, food security, nutrition, gender equality, resilience, innovation, partnerships and financing.
Inter-Institutional Relationship: IFAD partners with various organizations to achieve its mission of ending hunger and promoting food security through sustainable agriculture. This relationship is guided by Article 8 of the Agreement Establishing the International Fund for Agricultural Development (https://www.ifad.org/documents/38711624/39421015/agree_e.pdf/b06d3b8f-6fb5-4db1-8054-b1ef21d746a5). It works closely with the UN Rome-based agencies – the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and the World Food Programme (WFP) – with whom it shares a common vision and supports the Committee on World Food Security (CFS). It also collaborates with other UN programmes and funds such as UN Women (https://www.ifad.org/en/united-nations-agencies). Beyond the UN System, IFAD partners with multilateral development banks and international financial institutions, such as the African Development Bank, the Islamic Development Bank, the OPEC Fund for International Development and the World Bank. IFAD also works with regional organizations such as ASEAN, COMESA, ECOWAS, the European Union and Mercosur; multilateral climate and environment funds, such as the GCF and GEF; and other multilateral organizations, such as the OECD (https://www.ifad.org/en/multilateral-organizations#:~:text=IFAD%20also%20works%20with%20regional,organizations%2C%20such%20as%20the%20OECD.). In addition, IFAD facilitates the Global Environment Facility (GEF), established in 1991, to enhance environmental sustainability and resilience (https://www.ifad.org/en/gef). It also engages with the Green Climate Fund (GCF), established in 2010, to mobilise climate finance and support adaptation and mitigation actions (https://www.greenclimate.fund/ae/ifad).
Vertical Coordination: Vertical coordination within IFAD involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other specialized agencies, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and local authorities. This is achieved through partnership, alignment, and harmonization. This is structured under Article 6 of the Agreement Establishing the International Fund for Agricultural Development (https://www.ifad.org/documents/38711624/39421015/agree_e.pdf/b06d3b8f-6fb5-4db1-8054-b1ef21d746a5). IFAD operates through the Governing Council of all the 177 members, the Executive Board, and a secretariat headed by a President (https://www.ifad.org/en/governance). IFAD also has committees, working groups, and other subsidiary bodies (https://www.ifad.org/pt-BR/groups-and-committees). IFAD assists members in the implementation of its policies, strategies, and programmes and provides financial and technical support upon request (https://www.ifad.org/pt-BR/web/operations/projects-and-programmes). IFAD's work is organised around five regions, each overseen by a Regional Director who works closely with the President to implement projects and programmes across all levels of the Organization (https://www.ifad.org/pt-BR/leadership). There is also the Senior Management Team (consisting of the President, Vice-President, Associate Vice-President, Regional Directors, and Directors of Corporate Services and Global Engagement) providing strategic and operational guidance to the President on matters related to the programmatic and managerial work of IFAD; and ensuring coherence and alignment between the three levels of the Organization and the governing bodies (https://www.ifad.org/it/leadership). Also, a network of country offices and technical experts supports IFAD's work in promoting rural development and food security as an integral part of regional and national development policies (https://webapps.ifad.org/members/pmtgr/125893/docs/IFAD-Country-Offices-Presentation.pdf). Additionally, IFAD operates technical centres and in-country offices in 40 Member States (https://www.ifad.org/en/annualreport2019/regional.html). In addition, IFAD coordinates with the European Union and its agencies and is a partner of the Global Donor Platform for Rural Development (https://www.ifad.org/en/web/knowledge/-/ifad-and-the-eu-partnering-to-transform-rural-realities).
Horizontal Coordination:
Horizontal coordination within IFAD involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the rural development domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, the scientific community, and other UN agencies to ensure that rural poverty is reduced and food security is enhanced through sustainable agriculture and rural transformation. This coordination is guided by Article 8 of the  Agreement Establishing the International Fund for Agricultural Development (https://www.ifad.org/documents/38711624/39421015/agree_e.pdf/b06d3b8f-6fb5-4db1-8054-b1ef21d746a5). For example, IFAD works with the finance sector to promote inclusive rural financial services and access to credit for smallholder farmers and rural entrepreneurs (https://www.ifad.org/en/rural-finance), with the gender sector to empower rural women and girls and promote gender equality in rural development (https://www.ifad.org/en/gender), with the climate sector to support climate change adaptation and mitigation in agriculture and natural resource management (https://www.ifad.org/en/climate-and-environment), or with the nutrition sector to improve the availability, accessibility, and quality of food for rural populations (https://www.ifad.org/en/nutrition).
Horizontal coordination within IFAD can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Adaptation for Smallholder Agriculture Programme (ASAP) with FAO, WFP, and GEF (https://www.ifad.org/sv/asap) or the Rural Youth Action Plan with UNICEF, UNDP, and UN Women (https://www.ifad.org/documents/38711624/41190839/Action_Youth_web.pdf/f09a8d5c-36eb-f915-8b36-b521b1414b08), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the Committee on World Food Security (CFS) with FAO and WFP (https://www.ifad.org/en/web/latest/-/committee-on-world-food-security-50) or the UN Decade of Family Farming (2019-2028) with FAO and other partners (https://www.ifad.org/en/web/latest/-/news/launch-of-the-un-s-decade-of-family-farming-to-unleash-family-farmers-full-potential), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for rural development sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Rural Development Report (https://www.ifad.org/documents/38714170/43704363/rdr2021.pdf/d3c85b6a-229a-c6f1-75e2-a67bb8b505b2?t=1649073218696) or the Project Design Report (https://www.ifad.org/en/-/document/project-design-rep-13?p_l_back_url=%2Fit%2Fprogramme-and-project-documents%3Fp_p_id%3D2_WAR_kaleodesignerportlet%26p_p_lifecycle%3D0%26page%3D3%26delta%3D7%26start%3D70), and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for rural development issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the International Rural Women's Day (https://www.ifad.org/en/web/latest/-/international-rural-women-s-day-statement?p_l_back_url=%2Fen%2Fweb%2Flatest%2Fspeeches%3Fmode%3Dseench%26page%3D9%26stent%3D77%26delta%3D125) or the Rural Solutions Portal (https://ruralsolutionsportal.org/en/about).

Spatial Jurisdiction: IHO’s global jurisdiction represents the hydrographic interests of its 99 member states. IHO’s authority covers all the world’s seas, oceans and navigable waters, including the exclusive economic zones (EEZs), territorial seas, continental shelves, and inland waters of its members, as well as the international boundaries and limits of these zones. IHO’s jurisdiction extends from the coastlines' low water mark to the marine environment's outermost reaches (https://iho.int/uploads/user/pubs/misc/M1_Separatedocs/Convention_new_EN.pdf).
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: IHO is responsible for advancing the science and practice of hydrography, which measures and describes the physical features of the oceans and coastal areas. This includes developing and maintaining standards, charts, and nautical publications for safe navigation, maritime security, and environmental protection (https://www.hydro-international.com/content/article/iho-standards?output=pdf). IHO also coordinates the activities of national hydrographic offices, facilitates the exchange of hydrographic data and information, and provides capacity-building and technical assistance to its member states (https://iho.int/en/about-the-iho).
Source of Jurisdiction: IHO derives its mandate from the Convention on the IHO, which established IHO as an intergovernmental organization representing hydrography (https://iho.int/uploads/user/pubs/misc/M1_Separatedocs/Convention_new_EN.pdf). Specifically, Article 2 of the Convention defines the objectives and functions of IHO, and Article 3 outlines the structure and membership of IHO (https://iho.int/uploads/user/pubs/misc/M1_Separatedocs/Convention_new_EN.pdf). Additionally, IHO's general regulations, regulation 3 on the general function of the IHO secretariat, states that the secretariat shall execute the decisions of the Assembly and the Council and provide them with the necessary services (https://iho.int/uploads/user/pubs/misc/M1_Separatedocs/Convention_new_EN.pdf). IHO's jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by its organs, such as the Assembly, the Council, and the Finance Committee (https://iho.int/mtg_docs/misc_docs/basic_docs/NEW/New_EN/M_1_EN_062017.pdf). These resolutions and decisions provide guidance and direction for IHO's activities and programmes and cooperation and coordination with other organisations and stakeholders. IHO's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the International Maritime Organization (IMO) instruments, etc., which provide further legal frameworks for hydrography and nautical charting (https://ihr.iho.int/articles/geospatial-information-management-between-hydrography-and-the-law-of-the-sea-a-milestone-opportunity-for-their-further-integration/) (https://iho.int/uploads/user/About%20IHO/Assembly/Assembly3/DOCUMENTS/PRO%20A3/A3_2023_PRO-1.2_EN_ImplStrPln_CC_v1.pdf)
Defined Objectives: According to Article II f the IHO Convention (https://iho.int/uploads/user/pubs/misc/M1_Separatedocs/Convention_new_EN.pdf), the International Hydrographic Organization's objectives cover several key areas: promoting the use of hydrography for the safety of navigation and all other marine purposes and raising global awareness of the importance of hydrography (Object a); improving global coverage, availability and quality of hydrographic data, information, products and services and facilitating access to such data, information, products and services (Object b); improving global hydrographic capability, capacity, training, science and techniques (Purpose, Object c); establishing and enhancing the development of international standards for hydrographic data, information, products, services and techniques and achieving the greatest possible uniformity in the use of these standards (Object d); giving authoritative and timely guidance on all hydrographic matters to States and international organizations (Object e); facilitating coordination of hydrographic activities among the Member States (Object f); and enhancing cooperation on hydrographic activities among States on a regional basis (Object g). These objectives enable the Organization to fulfil its vision of being the authoritative, worldwide hydrographic body that actively engages all coastal and interested states to advance maritime safety and efficiency and supports the protection and sustainable use of the marine environment.
Strategies: The IHO executes its objectives via several strategies: firstly, a six-year Strategic Plan, revised annually by the Council, which identifies specific strategic goals and targets that will direct the IHO's Work Programme in a way that will foster the IHO vision, mission, and objectives. This plan, applicable for 2021-2026, addresses the growing need for hydrographic knowledge, the progress in sensors, carriers and IT technology, the data revolution, and the increasing environmental, societal and economic attention to the Ocean (https://iho.int/uploads/user/About%20IHO/Strategic%20Plan/IHOSP2021_2026_final.pdf). Secondly, a 3-yearly budgetary cycle and work programme, devised by the Secretariat and approved by the Assembly, details the activities, outputs, indicators, and resources corresponding to each strategic goal (https://iho.int/uploads/user/About%20IHO/WP_Budget%20for%202024-2026.pdf). The current budget and work programme for 2024-2026 are aligned with the Strategic Plan and the priorities of the Member States. Finally, various standards, specifications, guidelines, mechanisms, platforms, and initiatives provide an operational framework for implementing the IHO objects, addressing hydrographic data, products, services, techniques, capacity building, and cooperation, with key instruments listed here (https://iho.int/en/standards-and-specifications).
Inter-Institutional Relationship:
The IHO collaborates with various organisations to achieve its objectives. It engages with its 99 Member States and other stakeholders through the Assembly (https://iho.int/en/iho-welcomes-99th-member-state). The IHO enjoys observer status in the United Nations and is particularly active in a number of its subordinate organisations, most notably the International Maritime
Organisation (IMO) and the Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission (IOC) (https://iho.int/uploads/user/About%20IHO/Member%20States/Attachment_1-Brief_info_about_the_IHO.pdf). Additionally, the IHO supports the implementation of the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), especially SDG 14 on Life Below Water, by providing hydrographic data and information for safe, secure and sustainable use of the oceans (https://legacy.iho.int/mtg_docs/circular_letters/english/2017/Cl39.pdf). It also cooperates with other UN specialized agencies and programmes, such as IMO, IOC, UNEP, UNDP, and WMO, and other organizations, such as ISA, ITLOS, IALA, and ICG/IOC, addressing shared hydrographic and oceanographic issues (https://iho.int/uploads/user/About%20IHO/Work_Programme_for_2022.pdf). Moreover, the IHO contributes to the UN Decade of Ocean Science for Sustainable Development (2021-2030) (https://iho.int/en/the-un-ocean-decade-and-the-iho-join-forces-to-change-the-gender-climate-in-hydrography), offering expertise and standards for ocean mapping and observation, as acknowledged in UN resolution 72/73, paragraph 14 (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N17/421/90/PDF/N1742190.pdf?OpenElement).
Vertical Coordination: Vertical coordination connected to the IHO involves downward coordination into subsidiary bodies  and receipt of governance input from member states, other specialised agencies, regional and intergovernmental organisations, national hydrographic offices, and local authorities (https://iho.int/en/about-the-iho). This is achieved through reporting, cooperation, and assistance (https://iho.int/uploads/user/About%20IHO/Assembly/Assembly3/DOCUMENTS/A3_2023_G_05.1_EN_WP1_SG_Report_v2.pdf).  The IHO operates through the Assembly of all the Member States, the Council of 30 Member States, and a secretariat headed by a Secretary-General (Article 6 of the Convention on the IHO) (https://iho.int/mtg_docs/misc_docs/basic_docs/NEW/New_EN/M_1_EN_062017.pdf). The IHO also has committees, sub-committees, working groups, and other subsidiary bodies (Article 7 of the Convention on the IHO) (https://iho.int/uploads/user/pubs/misc/M1_Separatedocs/Convention_new_EN.pdf). The IHO assists Member States in the implementation of its standards, policies, and programmes, and provides technical cooperation and assistance upon request (Article 4 of the Convention on the IHO) (https://iho.int/uploads/user/pubs/misc/M1_Separatedocs/Convention_new_EN.pdf). The IHO's work is organised around four major programme areas, each overseen by a Director who works closely with the Secretary-General to implement strategies and programmes across all levels of the Organization. Also, inter-regional cooperation is fostered with the Inter-Regional Coordination Committee (https://iho.int/uploads/user/Inter-Regional%20Coordination/IRCC/MISC/IRCC_TOR.pdf), Regional Hydrographic Commissions (https://iho.int/en/rhcs), and the Capacity Building & Technical Cooperation (https://iho.int/en/capacity-building-and-technical-cooperation) supporting the IHO's work in promoting the use of hydrography for the safety of navigation and all other marine purposes and raising global awareness of the importance of hydrography.  The Hydrographic Services and Standards Committe is also setup to promote and coordinate the development of standards, specifications and guidelines for official products and services to meet the requirements of mariners and other users of hydrographic information. Additionally, the IHO operates the IHO Data Centre for Digital Bathymetry (DCDB), a key component of timplementing theIHO Resolution 2/2005 as amended on the Establishment of a Worldwide Electronic Navigational Chart Database (WEND) (https://iho.int/en/data-centre-for-digital-bathymetry). Besides the Secretary-General, at the IHO headquarters, there is a clear line of duty within the leadership team comprising of a Director of the International Hydrographic Bureau, a Director of the International Hydrographic Standards and Services, a Director of the International Hydrographic Cooperation and Development, and a Director of the International Hydrographic Administration and Finance (https://iho.int/en/iho-secretariat) (https://iho.int/mtg_docs/misc_docs/basic_docs/NEW/New_EN/M_1_EN_062017.pdf)
Horizontal Coordination: Horizontal coordination within IHO involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the hydrographic domain, such as governments, maritime authorities, oceanographic institutions, and other international organizations to ensure that all the world’s seas, oceans and navigable waters are surveyed and charted. This coordination is guided by the Convention on the IHO (https://iho.int/uploads/user/pubs/misc/M1_Separatedocs/Convention_new_EN.pdf). For example, IHO works with the safety of navigation sector to provide standards and services for nautical charts and publications (https://iho.int/en/standards-and-specifications), with the marine environment protection sector to support the implementation of the International Convention for the Control and Management of Ships’ Ballast Water and Sediments (http://library.arcticportal.org/1913/1/International%20Convention%20for%20the%20Control%20and%20Management%20of%20Ships%27%20Ballast%20Water%20and%20Sediments.pdf), with the ocean governance sector to contribute to the development of a global framework for ocean data management (https://iho.int/uploads/user/Inter-Regional%20Coordination/MSDIWG/Body%20of%20Knowledge/MSDI_white_paper.pdf) or with the capacity building sector to assist developing countries in enhancing their hydrographic capabilities (https://iho.int/en/capacity-building-and-technical-cooperation). Horizontal coordination within IHO can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Hydrographic Services and Standards Committee (https://iho.int/en/hssc), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the Joint IHO-IMO-WMO-IOC-IALA-IAEA-FIG-IMPA Capacity Building Coordination Meetings (https://iho.int/en/cb-international-partners) or the UN-GGIM Working Group on Marine Geospatial Information (https://ggim.un.org/UNGGIM-wg8/), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for hydrographic sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the S-100 Universal Hydrographic Data Model (https://iho.int/en/s-100-universal-hydrographic-data-model) or the Crowdsourced Bathymetry Working Group (https://iho.int/en/csbwg-home), (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for hydrographic issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the IHO Publication C-55 Status of Hydrographic Surveying and Nautical Charting Worldwide (https://iho.int/en/iho-c-55) or the World Hydrography Day (https://iho.int/en/world-hydrography-day). This collaboration enables IHO to provide leadership and direction on matters related to hydrography, shape the hydrographic agenda, sets norms and standards, articulate evidence-based policy options, provide technical support to countries, while also monitoring and assessing hydrographic trends (https://iho.int/en/about-the-iho).

Spatial Jurisdiction: ILO's authority is global, covering the labour standards and rights of its member states. This includes a focus on countries, territories and areas within the UN system, with authority reaching up to the national laws and policies of these states, respecting their sovereignty and diversity. The ILO also cooperates with regional and subregional organizations to promote decent work and social justice (https://www.ilo.org/wcmsp5/groups/public/---asia/---ro-bangkok/---ilo-hanoi/documents/publication/wcms_818973.pdf).
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: The International Labour Organization (ILO) is devoted to promoting social justice and internationally recognized human and labour rights, pursuing its founding mission that social justice is essential to universal and lasting peace (https://www.ilo.org/global/about-the-ilo/mission-and-objectives/lang--en/index.htm). This includes adopting and supervising Conventions and Recommendations, providing technical cooperation and assistance, conducting research and analysis, and facilitating tripartite consultations among governments, employers, and workers (https://www.ilo.org/tribunal/lang--en/index.htm). The ILO also collaborates with other UN agencies and regional and subregional organizations to advance the human rights and dignity of all workers, as well as supporting the achievement of the UN's development agenda and the Sustainable Development Goals  (https://www.ilo.org/inform/online-information-resources/research-guides/labour-law/lang--en/index.htm; https://www.ilo.org/dyn/normlex/en/f?p=NORMLEXPUB:91:0::NO:::)
Source of Jurisdiction: ILO derives its mandate from the Treaty of Versailles, cum The Covenant of the League of Nations, which established it as the first specialised agency of the League of Nations in 1919 (https://libraryresources.unog.ch/ld.php?content_id=32971179). Specifically, Article 23 of the Treaty provides the legal basis for ILO's jurisdiction over the improvement of labour conditions, the regulation of hours of work, the prevention of unemployment, and the protection of workers' rights (https://www.foundingdocs.gov.au/resources/transcripts/cth10_doc_1919.pdf). Additionally, ILO's jurisdiction is influenced by the Declaration of Philadelphia, which reaffirmed the principles and objectives of the ILO in 1944 (https://www.ilo.org/static/english/inwork/cb-policy-guide/declarationofPhiladelphia1944.pdf), and the Constitution of the International Labour Organization, which defines the structure, functions, and procedures of the ILO ((https://www.ilo.org/wcmsp5/groups/public/---asia/---ro-bangkok/---ilo-hanoi/documents/publication/wcms_818973.pdf). ILO also adopts and supervises international labour standards, such as Conventions and Recommendations, (including he Maritime Labour Convention - Maritime Labour Convention, 2006  - https://www.ilo.org/wcmsp5/groups/public/---ed_norm/---normes/documents/normativeinstrument/wcms_090250.pdf) which provide further legal frameworks for ILO's jurisdiction over specific labour issues and regions.
Defined Objectives: According to the Preamble and Chapter I of the ILO Constitution, the International Labour Organization's objectives encompass several key principles: promoting social justice and internationally recognized human and labour rights, based on the Declaration of Philadelphia and the Declaration on Fundamental Principles and Rights at Work (Preamble); establishing and adopting international labour standards in the form of Conventions and Recommendations, and ensuring their effective observance by the Members (Article 19, Article 22, Article 23, Article 24, Article 26); fostering cooperation among the Members and with other international organizations, especially the United Nations, in the fields of industry and employment (Article 12, Article 13); and providing technical assistance, information, and publications on various aspects of industrial life and labour (Article 10, Article 11) (https://www.ilo.org/wcmsp5/groups/public/---asia/---ro-bangkok/---ilo-hanoi/documents/publication/wcms_818973.pdf). These principles enable the Organization to fulfil its role as the specialized agency of the United Nations devoted to promoting rights at work, creating greater opportunities for women and men to decent employment and income, enhancing the coverage and effectiveness of social protection for all, and strengthen tripartism and social dialogue  (https://www.ilo.org/global/about-the-ilo/mission-and-objectives/lang--en/index.htm).
Strategies: ILO implements its objectives through strategic planning and operational frameworks. Its four-year Strategic Plan for 2022-2025, approved by the Governing Body, aligns with its mission of social justice and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (GB.340/PFA/1(Rev.1)) (https://www.ilo.org/wcmsp5/groups/public/---ed_norm/---relconf/documents/meetingdocument/wcms_757564.pdf). The biennial programme and budget for 2022-2023, adopted by the International Labour Conference, outlines policy outcomes, indicators, and resources to operationalize the Strategic Plan, reflecting constituents' needs (GB.341/PFA/22) (https://www.ilo.org/wcmsp5/groups/public/---ed_mas/---program/documents/genericdocument/wcms_831036.pdf). Furthermore, the ILO Administrative Tribunal, established in 1927, adjudicates complaints from officials of the ILO and affiliated organizations (following Chapter III  Article 37 (2) of the ILO Constitution), delivering around 120 judgments annually (https://www.ilo.org/wcmsp5/groups/public/---ed_norm/---relconf/documents/meetingdocument/wcms_413819.pdf). Likewise, the ILO’s Decent Work Agenda, comprising four pillars—rights at work, employment, social protection, and social dialogue—was formalized in 2008 (ILO’s Declaration on Social Justice for a Fair Globalization) is a key area of engagement for the ILO and its constituents (https://www.ilo.org/wcmsp5/groups/public/---dgreports/---dcomm/documents/instructionalmaterial/wcms_650144.pdf). Also, the DW4SD Resource Platform (https://www.ilo.org/global/topics/dw4sd/lang--en/index.htm) offers online resources on themes related to ILO’s mandate and SDGs, featuring good practices and policy outcomes (https://www.ilo.org/wcmsp5/groups/public/---dgreports/---dcomm/documents/instructionalmaterial/wcms_650144.pdf). These strategies collectively ensure the effective fulfilment of ILO's mandate for global labour standards and social justice.
Inter-Institutional Relationship: The ILO collaborates with various organizations to achieve its objectives. It works closely with its tripartite constituents - governments, employers and workers - through the International Labour Conference, the Governing Body, and the Regional Meetings, which are the supreme organs of the ILO and set its policies and programmes (https://www.ilo.org/global/about-the-ilo/how-the-ilo-works/lang--en/index.htm). As the first specialized agency of the UN, the ILO's relationship with the UN is based on the Agreement between the United Nations and the International Labour Organization, which was approved by the General Assembly in 1946 and by the International Labour Conference in 1947 (https://www.ilo.org/wcmsp5/groups/public/---dgreports/---jur/documents/genericdocument/wcms_433792.pdf). Additionally, the ILO cooperates with other UN agencies and regional and subregional organizations, such as the UN Economic and Social Council, the UN Development Group, UNEP, UNIDO, UNDP, UNITAR, the World Bank, the IMF, the OECD, the African Union, the European Union, and the Organization of American States, on various aspects of labour and social issues, as stipulated in Article 12 and Article 13 of the ILO Constitution (https://www.ilo.org/wcmsp5/groups/public/---asia/---ro-bangkok/---ilo-hanoi/documents/publication/wcms_818973.pdf; https://www.ilo.org/pardev/partnerships/partnerships-and-relations/interagency-partnerships/lang--en/index.htm). The ILO is member of the UN Cluster on Trade and Productive Capacity   through which it works with UNCTAD, ITC, UNIDO and UNOPS to enhance horticulture supply and sustainable tourism to develop business linkages in developing countries (https://tii.unido.org/sites/default/files/publications/TII_ImpactStory_SECO_Myanmar.pdf)  It also participates in the Regular Process for Global Reporting and Assessment of the Marine Environment, providing data on the social and economic dimensions of the marine sector, as recognized in resolution 57/141, paragraph  (https://www.un.org/en/development/desa/population/migration/generalassembly/docs/globalcompact/A_RES_57_141.pdf).
Vertical Coordination: Vertical coordination within ILO involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other specialized agencies, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and local authorities. This is structured under the Relationship with the United Nations and Other International Organizations section of the ILO Constitution, specifically in Articles 12-13 (https://www.ilo.org/wcmsp5/groups/public/---asia/---ro-bangkok/---ilo-hanoi/documents/publication/wcms_818973.pdf). The ILO operates through the International Labour Conference of all the members, the Governing Body of 56 members, and a secretariat headed by a Director-General (Articles 3-9) (https://www.ilo.org/wcmsp5/groups/public/---asia/---ro-bangkok/---ilo-hanoi/documents/publication/wcms_818973.pdf). The ILO also has committees, commissions, and other subsidiary bodies (Articles 14-18). The ILO assists members in the implementation of its standards, policies, and programmes, and provides technical cooperation and assistance upon request (Articles 10-11) (https://www.ilo.org/wcmsp5/groups/public/---asia/---ro-bangkok/---ilo-hanoi/documents/publication/wcms_818973.pdf). ILO’s work is organized around four clusters, each overseen by an Assistant Director-General (https://www.ilo.org/global/about-the-ilo/how-the-ilo-works/organigramme/lang--en/index.htm). Also, a network of field offices and technical specialists underpins the ILO’s work in promoting the Decent Work Agenda  as an integral part of regional and national development policies (https://www.ilo.org/global/about-the-ilo/where-we-are/lang--en/index.htm).
Horizontal Coordination: Horizontal coordination within ILO involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the labour domain, such as governments, employers, workers, social partners, and other international organizations (https://www.ilo.org/global/about-the-ilo/lang--en/index.htm). This coordination is structured under the Organization section of the ILO Constitution, specifically in Articles 1-13 (https://www.ilo.org/wcmsp5/groups/public/---asia/---ro-bangkok/---ilo-hanoi/documents/publication/wcms_818973.pdf). The ILO promotes social justice and decent work by setting international labour standards, providing technical assistance and capacity building, conducting research and analysis, and fostering social dialogue and tripartism (https://www.ilo.org/global/about-the-ilo/mission-and-objectives/lang--en/index.htm). The ILO facilitates the exchange of information and experience among its Members and cooperates with other specialized agencies and bodies of the United Nations on matters pertaining to its mandate (https://www.ilo.org/wcmsp5/groups/public/---ed_mas/---program/documents/genericdocument/wcms_831036.pdf).

Spatial Jurisdiction: The IMF does not have specific authority over maritime zones or territorial waters but rather covers global economic and political zones with 190 member countries and six regional offices through which it coordinates its activities (https://www.imf.org/en/About). Regional coverage of IMF's activities is guided by economic outlook reports which discuss recent economic developments and prospects for countries in different regions, as well as policy challenges and recommendations (https://www.imf.org/en/publications/reo).
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: The IMF is responsible for promoting international monetary cooperation, facilitating the expansion and balanced growth of international trade, and maintaining a stable system of exchange rates among its members (https://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/aa/pdf/aa.pdf). This includes overseeing the international monetary system and the compliance of each member with its obligations, providing financial and technical assistance to members facing balance of payments problems, and allocating and managing special drawing rights as a supplementary reserve asset (https://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/aa/pdf/aa.pdf). The IMF also conducts research and analysis, policy advice and dialogue, capacity development, and data and statistics on various aspects of the global economy, such as fiscal and monetary policy, financial stability, debt sustainability, poverty reduction, and environmental and social issues (https://www.imf.org/en/About/Factsheets/IMF-at-a-Glance).
Source of Jurisdiction:
The IMF mainly derives its mandate from its Articles of Agreement, which is a treaty that establishes the legal framework and objectives of the Fund. The Articles of Agreement were adopted at the United Nations Monetary and Financial Conference in Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, in July 1944, and entered into force in December 1945 (https://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/pam/pam45/pdf/chap1.pdf). The Articles of Agreement have been amended several times to reflect the changes in the global economic and financial system. The most recent amendment, which became effective in January 2016, was aimed at enhancing the representation and voice of emerging and developing countries in the Fund’s governance (https://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/aa/pdf/aa.pdf).
The Articles of Agreement define the obligations and rights of the Fund and its members, as well as the procedures and principles for the Fund’s operations and transactions. In addition to the Articles of Agreement, the Fund’s jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions of the Board of Governors, the decisions of the Executive Board, the agreements with other international organizations, and the jurisprudence of the Administrative Tribunal (https://www.imf.org/external/imfat/report.htm).
Defined Objectives: According to Article I of the Articles of Agreement of the IMF (https://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/aa/pdf/aa.pdf), the IMF's objectives cover several key areas: promoting international monetary cooperation through a permanent institution that provides the machinery for consultation and collaboration on international monetary problems (Objective i); facilitating the expansion and balanced growth of international trade, and contributing thereby to the promotion and maintenance of high levels of employment and real income and to the development of the productive resources of all members as primary objectives of economic policy (Objective ii); promoting exchange stability, maintaining orderly exchange arrangements among members, and avoiding competitive exchange depreciation (Objective iii); assisting in the establishment of a multilateral system of payments in respect of current transactions between members and in the elimination of foreign exchange restrictions which hamper the growth of world trade (Objective iv); giving confidence to members by making the general resources of the Fund temporarily available to them under adequate safeguards, thus providing them with opportunity to correct maladjustments in their balance of payments without resorting to measures destructive of national or international prosperity (Objective v); and in accordance with the above, shortening the duration and lessening the degree of disequilibrium in the international balances of payments of members (Objective vi).
Strategies: The IMF implements its objectives through several strategies. The IMF’s capacity development strategy is reviewed every five years to ensure its relevance and effectiveness (https://www.imf.org/-/media/Files/Publications/PP/2022/English/PPEA2022056.ashx). The latest review, conducted in 2023, reaffirmed the two main objectives of increasing the impact and efficiency of capacity development, and proposed several recommendations to achieve them. The review also highlighted the importance of integrating capacity development with surveillance and lending, tailoring and modernizing delivery, enhancing internal and external coordination and communication, and improving management processes and systems. The IMF’s capacity development strategy is guided by the principles and priorities set out in document IMF/18/4/Rev.1 (https://www.imf.org/~/media/Files/Publications/PP/2018/pp021518cd-strategy-review.ashx). The IMF’s surveillance strategy is also reviewed periodically to adapt to the changing global environment and the needs of the membership. The most recent review, completed in 2019, focused on enhancing the quality, traction, and evenhandedness of surveillance, and identified four priority areas for action: strengthening the analysis of macro-financial linkages, governance and corruption, external sector assessments, and policy trade-offs and spillovers. The IMF’s surveillance strategy is based on the principles and modalities specified in document IMF/19/68/Rev.1 (https://www.imf.org/~/media/Files/Publications/PP/2019/PP041719-2018-Review-of-Program-Design-and-Conditionality.ashx).
