The IMF’s lending strategy is designed to help members restore macroeconomic stability, foster growth and reduce poverty, and safeguard the stability of the international monetary system. The IMF’s lending strategy is informed by regular reviews of its lending policies and facilities, as well as the lessons learned from its program experience. The latest review, conducted in 2019, assessed the adequacy and effectiveness of the Fund’s lending toolkit, and proposed some modifications and enhancements to better meet the diverse needs of the membership. The IMF’s lending strategy is governed by the rules and procedures established in document IMF/19/69/Rev.1 (https://www.imf.org/~/media/Files/Publications/PP/2019/PP041719-2018-Review-of-Program-Design-and-Conditionality.ashx).
Inter-Institutional Relationship: The IMF collaborates with various institutions to achieve its goals and objectives, working closely with the World Bank in program design and monitoring. This collaboration is based on the IMF’s mandate and limited resources, drawing on the expertise of the World Bank and other relevant institutions as detailed in the IMF Pamphlet Series - No. 47, under the section “Collaboration with Other Institutions in Program Design and Monitoring” (https://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/pam/pam47/pam4705.htm). The IMF also maintains a relationship with the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and the International Labour Organization (ILO). The IMF assists member countries in integrating social policies in the macroeconomic framework developed in close collaboration with these institutions. Collaboration between the IMF and the World Trade Organization (WTO) has been substantially strengthened on trade issues. This is detailed in the IEO Update on the IMF’s involvement in international trade policies. The IMF’s engagement with regional development banks and bilateral donor agencies is also noteworthy (https://ieo.imf.org/-/media/IEO/Files/evaluations/completed/07-24-2017-the-imf-and-social-protection/sp-bd7-imf-collaboration-with-other-institutions-on-sp-web.ashx). Coordination between these institutions helps to minimize the burden on member countries, especially those with low administrative capacity that engage with multiple IOs (https://ieo.imf.org/-/media/IEO/Files/evaluations/completed/11-24-2020-imf-collaboration-with-the-world-bank/bfc-iii-wider-experience-of-fund-external-collaborationweb.ashx).
Vertical Coordination: Vertical coordination within IMF involves cooperation with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other international financial institutions, regional and subregional organizations, national authorities, and local agencies (https://www.imf.org/en/About). This is achieved through consultation, surveillance, policy advice, technical assistance, and financial support. This is structured under the Relations with Other International Organizations section of the IMF Articles of Agreement, specifically in Article X (https://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/aa/pdf/aa.pdf). The IMF operates through the Board of Governors of all the members, the Executive Board of 24 members, and a staff headed by a Managing Director (Article XII) (https://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/aa/pdf/aa.pdf). The IMF also has committees, councils, and other subsidiary bodies (Article XII, Section 1) (https://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/aa/pdf/aa.pdf). The IMF assists members in the design and implementation of its policies and programs and provides lending and other financial services upon request (Article V) (https://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/aa/pdf/aa.pdf). The IMF's work is organized around five departments, each overseen by a Deputy Managing Director who works closely with the Managing Director to oversee the operational, policy, and administrative work of the IMF across all levels of the organization (https://www.imf.org/external/np/obp/orgcht.htm). There is also the Management Implementation Group (consisting of the Managing Director, Deputy Managing Directors, and senior staff) providing guidance and oversight on the implementation of the IMF's strategic priorities and reforms (https://www.imf.org/external/np/obp/orgcht.htm). Also, a network of resident representatives and regional technical assistance centers supports the IMF's work in engaging with member countries and regional organizations on economic and financial issues (https://www.imf.org/external/np/rr/index.htm).
Horizontal Coordination: Horizontal coordination within the IMF involves working with external partners and stakeholders, such as governments, international organizations, civil society, private sector, and academia, to ensure coherence, consistency, and effectiveness of the IMF's policies and operations. This coordination is guided by the Articles of Agreement of the IMF (https://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/aa/index.htm), especially Article IV on obligations regarding exchange arrangements. For example, the IMF coordinates with the World Bank and other multilateral development banks to support low-income countries and fragile states (https://www.imf.org/en/About/Factsheets/Sheets/2016/08/01/16/31/IMF-World-Bank), with the Financial Stability Board and other standard-setting bodies to promote global financial stability (https://www.imf.org/en/About/Factsheets/Sheets/2016/08/01/16/32/Financial-Stability), with the United Nations and other agencies to advance the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://www.imf.org/en/About/Factsheets/Sheets/2016/08/01/16/33/IMF-and-the-Sustainable-Development-Goals), or with the World Health Organization and other health actors to respond to the COVID-19 pandemic (https://www.imf.org/en/About/Factsheets/Sheets/2020/04/16/imf-response-to-covid-19). Horizontal coordination within the IMF can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint analysis and policy advice on cross-cutting issues, such as climate change (https://www.imf.org/en/Topics/climate-change), inequality (https://www.imf.org/en/Topics/inequality), or digitalization (https://www.imf.org/en/Topics/imf-and-digital-money), (2) Participation in interdepartmental and interagency committees, working groups, and task forces, such as the Interdepartmental Working Group on Fund Engagement with Small States (https://www.imf.org/external/np/pp/eng/2013/061013.pdf) or the Inter-Agency Task Force on Financing for Development (https://developmentfinance.un.org/iatf), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, frameworks, and tools for policy coordination and collaboration, such as the Integrated Policy Framework (https://www.imf.org/en/Publications/Policy-Papers/Issues/2019/07/18/Integrated-Policy-Framework-47074) or the Debt Sustainability Framework (https://www.imf.org/en/About/Factsheets/Sheets/2016/08/01/16/10/Debt-Sustainability-Framework-for-Low-Income-Countries), (4) Consultation and communication with internal and external stakeholders to solicit feedback and build consensus on policy issues and reforms, such as the Article IV consultations (https://www.imf.org/en/About/Factsheets/Sheets/2016/08/01/21/46/IMF-Surveillance).

Spatial Jurisdiction: IOM's jurisdiction is global, covering all the regions and countries where it operates and provides services and advice to governments and migrants. This includes a presence in over 100 countries, with 175 member states and 8 observer states (https://www.iom.int/member-states). IOM does not have a specific authority on oceans and maritime zones, but it works closely with other UN agencies and partners to address the challenges and opportunities of migration by sea, such as rescue operations, human trafficking, environmental issues, and regional cooperation (https://governingbodies.iom.int/iom-governing-bodies).
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: The IOM is responsible for promoting humane and orderly migration for the benefit of all, as well as the link between migration and economic, social and cultural development (https://www.iom.int/who-we-are). This includes working in the four broad areas of migration management: migration and development, facilitating migration, regulating migration, and forced migration (https://www.iom.int/who-we-are). IOM also provides services and advice to governments and migrants on various migration issues, such as migration law, migrants' rights, migration health, and the gender dimension of migration (https://www.iom.int/our-work). Furthermore, IOM collaborates with other UN agencies and partners to address the challenges and opportunities of migration by sea, such as rescue operations, human trafficking, environmental issues, and regional cooperation (https://governingbodies.iom.int/who-we-are).
Source of Jurisdiction: IOM derives its mandate from the Constitution of the International Organization for Migration (https://publications.iom.int/system/files/pdf/iom-constitution-3rd-en.pdf), which established IOM as an intergovernmental organization in the field of migration. The present Constitution is an incoporation of the Constitution of 19 October 1953 of the Intergovernmental Committee for European Migration (former designation of the Organization), which entered into force on 30 November 1954, the amendments adopted on 20 May 1987 by the 55th Session of the Council (Resolution no. 724), which entered into force on 14 November 1989, the amendments adopted on 24 November 1998 by the 76th Session of the Council (Resolution No. 997), which entered into force on 21 November 2013 and the amendments adopted on 28 October 2020 by the Fourth Special Session of the Council (Resolution No.1385), which entered into force on 28 October 2020 (https://publications.iom.int/books/constitution-and-basic-texts). Specifically, Article 1 of the Constitution defines the purposes and functions of IOM, and Article 2 outlines the procedures of membership. Articles IV-VIII of the Constitution establish procedures for Council, Administration, Headquarters, Finance, and Legal Status respectively. IOM's jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by its governing bodies, such as the Council, the Executive Committee, and the Standing Committee on Programmes and Finance (https://governingbodies.iom.int/standing-committee-programmes-and-finance). These resolutions and decisions provide guidance and direction for IOM's activities and programmes, as well as cooperation and coordination with other organizations and stakeholders. IOM's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the Global Compact for Safe, Orderly and Regular Migration 9https://refugeesmigrants.un.org/sites/default/files/180711_final_draft_0.pdf), the 1951 Refugee Convention and its 1967 Protocol (https://www.unhcr.org/sites/default/files/legacy-pdf/4ec262df9.pdf), and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://sustainabledevelopment.un.org/content/documents/21252030%20Agenda%20for%20Sustainable%20Development%20web.pdf), which provide further legal frameworks for IOM's jurisdiction over specific migration issues and domains.
Defined Objectives: According to Chapter I (Article 1) of the Constitution of the International Organization for Migration (https://publications.iom.int/system/files/pdf/iom-constitution-3rd-en.pdf), the defined purposes and functions of the International Organization for Migration (IOM) are: (1) To arrange the transfer of migrants who need special assistance or who lack adequate facilities to move to countries offering opportunities for orderly migration, (2) To provide migration services such as recruitment, selection, processing, language training, orientation, medical examination, placement, integration, and return migration, at the request and in agreement with the States concerned, (3) To provide a forum for cooperation and coordination on international migration issues, including studies, research and consultation, among States and other relevant actors, such as international organizations and civil society, (4) To cooperate closely with other international organizations concerned with migration, refugees and human resources, in order to facilitate the harmonization of international activities in these fields, and (5) To recognize the linkages between migration and other areas such as economic, social and cultural development, human rights, humanitarian assistance, and environmental sustainability.
Strategies: The IOM executes its objectives via several strategies: firstly, a five-year Strategic Plan (https://publications.iom.int/system/files/pdf/pub2023-159-r_-_strategic_plan_2024-2028-en_0.pdf), revised annually by the Council, establishes the IOM's vision, mission, strategic objectives, enablers, and cross-cutting priorities. The current plan, applicable for 2024-2028, aligns with the Global Compact for Safe, Orderly and Regular Migration and the United Nations Secretary-General’s Action Agenda on Internal Displacement. Secondly, an annual budget and work plan, devised by the IOM and approved by the Council, detail activities, outputs, indicators, and resources corresponding to each strategic objective. The current budget and work plan for 2024 is tailored to the Member States' needs and stakeholders' priorities (https://www.iom.int/sites/g/files/tmzbdl486/files/developmentfund/iom-development-fund-financial-guidelines-2024.pdf). Thirdly, an IOM Development fund with a strategic plan applicable for 2022-2027 (https://www.iom.int/sites/g/files/tmzbdl486/files/documents/2023-05/iom-development-fund-strategic-plan-2022-2027_6.pdf) aimed at providing Member States with accountable and effective seed funding for innovative migration-related initiatives that align with national, regional, and global development strategies and priorities, as well as supporting the development and strengthening of the capacities of Member States to achieve effective and sustainable migration governance that benefits migrants and society. The IOM also maintains the Migration Data Portal (https://migrationdataportal.org/), a key aspect of the implementation of the Global Compact for Safe, Orderly and Regular Migration. Finally, various strategies, frameworks, platforms, and initiatives provide an operational framework for implementing the IOM's mandate, addressing migration, environment, and climate change, governance, resilience, and mobility (https://publications.iom.int/books/institutional-strategy-migration-environment-and-climate-change-2021-2030).
Inter-Institutional Relationship: IOM cooperates with various partners to advance migration governance and, in particular, achieve the 2030 Agenda. It engages with the United Nations (UN), implementing a relationship agreement (https://www.iom.int/sites/g/files/tmzbdl486/files/about-iom/IOM-UN-Agreement-Sept19-2016.pdf) effective since 19 September 2016, as per the UN General Assembly Resolution 70/296. Similarly, IOM collaborates with the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), providing technical support and policy advice (https://weblog.iom.int/partnerships-action-enabling-development-benefits-migration). Additionally, IOM works with the World Health Organization (WHO), promoting the health of migrants and refugees (https://apps.who.int/gb/ebwha/pdf_files/EB144/B144_27-en.pdf). It also participates in the Global Migration Group (GMG), contributing to inter-agency coordination and coherence, with its terms of reference in the GMG Principles of Working Arrangements (https://www.iom.int/sites/g/files/tmzbdl486/files/jahia/webdav/site/myjahiasite/shared/shared/mainsite/partnerships/docs/gmg_tor_eng.pdf). Moreover, IOM supports the Global Forum on Migration and Development (GFMD), facilitating dialogue and cooperation among stakeholders, involving a Steering Group and a Support Unit, with its objectives and modalities in the GFMD Operating Modalities (https://www.iom.int/global-forum-migration-and-development-gfmd).
Vertical Coordination: Vertical coordination within IOM involves cooperation with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other international organizations, Member States, regional and subregional bodies, and local actors. This is achieved through consultation, information sharing, and joint action. This is structured under Chapter III (Organs), Chapter IV (Council), Chapter V (Administration), and Chapter VI (Headquarters) of the IOM Constitution (https://publications.iom.int/system/files/pdf/iom-constitution-3rd-en.pdf), specifically in Articles 5-18. The IOM operates through the Council of all the Member States, the Administration headed by a Director General, and two Deputy Directors General. The Council may also set up subsidiary bodies as required (Article 10). IOM is present in 171 countries and has 9 regional offices worldwide (https://www.iom.int/iom-organizational-structure), and its work in each region led by a Regional Director who reports to the Director General and coordinates with the Headquarters and the Country Offices to implement policies and programmes across all levels of the Organization (https://www.iom.int/where-we-work). There is also the Senior Management Team (consisting of the Director General, the Deputy Directors General, the Chief of Staff, the Regional Directors, and the Directors of Departments) providing strategic guidance and oversight to the Director General on matters related to the operational and managerial work of IOM; and ensuring coherence and alignment between the three levels of the Organization and the governing bodies (https://www.iom.int/senior-management). Moreover, a network of 550 country offices and field locations supports IOM's work in delivering migration services and assistance to migrants, governments, and other stakeholders (https://www.iom.int/countries). Additionally, IOM operates Global Administrative Centres and Special Liaison Offices (https://www.iom.int/iom-organizational-structure).
Horizontal Coordination: Horizontal coordination within IOM involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the migration domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, academia, and other UN agencies to ensure that migration is humane, orderly, and beneficial for migrants and society. This coordination is guided by Article 8 of the IOM Constitution (https://publications.iom.int/system/files/pdf/iom-constitution-3rd-en.pdf). For example, IOM works with the health sector to promote the well-being of migrants and public health (https://www.iom.int/migration-health), with the development sector to enhance the contribution of migration to sustainable development (https://www.iom.int/migration-and-development), the humanitarian sector to provide assistance and protection to migrants in crisis situations (https://www.iom.int/sites/g/files/tmzbdl486/files/migrated_files/What-We-Do/docs/Assisting-migrants-caught-in-crisis-IOM-activities-2012.pdf) or with the human rights sector to uphold the rights and dignity of migrants (https://publications.iom.int/system/files/pdf/migrants_human_rights.pdf). Horizontal coordination within IOM can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Migration Governance Framework (https://www.iom.int/sites/default/files/about-iom/migof_brochure_a4_en.pdf) or the Global Compact for Safe, Orderly and Regular Migration (https://www.iom.int/global-compact-migration), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the Global Migration Group (https://www.ohchr.org/en/migration/global-migration-group) or the Platform on Disaster Displacement (https://disasterdisplacement.org/), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for migration sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Handbook of Migration and Development (https://publications.iom.int/system/files/pdf/booklet_migration_and_development_series_1mar2018.pdf) or the Migration Crisis Operational Framework (https://www.iom.int/mcof), and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for migration issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the International Dialogue on Migration (https://www.iom.int/idm) or the World Migration Report (https://worldmigrationreport.iom.int/).

Spatial Jurisdiction: The international seabed area – the part under ISA jurisdiction – is defined as “the seabed and ocean floor and the subsoil thereof, beyond the limits of national jurisdiction.” (https://www.isa.org.jm/exploration-contracts/exploration-areas/). This includes a vast expanse of ocean space, territory and maritime zones, covering about 50 per cent of the world’s oceans (https://www.un.org/depts/los/convention_agreements/texts/unclos/part11-4.htm).
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: The ISA is responsible for administering the international seabed area. This includes organising and controlling mineral exploration and exploitation activities in the area and protecting the marine environment from any harmful effects of such activities ((https://www.un.org/depts/los/convention_agreements/texts/unclos/part11-4.htm).). The ISA also assess prospecting and exploration data and the results of marine scientific research and international cooperation in the area and ensures the equitable sharing of benefits derived from the area (https://www.isa.org.jm/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/struct-funct.pdf).
Source of Jurisdiction: ISA derives its mandate from the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), which established the ISA as an autonomous international organization. Specifically, Part XI of UNCLOS ((https://www.un.org/depts/los/convention_agreements/texts/unclos/part11-4.htm) and Annexes III (https://www.un.org/depts/los/convention_agreements/texts/unclos/annex3.htm) and IV (https://www.un.org/depts/los/convention_agreements/texts/unclos/annex4.htm) of UNCLOS provide the legal framework for the ISA’s jurisdiction over the international seabed area and its mineral resources (https://www.un.org/depts/los/convention_agreements/texts/unclos/part11-4.htm). Additionally, ISA’s jurisdiction is influenced by the Agreement relating to the Implementation of Part XI of UNCLOS (http://www2.ecolex.org/server2neu.php/libcat/docs/TRE/Full/En/TRE-001196.pdf). The Agreement, particularly Section 5 and Annexes, ooutlinesthe procedures and mechanisms for the ISA’s administration of the international seabed area and its environmental protection (http://www2.ecolex.org/server2neu.php/libcat/docs/TRE/Full/En/TRE-001196.pdf).
Defined Objectives: According to Part XI, Section 4 of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, the International Seabed Authority's objectives encompass several key functions: organizing and controlling activities in the Area, particularly with a view to administering the resources of the Area (Article 157, paragraph 1); establishing specific policies for the Authority in conformity with the Convention and the general policies established by the Assembly (Article 162, paragraph 1); adopting and applying provisionally the rules, regulations and procedures of the Authority relating to prospecting, exploration and exploitation in the Area, as well as the financial management and internal administration of the Authority (Article 162, paragraph 2 o); supervising and coordinating the implementation of the provisions of Part XI and inviting the attention of the Assembly to cases of non-compliance (Article 162, paragraph 2 a); exercising control over activities in the Area in accordance with Article 153, paragraph 4, and the rules, regulations and procedures of the Authority (Article 162, paragraph 2 l); and ensuring the equitable sharing of financial and other economic benefits derived from activities in the Area, taking into account the interests and needs of developing States and peoples who have not attained full independence or other self-governing status (Article 160, paragraph 2 f and g; Article 162, paragraph 2 g). These functions enable the Authority to fulfil its role as the organization through which States Parties shall carry out their rights and obligations under the Convention with respect to activities in the Area (https://www.un.org/depts/los/convention_agreements/texts/unclos/part11-4.htm).
Strategies: The International Seabed Authority (ISA) fulfills its objectives through diverse strategies: firstly, a five-year Strategic Plan (https://www.isa.org.jm/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Strategic_Plan_Booklet.pdf), adopted in 2018 by the ISA Assembly (https://www.isa.org.jm/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/isba24_a10-en.pdf), aligns with UNCLOS, the 1994 Agreement (https://www.un.org/depts/los/convention_agreements/texts/unclos/part11-4.htm). Additionally, a High-Level Action Plan for 2019-2023, adopted in 2019 (https://www.isa.org.jm/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/25a-15-e.pdf), outlines necessary actions to achieve the Strategic Plan's objectives, including priorities, standards and guidelines (https://www.isa.org.jm/the-mining-code/standards-and-guidelines/). The ISA also employs a data management strategy initiated in August 2016 (https://www.isa.org.jm/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/isba-22ltc-15_1.pdf), focusing on enhancing data collection, storage, analysis, and dissemination, supported by the ISA DeepData database (https://www.isa.org.jm/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/DeepData-Brochure-final.pdf), as detailed in ISBA/23/A/3. Furthermore, ISA issues 15-year contracts for mineral resource exploration in the Area to various contractors, covering polymetallic nodules, polymetallic sulphides, and cobalt-rich ferromanganese crusts (https://dsm.gsd.spc.int/public/files/Deep%20Sea%20Minerals%20in%20the%20Pacific%20Islands%20Region%20Brochure%2015%281%29.pdf), governed by ISA's rules and requiring contractors to provide data and support training for personnel from developing States (https://www.isa.org.jm/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/isba_25_c_wp1-e_0.pdf). These strategies collectively ensure effective management and sustainable utilization of seabed resources.
Inter-Institutional Relationship: The ISA cooperates with various organizations to achieve its objectives and mandates. It maintains a relationship with the United Nations (UN), as an observer to the UN General Assembly, based on an agreement in accordance with UNCLOS Article 156, paragraph 2, and the 1994 Agreement Article 169 (https://www.isa.org.jm/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/UN-ISA-Agrmnt-1.pdf). Similarly, it maintains a relationship with the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS), as the principal judicial organ for the settlement of disputes relating to the activities in the Area, based on an agreement in accordance with UNCLOS Article 187 and the 1994 Agreement Article 178, detailed in resolution 51/205. Additionally, it consults and collaborates with the relevant specialized agencies of the UN, such as the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), and the Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission (IOC), as well as other international and regional organizations, such as the International Maritime Organization (IMO), the International Hydrographic Organization (IHO), and the regional fisheries management organizations (RFMOs), on matters of common interest, in accordance with UNCLOS Article 156, paragraph 3, and the 1994 Agreement Article 170 (https://treaties.un.org/doc/publication/CTC/Ch_XXI_6_english_p.pdf). It also participates in the Informal Consultative Process (ICP) on Oceans and the Law of the Sea, providing inputs and updates on its activities, with its role recognized in resolution 54/33 (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N00/237/93/PDF/N0023793.pdf?OpenElement). Moreover, it contributes to the Regular Process for Global Reporting and Assessment of the Marine Environment, providing data and information on the environmental aspects of the activities in the Area, with its involvement encouraged in resolution 57/141 (https://www.un.org/en/development/desa/population/migration/generalassembly/docs/globalcompact/A_RES_57_141.pdf).
Vertical Coordination: Vertical coordination within ISA involves cooperation with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other specialized agencies, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and local authorities. This is based on the general legal framework established by UNCLOS and the 1994 Agreement, specifically in Articles 156-170. The ISA operates through an Assembly of all the members, a Council of 36 members, and a Secretary-General (Articles 156-166). The ISA also has three subsidiary bodies: the Legal and Technical Commission, the Finance Committee, and the Enterprise (Articles 163-170). The ISA supports members in the administration of the resources and activities in the Area, and provides training and capacity building for personnel from developing States (Articles 143-144).
Horizontal Coordination: Horizontal coordination within the ISA involves collaboration among different sectors and stakeholders involved in the exploration and exploitation of the seabed and ocean floor beyond national jurisdiction, such as States Parties, contractors, the Enterprise, the United Nations and its specialised agencies, and other international and non-governmental organizations. This coordination is structured under the General Principles section of Part XI of the UNCLOS, specifically in Articles 156-185 (https://www.un.org/Depts/los/convention_agreements/texts/unclos/part11.htm). The ISA has established three principal organs: the Assembly, the Council, and the Secretariat, as well as two subsidiary organs: the Economic Planning Commission and the Legal and Technical Commission, to carry out its functions and responsibilities under the Convention (https://www.isa.org.jm/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/struct-funct.pdf). The ISA also has an organ for carrying out activities in the Area directly: the Enterprise, and all States Parties are ipso facto members of the Authority (https://www.un.org/depts/los/convention_agreements/texts/unclos/part11-4.htm). The ISA adopts and applies rules, regulations  and procedures for the management of activities in the Area, taking into account the protection of the marine environment, the equitable sharing of benefits, and the promotion of international cooperation ((https://www.isa.org.jm/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/isba_25_c_wp1-e_0.pdf)). The ISA also establishes a system of compensation or other measures of economic adjustment assistance for developing States that may be adversely affected by activities in the Area according to article 160 (10), Part XI of UNCLOS (https://www.un.org/depts/los/convention_agreements/texts/unclos/part11-4.htm). The ISA cooperates with other relevant international organizations and facilitates the exchange of scientific and technical information on activities in the Area (https://www.isa.org.jm/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/struct-funct.pdf).

Spatial Jurisdiction: ITU's geographical area is not confined to a specific ocean or region, but rather covers the whole world. This includes coordinating the global use of the radio spectrum, satellite orbits, and telecommunication standards,  based on the international treaties and agreements that its member states have ratified, as well as the ITU Constitution and Convention (https://www.itu.int/en/council/Documents/basic-texts/Constitution-E.pdf).
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: ITU is responsible for facilitating international connectivity in communications networks, allocating global radio spectrum and satellite orbits (including assigning country codes and geographical area codes for various services, such as telephone, telex, mobile, and data), developing the technical standards that ensure networks and technologies seamlessly interconnect, and striving to improve access to ICTs to underserved communities worldwide, thereby protecting and supportinng everyone's right to communicate.​ (https://www.itu.int/en/about/Pages/default.aspx).
Source of Jurisdiction: ITU derives its mandate from the Constitution (https://www.itu.int/en/council/Documents/basic-texts/Constitution-E.pdf) and the Convention of the International Telecommunication Union, which is an international treaty signed and ratified by almost all countries of the world (https://www.itu.int/en/council/Documents/basic-texts/Convention-E.pdf). The treaty is the founding document of the ITU, a specialized agency of the United Nations (https://www.itu.int/en/council/Documents/basic-texts/Constitution-E.pdf). Specifically, Article 1 of the Constitution defines the purposes and functions of the ITU, which include maintaining and extending international cooperation among all its Member States for the improvement and rational use of telecommunications of all kinds, promoting the development and efficient operation of technical facilities, and harmonizing the actions of Member States and Sector Members (https://www.itu.int/en/history/Pages/ConstitutionAndConvention.aspx). Additionally, ITU's jurisdiction is influenced by the resolutions and decisions of the Plenipotentiary Conference (https://search.itu.int/history/HistoryDigitalCollectionDocLibrary/5.23.61.en.100.pdf), which is the supreme organ of the ITU and has the power to amend the Constitution and the Convention (Article 8 of the Constitution). ITU also adopts and supervises the Administrative Regulations, such as the Radio Regulations and the International Telecommunication Regulations, which are binding on all ITU Member States and provide the legal framework for ITU's jurisdiction over the use of the radio-frequency spectrum, satellite orbits, and international telecommunication services (Article 4 of the Constitution). Also, The ITU Constitution and Convention are complemented by the Administrative Regulations, which comprise the ITU International Telecommunication Regulations and ITU Radio Regulations, and are binding on all ITU member states as well (https://www.itu.int/en/history/Pages/RegulationsCollection.aspx#:~:text=ITU's%20Administrative%20Regulations%20contain%20provisions,operation%20of%20international%20telecommunication%20services).
Defined Objectives: ITU, per its Constitution (Chapter I, Article 1), pursues objectives to enhance telecommunication globally. These include maintaining international cooperation for telecommunication improvements (Article 1, paragraph 2 a), enhancing participation and fostering partnerships between entities and Member States (Article 1, paragraph 2 abis), offering technical assistance to developing countries and mobilizing resources for telecommunications (Article 1, paragraph 2 b), developing technical facilities for efficient telecommunication services (Article 1, paragraph 2 c), extending new telecommunication technologies worldwide (Article 1, paragraph 2 d), using telecommunications to facilitate peaceful relations (Article 1, paragraph 2 e), harmonizing Member States' actions and promoting cooperation (Article 1, paragraph 2 f), and adopting a broader approach to telecommunication issues in cooperation with other organizations (Article 1, paragraph 2 g) (https://www.itu.int/en/council/Documents/basic-texts/Constitution-E.pdf). These objectives establish ITU as the UN's specialized agency for telecommunications, contributing to global information society development.
Strategies: The ITU executes its objectives via several strategies: firstly, a four-year Strategic Plan, revised every four years by the Plenipotentiary Conference, which establishes the ITU's vision, mission, strategic goals, core functions, and targets (https://www.itu.int/en/council/Documents/basic-texts-2023/RES-071-E.pdf). This plan, applicable for 2024-2027, aligns with the Connect 2030 Agenda and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, detailed in Resolution 71 (Rev. Bucharest, 2022) (https://www.itu.int/en/mediacentre/backgrounders/Pages/connect-2030-agenda.aspx). Secondly, a biennial programme budget and operational plan, devised by the ITU Council and ratified by the Plenipotentiary Conference, detail activities, outputs, indicators, and resources corresponding to each strategic goal. The current budget and operational plan for 2022-2023 are tailored to the Member States' and Sector Members' needs and priorities, as outlined in Resolution 154 (Rev. Dubai, 2018) (https://www.itu.int/dms_pub/itu-s/md/22/cl/c/S22-CL-C-0063!!MSW-E.docx). It also maintains the databases and registries for the allocation and assignment of radio frequencies, satellite orbits, and numbering resources, which are essential for the coordination and management of the global telecommunication network (https://www.itu.int/en/ITU-R/terrestrial/Pages/by-categories-faq.aspx?subcategorizedby=6). Finally, various standards, regulations, resolutions, recommendations, and initiatives provide a technical and regulatory framework for implementing the Constitution and Convention of the ITU, addressing connectivity, digital transformation, innovation, and partnership, with key instruments listed here (https://www.itu.int/dms_pub/itu-s/opb/conf/S-CONF-ACTF-2022-PDF-E.pdf).
Inter-Institutional Relationship: ITU collaborates with various organizations to achieve its objectives. It engages with 193 Member States and over 900 Sector Members and Associates through the Plenipotentiary Conference, the supreme organ of the ITU, established by Article 8 of the Constitution of the ITU (https://www.itu.int/en/about/Pages/default.aspx). As the specialized agency of the United Nations for telecommunications, information and communication technologies, ITU's relationship with the UN is based on the Agreement between the United Nations and the International Telecommunication Union, signed in 1947 (https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/212014/files/E_RES_90%28V%29-EN.pdf?ln=en). Additionally, ITU supports the implementation of the World Summit on the Information Society (WSIS) outcomes and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, providing a platform for multi-stakeholder dialogue and action on the role of ICTs in development, as recognized by resolution 70/125 of the UN General Assembly³. It also cooperates with other UN specialized agencies, such as UNESCO, WHO, and WMO, and other organizations, such as WTO, OECD, and ICANN, addressing common ICT issues and challenges (https://www.itu.int/net/wsis/review/inc/docs/phase6/v/r/wsis10-5-3.pdf). Moreover, ITU collaborated with the WMO and UNESCO-IOCJoint on the Joint Task Force on SMART Submarine repeaters equipped with scientific sensors for climate monitoring and disaster risk reduction (tsunami warnings) (https://www.itu.int/dms_pub/itu-t/oth/0b/11/T0B110000203302PDFE.pdf).
Vertical Coordination: Vertical coordination within ITU involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other specialized agencies, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and local authorities. This is structured under the Relations with the United Nations and Other International Organizations section of the ITU Constitution, specifically in Articles 48-50 (https://www.itu.int/en/council/Documents/basic-texts/Constitution-E.pdf). The ITU operates through the Plenipotentiary Conference of all the members, the Council of 48 members, and a secretariat headed by a Secretary-General (Articles 8-10) (https://www.itu.int/en/council/Documents/basic-texts/Constitution-E.pdf). The ITU also has three Sectors: Radiocommunication, Telecommunication Standardization, and Telecommunication Development, each with its own conference, assembly, and bureau (Articles 11-13) (https://www.itu.int/en/council/Documents/basic-texts/Constitution-E.pdf). The ITU assists members in the implementation of its standards, regulations, and programmes, and provides technical cooperation and assistance upon request (Article 14) (https://www.itu.int/en/council/Documents/basic-texts/Constitution-E.pdf). ITU's work is organized around five strategic goals: Growth, Inclusiveness, Sustainability, Innovation, and Partnership, each overseen by a Deputy Secretary-General or an Assistant Secretary-General (https://sdgs.un.org/un-system-sdg-implementation/international-telecommunication-union-itu-24522). Also, a network of regional and area offices and technical specialists supports the ITU's work in promoting the Connect 2030 Agenda as an integral part of regional and global development policies, in line with ITU RES 135 (https://www.itu.int/net4/proposals/PP18/Main/GetDocument?idProposal=49237&isSub=true&codeLang=E).
Horizontal Coordination: Horizontal coordination within ITU involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the telecommunication domain, such as radiocommunication, telecommunication standardization, telecommunication development, and other related fields (https://www.itu.int/en/about/Pages/whatwedo.aspx). This coordination is structured under the Structure of the Union section of the ITU Constitution, specifically in Articles 7-24 (https://www.itu.int/en/council/Documents/basic-texts/Constitution-E.pdf). The ITU, in particular, to "maintain and extend international cooperation among all the Member States of the Union for the improvement and rational use of telecommunications of all kinds", as defined in its mission according to  Article 1 of the ITU Constitution (https://www.itu.int/en/ITU-R/information/Pages/mission-statement.aspx#:~:text=This%20mission%20lies%20within%20the,of%20telecommunications%20of%20all%20kinds%22.) The ITU also allocates radio-frequency spectrum and satellite orbits, coordinates efforts to eliminate harmful interference, fosters the development of technical facilities and services, promotes the extension of the benefits of new technologies to all the world's inhabitants, and harmonizes the actions of its members and partners in the attainment of its purposes (https://www.itu.int/dms_pub/itu-r/oth/0A/0E/R0A0E0000010001PDFE.pdf). The ITU cooperates with other international organizations and facilitates the participation of concerned entities in its activities (https://www.itu.int/en/council/Documents/basic-texts/Constitution-E.pdf).

Spatial Jurisdiction: ITC's jurisdiction is global, covering all regions and countries that are members of the World Trade Organization (WTO) or the United Nations (UN). Nevertheless, it prioritizes project implementation in Least Developed Countries, Landlocked Developing Countries, Small Island Developing States, Sub-Saharan Africa, and post conflict and fragile states, which correspond to a wide range of ocean spaces, territories and maritime zones, depending on the specific trade agreements and policies of each country (https://intracen.org/our-work/regions-and-countries). ITC does not have a fixed spatial coverage, but rather adapts to the needs and preferences of its clients and partners.
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: ITC is responsible for fostering sustainable economic development and contributing to the UN Global Goals in developing countries and countries with transition economies through trade and international business development (https://intracen.org/about-us/who-we-are). This includes enhancing the trade competitiveness of micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) in various sectors, such as agriculture, textiles, services, and e-commerce (https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/devel_e/itc_e.htm). ITC also provides trade intelligence, capacity building, advisory services, and market linkages for MSMEs, as well as collaborating with trade support institutions and policymakers (https://intracen.org/). The ITC leverages technology and innovation to make trade more inclusive, sustainable, and digital (https://intracen.org/).
Source of Jurisdiction: ITC derives its mandate from the UN General Assembly Resolution 2297 (XXII) (https://documents.un.org/doc/resolution/gen/nr0/236/32/pdf/nr023632.pdf?token=KPeCl92Q67Vpf1B3TZ&fe=true), which established The International Trade Centre as a joint subsidiary organ of the World Trade Organization (WTO) and the United Nations (UN) through the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) in accordance with the recommendations of the 1964 Global Agreement on Tariff and Trade (GATT) (https://docs.wto.org/gattdocs/q/GG/SPEC/64-151.pdf). The Resolution defined the objectives and functions of ITC and also outlined the governance and administrative arrangements. Additionally, ITC is subject to the relevant provisions of the UN Charter, the WTO Agreement, and the UNCTAD resolutions ((https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/coher_e/wto_itc_e.htm).). ITC's jurisdiction is also influenced by the decisions and recommendations of its governing bodies, such as the Joint Advisory Group (JAG), the Consultative Committee of ITC Trust Fund (CCITF), and the parent organizations (WTO and UNCTAD) (https://intracen.org/about-us/governance). These decisions and recommendations provide strategic direction and oversight the for ITC's activities and programmes, as well as resource mobilization and partnership development (https://intracen.org/file/itcstrategicplan2022-2025pdf). Furthermore, ITC's mandate is supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the Paris Agreement on Climate Change, the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, and the Aid for Trade Initiative, which provide further legal frameworks for ITC's jurisdiction over specific trade and development issues and domains (https://intracen.org/file/operationalplan2023pdf).
Defined Objectives: According to paragraph 1 of resolution 2297 (XXII) of the UN General Assembly (https://documents.un.org/doc/resolution/gen/nr0/236/32/pdf/nr023632.pdf?token=KPeCl92Q67Vpf1B3TZ&fe=true), ITC's objectives are to provide international assistance in promoting the exports of the developing countries, in accordance with several recommendations of the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTD) adopted at its first Plenary (file:///C:/Users/Abiodun/Downloads/A_RES_1897(XVIII)-EN.pdf). Specific defined objectives of the ITc include (1) To help the developing countries in marketing and promoting their exports, especially in the fields of primary commodities, manufactured goods and services; (2 To provide the developing countries with reliable and up-to-date information on market opportunities, trade policies, trade regulations, trade statistics, and other aspects of international trade; (3) To assist the developing countries in organizing and participating in trade fairs and exhibitions, both at the national and international levels, as a means of showcasing their products and establishing business contacts; and (4) To facilitate the access of the developing countries to adequate and appropriate sources of trade financing, both short-term and long-term, and to encourage the development of trade financing institutions and mechanisms in the developing countries.
Strategies: ITC executes its objectives via several strategies: firstly, a four-year Strategic Plan, revised annually by the Joint Advisory Group, establishes ITC's vision, mission, strategic goals, core services, and impact areas. This plan, applicable for 2022-2025, aligns with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and its mandates (https://intracen.org/file/itcstrategicplan2022-2025pdf). The plan also articulates ITC's vision of a world where trade builds inclusive, sustainable and prosperous economies, one where the recovery from the COVID-19 pandemic creates resilience and ensures a green transition. Secondly, an annual Operational Plan, devised by ITC and approved by the Consultative Committee of the ITC Trust Fund, details activities, outputs, indicators, and resources corresponding to each strategic objective. The current Operational Plan for 2023 is tailored to the clients' needs and partners' priorities (https://intracen.org/file/operationalplan2023pdf). It also maintains the Trade Map, a key aspect of the provision of trade intelligence to micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) (https://intracen.org/resources/tools/trade-map). The plan also specifies how ITC will assist MSMEs in creating jobs through entrepreneurship and value chain development, with a focus on women, youth, people with disabilities, and those in vulnerable situations. ITC operates on an annual budget for its work programmes, and the 2024 budget is aligned with the ITC Strategic Plan 2022-2025 and the Operational Plan 2023, which focus on the 5 'Ps' of the Global Agenda - prosperity, people, planet, peace, and partnership 9https://intracen.org/file/proposedprogrammebudgetfor2024pdf). ITC’s Regular Budget (RB) is funded in equal parts by the UN and the WTO. Its extra budgetary resources (XB) consist of pledges from donor governments, governmental organizations, other international organizations and civil society, including NGOs, the business sector and a variety of foundations. These commitments often extend over multiyear periods (https://intracen.org/about-us/funding). In addition, various agreements, mechanisms, platforms, and initiatives provide an operational framework for implementing ITC's vision, mission, and principles, addressing trade competitiveness, inclusiveness, sustainability, and digitalization (https://intracen.org/file/itcstrategicplan2022-2025pdf). Finally, ITC Annual Report offers a comprehensive review of the organization’s activities and detailed information on the results and effectiveness of its work. The latest report for 2022 (https://intracen.org/file/itcannualreport2022eng-interactive20junepdf) showcases how ITC delivered above and beyond the call of duty to set the Sustainable Development Goals back on track and help small enterprises continue finding new pathways to prosperity through trade, despite the challenges posed by the ‘four Cs’ – COVID, climate, conflict and cost-of-living. The report also presents results from the first year of ITC’s Strategic Plan 2022–2025, which pushes its value proposition further than before, laying out a bold roadmap for creating trade that is sustainable, inclusive and transformative.
Inter-Institutional Relationship: ITC works with various institutions to achieve its goals of trade promotion and development. It is a joint agency of the WTO and the UN, operating under the guidance of the UN General Assembly and the WTO General Council (https://intracen.org/about-us/who-we-are). It also cooperates with the UN Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), the UN Development Programme (UNDP), and other UN specialized agencies and programmes, as well as regional and intergovernmental organizations, to implement trade-related technical assistance and capacity-building activities (https://intracen.org/our-work/partnerships). Furthermore, ITC collaborates with the International Trade Centre Trust Fund (ITF), which is a multi-donor trust fund that supports ITC’s projects and programmes. Additionally, ITC maintains relations with other trade-related institutions, such as the Codex Alimentarius Commission, the International Labour Organization (ILO), the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO), and the World Health Organization (WHO), to address various aspects of trade and development, as well as with the private sector, Governments, civil societies and philanthropic foundations, multilateral partners, academia, training and research partners, business support organizations, and regional partners (https://intracen.org/our-work/partnerships).
Vertical Coordination: Vertical coordination within ITC involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, the World Trade Organization, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and local authorities. This is achieved through strategic supervision, strategic management, and executive management. ITC is headed by an Executive Director who reports to the Secretary-General of the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) and the Director-General of the World Trade Organization (WTO) (https://intracen.org/about-us/who-we-are/structure-and-management). The ITC operates through the Joint Advisory Group of all the members, the Consultative Committee of the ITC Trust Fund, and a secretariat headed by the Executive Director (https://intracen.org/about-us/governance). ITC also has advisory bodies, such as the Global Network of Trade Promotion Organizations and the Global Network of Trade and Investment Support Institutions (https://intracen.org/about-us/who-we-are/structure-and-management). ITC’s work is organised around four divisions, each overseen by a Director who works closely with the Executive Director to implement strategies and programmes across all levels of the Organization (https://intracen.org/about-us/who-we-are/structure-and-management). There is also the Senior Management Committee, consisting of the Executive Director, the Deputy Executive Director, the Directors of the four divisions, and the Chief of Staff, providing strategic and internal policy advice to the Executive Director on matters related to the programmatic and managerial work of ITC and ensuring coherence and alignment between the three levels of the Organization and the governing bodies (https://intracen.org/about-us/who-we-are/structure-and-management). Additionally, a network of country offices and technical experts supports ITC’s work in promoting trade and private sector development as an integral part of regional and national development policies (https://www.intracen.org/about-us/where-we-work). In addition, ITC coordinates with the United Nations and its agencies and is a partner of the Enhanced Integrated Framework, the Aid for Trade Initiative, and the Standards and Trade Development Facility (https://www.intracen.org/about-us/who-we-are/partnerships).
Horizontal Coordination: Horizontal coordination within ITC involves working with different sectors and stakeholders within the trade and development domain, such as MSMEs, BSOs, governments, civil society, private sector, academia, and other UN agencies to ensure that trade contributes to inclusive, sustainable and prosperous economies (https://intracen.org/our-work/partnerships). This coordination is currently guided by its Strategic Plan for 2022-2025 (https://intracen.org/file/itcstrategicplan2022-2025pdf). For example, ITC works with the MSME sector to improve their competitiveness and access to markets, with the BSO sector to strengthen their capacity and service delivery, with the government sector to create conducive policy and regulatory environments, and with the civil society and private sector to foster partnerships and innovation (https://intracen.org/our-work/partnerships). Horizontal coordination within ITC can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint design and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the SheTrades Initiative (https://www.shetrades.com/en) or the Trade for Sustainable Development Programme (https://intracen.org/our-work/projects/trade-for-sustainable-development-t4sd), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the UN Inter-Agency Cluster on Trade and Productive Capacity (https://unctad.org/projects/UN-Inter-agency-Cluster#:~:text=and%20Productive%20Capacity-,United%20Nations%20Inter%2DAgency%20Cluster%20on%20Trade%20and%20Productive%20Capacity,levels%20within%20the%20UN%20system.) or the Enhanced Integrated Framework (https://www.enhancedif.org/en), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for trade sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the SME Competitiveness Outlook (https://intracen.org/resources/publications/sme-competitiveness-outlook) or the Market Access Map (https://www.macmap.org/), and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for trade issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the World Export Development Forum (https://intracen.org/news-and-events/events/world-export-development-forum-wedf) or the Trade Promotion Organization Network World Conference and Awards (https://intracen.org/news-and-events/events/world-trade-promotion-organizations-conference-and-awards-wtpo2024). The ITC provides leadership and direction on matters related to trade and development, shapes the trade and MSME agenda, sets norms and standards, articulates evidence-based policy options, provides technical support to countries, and monitors and assesses trade trends (https://intracen.org/about-us/governance/corporate-documents/itc-strategic-plan).

Spatial Jurisdiction: The Minamata Convention's jurisdiction is global, covering all 147 signatory states (https://minamataconvention.org/en/about). It, however, doesn’t specify authority over ocean spaces, particular maritime zones or distances from coastlines.
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: The Minamata Convention is responsible for protecting human health and the environment from the adverse effects of mercury and mercury compounds (https://minamataconvention.org/en). This includes regulating the entire life cycle of mercury, such as its mining, trade, use, emission, release, storage, and disposal. The Minamata Convention also provides controls over a range of products and processes that contain or use mercury, and requires parties to phase down or eliminate them by 2020 or later (https://minamataconvention.org/en/about). The Minamata Convention also supports the identification and management of contaminated sites, the monitoring and assessment of mercury levels, and the provision of information and public awareness on mercury risks (https://minamataconvention.org/en/about). Furthermore, the Minamata Convention facilitates technical and financial assistance, capacity-building, and cooperation among parties and stakeholders for the effective implementation of the treaty (https://minamataconvention.org/en/about).
Source of Jurisdiction:
The Minamata Convention derives its mandate from the Minamata Convention on Mercury, which established the Convention as an international treaty to protect human health and the environment from mercury and mercury compounds (https://minamataconvention.org/sites/default/files/2021-06/Minamata-Convention-booklet-Sep2019-EN.pdf). Article 1 of the Convention defines the objective of the Convention, and Article 15 lays out the mechanism for Implementation and Compliance Committee to promote implementation 
of, and review compliance with, all provisions of the Convention. Similarly Article 23 establishes the Conference of Parties to the Convention while Article 24 outlines the functions of the Convention's Secretariat. Additionally, the Convention's articles and annexes, which were adopted by the Conference of Plenipotentiaries on 10 October 2013 (https://minamataconvention.org/sites/default/files/2021-06/Minamata-Convention-booklet-Sep2019-EN.pdf), specify the obligations and commitments of the Parties to the Convention, such as regulating the sources and trade of mercury, controlling the emissions and releases of mercury, managing the mercury waste and contaminated sites, providing information and public awareness, and facilitating technical and financial assistance and cooperation. The Convention's jurisdiction is also influenced by the decisions and resolutions adopted by its governing bodies, such as the Conference of the Parties, the Implementation and Compliance Committee, and the Secretariat (https://minamataconvention.org/en/meeting-documents?f%5B0%5D=document_type_2%3A307). These decisions and resolutions provide guidance and direction for the Convention's implementation and review, as well as cooperation and coordination with other relevant organisations and stakeholders. The Convention's mandate is also supported by the participation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the Basel Convention on the Control of Transboundary Movements of Hazardous Wastes and their Disposal (https://www.pic.int/Portals/5/download.aspx?d=UNEP-FAO-RC-CONVTEXT-2019.English.pdf), the Rotterdam Convention on the Prior Informed Consent Procedure for Certain Hazardous Chemicals and Pesticides in International Trade (https://www.pic.int/Portals/5/ConventionText/UNEP-FAO-RC-CONVTEXT-2017.English.pdf), and the Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants (https://chm.pops.int/portals/0/repository/convention_text/unep-pops-cop-convtext-full.english.pdf), which provide further legal frameworks for the Convention's jurisdiction over specific mercury-related issues and domains.
Defined Objectives: According to Article 1 of the Minamata Convention on Mercury (https://minamataconvention.org/sites/default/files/2021-06/Minamata-Convention-booklet-Sep2019-EN.pdf), the objective of the Convention is to protect the human health and the environment from anthropogenic emissions and releases of mercury and mercury compounds. This objective is supported by provisions that relate to the entire life cycle of mercury, including controls and reductions across a range of products, processes and industries where mercury is used, released or emitted, as well as measures on the direct mining, trade, storage and disposal of mercury (https://minamataconvention.org/en/about). The Convention also addresses the impacts of mercury on vulnerable populations, especially women, children and indigenous communities, and provides for financial and technical assistance to developing countries and countries with economies in transition to implement the Convention (Article 13 and 14). Furthermore, the Convention establishes a mechanism for monitoring, reporting and reviewing the implementation and effectiveness of its provisions (Article 21 and 22).
Strategies: The Minamata Convention Secretariat executes its objectives through specific strategies. Firstly, the Secreatariat develops a programme of work and budget for each biennium, which is approved by the Conference of the Parties. The programme of work and budget, applicable for 2024-2025 (https://minamataconvention.org/sites/default/files/documents/2024-01/Programme_work_budget_for_2024-2025.pdf), outlines the activities, outputs, indicators, and resources for implementing the Convention based on the needs and priorities of the Parties and other stakeholders, as reflected in COP-5 decision document (https://minamataconvention.org/sites/default/files/documents/information_document/UNEP-MC-COP.5-INF36-POWB-Fact-sheets_English.pdf). Secondly, various mechanisms and tools provide technical and financial support to the Parties, especially developing countries and countries with economies in transition, to assist them in fulfilling their obligations under the Convention. These include the Implementation and Compliance Committee (https://minamataconvention.org/en/implementation/implementation-and-compliance-committee), the Specific International Programme (https://minamataconvention.org/en/implementation/specific-international-programme), the Global Environment Facility (https://minamataconvention.org/en/implementation/gef), the Special Programme (https://minamataconvention.org/en/implementation/special-programme), the Global Mercury Partnership (https://minamataconvention.org/en/about/partners/global-mercury-partnership), and the Minamata Online platform (https://minamataconvention.org/es/node/3136). The main sources of funding for the Minamata Convention are the Global Environment Facility Trust Fund (GEF) and the Specific International Programme (SIP) to support capacity-building and technical assistance (https://minamataconvention.org/en/about/financial-mechanism). The GEF has pledged $265 million for the four-year cycle starting in July 2022 (https://www.thegef.org/newsroom/news/minamata-convention-receives-increased-funding-pledge-global-environment-facility). Finally, various partnerships, initiatives, and platforms provide a framework for cooperation and information exchange among Parties, scientific communities, civil society, and other relevant stakeholders, on issues such as mercury supply and trade, mercury-added products, mercury waste, health and environmental impacts of mercury, and mercury-free technologies and alternatives (https://minamataconvention.org/en/resources/partnerships).
Inter-Institutional Relationship: The Minamata Convention collaborates with key organizations to protect human health and the environment from the adverse effects of mercury. It enhances cross-linkages with relevant international processes and bodies, such as the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) and the World Health Organization (https://enb.iisd.org/minamata-convention-mercury-cop5-1Nov2023). The Convention also cooperates with the secretariats of the Basel, Rotterdam, and Stockholm Conventions 9https://enb.iisd.org/minamata-convention-mercury-cop5-1Nov2023). The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) provides support to conduct Minamata Initial Assessment (MIA) and develop ASGM National Action Plans (NAPs), to undertake activities to reduce emissions of mercury and mercury compounds to the atmosphere from point sources and from ASGM, and to phase out mercury-containing products in the healthcare sector 9https://www.undp.org/chemicals-waste/chemicals-and-waste/minamata-convention). These relationships enable the Convention to fulfill its role as a global legally binding instrument on mercury to address the risks to human health and the environment from mercury pollution.
Vertical Coordination: Vertical coordination within the Minamata Convention Secretariat involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), other specialized agencies, national governments, and local authorities. This is achieved through delegation of authority, directing, and controlling (https://minamataconvention.org/en/about/secretariat). The Secretariat operates under the leadership of the Executive Secretary, supported by a team of officers responsible for programme management, coordination, administration, communications, and knowledge management (https://minamataconvention.org/en/about/secretariat). The Secretariat cooperates with the secretariats of the Basel, Rotterdam, and Stockholm conventions in areas of relevance to these conventions (https://minamataconvention.org/en/documents/cooperation-and-coordination-between-secretariats-minamata-convention-mercury-and-basel). It also facilitates assistance to Parties, particularly developing country Parties and Parties with economies in transition, on request, in the implementation of the Convention (https://wedocs.unep.org/bitstream/handle/20.500.11822/43171/Minamata.pdf). The Secretariat's work is organized around key operational articles under the Minamata Convention, each overseen by a Programme Management Officer who works closely with the Executive Secretary to implement strategies and programmes across all levels of the Organization (https://minamataconvention.org/sites/default/files/documents/2021-07/Key%20control%20measures%20under%20the%20Minamata%20Convention_05%2016_EN.pdf). There is also a network of country offices and technical experts supporting the Secretariat's work in promoting health and well-being as an integral part of regional and national development policies (https://minamataconvention.org/en/about/secretariat). In addition, the Secretariat coordinates with the Global Environment Facility and the Special Programme to support capacity-building and technical assistance (https://minamataconvention.org/en/documents/international-cooperation-and-coordination).
Horizontal Coordination: Horizontal coordination within the Minamata Convention Secretariat involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the mercury domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, the scientific community, and other UN agencies to protect human health and the environment from the adverse effects of mercury. This coordination is guided by Article 24 of the Minamata Convention on Mercury (https://minamataconvention.org/sites/default/files/2021-06/Minamata-Convention-booklet-Sep2019-EN.pdf) as part of the functions of the Secretariat. For example, the Secretariat works with the health sector to support the phase-out of mercury in medical devices and dental amalgam (https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health#:~:text=A%20significant%20example%20of%20mercury,included%20high%20concentrations%20of%20methylmercury.), with the mining sector to promote the reduction and elimination of mercury use in artisanal and small-scale gold mining (https://2009-2017.state.gov/e/oes/eqt/chemicalpollution/mercury/245187.htm), with the waste sector to ensure the environmentally sound management and transportation of mercury wastes (https://minamataconvention.org/sites/default/files/documents/submission_from_government/%28JPN%29Article11.pdf), or with the trade sector to regulate the import and export of mercury and mercury compounds (https://minamataconvention.org/en/news/minamata-online-article-3-trade-mercury). Horizontal coordination within the Minamata Convention Secretariat can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Global Environment Facility (https://www.thegef.org/topics/chemicals-and-waste) or the Special Programme on Institutional Strengthening (https://www.unep.org/explore-topics/chemicals-waste/what-we-do/special-programme/goal-special-programme), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the Inter-Organization Programme for the Sound Management of Chemicals (https://partnership.who.int/iomc) or the Global Mercury Partnership (https://minamataconvention.org/en/about/partners/global-mercury-partnership#:~:text=Initiated%20in%202005%20by%20a,legally%2Dbinding%20instrument%20on%20mercury.), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for mercury sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Minamata Initial Assessments (https://minamataconvention.org/en/parties/minamata-initial-assessments) or the Mercury Inventory Toolkit (https://www.unep.org/topics/chemicals-and-pollution-action/pollution-and-health/heavy-metals/mercury/mercury-inventory), and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for mercury issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the International Conference on Mercury as a Global Pollutant (https://minamataconvention.org/en/news/icmgp-2022-reducing-mercury-emissions-achieve-greener-world) or the Minamata Online E-Learning Platform (https://minamataconvention.org/en/resources/e-learning).

Institution: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
Spatial Jurisdiction: The OECD's jurisdiction is global, encompassing the economic zones of its 38 member countries (https://www.oecd.org/newsroom/oecd-welcomes-costa-rica-as-its-38th-member.htm#:~:text=The%20OECD's%2038%20members%20are,Norway%2C%20Poland%2C%20Portugal%2C%20Slovak). The OECD does not have specific authority over maritime zones or territorial waters, but rather, its influence is primarily on key global issues at national, regional and local levels (https://www.oecd.org/about/members-and-partners/).
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: The OECD is responsible for promoting economic cooperation and development, especially among its 38 member countries (https://www.oecd.org/about/). This includes addressing economic issues, such as tax cooperation, trade, investment, and technology transfer (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%20888/volume-888-I-12736-English.pdf). The OECD also provides technical assistance, research and analysis, intergovernmental consensus-building, and policy advice for sustainable development (https://www.oecd.org/greengrowth/47445613.pdf). It supports the implementation of economic policies and the development goals of its member countries (https://www.oecd.org/general/Key-information-about-the-OECD.pdf).
Source of Jurisdiction: The OECD derives its mandate from the Convention on the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, which established OECD as an intergovernmental organisation with 38 member countries, to stimulate economic progress and world tradem (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%20888/volume-888-I-12736-English.pdf). Specifically, Article 1 of the Convention defines the aims and objectives of OECD, and Article 2 outlines the functions and activities of OECD (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%20888/volume-888-I-12736-English.pdf). Additionally, OECD’s rules of procedure, rule 18 on the functions of the OECD secretariat, states that the secretariat shall assist the Council and its subsidiary bodies in carrying out their work and shall perform any other tasks entrusted to it by the Council (https://www.oecd.org/legal/Rules%20of%20Procedure%20OECD%20Oct%202013.pdf). OECD’s jurisdiction is also influenced by the decisions, agreements, recommendations, etc adopted by its governing bodies, such as the Council, the Ministerial Council, and the committees (https://legalinstruments.oecd.org/en/). These decisions and recommendations provide guidance and direction for OECD’s work and policy advice, as well as the cooperation and coordination with other organisations and stakeholders. OECD’s mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international standards and frameworks, such as the Common Reporting Standard (https://www.oecd.org/tax/automatic-exchange/common-reporting-standard/), the Base erosion and profit shifting (BEPS) (https://www.oecd.org/tax/beps/about/), which provide further legal and technical frameworks for the OECD.
Defined Objectives: According to Article 1 of the Convention on the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, the OECD's objectives encompass several key aims: achieving the highest sustainable economic growth and employment and a rising standard of living in member countries, while maintaining financial stability, and thus contributing to the development of the world economy (Article 1 a); contributing to sound economic expansion in member as well as non-member countries in the process of economic development (Article 1 b); and contributing to the expansion of world trade on a multilateral, non-discriminatory basis in accordance with international obligations (Article 1 c) (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%20888/volume-888-I-12736-English.pdf). These aims enable the OECD to fulfil its role as an intergovernmental organisation that works to build better policies for better lives, providing a platform to compare policy experiences, seek answers to common problems, identify good practices, and coordinate domestic and international policies of its members (https://www.oecd.org/about/).
Strategies: The OECD executes its objectives through multiple strategies, aligning with its mission to foster global development. The OECD Action Plan on the Sustainable Development Goals adopted by the Council of Minster outlines how the OECD supports the 2030 Agenda, highlighting key areas like tracking SDG progress, policy analysis and advice, global dialogue, and internal sustainability practices (https://www.oecd.org/belgium/50452316.pdf). Also, the OECD Biannual Strategic Orientations of the Secretary-General present the organization's vision and mission, guiding its work programme and activities, reflecting challenges like the COVID-19 pandemic, digital transformation, green transition, inclusiveness in globalization, and multilateralism, which the current document runing from 2023 to 2024 (https://www.oecd.org/mcm/2022-OECD-SG-Strategic-Orientations-EN.pdf). Furthermore, the OECD's result based budget and programme of work, determined biennially by member countries, detail strategic objectives, expected results, and resource allocation for work areas, aligned with the Secretary-General's Strategic Orientations (https://www.oecd.org/general/frequentlyaskedquestionsfaq.htm). Strategic Foresight Unit for structured future planning, using tools like scenarios and visioning to prepare for change (https://www.oecd.org/strategic-foresight/about-us/). The OECD develops strategic plans for different domains such as skills (https://www.oecd.org/skills/oecd-skills-strategies.htm), energy (https://www.oecd-nea.org/upload/docs/application/pdf/2022-01/nea_strategic_plan_2023-2028.pdf), etc. These comprehensive strategies enable the OECD to deliver effective policies and foster global development
Inter-Institutional Relationship: OECD collaborates with various organizations to promote economic co-operation and development. It maintains relations with the European Communities, established by the Treaties of Paris and Rome of 18th April, 1951, and 25th March, 1957, as defined in Supplementary Protocol No. 1 to the Convention on the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD Convention), article 13 (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%20888/volume-888-I-12736-English.pdf). It also enters into agreements with Members, non-member States and international organizations, as provided for in OECD Convention, article 5 (c) (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%20888/volume-888-I-12736-English.pdf). Additionally, OECD participates in the activities of other international organizations or institutions, such as the UN, the World Bank, the IMF, and the WTO, in a manner consistent with its obligations, as stated in OECD Convention, article 1 (c) (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%20888/volume-888-I-12736-English.pdf). It also contributes to the economic development of both Member and non-member countries in the process of economic development, by appropriate means and, in particular, by the flow of capital to those countries, as agreed in OECD Convention, article 2 (e) (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%20888/volume-888-I-12736-English.pdf). Moreover, OECD supports the further expansion of world trade on a multilateral, non-discriminatory basis, as one of the most important factors favouring the economic development of countries and the improvement of international economic relations, as affirmed in OECD Convention, article 1 (c) (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%20888/volume-888-I-12736-English.pdf).
Vertical Coordination: Vertical coordination connected to the OECD involves downward coordination into subsidiary bodies of OECD and receipt of governance input from member states. This is achieved through reporting, cooperation, and assistance (https://www.oecd.org/effective-public-investment-toolkit/Improving-coordination.pdf). This is structured under the Relations with the European Communities and Agreements with Members, non-member States and international organisations sections of the OECD Convention, specifically in Articles 13-15 (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%20888/volume-888-I-12736-English.pdf). The OECD operates through the Council of all the members, the Ministerial Council of ministers from member countries and the European Union, and a secretariat headed by a Secretary-General (Articles 3-8) (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%20888/volume-888-I-12736-English.pdf).
