The OECD also has committees, working parties, and other subsidiary bodies (Article 9) (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%20888/volume-888-I-12736-English.pdf). The OECD assists members and non-members in the implementation of its standards, policies, and programmes, and provides policy analysis and advice upon request (Article 2) (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%20888/volume-888-I-12736-English.pdf). The OECD's work is organised around 14 major substantive directorates, each overseen by Directors who works closely with the Secretary-General to implement strategies and programmes across all levels of the Organisation (https://www.oecd.org/about/document/list-of-departments-and-special-bodies.htm). There is also the Senior Management Team (consisting of the Secretary-General and Deputy Secretaries-General) providing strategic and operational guidance to the Secretary-General on matters related to the programmatic and managerial work of the OECD; and ensuring coherence and alignment between the different directorates and divisions of the Organisation and the governing bodies (https://www.oecd.org/about/document/list-of-departments-and-special-bodies.htm). Moreover, the OECD operates various centres, networks, and initiatives that facilitate dialogue, knowledge sharing, and policy innovation among its members and partners, such as the Development Centre (https://www.oecd.org/dev/), the Centre for Entrepreneurship, SMEs, Regions and Cities (https://www.oecd.org/cfe/), the Global Relations Secretariat (https://www.oecd.org/global-relations/), the Sahel and West Africa Club Secretariat (https://www.oecd.org/swac/), the OECD Eurasia Competitiveness Platform (https://www.oecd.org/eurasia/), the OECD Latin America and the Caribbean Regional Programme (https://www.oecd.org/latin-america/regional-programme/), the OECD Southeast Asia Regional Programme (https://www.oecd.org/southeast-asia/regional-programme/), the OECD Korea Policy Centre, the OECD Tokyo Centre, the OECD Mexico Centre for Latin America, the OECD Istanbul Centre, the OECD Brazil Centre, the OECD China Centre, the OECD India Centre, the OECD Eurasia Centre (https://www.oecd.org/general/oecdcentres.htm), the OECD Global Forum on Transparency and Exchange of Information for Tax Purposes (https://www.oecd.org/tax/transparency/), the OECD International Network on Financial Education (https://www.oecd.org/financial/education/oecd-international-network-on-financial-education.htm), the OECD International Transport Forum (https://www.itf-oecd.org/), and the OECD Nuclear Energy Agency (https://www.oecd-nea.org/), the OECD Partnership in Statistics for Development in the 21st Century (https://www.oecd-ilibrary.org/docserver/078f091a-en.pdf?expires=1704549733&id=id&accname=guest&checksum=1A5600A8424B7AA33B844179E9EE8441).
Horizontal Coordination: Horizontal coordination within the OECD involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the economic and social domains, such as governments, civil society, private sector, academic community, and other international organisations to ensure that economic co-operation and development are considered in all policies and that OECD policies are aligned with other sectoral policies (https://www.oecd.org/about/). This coordination is guided by Article 2 of the Convention on the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%20888/volume-888-I-12736-English.pdf). For example, the OECD works with the education sector to improve learning outcomes and skills development (https://www.oecd.org/education/), with the transport sector to enhance mobility and environmental performance (https://www.oecd.org/transport/), or with the ocean sector to promote sustainable management and use of marine resources (https://www.oecd.org/ocean/OECD-work-in-support-of-a-sustainable-ocean.pdf). Horizontal coordination within the OECD can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the OECD Action Plan on the Sustainable Development Goals (https://www.oecd.org/dac/Better%20Policies%20for%202030.pdf) or the OECD/G20 Base Erosion and Profit Shifting Project (https://www.oecd.org/tax/beps/), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the OECD Development Assistance Committee (https://www.oecd.org/dac/development-assistance-committee/) or the OECD Global Forum on Transparency and Exchange of Information for Tax Purposes (https://www.oecd.org/tax/transparency/), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for OECD sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the OECD Principles on Artificial Intelligence (https://legalinstruments.oecd.org/en/instruments/OECD-LEGAL-0449) or the OECD Due Diligence Guidance for Responsible Business Conduct (https://www.oecd.org/investment/due-diligence-guidance-for-responsible-business-conduct.htm), (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for economic co-operation and development issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the OECD Forum (https://www.oecd.org/forum/) or the OECD Economic Outlook (https://www.oecd-ilibrary.org/economics/oecd-economic-outlook_16097408). The OECD provides policy analysis and advice, based on its multidisciplinary expertise, peer learning and dialogue, and policy coherence for sustainable development (https://www.oecd.org/about/how-we-work/).

Spatial Jurisdiction: The Ramsar Secretariat's jurisdiction is based on the Convention on Wetlands, which applies to all wetlands within the territories of its 163 Contracting Parties (https://www.ramsar.org/about/bodies/secretariat), and includes a wide variety of habitats such as marshes, peatlands, floodplains, rivers and lakes, and coastal areas such as saltmarshes, mangroves, and seagrass beds, but also coral reefs and other marine areas no deeper than six metres at low tide, as well as human-made wetlands such as waste-water treatment ponds and reservoirs (https://leap.unep.org/sites/default/files/2020-09/manual6-2013-e.pdf). The Secretariat has authority over the conservation and wise use of these wetlands, as well as their designation for inclusion in the Ramsar List of Wetlands of International Importance (https://leap.unep.org/sites/default/files/2020-09/manual6-2013-e.pdf). The Secretariat does not have jurisdiction over the entire ocean space or maritime zones of its Contracting Parties, but only over the wetlands that fall within the definition of the Convention.
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: The Ramsar Secretariat is responsible for coordinating the implementation of the Convention on Wetlands, which aims to conserve and wisely use all wetlands within the territories of its 163 Contracting Parties (https://www.ramsar.org/about/bodies/secretariat). The Convention covers all aspects of wetland conservation and wise use, such as maintaining the ecological character of wetlands, promoting their sustainable use, enhancing their biodiversity, and ensuring their resilience to climate change (https://www.ramsar.org/sites/default/files/documents/library/manual6-2013-e.pdf). The Convention also identifies wetlands of international importance, especially those providing waterfowl habitat, and encourages international cooperation and information exchange on wetland issues (https://www.ramsar.org/sites/default/files/documents/pdf/lib/hbk4-17.pdf). The Secretariat provides administrative, scientific, and technical support to Contracting Parties, as well as funding programmes for wetland conservation and management projects, focusing on a wide variety of wetland habitats, such as marshes, peatlands, rivers, lakes, coastal and marine areas, and human-made wetlands (https://www.ramsar.org/about/bodies/secretariat).
Source of Jurisdiction: The Ramsar Secretariat derives its mandate from the Convention on Wetlands of International Importance especially as Waterfowl Habitat, also known as the Ramsar Convention, which was signed in Ramsar, Iran, in 1971, entered into force in 1975, and ammended in 1994 (https://www.ramsar.org/sites/default/files/documents/library/current_convention_text_e.pdf). Specifically, Article 8 of the Convention assigned bureau duties to the International Union for the Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources as a body to carry out the day-to-day coordination of the Convention's activities, as detailed in Paragraph 2 of article 8. Additionally, Rule 27 of the Convention's Rules of Procedure (https://www.ramsar.org/sites/default/files/documents/library/ramsar_rules_of_procedure_e_0.pdf) defines the functions of the Secretariat, which include performing all other work that the Conference of the Parties requires and directs (Rule 27 g), and Rule 26 states the duties of the Secretary General. The Secretariat's jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by the COP, the Standing Committee, and the STRP, which provide guidance and direction for the Secretariat's work, as well as cooperation and coordination with other conventions, intergovernmental institutions, and national and international NGOs (https://www.ramsar.org/sites/default/files/2023-07/list_resolutions_recommendations_e_1.pdf). The Secretariat's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the Convention on Biological Diversity, the Convention on Migratory Species, the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, and the UN Convention to Combat Desertification, which provide further legal frameworks for the Secretariat's jurisdiction over specific wetland-related issues and domains (https://www.ramsar.org/about/partnerships/partnerships-other-conventions).
Defined Objectives: According to the Ramsar Convention (https://www.ramsar.org/sites/default/files/documents/library/current_convention_text_e.pdf), Ramsar Secretariat’s objectives include the following key aspects: promoting the conservation and sustainable use of wetlands, recognizing their ecological, economic, cultural, and recreational value (Preamble; Article 3, paragraph 1); encouraging countries to identify and designate Wetlands of International Importance, which represent the best examples of wetland ecosystems of global significance (Article 2, paragraph 2); promoting international cooperation on wetland conservation and management, recognizing that the conservation of wetlands and their resources is a global concern that requires coordinated efforts (Article 5); equiring regular monitoring and reporting on the status of wetlands and their resources, the measures taken for their conservation and sustainable use, and the effectiveness of these measures (Article 3, paragraph 2; Article 6, paragraph 2 e); and promoting public awareness and education on the importance of wetlands and their conservation, recognizing that public support and involvement are essential for the success of wetland conservation efforts (Article 4, paragraph 3).
Strategies: The Ramsar Secretariat executes its defined objectives following certain strategies, including its fourth strategic plan which spans from 2016-2024 (https://www.ramsar.org/sites/default/files/documents/library/4th_strategic_plan_2022_update_e.pdf). This plan has three strategic goals: 1) address the drivers of wetland loss and degradation; 2) effectively conserve and manage the Ramsar Site Network; and 3) wisely use all wetlands. The Secretariat also has a Workplan that is structured around the seven core functions of the Secretariat and sets out principal activities and corresponding annual and triennial indicators for each, together with indicative lead responsibilities and principal funding source. The most recent Workplan is applicable for 2023-2025 (https://www.ramsar.org/sites/default/files/2023-09/secretariat_workplan_2023_2025_e.pdf). Ramsar Secretariat's core funding is based on contributions from Contracting Parties to the Convention 9https://www.ramsar.org/about/bodies/secretariat). The Secretariat also prepares an annual core budget which is approved by the Conference of the Contracting Parties. The core budget for 2022 was presented in Annex 1 of Resolution ExCOP3.2 (https://www.ramsar.org/sites/default/files/documents/library/excop3_2_financial_budgetary_matters_e.pdf). Finally, the Secretariat develops cooperation with other conventions, intergovernmental institutions, and national and international NGOs (https://www.ramsar.org/about/partnerships). It also organizes Ramsar Advisory Missions at the request of Contracting Parties and contributes to the follow-up of RAM reports (https://www.ramsar.org/our-work/activities/ramsar-advisory-missions). These strategies and mechanisms provide an operational framework for implementing the Convention's mission of conservation and wise use of all wetlands through local and national actions and international cooperation.
Inter-Institutional Relationship: The Ramsar Secretariat collaborates with various institutions to achieve its objectives. It is based at the headquarters of the International Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN) in Gland, Switzerland (https://www.ramsar.org/about/bodies/secretariat). The Secretariat develops cooperation with other conventions, intergovernmental institutions, and national and international NGOs (https://www.ramsar.org/about/partnerships) . It also works to strengthen collaboration with the World Bank and UN agencies, particularly UNEP, UNDP, FAO, WHO, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), and the Intergovernmental Science Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES). This collaboration is detailed in the draft resolution on enhancing the Convention's visibility (Ramsar COP14 Doc.18.8 Rev.2) (https://www.ramsar.org/sites/default/files/documents/library/cop14_18_8_rev2_dr_synergies_e.pdf). Furthermore, the Secretariat has interface procedures with the Joint Environment Unit (JEU) of the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) and the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) (https://www.ramsar.org/document/interface-procedures-between-ramsar-secretariat-joint-environment-unit-jeu-un-office).
Vertical Coordination: Vertical coordination within Ramsar Secretariat involves working with the International Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN), the Conference of the Contracting Parties (COP), the Standing Committee, the Scientific and Technical Review Panel (STRP), and the Contracting Parties to the Convention. This is achieved through organizing, supporting, and implementing the decisions and resolutions of the Convention's governing bodies. This is structured under the Secretariat section of the Convention text, specifically in Articles 8 and 9 (https://www.ramsar.org/sites/default/files/documents/library/current_convention_text_e.pdf). The Ramsar Secretariat is based at the headquarters of the IUCN in Gland, Switzerland, and follows IUCN procedures and policies on staffing and recruitment (https://www.ramsar.org/about/bodies/secretariat). The Secretariat is headed by a Secretary General, who is appointed by the Standing Committee with the approval of the COP, and reports to the Standing Committee. The Secretariat also consists of a Deputy Secretary General, a Senior Advisor on Environment and Development, and other staff members organized into five teams: Administrative and Financial Management, Communications, Convention and Policy Support, Regional Affairs, and Scientific and Technical Support (https://www.ramsar.org/sites/default/files/documents/library/hr_org_chart_20230601.pdf). The Secretariat's main functions are to maintain the List of Wetlands of International Importance, help convene and organize the meetings of the COP, the Standing Committee, and the STRP, provide administrative and communications support to the STRP, provide administrative, scientific, and technical support to Contracting Parties, organize Ramsar Advisory Missions, develop cooperation with other conventions and institutions, and administer funding programmes (https://www.ramsar.org/about/bodies/secretariat). The Secretariat also works closely with the six International Organization Partners of the Convention: BirdLife International, International Water Management Institute, IUCN, Wetlands International, WWF International, and Wildfowl & Wetlands Trust (https://www.ramsar.org/about/partnerships/international-organization-partners).
Horizontal Coordination: Horizontal coordination within the Ramsar Secretariat involves working with different partners and actors within the wetland domain, such as other global and regional conventions and agencies, national and local governments, civil society, private sector, and scientific and academic institutions to ensure that wetlands are conserved, wisely used, restored and valued by all. This coordination is supported by the Convention’s Strategic Plan 2016-2024 (https://www.ramsar.org/sites/default/files/documents/library/4th_strategic_plan_2016_2024_e.pdf). For example, the Ramsar Secretariat works with the biodiversity sector to support the implementation of other biodiversity-related conventions, such as the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) or the Convention on Migratory Species (CMS), with the water sector to promote the integration of wetlands into water resources management, such as the Integrated Water Resources Management (IWRM) or the Water Framework Directive (WFD), with the climate change sector to enhance the role of wetlands in climate change mitigation and adaptation, such as the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) or the Paris Agreement, or with the disaster risk reduction sector to highlight the importance of wetlands in reducing disaster risks, such as the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction or the Hyogo Framework for Action (https://www.ramsar.org/about/partnerships/partnerships-other-conventions). Horizontal coordination within the Ramsar Secretariat can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other partners and actors, such as the Ramsar Regional Initiatives (https://www.ramsar.org/activity/ramsar-regional-initiatives) or the Wetlands for the Future Fund (https://www.ramsar.org/wetlands-future), (2) Participation in intergovernmental and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the Biodiversity Liaison Group (https://www.cbd.int/blg/) or the Global Partnership for Plant Conservation (https://www.plants2020.net/), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for wetland sector engagement with other partners and actors, such as the Ramsar Handbooks (https://www.ramsar.org/sites/default/files/documents/pdf/lib/hbk4-18.pdf) or the Ramsar Advisory Missions (https://www.ramsar.org/activity/ramsar-advisory-missions), and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for wetland issues and policies among other partners and actors, such as the World Wetlands Day (https://www.worldwetlandsday.org/) or the Ramsar Awards (https://www.ramsar.org/our-work/activities/ramsar-awards).

Institution: Secretariat of the Basel, Rotterdam and Stockholm Conventions (BRS)
Spatial Jurisdiction: The BRS Secretariat's jurisdiction is global, covering all parties to the Basel, Rotterdam and Stockholm conventions (https://www.brsmeas.org/Decisionmaking/Overview/AboutSynergies/tabid/2614/language/en-US/Default.aspx). This includes all ocean space, territory and maritime zones of the parties, as well as areas beyond national jurisdiction where the conventions apply, such as the high seas and the Antarctic . BRS Secretariat does not have a specific distance limit within its jurisdiction, but rather follows the principles and rules of international law and the conventions themselves.
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: The BRS Secretariat is responsible for facilitating the implementation of the Basel, Rotterdam and Stockholm conventions, which aim to protect human health and the environment from hazardous chemicals and wastes (https://www.un.org/depts/los//general_assembly/contributions_2020/SecretariatBRS.pdf). This includes providing administrative, technical and legal support to the parties and their subsidiary bodies, as well as receiving and conveying information from and to the parties. The BRS Secretariat also coordinates with other international bodies and stakeholders, and delivers capacity-building, awareness-raising and outreach activities for the sound management of chemicals and wastes, in line with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. The BRS Secretariat contributes to the protection of the marine environment and the law of the sea by preventing and combating illegal traffic in hazardous wastes and other wastes, including through transboundary movements at sea. The Secretariat also supports the parties in reducing direct discharge or land runoff of hazardous pollutants or wastes into the marine and coastal environments, which can harm marine biodiversity and ecosystems (https://www.un.org/depts/los//general_assembly/contributions_2020/SecretariatBRS.pdf). The BRS Secretariat works closely with other relevant UN agencies, such as the International Maritime Organization and the Division for Ocean Affairs and the Law of the Sea, to ensure coherence and synergies in addressing these issues (https://www.un.org/depts/los/general_assembly/contributions_2014_2/BRS_Conventions.pdf).
Source of Jurisdiction: The BRS Secretariat derives its mandate from the Basel, Rotterdam and Stockholm conventions, which established the BRS Secretariat as a joint secretariat serving the three conventions (https://www.brsmeas.org/Secretariat/Overview/tabid/3609/language/en-US/Default.aspx). Specifically, Article 16 of the Basel Convention (https://www.basel.int/Portals/4/Basel%20Convention/docs/text/BaselConventionText-e.pdf), Article 19 of the Rotterdam Convention (https://www.pic.int/Portals/5/ConventionText/UNEP-FAO-RC-CONVTEXT-2017.English.pdf) and Article 20 of the Stockholm Convention (https://chm.pops.int/portals/0/repository/convention_text/unep-pops-cop-convtext-full.english.pdf) define the functions and responsibilities of the BRS Secretariat, which include providing administrative, technical and legal support to the parties and their subsidiary bodies, as well as receiving and conveying information from and to the parties. Additionally, the memoranda of understanding between the conferences of the parties and the entities administering the secretariats of the conventions, namely the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) and the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) (https://www.pic.int/Portals/5/download.aspx?d=UNEP-FAO-RC-COP.9-RC-9-14.En.pdf), clarify the institutional relationship between the parties and UNEP/FAO, including the delegation of authority, financial matters, reporting and programmatic cooperation. The BRS Secretariat's jurisdiction is also influenced by the decisions and resolutions adopted by the conferences of the parties and their subsidiary bodies, such as the Conference of the Parties serving as the meeting of the Parties to the Basel Convention, the Conference of the Parties to the Rotterdam Convention, and the Conference of the Parties to the Stockholm Convention (https://www.brsmeas.org/Secretariat/Overview/History/tabid/2690/language/en-US/Default.aspx). These decisions and resolutions provide guidance and direction for the BRS Secretariat's activities and programmes, as well as cooperation and coordination with other international bodies and stakeholders. The BRS Secretariat's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://www.brsmeas.org/Implementation/ProgrammeofWork/SustainableDevelopmentGoals/Overview/tabid/8490/language/en-US/Default.aspx), the Minamata Convention on Mercury (https://www.brsmeas.org/Partners/MEAs/MinamataConvention/tabid/4083/language/en-US/Default.aspx), and the Strategic Approach to International Chemicals Management (SAICM (https://www.brsmeas.org/Partners/UNEP/SAICM/tabid/4073/language/en-US/Default.aspx), which provide further legal frameworks for the BRS Secretariat's jurisdiction over specific issues and domains related to the sound management of chemicals and wastes.
Defined Objectives: The BRS Secretariat's objectives encompass several key tasks: (1) Mobilizing resources and support for the implementation of the BRS Conventions programmes of work, including from the private sector and other relevant stakeholders, (2) Strengthening relationship and cooperation with other international bodies and the UN system on the sound management of hazardous chemicals and wastes, within the context of the global development agenda, (3) Enhancing science-based action and information sharing in the implementation of the BRS Conventions at the global, regional and national levels, (4) Developing and managing the technical assistance programme for the conventions, based on the needs assessment and capacity-building activities of the Parties, (5) Managing the development of technical documents, including guidelines and guidance, and facilitating the work of the scientific and technical subsidiary bodies of the conventions, and (6) Managing and coordinating the meetings of the conferences of the Parties and their subsidiary bodies, and providing legal and governance support, including on compliance, strategic issues and partnerships (https://www.brsmeas.org/Secretariat/Vision/Vision201819/tabid/7862/language/en-US/Default.aspx).
Strategies: The Secretariats of the Basel and Stockholm conventions (BRS) execute their objectives via several strategies: Firstly, as laid out in Article 16 of the Basel Convention (https://www.basel.int/Portals/4/Basel%20Convention/docs/text/BaselConventionText-e.pdf), Article 19 of the Rotterdam Convention (https://www.pic.int/Portals/5/ConventionText/UNEP-FAO-RC-CONVTEXT-2017.English.pdf) and Article 20 of the Stockholm Convention (https://chm.pops.int/portals/0/repository/convention_text/unep-pops-cop-convtext-full.english.pdf), The budget of the Secretariats and their staffing are determined by the conferences of the parties and are funded by contributions from parties, based on the United Nations scale of assessment (https://www.brsmeas.org/Secretariat/Overview/tabid/3609/language/en-US/Default.aspx). The Secretariat also develop biennium work plans for how to implement the programmes of work of the Basel, Rotterdam, and Stockholm conventions. The work plans for the biennium 2024-2025 (https://www.brsmeas.org/Portals/4/download.aspx?d=UNEP-FAO-CHW-RC-POPS-MNGMT-REP-BRSWorkplan-2024-2025.English.xlsx) include 36 programme of work activities. In addition various agreements, mechanisms, platforms, and initiatives provide an operational framework for implementing the Conventions. The strategies that the BRS secretariat use to achieve its objectives and mandates include (1) Establishing and facilitating the work of small intersessional working groups, expert working groups, and project groups, composed of representatives of Parties and observers, to carry out the activities under the work programmes, (2) Providing information, best practices, lessons learned, and recommendations on various aspects of the environmentally sound management of hazardous wastes and other wastes, through the development and dissemination of briefs, reports, and other materials, (3) Organizing and conducting capacity-building activities, such as regional workshops, webinars, and online courses, to assist Parties and other stakeholders in implementing the provisions and obligations of the Convention, and (4) Strengthening the communication and outreach with potential partners and other initiatives, such as the regional centres, other multilateral environmental agreements, and relevant organizations and networks, to promote information sharing and collaboration on hazardous chemicals and wastes issues (https://www.brsmeas.org/Portals/4/download.aspx?d=UNEP-CHW.16-INF-46-Rev.1.English.pdf).
Inter-Institutional Relationship: The BRS Secretariat cooperates with key entities to support the sound management of chemicals and waste. It is administered by the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) and the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), as per Article 16 of the Basel Convention (https://www.basel.int/Portals/4/Basel%20Convention/docs/text/BaselConventionText-e.pdf), Article 19 of the Rotterdam Convention (https://www.pic.int/Portals/5/ConventionText/UNEP-FAO-RC-CONVTEXT-2017.English.pdf) and Article 20 of the Stockholm Convention (https://chm.pops.int/portals/0/repository/convention_text/unep-pops-cop-convtext-full.english.pdf). It also implements memoranda of understanding with UNEP and FAO, clarifying the institutional relationship and responsibilities of the entities (https://www.brsmeas.org/Partners2/CooperationWithPartners/tabid/2841/language/en-US/Default.aspx). Furthermore, the BRS Secretariat coordinates with other international bodies, such as the Strategic Approach to International Chemicals Management (SAICM), the Minamata Convention on Mercury, the Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer, and the World Health Organization (WHO), to promote synergies and avoid duplication of efforts (https://www.brsmeas.org/Partners/MEAs/MinamataConvention/tabid/4083/language/en-US/Default.aspx). It also engages with various stakeholders, such as industry, civil society, academia and media, to raise awareness and mobilize resources for the implementation of the conventions (https://www.brsmeas.org/Partners2/CooperationWithPartners/tabid/2841/language/en-US/Default.aspx). It also coordinates with the International Seabed Authority (ISA), the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS), the Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf (CLCS), the Informal Consultative Process (ICP) on Oceans and the Law of the Sea, and the Regular Process for Global Reporting and Assessment of the Marine Environment (https://www.brsmeas.org/Implementation/TechnicalAssistance/Partnerships/tabid/4900/language/en-US/Default.aspx). Furthermore, the BRS Secretariat engages with stakeholders, such as regional centres, non-governmental organizations, industry associations, and scientific institutions, to provide technical assistance, capacity building, and information exchange (https://www.brsmeas.org/Partners2/CooperationWithPartners/tabid/2841/language/en-US/Default.aspx).
Vertical Coordination:
Vertical coordination within BRS Secretariat involves cooperation with higher and lower level institutions, such as UNEP, the FAO, the conferences of the parties (COPs) and the subsidiary bodies of the three conventions, as well as the national focal points and regional centres of the parties. This is achieved through memoranda of understanding, reporting, and programmatic collaboration. The BRS Secretariat operates under the guidance of the COPs and their subsidiary bodies, such as the Chemical Review Committee (CRC) and the Persistent Organic Pollutants Review Committee (POPRC), and provides administrative and technical support to them (https://www.brsmeas.org/Secretariat/Overview/tabid/3609/language/en-US/Default.aspx). The BRS Secretariat is headed by an Executive Secretary, who is assisted by two Deputy Executive Secretaries, one for the Basel and Stockholm conventions and one for the Rotterdam Convention (https://www.brsmeas.org/Secretariat/Structure/OurTeam/tabid/2641/language/en-US/Default.aspx). The BRS Secretariat also has a matrix structure with four units: the Legal and Policy Unit, the Policy and Strategy Unit, the Programme Resources and Oversight Unit, and the Technical Assistance Unit (https://www.brsmeas.org/Secretariat/Structure/OurTeam/tabid/2641/language/en-US/Default.aspx). The BRS Secretariat assists parties in the implementation of the conventions, provides information and guidance, facilitates technical assistance and capacity building, and coordinates with other international bodies. The BRS Secretariat works closely with the UNEP and FAO, which jointly serve the Rotterdam Convention Secretariat, and reports to the UNEP Executive Director and FAO Director General on administrative and financial matters (https://www.brsmeas.org/Secretariat/Overview/tabid/3609/language/en-US/Default.aspx). The BRS Secretariat also cooperates with the regional offices of UNEP and FAO, as well as the regional centres designated under the Basel and Stockholm conventions, to deliver regional and national activities and services. There is also the Environmental Network for Optimizing Regulatory Compliance on Illegal Traffic (ENFORCE), which is a network of experts and practitioners that aims to enhance the implementation and enforcement of the Basel Convention and prevent and combat illegal traffic and trade in hazardous wastes (https://www.basel.int/Implementation/TechnicalAssistance/Partnerships/ENFORCE/Overview/tabid/4526/Default.aspx). Additionally, the BRS Secretariat engages with other relevant stakeholders, such as civil society, industry, academia, and media, to raise awareness and promote the sound management of chemicals and waste.

Horizontal Coordination:
Horizontal coordination within BRS Secretariat involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the chemicals and waste domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, the scientific community, and other UN agencies to ensure that the sound management of chemicals and waste is achieved and that human health and the environment are protected from their adverse effects. This coordination is guided by the preambles and the objectives of the Basel, Rotterdam and Stockholm conventions (https://www.brsmeas.org/Secretariat/Overview/tabid/3609/language/en-US/Default.aspx). For example, the BRS Secretariat works with the health sector to prevent and reduce the exposure to hazardous chemicals and waste (such as mercury, lead, asbestos, and pesticides) and to promote the implementation of the health-related provisions of the conventions (https://www.brsmeas.org/Secretariat/Vision/Vision201819/tabid/7862/language/en-US/Default.aspx), with the agriculture sector to support the environmentally sound management of pesticides and other chemicals used in agriculture and to promote alternatives to hazardous pesticides (https://www.brsmeas.org/Implementation/ProgrammeofWork/SustainableDevelopmentGoals/Overview/tabid/8490/language/en-US/Default.aspx), the trade sector to facilitate the exchange of information and the prior informed consent procedure for certain hazardous chemicals and waste in international trade or with the climate change sector to address the linkages between chemicals (https://www.brsmeas.org/Implementation/ProgrammeofWork/SustainableDevelopmentGoals/Overview/tabid/8490/language/en-US/Default.aspx), waste and climate change and to promote low-carbon and circular economy approaches (https://www.brsmeas.org/Implementation/ProgrammeofWork/SustainableDevelopmentGoals/Overview/tabid/8490/language/en-US/Default.aspx). Horizontal coordination within BRS Secretariat can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Special Programme on Institutional Strengthening for Chemicals and Waste Management or the Global Environment Facility (GEF) projects on persistent organic pollutants (POPs), mercury and integrated chemicals and waste management (https://www.brsmeas.org/Decisionmaking/COPsandExCOPs/20212022COPs/MeetingDocuments/tabid/8810/ctl/Download/mid/24689/language/en-GB/Default.aspx?id=111&ObjID=29473), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the Inter-Organization Programme for the Sound Management of Chemicals (IOMC) (https://www.brsmeas.org/Partners/IGOs/IOMC/tabid/4094/language/en-US/Default.aspx) or the Environmental Network for Optimizing Regulatory Compliance on Illegal Traffic (ENFORCE) (https://www.basel.int/Implementation/LegalMatters/IllegalTraffic/Meetings/ENFORCE8Brussels2024/tabid/9702/Default.aspx), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for chemicals and waste sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the technical guidelines for the environmentally sound management of waste or the guidance on best available techniques and best environmental practices for POPs 9https://www.brsmeas.org/Resources/Shared/scripts/appPubKit/docs/06a-StockholmConvention-GuidelinesBATBEP.English.pdf), (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for chemicals and waste issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Triple COPs (https://enb.iisd.org/basel-rotterdam-stockholm-conventions-brs-cops-2023) or the online briefings and webinars. The BRS Secretariat provides leadership and direction on matters related to chemicals and waste management, shapes the policy agenda, sets norms and standards, articulates evidence-based policy options, provides technical support to parties, and monitors and assesses chemicals and waste trends (https://www.brsmeas.org/Secretariat/Overview/tabid/3609/language/en-US/Default.aspx).

Institution: Secretariat of the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD)
Spatial Jurisdiction: The CBD's jurisdiction is based on the principle of national sovereignty over biological diversity, meaning that the CBD applies to the components of biological diversity in areas within the limits of each Contracting Party's national jurisdiction, and to the processes and activities carried out under its jurisdiction or control, regardless of where their effects occur (https://www.cbd.int/doc/legal/cbd-en.pdf). The CBD does not have authority over oceans and maritime zones beyond the limits of national jurisdiction, except for the responsibility to prevent or minimize damage to the environment of other States or of areas beyond the limits of national jurisdiction (https://www.cbd.int/doc/legal/cbd-en.pdf). Therefore, the CBD's jurisdiction varies depending on the extent of each Contracting Party's national jurisdiction, which may include exclusive economic zones (EEZs), territorial waters, contiguous zones, inland waters, and coastal areas.
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: The CBD Secretariat is responsible for facilitating the implementation of the Convention on Biological Diversity, which aims to conserve biological diversity, use its components sustainably, and share the benefits of genetic resources fairly and equitably (https://www.cbd.int/). This includes addressing biodiversity issues such as ecosystem restoration, invasive alien species, biosafety, access and benefit-sharing, traditional knowledge, marine and coastal biodiversity, forest biodiversity, and agricultural biodiversity (https://www.cbd.int/). The CBD Secretariat also provides scientific and technical support, coordination and cooperation, communication and outreach, and resource mobilization for the achievement of the global biodiversity framework and the Sustainable Development Goals (https://www.cbd.int/mainstreaming).
Source of Jurisdiction: The CBD derives its mandate from the Convention on Biological Diversity (https://www.cbd.int/doc/legal/cbd-en.pdf), which is the international legal instrument for "the conservation of biological diversity, the sustainable use of its components and the fair and equitable sharing of the benefits arising out of the utilization of genetic resources" that has been ratified by 196 nations (https://www.un.org/en/observances/biological-diversity-day/convention). Specifically, Article 1 of the Convention states the objectives of CBD, which are to conserve biological diversity, to use its components sustainably, and to share the benefits of genetic resources fairly and equitably; Article 23 establishes a Conference of the Parties, which shall be the supreme body of the convention and shall keep under review the implementation of the convention. It also specifies the functions, procedures and frequency of the meetings of the Conference of the Parties, and the participation of observers; Article 24 establishes the CBD Secretariat, which shall arrange for and service the meetings of the Conference of the Parties and perform other functions assigned to it by the convention or by any protocol. It also requires the Conference of the Parties to designate the secretariat from among the existing competent international organizations that have signified their willingness to carry out the secretariat functions; and Article 25 establishes a subsidiary body on scientific, technical and technological advice, which shall provide the Conference of the Parties and its other subsidiary bodies with timely advice relating to the implementation of the convention. The CBD's jurisdiction is also influenced by the decisions and recommendations adopted by its governing bodies, including the Conference of the Parties (https://www.cbd.int/cop), the Subsidiary Body on Scientific, Technical and Technological Advice (https://www.cbd.int/sbstta), and the Subsidiary Body on Implementation (https://www.cbd.int/sbi). These decisions and recommendations provide guidance and direction for the CBD's work programmes and thematic areas, as well as cooperation and coordination with other conventions and organisations. The CBD's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various protocols and frameworks, such as the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety (https://bch.cbd.int/protocol/#:~:text=The%20Cartagena%20Protocol%20on%20Biosafety%20to%20the%20Convention%20on%20Biological,diversity%2C%20taking%20also%20into%20account), the Nagoya Protocol on Access and Benefit-sharing (https://www.cbd.int/abs#:~:text=The%20Nagoya%20Protocol%20on%20Access%20to%20Genetic%20Resources%20and%20the,a%20fair%20and%20equitable%20way.), and the Post-2020 Global Biodiversity Framework (https://www.cbd.int/doc/c/409e/19ae/369752b245f05e88f760aeb3/wg2020-05-l-02-en.pdf), which provide further legal instruments and targets for the CBD's jurisdiction over specific biodiversity issues and domains.
Defined Objectives: According to the Convention on Biological Diversity (https://www.cbd.int/doc/legal/cbd-en.pdf), the CBD's objectives are to pursue the following goals in accordance with its relevant provisions: (1) Conservation of biological diversity: to protect and maintain the variability among living organisms and the ecological systems they form, as well as their intrinsic and instrumental values for humanity (preamble; Article 1), (2) Sustainable use of its components: to use the components of biological diversity, such as genetic resources, species and ecosystems, in a way and at a rate that does not lead to their long-term decline, thereby maintaining their potential to meet the needs and aspirations of present and future generations (preamble; Article 1), and (3) Fair and equitable sharing of the benefits arising from the utilization of genetic resources: to ensure that the benefits derived from the access to and exploitation of genetic resources, such as scientific, technological, economic and social benefits, are shared in a fair and equitable way with the countries and communities that provide such resources, as well as with the holders of traditional knowledge, innovations and practices relevant to the conservation and sustainable use of biological diversity (preamble; Article 1; Article 8 j; Article 15; Article 16; Article 19). This objective also includes the provision of appropriate access to genetic resources and the transfer of relevant technologies, taking into account all rights over those resources and technologies (Article 1; Article 15; Article 16).
Strategies: The CBD Secretariat executes its objectives via several strategies: firstly, a post-2020 global biodiversity framework, adopted by the Conference of the Parties at its fifteenth meeting, provide the vision, mission, goals and targets for biodiversity conservation and sustainable use for the next decade, aligning with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the Paris Agreement (https://www.cbd.int/doc/strategic-plan/Post2020/Bubb.pdf). This framework, based on extensive consultations and inputs from various stakeholders, build on the achievements and lessons learned from the Strategic Plan for Biodiversity 2011-2020 and the Aichi Biodiversity Targets (https://www.cbd.int/doc/strategic-plan/2011-2020/Aichi-Targets-EN.pdf), as well as the current state of knowledge and science on biodiversity and ecosystem services. Secondly, a four-year medium-term programme of work, approved by the Conference of the Parties, outlines the activities, expected outcomes, indicators and budget of the Secretariat for the period of interest, in support of the implementation of the Convention and its Protocols (https://www.cbd.int/information/adm-fin). This programme of work is structured around six core functions of the Secretariat, namely: servicing meetings of the governing bodies and subsidiary bodies; facilitating implementation; providing policy advice and support; fostering communication, outreach and partnerships; managing information and knowledge; and ensuring sound management and administration, as detailed in Article 24 of the Convention document (https://www.cbd.int/doc/legal/cbd-en.pdf). The programme of work also includes a results-based management framework and a resource mobilization strategy. The major source of funding for the CBD Secretariat is the General Trust Fund for the Convention on Biological Diversity (BY Trust Fund), which is funded from the assessed contributions of Parties to the CBD, based on the United Nations scales of assessment (https://www.cbd.int/convention/parties/contributions.shtml). In addition, various mechanisms, initiatives and partnerships provide a platform for cooperation and coordination among Parties, other Governments, international organizations, civil society, indigenous peoples and local communities, and the private sector, on various thematic and cross-cutting issues related to biodiversity (https://www.cbd.int/programmes). Some of these include: the Clearing-House Mechanism (https://www.cbd.int/chm), which facilitates the exchange of information and technical and scientific cooperation; the Global Taxonomy Initiative (https://www.cbd.int/gti/default.shtml), which enhances taxonomic knowledge and capacity; the LifeWeb Initiative (https://www.cbd.int/undb/media/factsheets/undb-factsheet-lifeweb-en.pdf), which supports the establishment and management of protected areas; the Bio-Bridge Initiative (https://www.cbd.int/biobridge/), which fosters technical and scientific collaboration among Parties; the Global Partnership for Plant Conservation, which supports the implementation of the Global Strategy for Plant Conservation (https://www.cbd.int/gspc/default.shtml); and the Biodiversity for Development Initiative ( Biodiversity for Development Initiative), which promotes the integration of biodiversity into development policies and plans.
Inter-Institutional Relationship: The CBD Secretariat collaborates with key organizations to support biodiversity conservation. It is institutionally linked to UN Environment, its host institution, as per decision II/19 (https://www.cbd.int/secretariat/role.shtml). The Secretariat also liaises with the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) to host the NBSAP Forum, through generous funding provided by the Global Environmental Facility (GEF) (https://www.undp.org/nature/our-flagship-initiatives/gbf-action-nbsap-support). Furthermore, the Secretariat has established Memoranda of Cooperation with numerous entities, outlining formally agreed activities or targets (https://www.cbd.int/secretariat). Guided by Article 22 of the Convention (https://www.cbd.int/convention/articles/default.shtml?a=cbd-22), the Secretariat has also established liaison groups with the secretariats of the Rio Conventions (Joint Liaison Group) (https://www.cbd.int/rio) and those of the biodiversity-related conventions (Liaison Group of Biodiversity-related Conventions) (https://www.cbd.int/brc), as well as for thematic areas, such as the Inter-agency Liaison Group on Invasive Alien Species (https://www.cbd.int/invasive/lg). The Executive Secretary of the Secretariat is accountable to the Conference of the Parties for programme delivery and policy-related issues and to the Executive Director of UNEP for administrative and financial issues (https://www.un.org/sites/un2.un.org/files/asg_cbd-2023-nv-english.pdf).
Vertical Coordination: Vertical coordination within the CBD Secretariat involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other international organizations, member governments, and local communities. This is achieved through organizing meetings, preparing reports, assisting member governments in the implementation of various programmes of work, coordinating with other international organizations, and collecting and disseminating information (https://www.cbd.int/secretariat). The CBD Secretariat, based in Montreal, Canada, operates under the guidance of the Executive Secretary, who is appointed by the United Nations Secretary-General 9https://www.cbd.int/secretariat/executive-secretary). The Executive Secretary leads the strategic and planning activities of the Secretariat, as well as the intergovernmental processes and activities under the Convention and its two protocols, guided by Article 32 of the Convention (https://www.cbd.int/convention/articles/default.shtml?a=cbd-32). The Secretariat is accountable to the Conference of the Parties (COP) and its subsidiary bodies as detailed in Article 23 (https://www.cbd.int/convention/articles.shtml?a=cbd-23) and Article 25 (https://www.cbd.int/convention/articles.shtml?a=cbd-25) of the Convention respectively (https://www.cbd.int/secretariat/role.shtml). There are various divisions within the Secretariat, each focusing on different aspects of the CBD's mandate (https://www.cbd.int/secretariat/staff/default.shtml). In addition, the CBD Secretariat collaborates with key organizations such as UN Environment, its host institution, and liaises with the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) to host the NBSAP Forum (https://www.cbd.int/secretariat/role.shtml).
Horizontal Coordination:
Horizontal coordination within the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) Secretariat involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the biodiversity domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, indigenous and local communities, the scientific community, and other UN agencies to ensure that biodiversity is conserved, sustainably used, and equitably shared in all activities and policies. This coordination is led by the Secretariat according to Article 24 of the Convention (https://www.cbd.int/convention/articles/?a=cbd-24). For example, CBD works with the agriculture sector to promote the conservation and sustainable use of agricultural biodiversity (https://www.cbd.int/agro/), with the health sector to enhance the linkages between biodiversity and human health (https://www.cbd.int/health/), with the ocean sector to protect and restore marine and coastal biodiversity (https://www.cbd.int/marine/), or with the climate change sector to address the impacts of climate change on biodiversity and ecosystem services (https://www.cbd.int/climate/). Horizontal coordination within CBD can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Programme of Work on Island Biodiversity (https://www.cbd.int/island/pow.shtml) or the Global Taxonomy Initiative (https://www.cbd.int/gti/), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the Biodiversity Liaison Group (https://www.cbd.int/blg/) or the Collaborative Partnership on Forests (https://www.cpfweb.org/), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for biodiversity sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Ecosystem Approach (https://www.cbd.int/ecosystem/) or the Access and Benefit-sharing Clearing-House (https://absch.cbd.int/), and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for biodiversity issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the International Day for Biological Diversity (https://www.cbd.int/idb/) or the Global Biodiversity Outlook (https://www.cbd.int/gbo/).
The CBD Secretariat provides leadership and direction on matters related to biodiversity, science and technology, shapes the biodiversity research agenda, sets norms and standards, articulates evidence-based policy options, provides technical support to countries, and monitors and assesses biodiversity trends (https://www.cbd.int/secretariat/).

Institution: Secretariat of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES)
Spatial Jurisdiction: CITES Secretariat operates globally, with its authority extending to the territories of its member states. However, it does not specify jurisdiction over particular maritime zones or distances from coastlines. Instead, its mandate covers the regulation of trade in specimens of species included in its appendices (https://cites.org/eng/prog/Permit_system). Therefore, its jurisdiction is not limited to specific ocean spaces, territories, or maritime zones, but rather focused on the trade of endangered species within its member states.
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: The CITES Secretariat is responsible for ensuring the effective implementation of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora, which aims to protect wildlife from over-exploitation and illegal trade (https://cites.org/eng/disc/what.php). This includes providing support and guidance to the Parties, the Conference of the Parties, and the scientific and standing committees of CITES (https://cites.org/eng/disc/what.php). The CITES Secretariat also coordinates and monitors various projects and activities related to wildlife conservation and management, such as the Monitoring the Illegal Killing of Elephants (MIKE) programme (https://cites.org/eng/prog/mike/index.php/portal), the e-permitting system 9https://cites.org/eng/prog/Permit_system), and the identification manual (https://cites.org/eng/resources/wiki_id.php). The CITES Secretariat also collaborates with other international organizations and stakeholders, such as the International Consortium on Combating Wildlife Crime (ICCWC) (https://cites.org/eng/prog/iccwc#:~:text=What%20is%20ICCWC%3F,World%20Customs%20Organization%20(WCO).), to enhance the global response to wildlife crime and promote sustainable use of natural resources.
Source of Jurisdiction: The CITES Secretariat derives its mandate from the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/eng/disc/CITES-Convention-EN.pdf), which established CITES as an international agreement between governments to regulate wildlife trade. Specifically, Article XII of the Convention defines the functions of the Secretariat, which include arranging and servicing meetings of the Parties and the committees, communicating with the Parties and other relevant organizations, preparing reports and studies, and providing advice and assistance to the Parties. Additionally, the CITES guidelines for developing legislation (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/eng/prog/Legislation/guidelines_legislation.pdf), which were adopted by the Conference of the Parties in Resolution Conf. 8.4 (Rev. CoP15) (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/documents/E-Res-08-04-R15_0.pdf), state that the Secretariat has the authority to review and assess the national legislation of the Parties and to provide them with recommendations and assistance to ensure compliance with the Convention. The CITES Secretariat's jurisdiction is also influenced by other resolutions and decisions adopted by the Conference of the Parties and the committees, such as the Standing Committee (https://cites.org/eng/disc/sc.php#:~:text=The%20Standing%20Committee%20provides%20policy,management%20of%20the%20Secretariat's%20budget.) and the Animals and Plants Committee (https://cites.org/eng/disc/ac_pc.php), which provide guidance and direction for the Secretariat's activities and projects, as well as cooperation and coordination with other organizations and stakeholders (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/eng/prog/Legislation/guidelines_legislation.pdf). The CITES Secretariat's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (https://treaties.un.org/Pages/ViewDetailsIII.aspx?src=TREATY&mtdsg_no=XXI-6&chapter=21&Temp=mtdsg3&clang=_en), the Convention on Biological Diversity (https://www.cbd.int/cooperation/final-report-CITES%20CBD_Vilm_Workshop_Report.doc#:~:text=The%20Convention%20on%20International%20Trade,international%20concerns%20about%20biodiversity%20loss.), and the United Nations General Assembly Resolution on Sustainable Fisheries (https://documents.un.org/doc/undoc/gen/n23/397/27/pdf/n2339727.pdf?token=d5POlAgiWYC8Gzyjxu&fe=true), which provide further legal frameworks for the Secretariat's jurisdiction over specific wildlife issues and domains.
Defined Objectives: According to Article XII of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/eng/disc/CITES-Convention-EN.pdf), the CITES Secretariat's objectives include the following tasks: (1) To arrange for and service meetings of the Parties (paragraph 2 a); (2) To perform the functions entrusted to it under the provisions of Articles XV and XVI of the Convention, which relate to amendments to Appendices I and II and Appendix III and amendments thereto (paragraph 2 b); (3) To undertake scientific and technical studies in accordance with programmes authorized by the Conference of the Parties as will contribute to the implementation of the Convention, including studies concerning standards for appropriate preparation and shipment of living specimens and the means of identifying specimens (paragraph 2 c); (4) To study the reports of Parties and to request from Parties such further information with respect thereto as it deems necessary to ensure implementation of the Convention (paragraph 2 d); (5) To invite the attention of the Parties to any matter pertaining to the aims of the Convention (paragraph 2 e); (6) To publish and distribute to the Parties current editions of Appendices I, II and III together with any information which will facilitate identification of specimens of species included in those Appendices (paragraph 2 f); (7) To prepare annual reports to the Parties on its work and on the implementation of the Convention and such other reports as meetings of the Parties may request (paragraph 2 g); (8) To make recommendations for the implementation of the aims and provisions of the Convention, including the exchange of information of a scientific or technical nature (paragraph 2 h);and (9) To perform any other function as may be entrusted to it by the Parties (paragraph 2 i).
Strategies: The CITES Secretariat executes its objectives via several strategies: firstly, a ten-year Strategic Vision, adopted by the Conference of the Parties, outlines the Convention’s direction for the 2021-2030 timeframe in fulfilment of its mandate (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/reports/Implementation/E-SV-indicators.pdf). This vision, annexed to Resolution Conf. 18.3 (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/documents/COP/19/resolution/E-Res-18-03.pdf), aligns with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and its Sustainable Development Goals, as well as the post-2020 Global Biodiversity Framework (https://www.cbd.int/doc/c/409e/19ae/369752b245f05e88f760aeb3/wg2020-05-l-02-en.pdf) being developed by Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity. It also recognizes the importance of global cooperation to address the threats posed by illegal trade in wildlife, as acknowledged by the United Nations General Assembly. The vision sets five broad goals and corresponding objectives and indicators to measure progress and performance. Secondly, a triennial budget and work programme, proposed by the Secretariat and approved by the Conference of the Parties, details the activities, outputs, and resources required to implement the Convention and the decisions of the Parties. The current budget and work programme for 2023-2025 is based on the priorities identified by the Parties and the Secretariat, as well as the expected income from the Trust Fund and external sources, as specified in Resolution Conf. 19.1 (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/documents/COP/19/resolution/E-Res-19-01.pdf). Thirdly various resolutions, decisions, agreements, and partnerships provide guidance and support for the implementation and enforcement of the Convention at the national, regional, and international levels, addressing legal and sustainable trade, compliance and enforcement, capacity-building, cooperation and collaboration, and awareness-raising, with key instruments listed here (https://cites.org/eng/res/index.php). The Convention is financed by core and external funds. The core funding, known as the CITES Trust Fund (CTL), finances the administrative costs of the Secretariat, the Conference of the Parties and its subsidiary bodies, the Standing Committee and other permanent committees. The CITES Trust Fund is replenished from contributions of the Parties to the Convention based on the United Nations scale of assessment, adjusted to take account of the fact that not all members of the United Nations are Parties to the Convention. The external funds, known as the CITES External Trust Fund (QTL) funds the voluntary programmes/projects activities costs. The CITES External Trust Fund consists of extrabudgetary contributions from Parties and other entities on a purely voluntary basis. Each offer of funding to the CITES External Trust Fund is negotiated and vetted by the Secretariat (https://cites.org/eng/disc/fund.php).
Inter-Institutional Relationship: CITES cooperates with various institutions to ensure the conservation and sustainable use of wildlife. It works closely with the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), which provides administrative and financial support to the CITES Secretariat, as per the Memorandum of Understanding signed in 1976 and revised in 1983 (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/common/disc/sec/CITES-UNEP_0.pdf). It also coordinates with other biodiversity-related conventions, such as the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), the Convention on Migratory Species (CMS), and the Ramsar Convention on Wetlands, through joint work plans, liaison groups, and mutual representation, as per Resolution Conf. 13.3 (Rev. CoP18) (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/documents/COP/19/resolution/E-Res-13-03.pdf). Furthermore, CITES collaborates with international organizations and initiatives, such as the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), the World Trade Organization (WTO), the World Customs Organization (WCO), and the International Consortium on Combating Wildlife Crime (ICCWC), to enhance technical expertise, trade regulation, enforcement, and capacity-building (https://cites.org/eng/node/6808) Additionally, CITES engages with non-governmental organizations, civil society, and the private sector, to promote awareness, participation, and compliance (https://cites.org/eng/node/6808).
Vertical Coordination: Vertical coordination within the CITES Secretariat involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions. This is achieved through the overall leadership and management of the Secretariat, strategic planning and policy matters of the Secretariat, Depositary Government and Parties’ liaison, resource mobilization, high level relationships with partner organizations, and relationships with UNEP Executive and Deputy (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/eng/disc/CITES_Functional_Stucture_Oct2021.pdf). The CITES Secretariat operates through various units such as the Governing Bodies Unit, Office of the Secretary-General, Outreach and Projects Unit, Science Unit, Administration & Finance Unit, Legal Unit, and Enforcement Unit. Each unit has specific roles and responsibilities that contribute to the overall functioning of the Secretariat (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/eng/disc/CITES_Functional_Stucture_Oct2021.pdf). The Office of the Secretary-General provides overall leadership and management of the Secretariat, leads on strategic planning and policy matters of the Secretariat, Depositary Government and Parties’ liaison, resource mobilization, leads on high level relationships with partner organizations, leads on the relationships with UNEP Executive and Deputy (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/eng/disc/CITES_Functional_Stucture_Oct2021.pdf). The Secretary-General serves serves as the chief executive officer of the Convention and reports to the Conference of the Parties (https://cites.org/eng/disc/cop.php). The CITES Secretariat’s work is organized around various units, each overseen by a unit head who works closely with the Secretary-General to implement strategies and programmes across all levels of the Organization (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/eng/disc/CITES_Functional_Stucture_Oct2021.pdf). The Enforcement Unit provides enforcement support, relationships with international organizations combatting wildlife crime (i.e. ICCWC partners), wildlife crime and illegal wildlife trade advice (anti-smuggling, anti-fraud, combatting organized crime, money laundering and illegal wildlife trade, etc.), national reporting on illegal wildlife trade, and capacity building for enforcement (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/eng/disc/CITES_Functional_Stucture_Oct2021.pdf). The Legal Unit provides support for compliance to Parties, National Legislation Project, legal and trade advice (legislation, annotations, etc), regulatory support to CoP and Committees, socio-economic / livelihoods issues, major groups liaison, relationships with international trade organizations and industry, national reporting, NIAPs, inter-agency affairs, legal advice on legal instruments and to the SG, and capacity building for legal/compliance matters (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/eng/disc/CITES_Functional_Stucture_Oct2021.pdf). There are also committees that facilitate knowledge-sharing within the Secretariat. The Standing Committee provides policy guidance to the Secretariat and oversees the management of the budget. It also coordinates and oversees the work of other committees and working groups, and carries out tasks given to it by the Conference of the Parties (https://cites.org/disc/sc.php). The Animals Committee provides scientific advice and guidance to the Secretariat and the Parties on all matters relating to the international trade in animal specimens. It also reviews the implementation of the Convention and the effectiveness of its resolutions for animals (https://cites.org/disc/ac_pc.php). The Plants Committee performs similar functions as the Animals Committee, but for plant specimens. It also cooperates with the Animals Committee on matters of common interest (https://cites.org/disc/ac_pc.php). Additionally, the CITES Secretariat operates through various projects and programmes such as the Monitoring the Illegal Killing of Elephants programme (MIKE), the CITES Tree Species Programme (CTSP), and others. The CITES Secretariat also underwent a restructuring as of September 2020 (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/documents/E-Annual%20Report%202020-2021.pdf).
Horizontal Coordination:
Horizontal coordination within the CITES Secretariat involves collaboration with different organizations, instruments and processes that are relevant to the conservation and sustainable use of biodiversity and wildlife trade, such as other biodiversity-related conventions, international organizations, enforcement agencies, scientific bodies, and civil society. This coordination is reflected in Goal 5 of the CITES Strategic Vision: 2021-2030 (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/reports/Implementation/E-SV-indicators.pdf), specifically under Indicators 5.14, and 5.15, as well as Objectives 5.2 and 5.3. For example, CITES works with the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) to align its objectives and actions with the post-2020 global biodiversity framework (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/documents/E-CoP19-Inf-11.pdf), with the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) to ensure the sustainable management of marine and tree species (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/eng/com/sc/62/E62-14-04-A1.pdf), with the World Health Organization (WHO) to address the links between wildlife trade and zoonotic diseases (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/documents/E-CoP19-23-02_0.pdf), or with the World Customs Organization (WCO) to enhance the capacity and effectiveness of customs officers in combating illegal wildlife trade (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/eng/disc/sec/CITES-WCO.pdf). Horizontal coordination within the CITES Secretariat can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other organizations and processes, such as the International Consortium on Combating Wildlife Crime (ICCWC) (https://cites.org/eng/prog/iccwc.php) or the Joint CITES-CMS African Carnivores Initiative (https://cites.org/eng/node/55702), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, groups, and platforms, such as the Biodiversity Liaison Group (BLG) (https://www.cbd.int/blg/) or the Environment Management Group (EMG) (https://unemg.org/), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for CITES implementation and cooperation with other organizations and processes, such as the CITES guidelines for developing legislation (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/eng/prog/Legislation/guidelines_legislation.pdf) or the CITES Trade Database (https://trade.cites.org/), (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for CITES issues and policies among other organizations and processes, such as the World Wildlife Day (https://www.wildlifeday.org/) or the CITES Newsletter (https://cites.org/eng/news/newsletter.php). The CITES Secretariat provides administrative and technical support to the Parties, facilitates the implementation and enforcement of the Convention, coordinates with other organizations and processes, and promotes the objectives and principles of CITES (https://cites.org/eng/disc/sec/index.php).
