Institution: Secretariat of the Convention on Migratory Species (CMS)
Spatial Jurisdiction: The CMS Secretariat's jurisdiction is global, covering all the regions and habitats where migratory species of wild animals occur. This includes terrestrial, aquatic and avian species that cross national boundaries or move between areas of jurisdiction. The CMS Secretariat does not have authority over specific ocean spaces, territories or maritime zones, but rather facilitates cooperation and coordination among the Parties to the Convention, which are currently 133 countries (https://www.cms.int/en/parties-range-states).
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: The CMS secretariat is the coordinating body of the Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals (CMS), an environmental treaty that aims to protect and conserve terrestrial, aquatic and avian migratory animals and their habitats. The CMS secretariat's functions include organizing and servicing meetings of the Conference of the Parties (COP), the Scientific Council (ScC) and the Standing Committee (StC), promoting and supporting the development of Agreements, stimulating and supervising research and conservation projects, promoting the exchange of information between the Parties and liaising with international governmental and non-governmental organizations (https://www.cms.int/en/about/partnerships). The CMS secretariat covers a wide range of topics and fields related to migratory species, such as ecology, population dynamics, habitat restoration, migration routes, taking and trade, research and monitoring, emergency procedures, climate change, bycatch, renewable energy, wildlife disease, illegal killing, and poisoning (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/publication/State%20of%20the%20Worlds%20Migratory%20Species%20report_E.pdf).
Source of Jurisdiction: The CMS Secretariat derives its mandate from the Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals (CMS) (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/instrument/CMS-text.en_.PDF), which established CMS as an environmental treaty that aims to protect and conserve terrestrial, aquatic and avian migratory animals and their habitats (https://www.cms.int/en/convention-bodies/secretariat). Specifically, Article IX of the Convention defines the functions of the CMS Secretariat, which include organizing and servicing meetings of the Conference of the Parties, the Scientific Council and the Standing Committee, promoting and supporting the development of Agreements, stimulating and supervising research and conservation projects, promoting the exchange of information between the Parties and liaising with international governmental and non-governmental organizations. The CMS Secretariat is provided and administered by the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) (https://www.cms.int/en/convention-bodies/secretariat). The CMS Secretariat's jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by the Conference of the Parties, the Scientific Council and the Standing Committee, which provide guidance and direction for the CMS Secretariat's activities and programmes, as well as cooperation and coordination with other organisations and stakeholders 9https://www.cms.int/en/documents/cop-resolutions). The CMS Secretariat's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the Convention on Biological Diversity (https://www.cbd.int/doc/legal/cbd-en.pdf), the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (https://www.wto.org/english/res_e/booksp_e/int_exp_regs_part1_1_e.pdf), and the Ramsar Convention on Wetlands (https://www.ramsar.org/sites/default/files/documents/library/current_convention_text_e.pdf), which provide further legal frameworks for the CMS Secretariat's jurisdiction over specific migratory species and issues.
Defined Objectives: According to Article IX of the Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/instrument/CMS-text.en_.PDF), the CMS Secretariat's objectives include several key functions: arranging for and servicing meetings of the Conference of the Parties, the Scientific Council and the Standing Committee (paragraph 4 a); maintaining liaison with and promoting liaison between the Parties, the standing bodies set up under AGREEMENTS and other international organizations concerned with migratory species (paragraph 4 b); obtaining from any appropriate source reports and other information which will further the objectives and implementation of this Convention and arranging for the appropriate dissemination of such information (paragraph 4 c); inviting the attention of the Conference of the Parties to any matter pertaining to the objectives of this Convention (paragraph 4 d); preparing for the Conference of the Parties reports on the work of the Secretariat and on the implementation of this Convention (paragraph 4 e); maintaining and publishing a list of Range States of all migratory species included in Appendices I and II (paragraph 4 f); promoting, under the direction of the Conference of the Parties, the conclusion of AGREEMENTS (paragraph 4 g); maintaining and making available to the Parties a list of AGREEMENTS and, if so required by the Conference of the Parties, providing any information on such AGREEMENTS (paragraph 4 h); maintaining and publishing a list of the recommendations made by the Conference of the Parties pursuant to subparagraphs (e), (f) and (g) of paragraph 5 of Article VII or of decisions made pursuant to sub-paragraph (h) of that paragraph (paragraph 4 i); providing for the general public information concerning this Convention and its objectives (paragraph 4 j); and performing any other function entrusted to it under this Convention or by the Conference of the Parties (paragraph 4 k). These functions enable the Secretariat to fulfil its role as the Convention's coordinating body.
Strategies:
The CMS Secretariat executes its objectives via several strategies:
Firstly, the CMS Secretariat has a Strategic Plan. This plan, proposed for 2024-2032, aligns with the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF) and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, as stated in the draft resolution UNEP/CMS/COP14/CRP14.2 (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/document/cms_cop14_crp14.2_spms_e.docx). The plan is revised periodically, with the latest revision published in February, 2024. The Strategic Plan outlines the Secretariat’s vision, mission, strategic goals, core functions, and targets. It aligns with the Convention’s mandate to conserve migratory species of wild animals. Secondly, the CMS operates on triennium budgets to fulfill its strategic plans, but may also operate interim budgets as deemed fit. The interim budget for 2024 (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/036_Interim%20Budget%20for%202024_ExCOP1%20%281%29_2.pdf) provides for the same funding levels as the 2023 budget that was approved by COP13. The budget period covers the calendar year, from January 1 to December 31 and details activities, outputs, indicators, and resources corresponding to each strategic objective. In February 2024, the CMS COP14 will adopt a budget for the triennium 2024-2026, which will supersede the interim budget for 2024 (https://www.cms.int/en/news/2023028-process-adoption-interim-cms-budget-2024-through-silence-procedure-and-convening). Thirdly, the CMS Secretariat promotes and supports the development of Agreements. These agreements are designed to address the conservation needs of specific groups of migratory species or specific migratory species that have an unfavorable conservation status (https://www.cms.int/en/cms-instruments/agreements). The CMS Secretariat engages closely with UNEP through various mechanisms to enhance cooperation and policy coherence between UNEP and the multilateral environmental agreements (MEAs). This includes periodic meetings with UNEP Executive Director and the Director of Law Division and the MEAs Focal Points Network coordinated by Law Division (https://www.cms.int/en/news/cms-and-unep-strengthen-mea-coordination). The Secretariat also collaborates with a number of organizations outside the framework of formal agreements (https://www.cms.int/en/about/partnerships). The CMS Secretariat crafts different action and strategic plans for different programs with varying cycles based on the decisions and resolutions of the Conference of the Parties (COP), the Scientific Council (ScC) and the Standing Committee (StC), while also accepting inputs from other environmental treaties and organizations (https://www.cms.int/en/documents/action-plans). It also supports the implementation of CMS instruments, such as Memoranda of Understanding (https://www.cms.int/en/cms-instruments/mou), Action Plans (https://www.cms.int/en/documents/action-plans) and Concerted Actions (https://www.cms.int/en/documents/concerted-actions), which provide cooperative frameworks for the conservation and management of migratory species, as listed here (https://www.cms.int/en/cms-instruments). Finally, various partnerships, mechanisms, platforms and initiatives provide an operational framework for implementing the Convention and its instruments, addressing threats, habitats, knowledge, governance and synergies, with key examples listed here (https://www.cms.int/en/partnerships).
Inter-Institutional Relationship: The CMS Secretariat works with various partners to implement the Convention and conserve migratory species. It cooperates with the secretariats of other biodiversity-related MEAs, such as CBD, CITES, Ramsar, and UNCCD, to harmonize policies and activities (https://www.cms.int/en/about/partnerships), as per Paragraph 4(b) of Article IX of the Convention (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/instrument/CMS-text.en_.PDF) and resolution 11.10 (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/document/cms_cop12_res.11.10%28rev.cop12%29_e.pdf). It also collaborates with other inter-governmental bodies, such as UNESCO, IWC, and ITTO, to promote joint initiatives and projects on specific species or habitats, as per resolution 12.7 (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/document/cms_cop13_res.12.7_rev.cop13_e.pdf). It engages with non-governmental organizations, such as IUCN, BLI, OceanCare, and IFAW, to support scientific research, conservation action, and public awarenes (https://www.cms.int/en/about/partnerships). It partners with the private sector, such as TUI AG, to raise funds and foster corporate social responsibility, following a code of conduct (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/basic_page_documents/code_of_conduct.pdf) adopted in resolution 10.21 (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/document/10_21_synergies_e_0_0.pdf). It participates in the IPBES as an observer and contributes to its assessments and work programme (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/document/Doc_04_1_IPBES_E.pdf). It also supports the development and implementation of regional and thematic agreements and initiatives under the Convention, such as EAAFP, WHMSI, and SCF, as per Article IV and V of the Convention and Paragraph 6 of resolution 12.3 (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/document/cms_cop12_res.12.3_manila-declaration_e_1.pdf).
Vertical Coordination: Vertical coordination within the CMS Secretariat involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), other multilateral environmental agreements (MEAs), regional and sub-regional organisations, national governments, and local authorities. This is achieved through reporting, advising, and supporting. This is guided by Articles VII-IX of the Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/instrument/CMS-text.en_.PDF) as well as by the three Rules of Procedures for the Convention (https://www.cms.int/en/documents/rules-procedures). The CMS operates through the Conference of the Parties (COP) of all the members, the Standing Committee (StC) of 10 members, and a secretariat headed by an Executive Secretary (Article VII). It also has a Scientific Council (ScC) and other subsidiary bodies (Article VIII). The CMS Secretariat develops and promotes Agreements, services meetings, supports and supervises research and conservation projects and co-operates with governments and partner organizations (Article IX). The CMS Secretariat is provided by UNEP and is based in Bonn, Germany and has an out-posted office in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates (https://www.cms.int/en/about/structure). Also, a network of focal points and experts supports the CMS's work in promoting the conservation and sustainable use of migratory species across their range states (https://www.cms.int/en/page/focal-points). Additionally, CMS operates 21 Agreements and Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs) covering more than 500 species of migratory animals (https://www.cms.int/en/cms-instruments/agreements). Besides the Executive Secretary, at the CMS Secretariat, there is a clear line of duty within the leadership team comprising of a Deputy Executive Secretary and 5 Unit Coordinators with portfolios focusing on different aspects of the CMS's mandate (https://www.cms.int/en/convention-bodies/cms-organizational-structure). In addition, CMS Secretariat coordinates with other MEAs and their secretariats, such as the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES), the Ramsar Convention on Wetlands, and the Convention on the Conservation of European Wildlife and Natural Habitats (Bern Convention) (https://www.cms.int/en/about/partnerships).
Horizontal Coordination: Horizontal coordination within the CMS Secretariat involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the wildlife conservation domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, the scientific community, and other UN agencies to ensure that migratory species are protected and their habitats are conserved in all activities and policies. This coordination is guided by Article IX of the Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals (CMS) (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/instrument/CMS-text.en_.PDF). For example, CMS works with the aquatic species sector to promote the conservation and management of marine mammals, fish, and turtles (https://www.cms.int/iosea-turtles/en/page/mou-text-cmp), with the avian species sector to enhance the conservation and management of migratory birds (https://www.cms.int/en/publication/review-migratory-bird-flyways-and-priorities-management-0), the terrestrial species sector to develop the conservation and management of migratory land mammals and bats (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/document/Doc_13_Bats_Study_combined_E_0.pdf) or with the cross-cutting conservation issues sector to address common threats and challenges to migratory species, such as climate change, illegal killing, and renewable energy (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/document/cms_scc-sc5_crp.3_e_cross-cutting-conservation-issues_e.pdf). Horizontal coordination within CMS can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the CMS Family Strategic Plan (2018-2023) (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/document/10_05_strategic_plan_e_0_0.pdf) or the CMS Family Guidelines on Environmental Impact Assessments for Marine Noise-generating Activities (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/CMS%20Noise%20EIA%20Guidelines%20Panel%20Segment%202.pdf), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES) (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/document/Doc_04_1_IPBES_E.pdf), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for wildlife conservation sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the CMS Guidelines on the Integration of Migratory Species into National Biodiversity Strategies and Action Plans (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/document/10_18_nsbaps_e_0_0.pdf) or the CMS Online Reporting System (https://cms-ort.ort-production.linode.unep-wcmc.org/), (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for migratory species issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the World Migratory Bird Day (https://www.cms.int/en/campaign/world-migratory-bird-day-wmbd#:~:text=Every%20year%2C%20on%20the%20second,exhibitions%20and%20bird%2Dwatching%20excursions.) or the CMS Migratory species Champions Programme (https://www.migratoryspecies.org/en/champion). The CMS Secretariat provides leadership and direction on matters related to migratory species conservation, science and technology, shapes the wildlife conservation agenda, sets norms and standards, articulates evidence-based policy options, provides technical support to countries, and monitors and assesses conservation trends (https://www.cms.int/en/about/secretariat).

Institution: Secretariat of the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD)
Spatial Jurisdiction: The UNCCD Secretariat's jurisdiction is focused on dry and semi-arid lands regions, where desertification and drought are prevalent. This includes a range of political and economic zones as represented by countries in Africa, Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean, Central and Eastern Europe, and the Northern Mediterranean (https://www.unccd.int/convention/regions). The Secretariat does not have authority over oceans and maritime zones, as its mandate is to combat land degradation and mitigate the effects of drought on land-based ecosystems and populations.
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: The UNCCD Secretariat is responsible for combating land degradation and drought, especially in dry and semi-arid lands regions, where these issues are prevalent (https://www.unccd.int/convention/secretariat). This includes addressing land and soil-related issues like land degradation neutrality, climate change adaptation and mitigation, sustainable land management & restoration, poverty eradication, biodiversity loss, peace & security, sand and dust storms, land tenure, gender, food security & agriculture, drought, desertification, and cooperation among affected country Parties (https://www.unccd.int/land-and-life). The UNCCD also provides advocacy, awareness raising, education, science, technology, knowledge, capacity building, financing, and technology transfer for sustainable land use, as well as supporting the 2030 Agenda's Sustainable Development Goals, especially Goal 15 (Life on Land) (https://www.unccd.int/our-work/overview).
Source of Jurisdiction: The UNCCD Secretariat derives its mandate from the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD), which established the UNCCD as a legally binding framework to address desertification and the effects of drought (https://catalogue.unccd.int/936_UNCCD_Convention_ENG.pdf). Specifically, Article 23 of the Convention defines the functions and location of the Secretariat, Article 22 establishes modalities for the Conference of Parties, and Articles 20-21 outline the financial resources and funding mechanism of the Secretariat. Additionally, the UNCCD 2018-2030 Strategic Framework, adopted by the Conference of the Parties (COP) in 2017, specifies the vision, mission, strategic objectives, and expected impacts of the UNCCD for the period 2018-2030 (https://www.unccd.int/sites/default/files/inline-files/ICCD_COP%2813%29_L.18-1716078E_0.pdf). The Strategic Framework also defines the roles and responsibilities of the Secretariat, the COP, and its subsidiary bodies, as well as the affected country Parties and other stakeholders. The UNCCD Secretariat's jurisdiction is also influenced by the decisions and recommendations adopted by the COP and its subsidiary bodies, such as the Committee for the Review of the Implementation of the Convention (CRIC) and the Committee on Science and Technology (CST) (https://www.unccd.int/convention/governance/cric). These decisions and recommendations provide guidance and direction for the implementation of the Convention and the Strategic Framework, as well as cooperation and coordination with other relevant international bodies and conventions. Furthermore, UNCCD Secretariat's mandate is supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, the Paris Agreement on Climate Change, United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), and the African Union Agenda 2063, which provide further legal frameworks for the UNCCD Secretariat's jurisdiction over specific land and soil-related issues and domains (https://www.unccd.int/land-and-life/sdgs/unccd-cbd-and-unfccc-joint-liaison-group).
Defined Objectives: According to Article 23 of the UNCCD Convention (https://catalogue.unccd.int/936_UNCCD_Convention_ENG.pdf), the UNCCD Secretariat's objectives encompass several key functions: making arrangements for sessions of the Conference of the Parties (COP) and its subsidiary bodies established under the Convention, and providing them with services as required (Article 23, paragraph 1); compiling and transmitting reports submitted to it (Article 23, paragraph 2); facilitating assistance to affected developing country Parties, on request, particularly those in Africa, in the compilation and communication of information required under the Convention (Article 23, paragraph 3); and coordinating its activities with the secretariats of other relevant international bodies and conventions (Article 23, paragraph 4). Additionally, according to the UNCCD 2018-2030 Strategic Framework, the UNCCD Secretariat's objectives also include: acting as an advocate for land, ensuring land-related issues are put front and center on the development agenda; championing for healthy, productive and accessible land around the world; supporting countries in achieving land degradation neutrality, integrating strategies for poverty eradication, and promoting cooperation among affected country Parties; and providing access to the latest data and knowledge, ensuring that best practices are shared and opportunities for capacity-building are increased. These functions enable the Secretariat to fulfil its role as the main facilitator of the implementation of the Convention and the Strategic Framework (https://www.unccd.int/sites/default/files/inline-files/ICCD_COP%2813%29_L.18-1716078E_0.pdf).
Strategies: The UNCCD Secretariat executes its objectives via several strategies: Firstly, a 12-year Strategic Framework (2018-2030) is its most comprehensive global commitment to achieve Land Degradation Neutrality (LDN) (https://www.unccd.int/sites/default/files/inline-files/ICCD_COP%2813%29_L.18-1716078E_0.pdf). It aims to restore the productivity of vast expanses of degraded land, improve the livelihoods of more than 1.3 billion people, and reduce the impacts of drought on vulnerable populations (https://www.unccd.int/convention/secretariat#:~:text=It%20aims%20to%20restore%20the,is%20located%20in%20Bonn%2C%20Germany.). Secondly, the Secretariat prepares a triennial programme and budget. The Programme and budget for the triennium 2022–2024 as detailed in Decision 10/COP.15 provides an overview of the human and financial resources requirements as well as the programme priorities (https://www.unccd.int/sites/default/files/2022-10/10_cop15.pdf). Thirdly, the Secretariat supports countries that want to achieve national/regional land degradation neutrality, identify how land and soil are critical for climate change adaptation and mitigation, implement land management practices, design programmes and projects that transform communities, and provide science and research needed to take informed decisions (https://www.unccd.int/convention/secretariat). Finally, the Secretariat has been granted additional mandates to play a leading role with regards to operational objectives on advocacy, awareness raising and education, policy framework, and science, technology, and knowledge, as well as a support role in other operational objectives on capacity building and financing and technology transfer (https://knowledge.unccd.int/sites/default/files/inline-files/The%20secretariat.pdf). The Secretariat also collaborates with various partners at all levels, from global to local, to advance the implementation of the Convention (https://www.unccd.int/sites/default/files/2022-02/Partnership%20evaluation%20report%20%20final%20corrected.pdf).
Inter-Institutional Relationship: The UNCCD Secretariat collaborates with various institutions to implement its goals and objectives. This collaboration is guided by Articles 8 & 25 of the UNCCD Convention (https://catalogue.unccd.int/936_UNCCD_Convention_ENG.pdf). The UNCCD works closely with the Rio conventions and the Global Environment Facility to develop common indicators and synergies in reporting processes and capacity-building (https://www.unccd.int/sites/default/files/sessions/documents/2017-07/ICCD_COP%2813%29_6-1710495E.pdf). The Secretariat also collaborates with other United Nations entities on issues of food security, climate change, land degradation and restoration, forests, gender, drought, sand and dust storms, and migration (https://www.unccd.int/sites/default/files/sessions/documents/2017-07/ICCD_COP%2813%29_6-1710495E.pdf). In addition, it has established a strategic working partnership with the UN Development Programme (UNDP) to raise awareness and catalyze international cooperation to address the needs of the world’s poorest living in the drylands, particularly under scenarios of climate change (https://sdg.iisd.org/news/unccd-and-undp-agree-to-establish-strategic-working-partnership-summary/).
Vertical Coordination: Vertical coordination within UNCCD Secretariat involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other environmental agreements, regional and sub-regional organisations, national governments, and local authorities. This is structured under Articles 8, 22, 23, and 24 of the UNCCD Convention (https://catalogue.unccd.int/936_UNCCD_Convention_ENG.pdf). The UNCCD operates through the Conference of the Parties, the Committee on Science and Technology, and the Committee for the Review of the Implementation of the Convention as subsidiary bodies, and a secretariat headed by an Executive Secretary (Articles 22-24). Other UNCDD subsidiary bodies include intergovernmental working groups, regional coordination units, and Global Mechanism groups (https://www.unccd.int/convention/governance). UNCCD's work is organised around five regional implementation annexes, each overseen by a Regional Coordinator (https://www.unccd.int/convention/governance). There is also the Management and Coordination Unit providing strategic and internal policy advice to the Executive Secretary. A network of regional coordination units and technical experts supports the UNCCD's work in promoting land degradation neutrality and sustainable land management (https://www.unccd.int/resources/reports/2019-evaluation-regional-coordination-units-august-2019).
Horizontal Coordination: Horizontal coordination within the UNCCD Secretariat involves collaboration with different regions and stakeholders within the land degradation domain, such as affected countries, civil society, private sector, the scientific community, and other UN agencies to ensure that desertification, land degradation and drought are addressed effectively and efficiently in all activities and policies. This coordination is guided by Articles 8, 12, and 25 of the UNCCD Convention (https://catalogue.unccd.int/936_UNCCD_Convention_ENG.pdf), as well as by the UNCCD 2018-2030 Strategic Framework (https://www.unccd.int/sites/default/files/inline-files/ICCD_COP%2813%29_L.18-1716078E_0.pdf). For example, the UNCCD Secretariat works with the regional coordination units (RCUs) to support regional coordination mechanisms and facilitate the implementation of the Convention in each region (https://www.unccd.int/sites/default/files/2022-02/RCU%20eval%20report%20final_0.pdf), with the Committee on Science and Technology (CST) to provide scientific advice and guidance for the assessment and implementation of the Convention (https://knowledge.unccd.int/sites/default/files/inline-files/The%20secretariat.pdf), with the Global Mechanism (GM) to mobilize financial and non-financial resources for the implementation of the Convention (https://www.unccd.int/about-us/global-mechanism), or with the Science-Policy Interface (SPI) to enhance the science-policy dialogue and ensure the delivery of policy-relevant information, knowledge and advice on desertification, land degradation and drought (https://www.unccd.int/science-policy-interface). Horizontal coordination within the UNCCD Secretariat can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other regions and stakeholders, such as the Land Degradation Neutrality Target Setting Programme (https://www.unccd.int/actions/ldn-target-setting-programme) or the Drought Initiative (https://www.unccd.int/actions/drought-initiative), (2) Participation in interregional and multistakeholder committees, networks, and platforms, such as the Regional Coordination Mechanisms (https://www.unccd.int/sites/default/files/2022-02/RCU%20eval%20report%20final_0.pdf) or the UNCCD Knowledge Hub (https://knowledge.unccd.int/), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for land degradation sector engagement with other regions and stakeholders, such as the Good Practice Guidance for SDG Indicator 15.3.1 (https://www.unccd.int/resources/manuals-and-guides/good-practice-guidance-sdg-indicator-1531-proportion-land-degraded) or the National Reporting Process (https://www.unccd.int/data-knowledge/unccd-national-reporting-process), and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for land degradation issues and policies among other regions and stakeholders, such as the UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration (https://www.decadeonrestoration.org/) or the UNCCD Capacity Building Marketplace (https://www.unccd.int/our-work/capacity-building-marketplace).

Institution: The Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES)
Spatial Jurisdiction: Although no specific spatial coverage stated, the jurisdiction of IPBES covers global terrestrial, freshwater, coastal, and marine biodiversity, ecosystem functions, and ecosystem services through its periodic assessments of the state of biodiversity and ecosystem services worldwide (https://www.ipbes.net/regional-assessments), performing regular and timely assessments at regional and subregional levels. In 2015, IPBES launched four regional assessments for Africa, the Americas, Asia Pacific, and Europe and Central Asia (https://www.ipbes.net/regional-assessments).
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: The IPBES is an independent intergovernmental body established to strengthen the science-policy interface for biodiversity and ecosystem services (https://www.ipbes.net/about). It focuses on the conservation and sustainable use of biodiversity, long-term human well-being, and sustainable development . IPBES' work is broadly grouped into four areas: assessments on specific themes, methodological issues, and at both the regional and global levels. It also provides policy-relevant knowledge and catalyzes the implementation of knowledge-based policies (https://www.ipbes.net/about).
Source of Jurisdiction:
IPBES derives its mandate from the 2010 Busan Outcome document (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/3115), which was adopted by the United Nations General Assembly resolution 65/162 on 20 December 2010 and Decision 26/4 
of 24 February 2011. The first session of Plenary convened in Nairobi in 2011 to determine modalities 
and institutional arrangements for IPBES (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/3377) and a second session of Plenary in Panama in 2012 established IPBES as an independent intergovernmental body to strengthen the science-policy interface for biodiversity and ecosystem services (https://www.ipbes.net/history-establishment). Specifically, paragraph 4 of the Busan Outcome defines the objectives and functions of IPBES, and paragraph 5 outlines the operating principles and modalities of IPBES. Additionally, the IPBES rules of procedure, rule 2 on the functions of the IPBES secretariat (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/2675), states the duties of the secretariat in servicing and supporting the sessions of the Plenary and other subsidiary bodies, and in performing other tasks entrusted to it by the Plenary. IPBES's jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by its Plenary, such as the IPBES work programme (https://www.ipbes.net/work-programme), the IPBES conceptual framework (https://www.ipbes.net/conceptual-framework), and the IPBES assessment process (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/18538#:~:text=An%20IPBES%20assessment%20is%20a,ensure%20legitimacy%2C%20relevance%20and%20credibility.). These resolutions and provisional documents provide guidance and direction for IPBES's activities and deliverables, as well as cooperation and coordination with other organisations and stakeholders (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/24663). IPBES's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the Convention on Biological Diversity (https://www.cbd.int/doc/legal/cbd-en.pdf), the Convention on Migratory Species (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/instrument/CMS-text.en_.PDF), and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://sustainabledevelopment.un.org/content/documents/21252030%20Agenda%20for%20Sustainable%20Development%20web.pdf), which provide further legal frameworks for IPBES's jurisdiction over specific biodiversity and ecosystem services issues and domains.
Defined Objectives: According to the Resolution on the IPBES during second session of Plenary in 2012 (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/2674), the overarching objective of the IPBES platform is to strengthen the science-policy interface for biodiversity and ecosystem services for the conservation and sustainable use of biodiversity, long-term human well-being and sustainable development (Section I, Paragraph 1). Other functions of IPBES defined in the resolution include responding to requests from Governments and other stakeholders on biodiversity and ecosystem services issues (Section I, Paragraph 1a); identifying and prioritizing key scientific information needed for policymakers and catalysing efforts to generate new knowledge (Section I, Paragraph 1b); performing regular and timely assessments of knowledge on biodiversity and ecosystem services and their interlinkages (Section I, Paragraph 1c); supporting policy formulation and implementation by identifying policy-relevant tools and methodologies (Section I, Paragraph 1d); and prioritizing and providing capacity-building for the science-policy interface (Section I, Paragraph 1e).
Strategies: The IPBES Secretariat executes its defined objectives and functions via several strategies: firstly, a rolling work programme up to 2030 backed by Decision IPBES-7/1 (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/27458) and based on requests, inputs and suggestions from relevant bodies under multilateral environmental agreements as well as governments and other stakeholders. The rolling work program aims to strengthen the science-policy interface for biodiversity and ecosystem services for the conservation and sustainable use of biodiversity, long-term human well-being and sustainable development. This work programme corresponds to the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, including the Sustainable Development Goals (http://www.un.org/sustainabledevelopment/sustainable-development-goals/), the biodiversity-related conventions and other biodiversity and ecosystem service processes (https://www.ipbes.net/work-programme). It initially focuses on three topics: the interlinkages between biodiversity and other relevant issues reflected in the 2030 Agenda, the determinants of transformative change, and the tools and solutions for conservation and sustainable use of biodiversity (https://www.ipbes.net/work-programme). Secondly, a biennial budget and work programme, approved by the Plenary, detail the activities, outputs, indicators, and resources corresponding to each deliverable of the work programme (https://www.ipbes.net/work-programme). The current budget and work programme for 2022-2023 is based on the priorities identified by the Plenary and the available resources, as outlined in decision IPBES-8/1 (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/102793). It also supports the development and use of policy support tools and methodologies, such as the IPBES online catalogue of policy support tools and methodologies (https://www.ipbes.net/catalogue-policy-support-tools-and-methodologies), the IPBES guide on the production and integration of assessments from and across all scales (https://www.ipbes.net/guide-production-assessments), and the IPBES conceptual framework (https://www.ipbes.net/conceptual-framework). Finally, various assessments, task forces, expert groups, and platforms provide an evidence base for informing policy and decision-making, addressing the state of knowledge on the interactions between human societies and the natural world, the drivers and impacts of biodiversity change, and the options and pathways for achieving conservation and sustainable use of biodiversity (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/104403). Some of the key assessments include the global assessment report on biodiversity and ecosystem services (https://www.ipbes.net/global-assessment), the assessment report on invasive alien species (https://www.ipbes.net/ias), the assessment report on the sustainable use of wild species (https://www.ipbes.net/sustainable-use-assessment), and the assessment report on the diverse conceptualization of multiple values of nature and its benefits (https://files.ipbes.net/ipbes-web-prod-public-files/downloads/IPBES-4-INF-13_EN.pdf).
Inter-Institutional Relationship: IPBES collaborates with key organisations to support biodiversity and ecosystem services. It has an institutional link with the United Nations Environment Programme, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization, the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations and the United Nations Development Programme, based on a collaborative partnership arrangement approved by the Plenary in its decision IPBES-2/8 (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/4911) . Similarly, IPBES has memoranda of understanding with several strategic partners, such as Future Earth, the Global Biodiversity Information Facility, the Inter-American Institute for Global Change Research, and the International Union for Conservation of Nature, as requested by the Plenary in its decision IPBES-4/4 (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/5979) . Additionally, IPBES engages with various multilateral environmental agreements related to biodiversity and ecosystem services, such as the Convention on Biological Diversity, the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora, the Convention on Migratory Species, the Ramsar Convention on Wetlands, and the World Heritage Convention, as reported by the Executive Secretary in document IPBES/5/INF/16 (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/7303). It also involves a large number of NGOs, organizations, conventions and civil society groupings as observers in the formal IPBES process, with several thousand individual stakeholders contributing to and benefiting from its work (https://www.ipbes.net/about). Moreover, IPBES supports the recognition and engagement of Indigenous peoples and local communities and their knowledge systems in its activities, as outlined in its approach adopted by the Plenary in its decision IPBES-4/1 (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/5976).
Vertical Coordination:
Vertical coordination within IPBES involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other multilateral environmental agreements, intergovernmental and non-governmental organizations, scientific and academic institutions, indigenous peoples and local communities, and other stakeholders. This is achieved through the establishment of partnerships, the provision of policy support, the facilitation of knowledge generation and the enhancement of capacity-building. This is structured under the Operating Principles and Procedures of the Platform section of the IPBES document (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/2675), specifically in paragraphs 9-14. The IPBES operates through the Plenary, which is the decision-making body of the Platform and consists of all the members, the Multidisciplinary Expert Panel, which provides scientific and technical guidance to the Plenary, and the secretariat, which is responsible for the day-to-day operations of the Platform (paragraphs 9-12). The IPBES also has task forces, expert groups and other subsidiary bodies to carry out specific tasks and functions (https://www.ipbes.net/about). The IPBES supports the implementation of its work programme and the delivery of its products and services by engaging with various partners and stakeholders at different levels, such as the United Nations Environment Programme, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization, the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations and the United Nations Development Programme, which provide administrative and technical support to the Platform (paragraph 21). The IPBES also collaborates with other relevant international initiatives and processes, such as the Convention on Biological Diversity, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, the Global Biodiversity Information Facility and the International Union for Conservation of Nature, to ensure coherence and avoid duplication of efforts (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/102783). Lastly, the IPBES promotes the involvement of a wide range of stakeholders, such as scientific and academic institutions, civil society organizations, the private sector and the media, in its activities and processes, and encourages the establishment of national, subregional and regional platforms and networks to support its work (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/102793).

Horizontal Coordination: Horizontal coordination within IPBES involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the biodiversity and ecosystem services domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, the scientific community, and other UN agencies to ensure that biodiversity and ecosystem services are conserved, restored and used sustainably for human well-being and nature's balance. This coordination is guided by the Functions, Operating Principles and Institutional Arrangements of IPBES document (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/2675). IPBES works with the conservation sector to assess the status and trends of biodiversity and ecosystem services and their values (https://www.ipbes.net/assessment-reports), with the development sector to identify policy options and actions for achieving the Sustainable Development Goals and other global targets (https://www.ipbes.net/global-assessment), with the education sector to enhance capacity-building and knowledge generation and sharing (https://www.ipbes.net/capacity-building), or with the indigenous and local communities sector to recognize and respect their diverse knowledge systems and practices (https://www.ipbes.net/deliverables/1c-ilk). Horizontal coordination within IPBES can take various forms, such as (1) Joint planning and implementation of assessments and other deliverables with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the regional assessments of biodiversity and ecosystem services (https://www.ipbes.net/regional-assessments) or the thematic assessment of land degradation and restoration (https://www.ipbes.net/assessment-reports/ldr) with FAO, UNCCD and other partners, (2) Participation in intergovernmental and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the Multidisciplinary Expert Panel (https://www.ipbes.net/multidisciplinary-expert-panel) or the Stakeholder Engagement Network (https://www.ipbes.net/stakeholders) (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for biodiversity and ecosystem services sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the IPBES conceptual framework (https://www.ipbes.net/conceptual-framework) or the IPBES guide on the production and integration of assessments from and across all scales (https://www.ipbes.net/guide-production-and-integration-assessments-all-scales), and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for biodiversity and ecosystem services issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the IPBES #PledgeToAct campaign (https://www.ipbes.net/pledgeact) or the IPBES media centre (https://www.ipbes.net/media-centre).

Institution: UN Entity for Gender Equality and the Empowerment of Women (UN-Women)
Spatial Jurisdiction: UN-Women’s jurisdiction is global, encompassing all regions and countries where the United Nations operates. This includes a focus on conflict-affected and fragile states, where women’s rights and participation are often most at risk. UN Women does not have specific authority over ocean space, territory, or maritime zones, but rather works with governments, civil society, and other UN entities to promote gender equality and women’s empowerment in all spheres of life (https://www.unwomen.org/en/about-us/about-un-women).
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: UN-Women is responsible for advancing gender equality and the empowerment of women and girls. This includes addressing issues like women's leadership and political participation, women's economic empowerment, ending violence against women and girls, peace and security, humanitarian action, and youth and gender equality (https://www.unwomen.org/en/what-we-do). UN-Women also provides normative support, UN system coordination, and operational activities to promote gender equality and women's empowerment in all spheres of life, as well as supporting the implementation of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the Sustainable Development Goals (https://www.unwomen.org/sites/default/files/Headquarters/Attachments/Sections/Library/Publications/2021/UN-Women-Strategic-Plan-2022-2025-brochure-en.pdf).
Source of Jurisdiction: UN-Women derives its mandate from the UN General Assembly resolution 64/289 (https://undocs.org/en/A/RES/64/289), which established UN-Women as a multi-tiered intergovernmental governance structure. Specifically, Paragraphs 48-56 define the Purpose and General Principles of UN-Women, Paragraphs 57-67 outline the structure of Governance of the Entity, Paragraphs 68-74 define the provisions for Administration and Human Resources, Paragraphs 75-80 define Financing operations, and 81-89 describe Transitional arrangements and Review of Implementation. Additionally, UN-Women's strategic plan (https://www.unwomen.org/sites/default/files/Headquarters/Attachments/Sections/Library/Publications/2021/UN-Women-Strategic-Plan-2022-2025-brochure-en.pdf), which is approved by the Executive Board, states the vision, goals, and outcomes of UN-Women, and guides its operational activities and resource allocation. UN-Women's jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by its governing bodies, such as the Commission on the Status of Women (https://www.unwomen.org/en/csw), the Economic and Social Council (https://www.unwomen.org/en/how-we-work/intergovernmental-support/economic-and-social-council#:~:text=The%20UN%20Economic%20and%20Social,bodies%2C%20particularly%20its%20functional%20commissions.), and the General Assembly (https://www.un.org/womenwatch/ianwge/resolutions/ga_res_by_topic.htm). These resolutions and decisions provide policy guidance and recommendations for UN-Women's work on gender equality and women's empowerment, as well as cooperation and coordination with other UN entities and stakeholders. UN Women's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (https://www.unwomen.org/sites/default/files/Headquarters/Attachments/Sections/Library/Publications/2016/CEDAW-for-Youth.pdf), the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action (https://www.unwomen.org/sites/default/files/Headquarters/Attachments/Sections/CSW/PFA_E_Final_WEB.pdf), and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://www.unwomen.org/en/what-we-do/2030-agenda-for-sustainable-development), which provide further legal frameworks for UN Women's jurisdiction over specific gender issues and domains.
Defined Objectives: According to the Report of the Secretary-General A/64/588 on the Comprehensive Proposal for the Composite Entity for Gender Equality and the Empowerment of Women (https://documents.un.org/doc/undoc/gen/n10/202/88/pdf/n1020288.pdf?token=g8uLB3qijkKMoS6hAv&fe=true), the objectives of the UN-Women are to (1) Work for the elimination of discrimination against women and girls; the empowerment of women; and the achievement of equality between women and men as partners and beneficiaries of development, human rights, humanitarian action and peace and security (Paragraph 5), (2) Lead and coordinate United Nations system efforts to ensure that commitments on gender equality and gender mainstreaming translate into action throughout the world (Paragraph 5), (3) Provide strong and coherent leadership in support of Member States’ priorities and efforts, building effective partnerships with civil society and other relevant actors (Paragraph 5), (4) Perform eight functions, as outlined in the Deputy Secretary-General’s papers of August 2007 and July 2008, which include providing substantive support to intergovernmental bodies, supporting national efforts through innovative and catalytic programming, undertaking advocacy on critical issues, supporting Member States in implementing and monitoring intergovernmental agreements, undertaking research and analytical work, leading and coordinating United Nations system strategies and actions, strengthening the accountability of the United Nations system, and monitoring and reporting on system-wide compliance with gender balance (Paragraphs 5-6), and (5) Add value by providing capacity to meet the need for a strong voice for women and girls at the global, regional and local levels; better support for Member States as they enhance the normative and policy environment for accelerating progress towards full equality for women and girls; assistance for national partners as they respond to critical gaps and challenges; and an enhanced United Nations response to the country-defined needs and priorities of women and girls (Paragraph 21).
Strategies: UN-Women executes its objectives via several strategies. Firstly, a four-year Strategic Plan, revised annually by the Executive Board, establishes the organization’s vision, mission, strategic goals, core functions, and targets (https://www.unwomen.org/en/un-women-strategic-plan-2022-2025). This plan, applicable for 2022-2025 (https://www.unwomen.org/sites/default/files/Headquarters/Attachments/Sections/Library/Publications/2021/UN-Women-Strategic-Plan-2022-2025-brochure-en.pdf), aligns with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action (https://www.unwomen.org/sites/default/files/Headquarters/Attachments/Sections/CSW/PFA_E_Final_WEB.pdf). Secondly, an integrated results and resources framework (https://www.unwomen.org/sites/default/files/2021-02/irrf_updated%20on%2028%20may.pdf), devised by UN-Women and approved by the Executive Board, details the specific results that UN Women aims to achieve and their respective set of indicators and resources. The current framework for 2022-2025 is based on the needs and priorities of women and girls worldwide, as outlined in the Annex I of the UN Women Strategic Plan 2022–2025. It also monitors and reports on the progress and challenges of achieving gender equality and the empowerment of all women and girls, a key aspect of the implementation of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://www.unwomen.org/en/news/in-focus/women-and-the-sdgs). Thirdly, a biennial Integrated Budget and work plan, devised by the entity and ratified by the Executive Board, detail activities, outputs, indicators, and resources corresponding to each strategic objective. The current Budget for 2024-2025 (https://www.unwomen.org/sites/default/files/2023-05/Integrated%20Budget%202024-2025%20final.pdf) is tailored to the needs and priorities of the countries and regions where UN-Women operates, as outlined in the integrated results and resources framework. It also maintains the Women Count programme (https://data.unwomen.org/women-count), a global initiative to improve the production, accessibility and use of gender data for evidence-based advocacy and policy-making. Finally, various partnerships, platforms, and initiatives provide an operational framework for implementing the UN-Women Strategic Plan, addressing governance and participation in public life, women’s economic empowerment, ending violence against women and girls, and women, peace and security, humanitarian action, and disaster risk reduction (https://www.unwomen.org/en/partnerships/businesses-and-foundations/why-un-women).
Inter-Institutional Relationship: UN-Women collaborates with key institutions to advance gender equality and women's empowerment. It supports UN Member States as they set global standards for achieving gender equality, and works with governments and civil society to design laws, policies, programmes and services needed to ensure that the standards are effectively implemented and truly benefit women and girls worldwide (https://www.unwomen.org/en/about-us/about-un-women). Similarly, UN-Women liaises with the UN Development Programme (UNDP), implementing a relationship agreement effective since 1 January 2011, as per General Assembly resolution 64/289 (https://www.unwomen.org/sites/default/files/Headquarters/Attachments/Sections/Executive%20Board/GA-Res-64-289-en-Adopted%20by%20the%20General%20Assembly%20on%202%20July%202010%20pdf.pdf), which established UN Women as a composite entity of the UN system, comprising the Division for the Advancement of Women, the International Research and Training Institute for the Advancement of Women, the Office of the Special Adviser on Gender Issues and Advancement of Women, and the United Nations Development Fund for Women (Paragraph 53). Additionally, UN-Women facilitates linkages and influences between women’s lived experiences and efforts with regional intergovernmental policy and programme processes, and leverages spaces for women leaders to directly engage regional institutions, participate in mediation and other conflict resolution and peace initiatives (https://africa.unwomen.org/en/what-we-do/peace-and-security_africa). It also services the Commission on the Status of Women (CSW) (https://www.unwomen.org/en/csw#:~:text=The%20Commission%20on%20the%20Status,II)%20of%2021%20June%201946.) with its mandate in Economic and Social Council resolution 11(II) of 21 June 1946(https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/3845514/files/E_2ndsess-_Resolutions-EN.pdf?ln=en) by preparing related reports. Moreover, UN-Women maintains a relationship with the Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW) (https://www.ohchr.org/en/treaty-bodies/cedaw#:~:text=The%20Committee%20on%20the%20Elimination,rights%20from%20around%20the%20world.), providing substantive support and servicing its sessions, with its functions detailed in the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (https://www.ohchr.org/sites/default/files/Documents/ProfessionalInterest/cedaw.pdf) and its Optional Protocol.
Vertical Coordination: Vertical coordination within UN-Women involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the General Assembly, the Economic and Social Council, the Commission on the Status of Women, the Executive Board, regional and country offices, and national partners (https://www.unwomen.org/en/how-we-work/un-system-coordination). This is achieved through reporting, oversight, guidance, support, and partnership. This is structured under the Organizational arrangements section of the Comprehensive Proposal for the Composite Entity for Gender Equality and the Empowerment of women (https://documents.un.org/doc/undoc/gen/n10/202/88/pdf/n1020288.pdf?token=g8uLB3qijkKMoS6hAv&fe=true), specifically under Article III (Functions and Structure), Subarticle E (Organization Chart and structure), as well as under Article IV (Organizational Arrangements), Subarticle B (Governance). The UN-Women is a subsidiary organ of the General Assembly and reports to the General Assembly through the Economic and Social Council. The Commission on the Status of Women is the principal global policymaking body on gender equality and provides recommendations to guide the activities and operations of UN-Women. The Executive Board oversees the operational activities of UN-Women and applies the overall policy guidance of the General Assembly and the Economic and Social Council. The UN-Women is led by an Executive Director at the Under-Secretary-General level, who has full authority in financial and administrative matters and delegated authority from the Secretary-General. The UN-Women has three main divisions at the Headquarters level: the Intergovernmental Support and Strategic Partnerships Division, the Programme and Policy Division, and the Operations Division. The UN-Women also has regional divisions and subregional and country offices to provide technical support, oversight, and guidance to its country-level staff and to work with the United Nations country teams and national partners (https://www.unwomen.org/sites/default/files/Headquarters/Attachments/Sections/Executive%20Board/EB-2012-S2-UNW-2012-10-RegionalArchitecture-en.pdf). The UN-Women works as a full member of the resident coordinator system at the country level and as a leader of the United Nations gender theme group. The UN-Women also develops strategic partnerships with multilateral and regional organizations, civil society and women's organizations, and other relevant actors, fostering strong linkages between the normative and the operational aspects of gender equality and women's empowerment at all levels (https://www.unwomen.org/en/partnerships).
Horizontal Coordination: Horizontal coordination within UN-Women involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the gender equality and women's empowerment domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, the academic community, and other UN agencies to ensure that gender equality and women's rights are promoted and protected in all activities and policies. This coordination is guided by the General Assembly resolution 64/289 (https://undocs.org/en/A/RES/64/289) that established UN-Women as a composite entity with a dual mandate of normative support and operational activities. For example, UN-Women works with the human rights sector to support the implementation of the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (https://www.unwomen.org/en/csw), with the peace and security sector to advance the women, peace and security agenda (https://www.unwomen.org/en/what-we-do/ending-violence-against-women), with the development sector to promote women's economic empowerment and social protection (https://www.unwomen.org/en/what-we-do/economic-empowerment), or with the humanitarian sector to ensure that women and girls are protected and empowered in crisis situations (https://www.unwomen.org/en/what-we-do/economic-empowerment). Horizontal coordination within UN-Women can take various forms, such as: (1) UN System Coordination: UN-Women leads and coordinates the efforts of the UN system to ensure that commitments on gender equality and gender mainstreaming translate into action. It provides substantive and technical support to UN intergovernmental bodies, such as the Commission on the Status of Women, the Economic and Social Council, the General Assembly and the Security Council. It also works with the UN System Chief Executives Board for Coordination, the regional directors teams and the resident coordinator system to enhance coherence and accountability for gender equality across the UN system (https://www.unwomen.org/en/how-we-work/un-system-coordination), (2) Regional and country coordination: UN-Women has a staff presence in six regional offices and more than 80 countries, where it works as a member of the UN country teams and the regional coordination mechanisms. It provides policy advice, technical support, capacity development and advocacy to national and regional partners, as well as innovative and catalytic programming to address the needs and priorities of women and girls. It also leads the UN gender theme groups and supports the development and implementation of the UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Frameworks (https://www.unwomen.org/en/how-we-work/un-system-coordination/regional-and-country-coordination), (3) Strategic partnerships: UN-Women engages in policy dialogue, fosters knowledge exchange, and supports joint initiatives and campaigns to advance gender equality and women's empowerment. It also participates in various interagency and multisectoral platforms and networks, such as the Generation Equality Forum, the Spotlight Initiative, the Action Coalition on Economic Justice and Rights, and the UN Girls' Education Initiative (https://www.unwomen.org/en/partnerships), and (4) Advocacy and communication: UN-Women communicates and disseminates information on the achievements, challenges and opportunities for gender equality, using various media channels and tools, such as WomenWatch, UN Women Data Hub, UN Women Annual Report, and UN-Women social media accounts (https://www.unwomen.org/en/news/in-focus/strengthening-womens-access-to-justice/un-women-events).

Spatial Jurisdiction: The UN Global Compact's authority is global, covering all ocean spaces and maritime zones, as well as the adjacent coastal areas and inland waters of its signatory states (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N18/463/65/PDF/N1846365.pdf?OpenElement).
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: The UN Global Compact  Office is responsible for advancing corporate sustainability and social responsibility, especially among businesses and firms worldwide that adopt its ten principles on human rights, labour, environment and anti-corruption (https://unglobalcompact.org/about/faq). This includes promoting best practices, learning, dialogue and partnerships on these issues, such as climate action, gender equality, decent work, peace and justice, and ocean health (https://unglobalcompact.org/what-is-gc/our-work/environment). The UN Global Compact also provides guidance, tools, resources, networks and platforms for its participants and stakeholders, as well as supporting the alignment of business strategies and operations with the UN's development agenda and the Sustainable Development Goals (https://unglobalcompact.org/about/un-business-agenda).
Source of Jurisdiction:
The UN Global Compact Office derives its mandate from the UN Secretary-General, who launched the initiative in 1999 as a voluntary platform for businesses to adopt sustainable and socially responsible policies and practices (https://unglobalcompact.org/take-action/20th-anniversary-campaign#:~:text=Launched%20in%202000%20by%20former,face%20to%20the%20global%20market.). Additionally, the UN Global Compact's jurisdiction is influenced by the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (https://www.un.org/en/udhrbook/pdf/udhr_booklet_en_web.pdf), the International Labour Organization's Declaration on Fundamental Principles and Rights at Work (https://www.ilo.org/wcmsp5/groups/public/---ed_norm/---declaration/documents/publication/wcms_467653.pdf), the Rio Declaration on Environment and Development (https://www.un.org/en/development/desa/population/migration/generalassembly/docs/globalcompact/A_CONF.151_26_Vol.I_Declaration.pdf), and the United Nations Convention Against Corruption (https://www.unodc.org/documents/treaties/UNCAC/Publications/Convention/08-50026_E.pdf), which provide the basis for its ten principles on human rights, labour, environment and anti-corruption (https://unglobalcompact.org/what-is-gc/mission/principles). The UN Global Compact also supports the implementation of the UN's development agenda and the Sustainable Development Goals, which provide further guidance for its participants and stakeholders on advancing societal goals with an emphasis on collaboration and innovation (https://unglobalcompact.org/what-is-gc/mission).

Furthermore, the UN Global Compact's jurisdiction is endorsed by the UN General Assembly, which has adopted several resolutions and a decision that recognize its role and activities, encourage its expansion and participation, and call for its strengthening and alignment with the UN's values and principles. These include resolutions 55/215 of 21 December 2000, 56/76 of 11 December 2001, 58/129 of 19 December 2003, 60/215 of 22 December 2005, 62/211 of 19 December 2007, 64/223 of 21 December 2009, 66/223 of 22 December 2011, 68/234 of 20 December 2013 and 70/224 of 22 December 2015, as well as decision 72/543 of 20 December 2017 (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N18/463/65/PDF/N1846365.pdf?OpenElement). These resolutions and decision reflect the support and recognition of the UN General Assembly for the UN Global Compact as a strategic partner and a leading initiative for corporate sustainability and social responsibility.
Defined Objectives: According to the General Assembly resolution 73/254, entitled "Towards global partnerships: a principle-based approach to enhanced cooperation between the United Nations and all relevant partners" (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N18/463/65/PDF/N1846365.pdf?OpenElement), the UN Global Compact's objectives include several key aspects: promoting the core values and principles of the United Nations, as reflected in the Charter of the United Nations and other relevant conventions and treaties, and encouraging businesses to adopt principles for responsible business and investing (preamble; paragraph 14); facilitating and stimulating innovation in the implementation of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, in particular by leveraging private sector competencies and technologies (paragraph 9); enhancing the involvement of the private sector in combating climate change and supporting leadership on climate action (paragraph 23); promoting the Women’s Empowerment Principles and creating awareness of the ways in which business can advance gender equality (paragraph 29); and supporting and participating in multi-stakeholder partnerships to contribute to the realization of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (paragraph 24). These objectives enable the UN Global Compact to fulfil its role as a strategic and operational framework for the United Nations to partner with the private sector, in accordance with its mandate from the General Assembly, to advance United Nations values and responsible business practices within the United Nations system and among the global business community (https://undocs.org/en/A/RES/73/254).
Strategies: The UN Global Compact implements its objectives through several strategies: firstly, a three-year Strategy, endorsed by the UN Secretary-General and the UN Global Compact Board, which sets the vision, mission, strategic goals, core functions, and targets for the initiative (https://ungc-communications-assets.s3.amazonaws.com/docs/about_the_gc/UN-GLOBAL-COMPACT-STRATEGY-2021-2023.pdf). This strategy, applicable for 2021-2023, aligns with the Ten Principles of the UN Global Compact and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, detailed in resolution 73/254 of the UN General Assembly (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N18/463/65/PDF/N1846365.pdf?OpenElement). It also maintains the Communication on Progress (COP) policy, which requires participating companies to report annually on their progress in implementing the Ten Principles and contributing to the Global Goals, a key aspect of the accountability and transparency of the UN Global Compact (https://unglobalcompact.org/participation/report/cop). Finally, various programmes, platforms, networks, and initiatives provide an operational framework for advancing the Ten Principles and the Global Goals, addressing human rights, labour, environment, and anti-corruption (https://www.un.org/en/un-chronicle/un-global-compact-finding-solutions-global-challenges)
Inter-Institutional Relationship: The UN Global Compact cooperates with various organizations to achieve its objectives. It works with the UN Secretary-General and the UN Global Compact Board, which provide strategic guidance and oversight for the initiative, as per resolution 73/254, paragraph 15 ([1](https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N18/463/65/PDF/N1846365.pdf?OpenElement). As a voluntary platform for businesses to align with the UN values and principles, the UN Global Compact's relationship with the UN is based on resolution 55/215, which endorsed the initiative in 2000 (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N00/572/05/PDF/N0057205.pdf?OpenElement). Additionally, the UN Global Compact supports the UN's development agenda and the Sustainable Development Goals, providing a framework for business action and partnerships, as affirmed in resolution 70/1, paragraph 67 (https://www.un.org/en/development/desa/population/migration/generalassembly/docs/globalcompact/A_RES_70_1_E.pdf). It also partners with UN specialized agencies, funds and programmes, such as UNDP, UNICEF, UN Women, and UNEP, as well as other organizations such as the International Labour Organization, the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights, and the UN Office on Drugs and Crime, addressing relevant issues and sectors (https://unglobalcompact.org/about/un-business-agenda). Moreover, the UN Global Compact engages with its participants and stakeholders, including over 13,000 companies and 3,800 non-business signatories from 160 countries, through its Local Networks, platforms, programmes, and initiatives (https://unglobalcompact.org/participation/join/benefits), as outlined in resolution 73/254, paragraph 16 (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N18/463/65/PDF/N1846365.pdf?OpenElement).
Vertical Coordination:
Vertical coordination within the UN Global Compact involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions such as the  UN Secretary-General, the UN Global Compact Board, the Global Compact Office, Local Networks, and participating entities (https://unglobalcompact.org/about/un-business-agenda) (https://unglobalcompact.org/about/governance). This is achieved through strategic guidance, oversight, coordination, implementation, and reporting, structured under the Governance section of the UN Global Compact Strategy 2021-2023 (https://ungc-communications-assets.s3.amazonaws.com/docs/about_the_gc/UN-GLOBAL-COMPACT-STRATEGY-2021-2023.pdf). The Global Compact Office, managed by an Executive Director, coordinates overall initiative management and upholds integrity measures (https://unglobalcompact.org/about/governance).
The Global Network Council, a joint committee of Local Network representatives and Global Compact Office chiefs, advises the Executive Director. Additionally, Regional Network Councils offer platforms for Local Networks to collaborate and provide systematic recommendations. Local Networks, business-led multi-stakeholder platforms, assist businesses in implementing the Ten Principles and advancing Sustainable Development Goals, adapting to national contexts (https://unglobalcompact.org/engage-locally/about-local-networks). With 69 Local Networks globally, each network is led by a Local Board and Representative, working closely with the Global Compact Office and Regional Teams (https://unglobalcompact.org/engage-locally/about-local-networks). There is also the Communication on Progress (COP) policy, which requires participating companies to report annually on their progress in implementing the Ten Principles and contributing to the Global Goals, a key aspect of the accountability and transparency of the UN Global Compact (https://unglobalcompact.org/participation/report/cop). Additionally, the Global Network Council, with regionally elected Local Network representatives, advises the Executive Director. Also, the Regional Network Councils in five regions collaborate and share best practices, electing a chair to join the Global Network Council (https://unglobalcompact.org/about/governance/local-network-advisory-group). UN Global Compact engages with its Local Networks, which are clusters of participants and stakeholders who work together to promote the UN Global Compact and its principles at the country level, as well as to support local learning, dialogue, and partnerships (https://unglobalcompact.org/about/governance).
Horizontal Coordination: Horizontal coordination within the UN Global Compact involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the sustainable development domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, scientific community, and other UN agencies to ensure that the core values and principles of the UN are respected and supported by all partners and that the partnerships are aligned with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://unglobalcompact.org/about/un-business-agenda). This coordination is guided by the Guidelines on a Principle-based Approach to the Cooperation between the United Nations and the Business Sector (https://www.un.org/en/ethics/assets/pdfs/Guidelines-on-Cooperation-with-the-Business-Sector.pdf). For example, the UN Global Compact works with the human rights sector to promote the Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights (https://www.ohchr.org/documents/publications/GuidingprinciplesBusinesshr_eN.pdf), with the labour sector to provide guidance and support to strengthen business respect for labour standards by embedding and implementing the UN Global Compact labour principles (Principles 3, 4, 5 and 6) (https://unglobalcompact.org/what-is-gc/our-work/labour#:~:text=The%20UN%20Global%20Compact%20provides,decent%20work%20for%20all%20workers.), or with the environment sector to foster climate action and circular economy (https://unglobalcompact.org/take-action/action/climate). Horizontal coordination within the UN Global Compact can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Action Platform for Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions (https://d306pr3pise04h.cloudfront.net/docs/publications%2FActionPlatform_Launch_Flyer.pdf) with UNDP, UNODC and OHCHR, (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the UN Global Compact Action Platform (https://unglobalcompact.org/take-action/action/globalallianceforsdgfinance) or the UN Global Compact Network (https://www.unglobalcompact.org/engage-locally), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for partnership engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the UN-Business Partnership Guidebook (https://d306pr3pise04h.cloudfront.net/docs/issues_doc%2Fun_business_partnerships%2FUNBusinessPartnershipHandbook.pdf) or the SDG Compass (https://sdgcompass.org/), (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for sustainable development issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the UN Global Compact Leaders Summit (https://unglobalcompact.org/take-action/events/2137-un-global-compact-leaders-summit) or the UN Global Compact Annual Report (https://ungc-communications-assets.s3.amazonaws.com/docs/publications/UN%20GLOBAL%20COMPACT_2022%20ANNUAL%20REPORT.pdf). The UN Global Compact provides a framework and a platform for businesses to align their strategies and operations with the UN values and principles, to engage in collective action for sustainable development, and to report on their progress and impact (https://www.unglobalcompact.org/what-is-gc). The UN Global Compact facilitates the participation of various actors in the sustainable development sector and enhances cooperation and coordination within the UN system on partnership matters (https://unglobalcompact.org/take-action/partnerships), (https://unglobalcompact.org/about/un-business-agenda).

Spatial Jurisdiction: The UNFPA does not have jurisdiction over specific geographical areas, oceans, or maritime zones. Instead, its mandate is to address population and development issues worldwide, operating within political regions such as Arab States, Asia & the Pacific, East & Southern Africa, Eastern Europe & Central Asia, Latin America & the Caribbean, and West & Central Africa (https://www.unfpa.org/worldwide).
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: The UNFPA Secretariat is responsible for advancing sexual and reproductive health and rights, especially for women, young people, and marginalized groups, and for addressing population and development challenges, such as ageing, migration, urbanization, and climate change (https://www.unfpa.org). This includes providing family planning, maternal health, HIV and AIDS, and gender-based violence services, as well as supporting the collection and analysis of population data, such as censuses and civil registration (https://www.unfpa.org/data). UNFPA also promotes human rights and gender equality, such as ending female genital mutilation, child marriage, and son preference, and engaging men and boys as partners and allies (https://www.unfpa.org). UNFPA works in partnership with governments, civil society, and other UN agencies to achieve the Programme of Action of the International Conference on Population and Development (https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/event-pdf/PoA_en.pdf) and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/resource-pdf/Resolution_A_RES_70_1_EN.pdf).
Source of Jurisdiction: UNFPA derives its mandate from the United Nations General Assembly, which established UNFPA as a subsidiary organ of the United Nations (https://www.unfpa.org/unfpa-un-system). UNFPA receives overall policy guidance from the General Assembly and the Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC). It reports to its governing body, the UNDP/UNFPA Executive Board, on administrative, financial and programme matters (https://www.unfpa.org/unfpa-un-system).
