UNFPA's jurisdiction is also influenced by the International Conference on Population and Development (ICPD), which was convened by the General Assembly in 1994 and adopted the Programme of Action 9https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/event-pdf/icpd_eng_2.pdf). The Programme of Action (https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/programme_of_action_Web%20ENGLISH.pdf) defines the scope and objectives of UNFPA's work on population and development issues, with an emphasis on reproductive health and gender equality. The Programme of Action also provides a framework for cooperation and coordination with other UN entities, governments, civil society and other stakeholders. UNFPA's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/resource-pdf/Resolution_A_RES_70_1_EN.pdf), the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action (https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/beijing-at-ten.pdf), the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/resource-pdf/Statement_of_CEDAW.pdf), and the Convention on the Rights of the Child (https://www.ohchr.org/sites/default/files/Documents/ProfessionalInterest/crc.pdf), which provide further legal frameworks for UNFPA's jurisdiction over specific population and development issues and domains.
Defined Objectives: The objectives of UNFPA as defined by the Programme of Action adopted at the 1994 International Conference on Population and Development (ICPD) (https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/programme_of_action_Web%20ENGLISH.pdf) and later Executive Resolutions are: (1) To achieve universal access to sexual and reproductive health and realize reproductive rights for all, especially women and young people, (2) To reduce maternal mortality and improve the lives of women, adolescents and youth, enabled by population dynamics, human rights and gender equality, and (3) To contribute to the implementation of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals.
Strategies: The UNFPA executes its objectives via several strategies: firstly, a four-year Strategic Plan, revised annually by the Executive Board, establishes the UNFPA's vision, mission, strategic goals, core functions, and targets. This plan, applicable for 2022-2025 as detailed in document DP/FPA/2021/8 (https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/board-documents/main-document/DP.FPA_.2021.8_-_UNFPA_strategic_plan_2022-2025_-_FINAL_-_14Jul21_-_Corrected_19Jul21.pdf), aligns with the Programme of Action of the International Conference on Population and Development (ICPD) (https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/programme_of_action_Web%20ENGLISH.pdf), the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/resource-pdf/Resolution_A_RES_70_1_EN.pdf), and the United Nations reforms. Secondly, an Integrated Budget, devised by the UNFPA and ratified by the Executive Board, detail activities, outputs, indicators, and resources corresponding to each strategic objective. The current Integrated Budget for 2022-2025 is tailored to the needs of people left furthest behind and the priorities of stakeholders, as outlined in document DP/FPA/2021/9 (https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/board-documents/main-document/ENG_DP.FPA_.2021.9_-_Integrated_budget_2022-2025.pdf). It also maintains the Data for Development Platform, a key aspect of the implementation of the ICPD agenda and the Sustainable Development Goals (https://www.unfpa.org/data). UNFPA evaluation is a key function that supports accountability, evidence-based decision-making and learning for the organization (https://www.unfpa.org/evaluation). It helps UNFPA become more agile and adaptive amid changing contexts, to reach the furthest behind first. UNFPA evaluation is governed by the evaluation policy, approved by the Executive Board, and implemented by the Independent Evaluation Office (IEO), which reports directly to the Executive Board. UNFPA evaluation covers various topics and levels, such as population dynamics, sexual and reproductive health, gender equality, humanitarian action, and organizational effectiveness. UNFPA evaluation also engages with various stakeholders, such as UNFPA staff, partners, donors, governments, civil society, and youth, to ensure relevance, quality, and use of evaluation findings and recommendations.
Inter-Institutional Relationship: UNFPA works with various partners to advance sexual and reproductive health and rights. It partners with other UN agencies through joint programmes, multi-donor trust funds and other funding arrangements, such as UNICEF, UN Women, UNDP and others, to deliver on the Sustainable Development Goals and the 2030 Agenda (https://www.unfpa.org/strategic-partnerships/united-nations-agencies). It also engages with international financial institutions to scale-up financing and leverage their expertise and influence, such as the World Bank Group and the African Development Bank, supporting governments in both their loan and grant implementations in line with national development priorities (https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/board-documents/main-document/UNFPA%20paper%20on%20engagement%20with%20IFIs%20-%20FINAL%20-%206Jan23.pdf). Furthermore, UNFPA collaborates with civil society organizations, foundations, academia, private sector and media to advocate, mobilize resources and implement programmes for its three transformative results (https://www.unfpa.org/strategic-partnerships).
Vertical Coordination: Vertical coordination within UNFPA involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other funds and programmes, regional and subregional offices, country and territory offices, and implementing partners (https://www.unfpa.org/unfpa-un-system). This is achieved through consultative strategic planning, clear organizational structure, robust contractual framework, and solid oversight functions. The UNFPA operates under the guidance and oversight of the Executive Board of the United Nations Development Programme, the United Nations Population Fund and the United Nations Office for Project Services, which consists of 36 members elected by the Economic and Social Council (https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/resource-pdf/Background_Document_on_the_Population_Programme_of_the_UN.pdf). The UNFPA also engages with other United Nations entities through the United Nations Sustainable Development Group and the United Nations Development Coordination Office (https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/board-documents/main-document/UNFPA%20Information%20Note%20on%20UNDS%20reform%20-%20FINAL%20-%2020May2022.pdf). The UNFPA has a well-defined organizational structure, with its headquarters in New York, consisting of 14 divisions, offices, services and units, with some headquarters functions located in Geneva (humanitarian) and Copenhagen (supply chain) (https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/board-documents/main-document/Management%20Response%20-%20JIU%20MAR%20-%20FINAL%20-%20FINAL%20-%2026Apr23%20_0.pdf). Furthermore, UNFPA has six regional offices, eight representational offices, three subregional offices, and 121 country and territory offices (https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/board-documents/main-document/Management%20Response%20-%20JIU%20MAR%20-%20FINAL%20-%20FINAL%20-%2026Apr23%20_0.pdf). The UNFPA supports the implementation of its strategic plan and the achievement of its three transformative results through various modalities, such as country programme documents, intergovernmental and inter-agency processes, global and regional initiatives, and thematic funds (https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/board-documents/main-document/ENG_DP.FPA_.2021.8_-_UNFPA_strategic_plan_2022-2025_-_FINAL_-_14Jul21.pdf). The UNFPA has established a solid oversight framework for its activities, consisting of the Office of Audit and Investigation Services, the Evaluation Office, and the Ethics Office (https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/board-documents/main-document/Management%20Response%20-%20JIU%20MAR%20-%20FINAL%20-%20FINAL%20-%2026Apr23%20.pdf). The oversight structure is supplemented by external oversight provided by the Oversight Advisory Committee, the Board of Auditors and the Joint Inspection Unit (https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/board-documents/main-document/Management%20Response%20-%20JIU%20MAR%20-%20FINAL%20-%2025Apr23-updated.pdf).
Horizontal Coordination: Horizontal coordination within UNFPA involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the population and development domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, the academic community, and other UN agencies to ensure that sexual and reproductive health and rights, gender equality and empowerment of women, and population data and analysis are integrated in all activities and policies. This coordination is currently guided by the UNFPA Strategic Plan (2022-2025) (https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/board-documents/main-document/DP.FPA_.2021.8_-_UNFPA_strategic_plan_2022-2025_-_FINAL_-_14Jul21_-_Corrected_19Jul21.pdf). For example, UNFPA works with the health sector to provide quality maternal and newborn health services, family planning, and prevention and response to gender-based violence and harmful practices (https://www.unfpa.org/sexual-reproductive-health), with the education sector to promote comprehensive sexuality education and youth leadership (https://www.unfpa.org/comprehensive-sexuality-education), with the humanitarian sector to ensure the delivery of the Minimum Initial Service Package for reproductive health in crisis settings (https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/resource-pdf/MISP-Reference-English.pdf) or with the data sector to support the production and use of population and housing censuses, surveys, and civil registration and vital statistics systems (https://www.unfpa.org/data). Horizontal coordination within UNFPA can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the UNFPA-UNICEF Joint Programme on the Elimination of Female Genital Mutilation (https://www.unfpa.org/unfpa-unicef-joint-programme-female-genital-mutilation) or the Spotlight Initiative to eliminate violence against women and girls with the EU and other UN agencies (https://esaro.unfpa.org/en/news/spotlight-initiative-dialogue-emphasizes-need-partnerships-local-ownership-and-strategic), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the Inter-Agency Working Group on Reproductive Health in Crises (https://iawg.net/) or the UN Population Division (https://www.un.org/development/desa/pd/), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for population and development sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Essential Services Package for Women and Girls Subject to Violence (https://www.unfpa.org/publications/essential-services-package-women-and-girls-subject-violence) or the UNFPA Supplies Partnership (https://www.unfpa.org/unfpa-supplies), and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for population and development issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the International Conference on Population and Development (https://www.unfpa.org/icpd) or the State of World Population Report (https://www.unfpa.org/swop).

Institution: UN Research Institute for Social Development (UNRISD)
Spatial Jurisdiction: UNRISD's work is global in nature as an autonomous research institute within the United Nations, focusing primarily on the developing world, although not  limited to exclusive economic or political zones (https://www.unrisd.org/en/about). It does not have jurisdiction over any specific geographical area, ocean space, territory, or maritime zones.
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: The UNRISD Secretariat is a research and policy institute within the UN system that studies the social dimensions of development issues and provides innovative solutions for social change. It conducts multidisciplinary research and policy analysis on topics such as poverty, inequality, democracy, human rights, and environmental justice, and explores how they affect and are affected by development processes. Specific priority concerns of UNRISD include Inequalities, New eco-social contracts, Justice, Low-carbon transitions, Climate justice, Social policy, Economy of care, Alternative economies, Intersectionality, Social development, Gender, Resilience, Migration, Social and solidarity economy, Capacity development, and Measurement and indicators that support the integration of social aspects into the UN's development policies and practices (https://cdn.unrisd.org/assets/about/outreach-unrisd-2023.pdf). UNRISD also engages in knowledge sharing and advocacy for sustainable development (https://www.unrisd.org/en/about).
Source of Jurisdiction: UNRISD derives its mandate from the Statutes of UNRISD (https://documents.un.org/doc/undoc/gen/n63/166/83/pdf/n6316683.pdf?token=yYyPtTVGKo5T95bmTP&fe=true), which established UNRISD as an autonomous research institute within the United Nations that undertakes multidisciplinary research and policy analysis on the social dimensions of contemporary development issues. Specifically, the Statutes defines the Purposes and general organization of the Institute (Articles 1-3); Administrative and financial arrangements (Articles 4-9); and Personnel arrangements (Articles 10-14). Articles 2 and 3 specify that the Institute is supervised by a Board composed of five members nominated by the Social Commission, a representative of the Secretary-General, the Directors of the regional planning institutes, the representatives of two specialized agencies, and the Director of the Institute. The Board lays down general rules, approves work programmes and budgets, and reports to the Social Commission. UNRISD's jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by its Board, which is composed of eminent social scientists and representatives of the United Nations and its specialized agencies (https://www.unrisd.org/en/about/our-team). These resolutions and decisions provide guidance and direction for UNRISD's research agenda and activities, as well as cooperation and coordination with other organisations and stakeholders. UNRISD's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://www.unrisd.org/en/research/projects/2030-agenda-for-sustainable-development), the Paris Agreement on Climate Change (https://cdn.unrisd.org/assets/legacy-files/301-info-files/ED0B565D0ADD38A1C125804F00333F7E/Flagship2016_Ch5.pdf), and the Addis Ababa Action Agenda on Financing for Development (https://sustainabledevelopment.un.org/content/documents/2051AAAA_Outcome.pdf), which provide further legal frameworks for UNRISD's jurisdiction over specific social development issues and domains.
Defined Objectives: According to the Statutes of UNRISD (https://documents.un.org/doc/undoc/gen/n63/166/83/pdf/n6316683.pdf?token=yYyPtTVGKo5T95bmTP&fe=true), the UNRISD’s objectives encompass several key functions: conducting research into problems and policies of social development and relationships between various types of social development and economic development during different phases of economic growth (Article 1, paragraph 1); carrying out research and studies that are urgent and important to the work of the United Nations Secretariat, regional and national planning institutes, and specialized agencies in the field of social policy, social development planning and balanced economic and social development (Article 1, a, b, c); coordinating its work with the United Nations Secretariat, regional and national planning institutes, specialized agencies, and other relevant bodies, and making its results available to them (Article 1).
Strategies: The UNRISD pursues its objectives and mandates through several strategies: firstly, a five-year institutional strategy, developed through consultation with its stakeholders, defines the Institute’s vision, mission, research programmes, and expected results. The current strategy, applicable for 2021-2025 (https://cdn.unrisd.org/assets/legacy-files/301-info-files/4A1D94EBE95DA31A802586D8004198E8/UNRISD-Strategy-2021-2025.pdf), focuses on overcoming inequalities and achieving a new eco-social contract. This plan aligns with the UN's Sustainable Development Goals and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. The present strategy sets out five research programmes: Transformative Social Policy, Gender Justice and Development, Alternative Economies for Transformation, Environmental and Climate Justice, and Translating Research into Policy and Practice—Bonn Programme. UNRISD engages with its network and partners through a co-production process (https://cdn.unrisd.org/assets/about/outreach-unrisd-2023.pdf). The Institute is committed to comprehensive consultation with its stakeholders on where its research activities are directed, as well as how UNRISD conducts and communicates about its research (https://cdn.unrisd.org/assets/legacy-files/301-info-files/C393FC7BBDCA9A1B8025859D00490220/UNRISD-Institutional-Strategy-2021-2025-Consultation-Document-V1.2.pdf).  It also maintains the UNRISD Flagship Report, a key publication that synthesizes the Institute’s research and policy analysis on the social dimensions of contemporary development issues (https://www.un-ilibrary.org/content/books/9789290851332#:~:text=This%20UNRISD%20Flagship%20Report%20shows,are%20built%20in%20by%20design.). UNRISD receives no funding from the regular budget of the United Nations but depends entirely on voluntary contributions from national governments, multilateral donors, foundations and other sources and must fully mobilize all the financial resources necessary to cover the institutional and staff costs required to implement the UNRISD Strategy 2021–2025 ((https://cdn.unrisd.org/assets/legacy-files/301-info-files/4A1D94EBE95DA31A802586D8004198E8/UNRISD-Strategy-2021-2025.pdf). The underlying assumption in terms of delivering results, therefore, is that UNRISD will design and successfully implement a fundraising strategy that will diversify the Institute’s funding sources, and generate predictable, stable and increased revenues. Various institutional initiatives, collaborations, and regulatory mechanisms also provide an operational framework for implementing the Institute's objectives. For instance, the work programme of the UNRISD Bonn office aims to create new interagency collaborations and enhance synergies between research and learning activities (https://www.unbonn.org/UNRISD#:~:text=The%20work%20programme%20of%20the,and%20contributing%20to%20training%20and). The Institute also organises regular Seminar Series to provide a space for open, informed, and insightful conversation around contemporary issues of concern to social development research and policy (https://www.unrisd.org/en/activities/events).
Inter-Institutional Relationship: UNRISD engages with various institutions to advance social development research and policy. It works closely with the UN system, especially the UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs (DESA) (https://www.un.org/en/desa/fifty-second-session-unrisd-board), the UN Development Programme (UNDP), and the UN Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC), to contribute to UN agendas and processes, such as the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://www.un.org/en/ecosoc/integration/2015/pdf/unrisd.pdf). It also collaborates with other UN agencies, funds and programmes, such as UN Women (https://evaw-un-inventory.unwomen.org/en/agencies/unrisd), UNICEF (https://cdn.unrisd.org/assets/legacy-files/301-info-files/1D84B2B1C806FBC5C1257C23003D591D/UNRISD-UNICEF%20Project%20Description.pdf), and UNFPA (https://www.unfpa.org/), on specific research projects and events, as detailed in its annual reports. Furthermore, UNRISD partners with academic institutions, the private sector, think tanks, civil society organisations, and foundations, to co-produce and disseminate knowledge on social development issues (https://cdn.unrisd.org/assets/about/outreach-unrisd-2023.pdf) . Additionally, UNRISD organises regional roundtables on the social sciences and social issues in development, to strengthen its links with other research networks (https://cdn.unrisd.org/assets/legacy-files/301-info-files/A4F723F019D0DEAE8025848D00533928/UNRISD_Annual_Report_2018.pdf).
Vertical Coordination: Vertical coordination within UNRISD involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, the Economic and Social Council, the Social Commission, the specialized agencies, and the regional and national development planning institutes. This is achieved through supervision, review, approval, and reporting of the Institute's work programmes, budgets, and progress. This is structured in the Statutes of UNRISD (https://documents.un.org/doc/undoc/gen/n63/166/83/pdf/n6316683.pdf?token=yYyPtTVGKo5T95bmTP&fe=true), specifically under Paragraphs 2-3 (General Organization), Paragraphs 4-9 (Administrative and Financial Arrangements), and Paragraphs 10-14 (Personnel Arrangements). UNRISD is an autonomous research institute within the UN system that undertakes multidisciplinary research and policy analysis on the social dimensions of contemporary development issues (https://www.ungeneva.org/en/about/organizations/unrisd). UNRISD is not a subsidiary organ of the UN General Assembly, but reports to the UN Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC) through the UN Secretary-General. UNRISD also collaborates with other UN agencies, funds and programmes, as well as academic and civil society partners, to disseminate its research findings and influence policy debates (https://cdn.unrisd.org/assets/library/reports/2023/annual-report-2022.pdf). UNRISD is overseen by a Board of 12 members (https://www.unrisd.org/en/about/our-team), headed by a Chairperson who is appointed by the UN Secretary-General. Board members are selected based on their expertise and qualifications, and membership is confirmed by the UN Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC). Board members participate in their individual capacity and do not represent UN member states. The Board reports to the Commission for Social Development biennially. The Board is composed of eminent social scientists and representatives of governments and civil society organizations. The Board approves the research agenda and budget of UNRISD, monitors its activities and evaluates its work. UNRISD has a small core staff, including researchers, administrative and support personnel, based at its headquarters in Geneva, Switzerland (https://www.unrisd.org/en/about/our-team).
Horizontal Coordination: Horizontal coordination within UNRISD involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the social development domain, such as governments, civil society, academia, the private sector, and other UN agencies to ensure that social equity, inclusion and justice are central to development thinking, policy and practice. This coordination is currently guided by the UNRISD Strategy 2021-2025 (https://cdn.unrisd.org/assets/legacy-files/301-info-files/4A1D94EBE95DA31A802586D8004198E8/UNRISD-Strategy-2021-2025.pdf). For example, UNRISD works with the social policy sector to promote transformative social policy for inclusive and sustainable development (https://www.unrisd.org/en/research/programme-areas/social-policy-and-development-2000-2009), with the gender sector to advance gender justice and development (https://www.unrisd.org/en/research/programme-areas/gender-justice-and-development), with the economy sector to explore alternative economies for transformation (https://cdn.unrisd.org/assets/legacy-files/301-info-files/4E6DACF58A13FA328025870B0047E2B3/AE4T---A5-Prospectus-UNRISD-Programme.pdf), and with the environment sector to foster environmental and climate justice (https://cdn.unrisd.org/assets/legacy-files/301-info-files/CACDA014C224E6978025870B0047F8BF/Climate---A5-Prospectus-UNRISD-Programme.pdf). Horizontal coordination within UNRISD can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint research and policy analysis with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the project on Politics of Domestic Resource Mobilization for Social Development with UNDP, UNICEF and the International Policy Centre for Inclusive Growth (https://www.unrisd.org/pdrm) or the project on Sustainable Development Performance Indicators with the Bertelsmann Stiftung (https://www.unrisd.org/sdpi), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral networks and platforms, such as the Social Protection Inter-Agency Cooperation Board (https://www.social-protection.org/gimi/ShowWiki.action?id=62) or the UN Inter-Agency Task Force on Social and Solidarity Economy (https://unsse.org/), (3) Development and dissemination of knowledge products and tools for social development engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the flagship report on Overcoming Inequalities in a Fractured World: Between Elite Power and Social Mobilization (http://213.219.61.110/unrisd/website/projects.nsf/(httpProjects)/259326031472FE1BC125834C0038A3B9?OpenDocument), and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for social development issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the UNRISD Conference on Overcoming Inequalities in a Fractured World (https://geneva.fes.de/fileadmin/user_upload/documents/2018/Booklet---UNRISD-Conference-2018.pdf) or the UNRISD Podcast Series on New Directions in Social Policy (https://www.unrisd.org/en/library/podcasts).

Spatial Jurisdiction: UNICEF’s authority is global, covering over 190 countries and territories across all continents and oceans to uphold the rights of every child, regardless of their location, nationality, or situation. UNICEF has no specific distance or boundary within its jurisdiction, as it operates in accordance with the United Nations Charter and the Convention on the Rights of the Child (https://www.unicef.org/media/52626/file).
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: UNICEF's subject matter jurisdiction is focused on protecting and promoting the rights of every child, especially those in greatest need, in accordance with the Convention on the Rights of the Child (https://www.unicef.org/media/52626/file). This includes addressing child rights issues, such as health, education, nutrition, water, sanitation, hygiene, protection, participation, and emergency response (https://www.unicef.org/what-we-do). UNICEF also provides humanitarian and development assistance, advocacy, communication, research and evaluation, partnership and coordination, and innovation for children's well-being, as well as supporting the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals (https://www.unicef.org/sites/default/files/2022-02/UNICEF-strategic-plan-2022-2025-publication-EN.pdf).
Source of Jurisdiction: UNICEF derives its mandate from the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), establishing it as the leading global child rights authority within the United Nations system (https://www.un.org/en/global-issues/children). Specifically, Resolution 57/60 of the UNGA provides the legal basis for UNICEF's jurisdiction over the protection and promotion of the rights of every child, everywhere (http://www.worldlii.org/int/other/UNGA/2002/125.pdf). Additionally, UNICEF's jurisdiction is guided by the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC), which is the most widely ratified human rights treaty in history (https://www.unicef.org/media/52626/file). UNICEF also supports the implementation of other international and regional instruments and mechanisms that advance the rights and well-being of children and young people, such as the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW) (https://www.unwomen.org/sites/default/files/Headquarters/Attachments/Sections/Library/Publications/2016/CEDAW-for-Youth.pdf), the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child (ACRWC) (https://au.int/sites/default/files/treaties/36804-treaty-african_charter_on_rights_welfare_of_the_child.pdf), and the Committee on the Rights of the Child (CRC Committee) (https://www.ohchr.org/en/documents/legal-standards-and-guidelines/crcc156-guidelines-regarding-implementation-optional).
Defined Objectives: According to the Preamble and Part I of the Convention on the Rights of the Child, the objectives of the UNICEF have been mandated to fulfil, as specified in this document, include several key functions: promoting and protecting the rights of every child, in accordance with the principles proclaimed in the Charter of the United Nations and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (Preamble, paragraph 2); ensuring that each child enjoys a full and decent life, in conditions that ensure dignity, promote self-reliance and facilitate the child's active participation in the community (Article 23, paragraph 1); providing appropriate assistance and protection to children who are living in exceptionally difficult conditions, such as those affected by armed conflict, disability, displacement, exploitation, abuse or neglect (Preamble, paragraph 9; Article 22, 23, 32, 34, 35, 36, 37, 38, 39); respecting the responsibilities, rights and duties of parents or other persons legally responsible for the child, and providing them with the necessary support for the child's well-being and development (Article 5, 18, 27); and fostering international cooperation for improving the living conditions of children in every country, in particular in the developing countries (Preamble, paragraph 10; Article 4, 17, 23, 24, 28, 29, 45) (https://www.unicef.org/media/52626/file). These functions enable the UNICEF to fulfil its role as the United Nations Children's Fund, which is responsible for providing humanitarian and developmental aid to children worldwide (https://www.unicef.org/what-we-do).
Strategies: UNICEF implements its objectives through several key strategies: firstly, a four-year Strategic Plan (2022-2025), revised by the Executive Board, outlining UNICEF’s vision, mission, and goals aligned with the Convention on the Rights of the Child and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) (https://www.unicef.org/sites/default/files/2022-02/UNICEF-strategic-plan-2022-2025-publication-EN.pdf), detailed in document E/ICEF/2021/11 (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N21/108/01/PDF/N2110801.pdf?OpenElement). Secondly, a biennial Integrated Results and Resources Framework (2022-2025) specifies expected results, indicators, and resources for each Strategic Plan outcome, based on a theory of change and results-based management (https://www.unicef.org/executiveboard/media/7426/file/2021-25-Add1-Strategic_Plan_2022-2025-IRRF-EN-ODS.pdf), as outlined in document E/ICEF/2021/12 (https://www.unicef.org/executiveboard/media/5316/file/2021-12-Draft_Strategic_Plan_2022-2025-EN-2021.05.04.pdf). UNICEF also focuses on monitoring the implementation of the Convention on the Rights of the Child (https://www.unicef.org/child-rights-convention/unicef-role). Additionally, UNICEF's Data for Children Strategic Framework sets principles for data work, including action, innovation, and trust, with strategic objectives like improving data quality and fostering data partnerships (https://data.unicef.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Data-for-Children-Strategic-Framework-UNICEF.pdf). The UNICEF Disability Inclusion Policy and Strategy (DIPAS) 2022-2030 aligns with the CRPD, CRC, and UNDIS, setting priorities for disability-inclusive services and participation (https://www.unicef.org/media/134511/file/An%20inclusive%20world,%20starts%20with%20me,%20with%20you,%20with%20all%20of%20us.pdf). Finally, the UNICEF 2021-2030 Child Protection Strategy aligns with the CRC and SDGs, focusing on strengthening child protection systems, addressing harmful social norms, leveraging partnerships, and enhancing evidence for child protection (https://www.unicef.org/media/104416/file/Child-Protection-Strategy-2021.pdf). These comprehensive strategies enable UNICEF to deliver results for children globally, including in humanitarian and fragile contexts.
Inter-Institutional Relationship: UNICEF collaborates with a diverse range of organizations to achieve its objectives. It works with 193 Member States and various stakeholders through the Executive Board, serving as the governing body of UNICEF (https://www.unicef.org/executiveboard/media/14411/file/2023-EB-Informal_Guide_2023-EN-2022.12.19.pdf). As the leading UN agency for children's rights, UNICEF's relationship with the UN is based on resolution  57 (I) (https://www.unicef.org/media/85596/file/UN-resolutions-UNICEF-1940s.pdf)57/60, which reaffirmed UNICEF's mandate and role within the UN system (https://undocs.org/en/A/RES/57/60). Additionally, UNICEF supports the implementation of the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC) and other international and regional instruments and mechanisms that advance the rights and well-being of children and young people, as stated in resolution 57/60, paragraph 2 (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N02/541/87/PDF/N0254187.pdf?OpenElement). It also partners with UN agencies and international financial institutions such as WHO, UNESCO, UNHCR, WFP, UNDP, and the World Bank, and other organizations such as the Global Partnership for Education, the Global Fund, and Gavi, addressing common challenges and opportunities for children (https://www.unicef.org/eca/what-we-do/our-partners). Moreover, UNICEF contributes to the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, aligning its Strategic Plan 2022-2025 with the Sustainable Development Goals, as endorsed in resolution 70/1 (https://undocs.org/en/A/RES/70/1).
Vertical Coordination: Vertical coordination within UNICEF involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other specialized agencies, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and local authorities. This is achieved through delegation of authority, directing, and controlling. The body responsible for guiding UNICEF’s global work is a 36-member Executive Board made up entirely of government representatives (https://www.unicef.org/executiveboard/media/14411/file/2023-EB-Informal_Guide_2023-EN-2022.12.19.pdf). The executive board is responsible for establishing policies, approving new programmes, and making key decisions on administrative and financial plans. The Office of the Secretary of the Executive Board (OSEB) is responsible for maintaining an effective relationship between the Executive Board and the UNICEF secretariat 9https://www.unicef.org/executiveboard/board-secretariat). UNICEF operates through its country offices that are responsible for carrying out the organization’s mission through a programme of cooperation developed in partnership with the host government (https://www.unicef.org/where-we-work). These programs are planned and delivered in five-year stints, and they are designed to focus on practical ways to improve the rights and prospects of women and children in that country (https://www.unicef.org/executiveboard/country-programme-documents). Regional Offices within host countries are responsible for guiding the delivery of this work, and they report and provide technical assistance to country offices when needed. There are also a range of specialized offices dotted around the world, such as UNICEF’s Supply Division which is responsible for procuring and delivering most of life-saving vaccines that UNICEF delivers in developing countries (https://www.unicef.org/supply/). The overall management and administration of UNICEF as a global organization takes place at its headquarters in New York, USA, where UNICEF’s global policy on children is formed under the supervision of the UNICEF executive team. UNICEF’s operational framework aims to help UNICEF staff and partners develop programmes across the social ecological model and the mental health continuum of prevention, promotion and treatment to improve the mental health and psychosocial wellbeing of children, adolescents and their caregivers globally, working together with a broad range of partners at the country, regional and global levels (https://www.unicef.org/reports/global-multisectoral-operational-framework).
Horizontal Coordination:
Horizontal coordination within UNICEF involves working with different sectors and stakeholders within the child rights domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, foundations, philanthropists, and other UN agencies to ensure that every child survives, thrives, learns, is protected, has a voice, and lives in a safe and clean environment. This coordination is guided by the Convention on the Rights of the Child (https://www.unicef.org/media/52626/file) and the UNICEF Strategic Plan (2022-2025) (https://www.unicef.org/sites/default/files/2022-02/UNICEF-strategic-plan-2022-2025-publication-EN.pdf). For example, UNICEF works with the health sector to provide immunization, nutrition, and maternal and newborn care services (https://www.unicef.org/health), with the education sector to ensure quality and inclusive learning opportunities for all children (https://www.unicef.org/education), with the humanitarian sector to prevent and respond to violence, abuse, and exploitation of children (https://www.unicef.org/protection), or with the environment sector to address the impacts of climate change and environmental degradation on children (https://www.unicef.org/environment-and-climate-change). Horizontal coordination within UNICEF can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Global Partnership to End Violence Against Children (https://www.end-violence.org/) or the Generation Unlimited initiative (https://www.generationunlimited.org/), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the Inter-Agency Standing Committee (https://interagencystandingcommittee.org/) or the Scaling Up Nutrition Movement (https://scalingupnutrition.org/), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for child rights sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Core Commitments for Children in Humanitarian Action (https://www.corecommitments.unicef.org/) or the Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys (https://mics.unicef.org/), and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for child rights issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the State of the World’s Children report (https://www.unicef.org/reports/state-of-worlds-children) or the World Children’s Day (https://www.unicef.org/world-childrens-day)
Through its coordination, UNICEF provides leadership and direction on matters related to child rights, while shaping the child rights agenda, setting standards, articulating evidence-based policy options, providing technical support to countries, and monitoringand assessesing child rights trends (https://www.unicef.org/about/what-we-do).

Institution: United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD)
Spatial Jurisdiction: The UNCTAD Secretariat’s authority is not limited to a specific geographical area, but rather covers the entire field of trade and related problems of economic development, as stated in paragraph 3 (a) of the UNGA Resolution A/RES/1995(XIX) (https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/203700/files/A_RES_1995%28XIX%29-ES.pdf?ln=en)
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: The UNCTAD Secretariat is responsible for promoting international trade, especially between countries at different stages of development and with different systems of economic and social organisation, and for formulating principles and policies on these matters (https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/edmmisc232add4_en.pdf). This includes addressing trade and development issues, such as market access, trade facilitation, debt management, investment, technology transfer, and e-commerce (https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/edmmisc232add19_en.pdf). UNCTAD also provides technical assistance, research and analysis, intergovernmental consensus-building, and policy advice for sustainable development, as well as supporting the implementation of the UN's development agenda and the Sustainable Development Goals (https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/edmmisc232add39_en.pdf).
Source of Jurisdiction: UNCTAD derives its mandate from the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), establishing it as the main organ of the United Nations dealing with trade, investment and development issues. Specifically, Resolution 1995 (XIX) of the UNGA provides the legal basis for UNCTAD's jurisdiction over the promotion of international trade, especially between countries at different stages of development and with different systems of economic and social organization, and the formulation of principles and policies on these matters (https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/edmmisc232add19_en.pdf). Additionally, UNCTAD's jurisdiction is influenced by the outcomes of its quadrennial conferences, which set the priorities and work programme of the organization (https://investmentpolicy.unctad.org/investment-dispute-settlement). UNCTAD also supports the implementation of the UN's development agenda and the Sustainable Development Goals including the ocean ((https://unctad.org/news/conservation-and-sustainable-use-marine-biodiversity-areas-beyond-national-jurisdiction-recent)), which provide further legal frameworks for UNCTAD's jurisdiction over specific trade and development issues and regions (https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/iteiit16_en.pdf)
Defined Objectives: As per the  General Assembly resolution 1995 (XIX) of 30 December 1964 (https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/edmmisc232add19_en.pdf),  Key objectives of UNCTAD include promoting international trade, especially to accelerate economic development, and enhancing trade between countries at varied development stages, including developing countries and those with different economic systems (section II, paragraph 3 a). It formulates principles and policies on international trade and economic development (section II, paragraph 3 b), proposes effective implementation strategies, considering economic system diversity and development stages (section II, paragraph 3 c). UNCTAD reviews and coordinates United Nations system activities in international trade and economic development, collaborating with the General Assembly and Economic and Social Council (section II, paragraph 3 d). It initiates actions for negotiating and adopting multilateral trade legal instruments (section II, paragraph 3 e), harmonizes trade and development policies of governments and regional groups (section II, paragraph 3 f), and addresses other relevant matters (section II, paragraph 3 g). Additionally, UNCTAD evaluates and recommends institutional arrangement improvements, including comprehensive organization establishment within the UN system (section III, paragraphs 30 and 31). These functions establish UNCTAD as the General Assembly's principal organ in trade and development (section I, paragraph 1).
Strategies:
The UNCTAD Secretariat implements its objectives and mandates through various strategies, such as the UNCTAD conference, held every four years, serving as the highest-level decision-making body on trade and development issues (https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/dtltlb2016d1_en.pdf).  The Conferene sets the priorities and work programme of the organization (https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/wpl94.en.pdf). The current cycle is based on the Nairobi Maafikiano, adopted by the fourteenth session of the UNCTAD conference in 2016 (https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/td519add2_en.pdf), and detailed in the UNGA resolution 71/215 (https://financing.desa.un.org/sites/default/files/2023-03/N1645944.pdf). Another strategy is a biennial programme plan and budget, which is prepared by the UNCTAD Secretariat and approved by the General Assembly, and outlines the expected accomplishments, indicators, and resources for each subprogramme of the organization (https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/a77d6-sect12_en.pdf). The current plan and budget for 2022-2023 are aligned with the UN development agenda and the Sustainable Development Goals, and detailed in [document A/76/6 (Sect. 12)] (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N21/084/27/PDF/N2108427.pdf?OpenElement). A third is the UNCTAD technical cooperation strategy that lays out UNCTAD's technical cooperation objectives and provide the basis for systematic and robust,
strategic secretariat-level coordination and decision-making for technical cooperation (https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/tdb69_crp1_en_1.pdf).
Inter-Institutional Relationship: UNCTAD collaborates with various organizations to achieve its objectives and mandates. It engages with 195 Member States and various stakeholders through the UNCTAD conference, held every four years, serving as the highest-level decision-making body on trade and development issues (https://unctad.org/about/partnership). As the main organ of the General Assembly in the field of trade and development, UNCTAD's relationship with the UN is based on resolution 1995 (XIX), which established UNCTAD in 1964 (https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/edmmisc232add19_en.pdf). Additionally, UNCTAD leads the UN Inter-Agency Cluster on Trade and Productive Capacity, involving 15 UN agencies, providing a mechanism for the coordination of trade and development operations at the national and regional levels within the UN system, as endorsed by the UN Chief Executives Board for Coordination (https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/tc2010d1rev9_en.pdf). It also cooperates with other international and regional organizations, such as WTO, OECD, World Bank, ILO, and CITES, UNDP, UNIDO, IMF, etc addressing common trade and development challenges (https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/dom20092rev1_en.pdf). Moreover, UNCTAD supports the implementation of the UN development agenda and the Sustainable Development Goals, offering research and analysis, technical assistance, intergovernmental consensus-building, and policy advice for developing countries, as recognized in resolution 71/215 (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N16/459/44/PDF/N1645944.pdf?OpenElement).
Vertical Coordination: Vertical coordination within UNCTAD involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other specialized agencies, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and local authorities. This is structured under the Relationship with Other Institutions within the United Nations System section of the General Assembly resolution 1995 (XIX), specifically in section II, paragraph 3 d (https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/edmmisc232add19_en.pdf). UNCTAD also has a Trade and Development Board of 55 members, a secretariat headed by a Secretary-General, and various commissions, committees, and intergovernmental groups (section IV, paragraphs 32-40) (https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/dtltlb2016d1_en.pdf). UNCTAD supports the implementation of the UN development agenda and the Sustainable Development Goals, offering research and analysis, technical assistance, intergovernmental consensus-building, and policy advice for developing countries (section II, paragraph 3 c) (https://elearning.unctad.org/pluginfile.php/34150/mod_page/content/12/UNCTAD_Competition_Consumer_Policies_short_course_part1.pdf). UNCTAD also leads the UN Inter-Agency Cluster on Trade and Productive Capacity, involving 15 UN agencies, providing a mechanism for the coordination of trade and development operations at the national and regional levels within the UN system, as endorsed by the UN Chief Executives Board for Coordination (https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/dom20092rev1_en.pdf). UNCTAD also cooperates with other international and regional organizations, such as WTO, OECD, World Bank, ILO, and CITES, addressing common trade and development challenges (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N16/459/44/PDF/N1645944.pdf?OpenElement).
Horizontal Coordination: Horizontal coordination within UNCTAD involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the trade and development domain, such as governments, international organizations, private sector, civil society, academia, and regional commissions (https://unctad.org/about/partnership). This coordination is structured under the Terms of Reference and Rules of Procedure of the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/issmisc2019d2_en.pdf). The UNCTAD promotes the integration of developing countries into the world economy and supports their efforts to achieve inclusive and sustainable development (https://unctad.org/about). Also, UNCTAD conducts research and analysis, provides policy advice and technical assistance, and organizes intergovernmental deliberations and consensus-building on trade and development issues (https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/tdsxxiiid3_en.pdf). In addition, UNCTAD fosters cooperation and dialogue among its member States and other stakeholders, and enhances the coherence and coordination of the UN system on trade and development matters (https://unctad.org/annualreport/2019/Pages/index.html).

Spatial Jurisdiction: UNDP's jurisdiction is global, operating in more than 170 countries and territories that cut across diverse political and economic zones with particular focus on low-income and middle-income nations and regions within Africa, Asia, Europe, Latin America, and the Caribbean (https://www.undp.org/). However, the UNDP does not have specific jurisdiction over oceans, maritime zones, or territorial waters. Its authority is not limited to exclusive economic or political zones, contiguous zones, territorial seas, or inland waters within state waters. Instead, its focus is on sustainable development across all territories of its member states.
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: UNDP’s work is concentrated in three focus areas: sustainable development, democratic governance and peacebuilding, and climate and disaster resilience. Its operations cut across a wide range of themes, including but not limited to: poverty reduction, democratic governance, crisis prevention and recovery, environment and energy, HIV/AIDS, gender equality, private sector development, and rule of law (https://www.undp.org/about-us). UNDP provides assistance ranging from policy advice and technical support to financial and human resources, covering key social and environmental issues. UNDP’s work in the area of sustainable development includes promoting sustainable livelihoods, conserving biodiversity, and mitigating the impact of climate change (https://www.undp.org/expertise). UNDP also works to ensure that the benefits of development are shared equitably among all people, regardless of their gender, race, or socio-economic status (https://www.undp.org/sustainable-development-goals).
Source of Jurisdiction: UNDP derives its mandate from the United Nation's General Assembly resolution 2029 (XX), establishing it in 1965 as a merger of two previous programmes, the United Nations Expanded Programme of Technical Assistance (EPTA) (1949) and the United Nations Special Fund (1958) to provide technical assistance to developing countries and to be responsible for the coordination of development activities on the country level, as well as the monitoring and reporting of the progress made in achieving the development goals (UNDP-MX-SpecialFundandTechnicalAssistanceMX.pdf). Specifically, Paragraph 4 of the Resolution states that a single inter-governmental committee of thirty-seven members, to be known as the Governing Council of the UNDP, shall be established to perform the funtions previously exercised by the Governing Council of the Special Fund and the Technical Assistance Committee, including the consideration and approval of projects and programmes and the allocation of funds, and Paragraph 5 requests the Economic and Social Council to elect the members of the Governing Council from among States Members of the United Nations or members of the specialized agencies or of the International Atomic Energy Agency, providing for equitable and balanced representation. Similarly, Paragraph 6 of the Resolution establishes the Inter-Agency Consultative Board of the UNDP to meet under the chairmanship of the Administrator or Co-Administrator. UNDP’s mandate is also influenced by the quadrennial comprehensive policy review of operational activities for development of the United Nations system (QCPR), which provides guidance and direction for UNDP and other UN development agencies (https://www.undp.org/sites/g/files/zskgke326/files/dp2022-17_Annex%203.docx). Its mandate is likewise supported by its Financial Regulations Rules (https://popp.undp.org/document/undp-financial-regulations-and-rules) and by its Programme and Operations Policies and Procedures (https://popp.undp.org/). In addition, the UNDP's mandate is influenced by the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://www.undp.org/sustainable-development-goals/life-on-land?gad_source=1&gclid=CjwKCAiA_tuuBhAUEiwAvxkgTs0LJirFb70iqfh78qtj276maQH96QDdTQEyrmw-FYYh6IPHZd3pDxoCO5IQAvD_BwE).
Defined Objectives: The objectives of UNDP as defined include: to help countries achieve the simultaneous eradication of poverty and significant reduction of inequalities and exclusion (https://www.undp.org/about-us); to support countries in achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and other internationally agreed development goals, through policy and technical support, capacity development, and advocacy; to promote the coordination, efficiency and effectiveness of the UN development system at the country level, through the UN Resident Coordinator system, the Delivering as One approach, the UN Partnership Framework, and the UN Development Group; to report on human development and provide innovative analysis and policy recommendations through the Human Development Report and other publications; and to advocate for development through goodwill ambassadors and partnerships with governments, civil society, the private sector, and other stakeholders (https://www.undp.org/sites/g/files/zskgke326/files/migration/jposc/fa75c5d1f0f92a14a8d8045068322deec92ce947ba03cb3c2f60d8904dbbb5ae.pdf).
Strategies: The UNDP executes its objectives via several strategies: firstly, a four-year Strategic Plan, revised annually by the Executive Board, establishes the UNDP's vision, mission, directions of change, signature solutions, and enablers. This plan, applicable for 2022-2025 (https://www.undp.org/sites/g/files/zskgke326/files/2021-09/UNDP-Strategic-Plan-2022-2025_1.pdf), aligns with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the Paris Agreement, and is structured around “3x6x3” - 3 directions of change, 6 signature solutions, and 3 enablers - to help countries expand human capabilities and development choices, build a more equitable world, and achieve the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). The three directions of change are structural transformation, leaving no one behind, and resilience. The six signature solutions are poverty and inequality, governance, resilience, environment, energy, and gender equality. The three enablers are strategic innovation, digitalization, and development financing. Secondly, an annual integrated budget and workplan, devised by the UNDP and ratified by the Executive Board, detail activities, outputs, indicators, and resources corresponding to each signature solution. The budget and workplan for 2024 is tailored to the countries' needs and stakeholders' priorities (https://www.undp.org/sites/g/files/zskgke326/files/2023-12/dp2024-CRP1_3.pdf). The UNDP also maintains the SDG Accelerator Lab Network, a key aspect of the innovation and digitalisation of the UNDP (https://www.undp.org/acceleratorlabs). UNDP proposes a total budget of $5.4 billion for 2022-2025, comprising $1.4 billion for institutional effectiveness and $4 billion for development activities based on projected income and in alignment with the strategic plan outcomes and outputs. In order to achieve its mandate, UNDP relies entirely on voluntary contributions from UN Member States, multilateral organizations, private sector and other sources, in the form of unrestricted regular resources (core), and contributions earmarked for a specific theme, programme or project (https://www.undp.org/funding). Finally, various agreements, mechanisms, platforms, and initiatives provide an operational framework for implementing the UNDAF, the UNDP Strategic Plan, and the SDGs, addressing poverty and inequality, governance, resilience, environment, energy, and gender equality (https://www.undp.org/sites/g/files/zskgke326/files/2022-07/UNDP%20Strategic%20Plan%202022-2025.pdf).
Inter-Institutional Relationship: UNDP collaborates with various partners to advance sustainable development. It works with governments, providing policy advice, technical assistance, and financial support, based on the UN Development Assistance Framework (UNDAF) and the Country Programme Documents (CPDs) that outline the country-specific priorities and results (https://www.undp.org/our-partners). It coordinates with the UN development system, ensuring coherent and effective support to countries, with its Administrator as the Vice-Chair of the UN Sustainable Development Group, which unites the 40 UN entities that contribute to the attainment of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development at the country level (https://popp.undp.org/policy-page/managing-partnerships). Furthermore, UNDP partners with international financial institutions, mobilizing non-core funding and implementing joint projects, such as the World Bank, the African Development Bank, the Asian Development Bank and the Inter-American Development Bank, with whom UNDP has formal agreements (https://www.undp.org/our-partners). It likewise collaborates with other UN entities, such as the UN Environment Programme, the UN Human Settlements Programme, the UN Office on Drugs and Crime, and the UN Entity for Gender Equality and the Empowerment of Women, on various thematic areas and initiatives, while also engaging with the private sector to foster innovation and entrepreneurship, and with foundations, civil society organizations, and goodwill ambassadors, leveraging their knowledge, networks, and resources, through various platforms and initiatives like the SDG Philanthropy Platform, the Business Call to Action, and the UNDP Innovation Facility (http://web.undp.org/evaluation/documents/directors-desk/papers/UNDPs_partnership_with_private_sector-12_2017.pdf). These partnerships are essential for UNDP to fulfill its strategic plan and contribute to the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.
Vertical Coordination: Vertical coordination within UNDP involves working with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other specialized agencies, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and local authorities. This is achieved through alignment, integration, and coherence for SDG implementation and review. This is structured under the Institutional and Coordination Mechanisms guidance note, which provides information on how countries have adapted their existing institutional and coordination frameworks or established new ones in order to implement the SDGs (https://www.undp.org/sites/g/files/zskgke326/files/publications/Institutional_Coordination_Mechanisms_GuidanceNote.pdf). The UNDP operates through the Executive Board of 36 members, which oversees and supports the activities of UNDP, UNFPA, UNOPS, and UN Women. The UNDP also has a leadership team headed by an Administrator, who is the third highest-ranking official of the United Nations after the United Nations Secretary-General and Deputy Secretary-General (https://www.undp.org/organizational-chart). The UNDP leadership team consists of an Associate Administrator, five Assistant Administrators, a Director of the Bureau of External Relations and Advocacy, a Director of the Bureau of Management Services, and a Chief of Staff (https://www.undp.org/organizational-chart). It has six regional bureaus, each led by a Regional Director, who works closely with the Administrator and the leadership team to implement strategies and programmes across all levels of the organization (https://www.undp.org/organizational-chart). There is also the UN Development Group (UNDG), which unites the 40 UN funds, programmes, specialized agencies, departments, and offices that play a role in development (https://unsceb.org/united-nations-development-group-undg). The UNDG is led by the UNDG Chair, who is the UNDP Administrator, and supported by the UNDG secretariat, which is hosted by UNDP. The UNDG ensures coordination and coherence among the UN entities at the global, regional, and country levels, and supports the Resident Coordinators and UN Country Teams in delivering effective and efficient support to countries (https://unsceb.org/about). The UNDP also has country offices and technical experts that support the UNDP's work in promoting sustainable development, democratic governance, and peacebuilding in 170 countries and territories (https://www.undp.org/acceleratorlabs/our-locations). Additionally, the UNDP hosts the UN Office for South-South Cooperation, which promotes and facilitates South-South and triangular cooperation among countries across the world (https://data.undp.org/insights/south-south-cooperation).
Horizontal Coordination: Horizontal coordination within UNDP involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the development domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, foundations, the academic community, and other UN agencies to ensure that sustainable development goals are achieved in all activities and policies. This coordination is guided by the UNDP Strategic Plan (2022 - 2025) (https://www.undp.org/sites/g/files/zskgke326/files/2021-09/UNDP-Strategic-Plan-2022-2025_1.pdf). For example, UNDP works with the governance sector to promote democratic institutions and human rights (https://www.undp.org/sites/g/files/zskgke326/files/2022-07/Renewed%20Governance%20and%20Peacebuilding%20Framework%20for%20Africa%202022-2025_Summarised%20Document_0.pdf), with the environment sector to address climate change and biodiversity loss (https://www.undp.org/nature/our-work-areas/biodiversity-conservation), with the crisis prevention and recovery sector to support peacebuilding and resilience (https://www.undp.org/tag/crisis-response), or with the poverty reduction and inclusive growth sector to reduce inequalities and enhance social protection (https://www.undp.org/tag/poverty-reduction-and-inequality). Horizontal coordination within UNDP can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the UNDP-UNEP Poverty-Environment Action for Sustainable Development Goals (https://www.undp.org/policy-centre/nairobi/poverty-environment-action-sdgs#:~:text=Poverty%2DEnvironment%20Action%20aims%20at,and%20private%20finance%20and%20investment.), the UNDP-UN Women Joint Programme on Electoral Assistance (https://www.undp.org/publications/preventing-violence-against-women-elections-programming-guide) or the UNDP-UNICEF-UNFPA Joint Programme on Local Governance and Decentralized Service Delivery (http://web.undp.org/evaluation/evaluations/documents/decentralization_final_Report.PDF), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the UN Sustainable Development Group (https://unsdg.un.org/about) or the Global Partnership for Effective Development Cooperation (http://effectivecooperation.org/), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for development sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Human Development Report (http://hdr.undp.org/en) or the Socio-Economic Impact Assessment (https://www.undp.org/coronavirus/socio-economic-impact-covid-19), and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for development issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the UNDP Goodwill Ambassadors and Advocates (https://www.undp.org/goodwill-ambassadors-and-advocates) or the UNDP Shop (https://shop.undp.org/).

Spatial Jurisdiction: The UNEP Secretariat’s authority is global, covering the marine and coastal environment of all regions and subregions of the world (http://undocs.org/en/a/res/2997(XXVII).
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: UNEP is responsible for coordinating the environmental activities of the United Nations and assisting countries in implementing environmentally sound policies and practices (http://undocs.org/en/a/res/2997(XXVII)). This includes addressing global and regional environmental challenges, such as climate change, biodiversity loss, pollution, land degradation, and resource efficiency (https://www.unenvironment.org/about-un-environment/what-we-do). UNEP also provides environmental leadership, science, and solutions for sustainable development, as well as supporting the implementation of multilateral environmental agreements (MEAs) and regional seas conventions and action plans ((https://www.unenvironment.org/about-un-environment/mandate-and-vision).
Source of Jurisdiction: UNEP derives its mandate from the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), establishing it as the leading global environmental authority within the United Nations system. Specifically, Resolution 2997 (XXVII) of the UNGA  provides the legal basis for UNEP’s jurisdiction over the coordination of environmental activities and the promotion of environmental policy across the UN (http://undocs.org/en/a/res/2997(XXVII)). Additionally, UNEP’s jurisdiction is influenced by the Stockholm Declaration on the Human Environment (https://wedocs.unep.org/bitstream/handle/20.500.11822/29567/ELGP1StockD.pdf) and the Rio Declaration on Environment and Development (https://www.un.org/en/development/desa/population/migration/generalassembly/docs/globalcompact/A_CONF.151_26_Vol.I_Declaration.pdf). UNEP also supports the implementation of multilateral environmental agreements (MEAs) and regional seas conventions and action plans, which provide further legal frameworks for UNEP’s jurisdiction over specific environmental issues and regions (https://www.unep.org/about-un-environment/why-does-un-environment-matter/secretariats-and-conventions).
Defined Objectives: According to the Governing Council decision 2/1 of 15 June 1972, the UNEP’s objectives encompass several key functions: providing general policy guidance for the direction and coordination of environmental programmes within the United Nations system (paragraph 2 a); keeping under review the world environmental situation in order to ensure that emerging environmental problems of wide international significance receive appropriate and adequate consideration by Governments (paragraph 2 b); promoting international cooperation in the field of the environment and recommending, as appropriate, policies to this end (paragraph 2 c); providing assistance to developing countries and regions in the implementation of environmental programmes and policies (paragraph 2 d); and initiating and coordinating scientific research and technological development in the field of the environment (paragraph 2 e) (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/RESOLUTION/GEN/NR0/270/27/IMG/NR027027.pdf?OpenElement). Additionally, UNEP is responsible for disseminating information and raising public awareness on environmental issues, facilitating the exchange of information and experience among countries, and providing advisory services and technical assistance to Governments and intergovernmental bodies on environmental matters (https://www.unep.org/news-and-stories). These functions enable UNEP to fulfil its role as the leading global authority on the environment and the principal advocate for environmental action within the United Nations system (https://www.unep.org/who-we-are/about-us).
Strategies: UNEP fulfills its objectives through diverse strategies: firstly, a four-year Medium-Term Strategy (MTS) for the period 2022–2025 set by and adopted by the UN Environmental Assembly (UNEA), adopted in 2021 (https://wedocs.unep.org/bitstream/handle/20.500.11822/35162/Doc3%20Reve1%20EnglishK2100501.pdf?sequence=1&isAllowed=y), aligns with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, the Stockholm Declaration on the Human Environment, and the Rio Declaration on Environment and Development. The MTS defines UNEP’s vision, mission, strategic objectives, core functions, subprogrammes and indicators for measuring progress (https://www.unep.org/about-un-environment/policies-and-strategies). Secondly, a biennial Programme of Work and Budget 2022-2023, based on the MTS, devised by UNEP and ratified by UNEA, details the activities, outputs, resources, and partnerships corresponding to each subprogramme (https://wedocs.unep.org/bitstream/handle/20.500.11822/38040/MTS_PoW2022.pdf?sequence=3&isAllowed=y). UNEP also supports the implementation of multilateral environmental agreements (MEAs) and regional seas conventions and action plans, which provide legal frameworks and operational mechanisms for addressing specific environmental issues and regions (https://www.unep.org/about-un-environment/why-does-un-environment-matter/secretariats-and-conventions). Furthermore, UNEP's work is guided by a number of over-arching strategies, policies and guidelines for ensuring access to information, preventing and responding to misconduct and fraud, enhancing sustainability, and engaging with civil society and the private sector, etc. (https://www.unep.org/about-un-environment/policies-and-strategies). Every two years, UNEA also adopts resolutions and decisions on various environmental topics, which guide UNEP’s implementation of its objectives and mandates (https://www.unep.org/news-and-stories/story/what-you-need-know-about-un-environment-assembly). These strategies collectively ensure effective coordination and promotion of environmental action within the United Nations system and beyond.
Inter-Institutional Relationship: UNEP collaborates with a wide range of organizations to fulfill its objectives. It engages with 193 Member States and various stakeholders through the UN Environment Assembly (UNEA), established in 2013 by resolution 67/251, serving as the highest-level environmental decision-making body (https://undocs.org/A/Res/67/251). As the primary environmental authority within the UN system, UNEP's relationship with the UN is grounded in resolution 2997 (XXVII), which established UNEP in 1972 (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/RESOLUTION/GEN/NR0/270/27/IMG/NR027027.pdf?OpenElement). Additionally, UNEP supports multilateral environmental agreements (MEAs) and regional seas conventions and action plans, providing legal and operational frameworks for specific environmental issues and regions, as stipulated in resolution 2997 (XXVII), paragraph 2 c (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/RESOLUTION/GEN/NR0/270/27/IMG/NR027027.pdf?OpenElement), and resolution 58/240, paragraph 4 of the UN General Assembly (https://www.un.org/en/development/desa/population/migration/generalassembly/docs/globalcompact/A_RES_58_240.pdf). It also collaborates with UN specialized agencies like FAO, IMO, and IOC, and other organizations such as ISA, ITLOS, and RFMOs, addressing shared environmental concerns. Moreover, UNEP contributes to the Regular Process for Global Reporting and Assessment of the Marine Environment, offering data on marine environmental conditions, as recognized in resolution 57/141, paragraph 6 (https://www.un.org/en/development/desa/population/migration/generalassembly/docs/globalcompact/A_RES_57_141.pdf).
Vertical Coordination: Vertical coordination within UNEP involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other specialized agencies, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and local authorities. This is structured under the Relationship with the United Nations and Inter-Agency Cooperation section of the Governing Council decision 2/1, specifically in paragraphs 3-5. UNEP operates through the UN Environment Assembly (UNEA) of all the members, a Committee of Permanent Representatives of 58 members, and a secretariat headed by an Executive Director (paragraphs 6-8) (http://wedocs.unep.org/bitstream/handle/20.500.11822/17307/K1607113_UNEPEA2_RES1E.docx?sequence=5&isAllowed=y). UNEP also has six regional offices and various thematic divisions and centres (paragraph 9) (http://wedocs.unep.org/bitstream/handle/20.500.11822/17307/K1607113_UNEPEA2_RES1E.docx?sequence=5&isAllowed=y). UNEP supports the implementation of multilateral environmental agreements (MEAs) and regional seas conventions and action plans, which provide legal frameworks and operational mechanisms for addressing specific environmental issues and regions (paragraph 10) (http://wedocs.unep.org/bitstream/handle/20.500.11822/17307/K1607113_UNEPEA2_RES1E.docx?sequence=5&isAllowed=y). UNEP also chairs the Environment Management Group (EMG), a system-wide coordination body established to enhance inter-agency cooperation on environmental issues, and builds on close cooperation with the UN Development Group (UNDG) and the UN’s coordination mechanisms of the Chief Executives Board (CEB) (paragraph 11). (https://wedocs.unep.org/bitstream/handle/20.500.11822/12698/CASM_web.pdf?sequence=1&amp%3BisAllowed=)
Horizontal Coordination: Horizontal coordination within UNEP involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the environmental domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, scientific community, and other UN agencies. This coordination is structured under  paragraph 3 of resolution 2997 (XXVII) of the General Assembly (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/RESOLUTION/GEN/NR0/270/27/IMG/NR027027.pdf?OpenElement) (https://www.unep.org/resources/report/functions-un-environment-programme). The UNEP provides leadership and encourages partnership in caring for the environment by inspiring, informing, and enabling nations and peoples to improve their quality of life without compromising that of future generations (https://www.unep.org/news-and-stories/press-release/buildings-breakthrough-global-push-near-zero-emission-and-resilient). The UNEP also monitors, assesses and reports on the state of the global environment, develops international environmental agreements and norms, supports the implementation of environmental policies and laws, and promotes the integration of environmental considerations into social and economic development1. The UNEP facilitates the participation of major groups and stakeholders in its work, and enhances cooperation and coordination within the UN system on environmental matters (https://www.unenvironment.org/about-un-environment/who-we-are/our-mission).

Spatial Jurisdiction: UN-Habitat's jurisdiction is not limited to any specific geographical area, but rather covers all human settlements and sustainable urban development issues worldwide with presence in more than 90 countries in five continents and a focus on cities and towns, as well as rural and peri-urban areas (https://unhabitat.org/about-us). UN-Habitat does not have a direct jurisdiction on oceans and maritime zones, but supports the implementation of the SDGs and other international agendas that relate to urbanization and human settlements.
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: UN-Habitat is responsible for promoting socially and environmentally sustainable towns and cities, with adequate housing, infrastructure, and basic services for all (https://unhabitat.org/about-us). This includes addressing urbanization and human settlement issues such as poverty, inequality, climate change, fragility and conflict. UN-Habitat also provides knowledge, policy advice, technical assistance and collaborative action for transformative change in cities and communities, reducing spatial inequality and leaving no one and no place behind (https://unhabitat.org/about-us). UN-Habitat works in seven focus areas: urban legislation, land, and governance; urban planning and design; urban economy; urban basic services; housing and slum upgrading; risk reduction and rehabilitation; and research and capacity development (https://unhabitat.org/goals-and-strategies-of-un-habitat).
Source of Jurisdiction:
UN-Habitat derives its mandate from several UN General Assembly resolutions, which established UN-Habitat as the focal point for all urbanization and human settlement matters within the UN system. Specifically, resolution 3327 (XXIX) of 1975 (https://undocs.org/en/A/RES/3327(XXIX)) created the United Nations Habitat and Human Settlements Foundation (UNHHSF), the first official UN body dedicated to urbanization. Resolution 32/162 of 1977 (https://undocs.org/en/A/RES/32/162) transformed the Committee on Housing, Building, and Planning into the Commission on Human Settlements, an intergovernmental body serviced by the Centre for Human Settlements (also known as “Habitat”). Resolution 56/206 of 2002 (https://undocs.org/en/A/RES/56/206) merged the UNHHSF, the Commission on Human Settlements, and Habitat into UN-Habitat, a fully-fledged UN programme managed by its own secretariat and headed by its own Executive Director. UN-Habitat's mandate is also shaped by the outcomes of the three UN conferences on human settlements: Habitat I in Vancouver (1976), Habitat II in Istanbul (1996), and Habitat III in Quito (2016). These conferences resulted in the adoption of the Vancouver Declaration on Human Settlements (https://unhabitat.org/sites/default/files/download-manager-files/1396335538wpdm_Vancouver_Declaration_EN.pdf), the Istanbul Declaration on Human Settlements (https://unhabitat.org/sites/default/files/download-manager-files/Istanbul_Declaration_EN.pdf) and the Habitat Agenda (https://unhabitat.org/sites/default/files/download-manager-files/Habitat_Agenda_EN.pdf), and the New Urban Agenda (https://unhabitat.org/sites/default/files/download-manager-files/The%20New%20Urban%20Agenda%20_%20Revised%20Low%20Res.pdf), respectively. These documents define the global standards and principles for achieving sustainable urban development and adequate shelter for all. UN-Habitat's jurisdiction is also influenced by the alignment of its work with other internationally agreed upon development goals, such as the Sustainable Development Goals (2015) (https://unhabitat.org/sustainable-development-goals), and the Paris Agreement on Climate Change (2015) (https://unhabitat.org/climate-change).
