These goals provide further legal frameworks and targets for UN-Habitat's jurisdiction over specific urban issues and domains. UN-Habitat's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the Framework Convention on Climate Change (https://unfccc.int/files/essential_background/background_publications_htmlpdf/application/pdf/conveng.pdf), the Vienna Convention on the Protection of the Ozone Layer (https://ozone.unep.org/sites/default/files/2019-12/The%20Ozone%20Treaties%20EN%20-%20WEB_final.pdf), and the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction (https://unfccc.int/sites/default/files/resource/UNDRR%20Presentation_Sendai%20Framework-GGA6%20%281%29.pdf).

Defined Objectives: According to the annex of UN General Assembly Rsolution 3327 (XXIX) (https://undocs.org/en/A/RES/3327(XXIX)), the United Nations Habitat and Human Settlements Foundation's objectives include the following key aspects: (1) Assisting in strengthening national environmental programmes relating to human settlements, particularly in the developing countries, through the provision of seed capital and the extension of the necessary technical and financial assistance to permit an effective mobilization of domestic resources for human habitat and environmental design and improvement of human settlements (paragraph 1 a); (2) Stimulating innovative approaches to pre-investment, pre-project and financing strategies of human settlements activities, while drawing on the accumulated practical experience of both the public and private sectors for mobilization of financial resources for human habitat and human settlements projects (paragraph 1 a i); (3) Organizing technical assistance services in human settlements and human habitat management, including training facilities and human habitat projects (paragraph 1 a ii); and (4) Promoting the adaptation and transfer of appropriate scientific and technical knowledge on human settlements projects (paragraph 1 a iii).
Strategies: The UN-Habitat executes its objectives via several strategies. Its programmes and initiatives are currently guided by a four-year Strategic Plan (https://unhabitat.org/sites/default/files/documents/2019-09/strategic_plan_2020-2023.pdf), endorsed by the Committee of Permanent Representatives and approved by the UN-Habitat Assembly, which sets out the vision, mission, objective, domains of change, drivers of change, and organizational performance enablers of the organization. This plan, applicable for 2020-2023, aligns with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, the New Urban Agenda, and other global frameworks (https://unhabitat.org/about-us/our-strategy). Some of the specific strategies in place for UN-Habitat to achieve its objectives and mandates according to the Strategic Plan include: (1) Refocusing its niche as the thought leader and go-to agency that sets the global discourse and agenda on sustainable urban development, (2) Aligning its work with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, the New Urban Agenda, and other relevant global frameworks and commitments, (3) Delivering four domain-specific goals that address the key challenges and opportunities of urbanization: reduced spatial inequality and poverty, enhanced shared prosperity, strengthened climate action, and effective urban crises prevention and response, (4) Integrating cross-cutting themes such as social inclusion, resilience, and safety throughout its programmes and projects, (5) Strengthening its partnerships with various stakeholders, including national and local governments, civil society, private sector, academia, and media, and (6) Improving its organizational effectiveness by enhancing its governance, accountability, transparency, innovation, and resource mobilization.  According to the document, the estimated budget for the strategic plan for 2020-2023 is $1.2 billion, of which $500 million is expected to come from the regular budget and $700 million from extrabudgetary sources. The budget is based on the projected resource requirements for the implementation of the four domains of change, the drivers of change and the organizational performance enablers.
Inter-Institutional Relationship: UN-Habitat establishes and strengthens strategic relationships with a diverse range of partners at national, regional, and international levels, including political actors, civil society, professional organizations, and the private sector (https://unhabitat.org/partnerships-at-un-habitat). It works with partners through the World Urban Forum (https://wuf.unhabitat.org/), multi-stakeholder thematic partnerships, and advisory boards. These partnerships include the Cities and Climate Change Initiative (https://unhabitat.org/initiative/cities-and-climate-change-initiative), Gender Equality Network (https://unhabitat.org/network/gender-equality-network), Global Alliance for Urban Crisis (https://unhabitat.org/network/global-alliance-for-urban-crises#:~:text=The%20Global%20Alliance%20for%20Urban,humanitarian%20crises%20in%20urban%20settings.), Global Housing Strategy Platform (https://unhabitat.org/programme/global-housing-strategy-making-housing-affordable-for-all), Global Land Tool Network (GLTN), (https://unhabitat.org/programme/global-land-tool-network-gltn) and others. UN-Habitat also services the World Urban Campaign, an advocacy and partnership platform to raise awareness about positive urban change (https://unhabitat.org/partnerships-at-un-habitat). Furthermore, UN-Habitat partners with sister agencies across the UN, such as UNDESA, UNDP, and UNRCOs, as well as with a large network of local and national partners across the globe to advance SDG localization (https://sdgs.un.org/un-system-sdg-implementation/united-nations-habitat-un-habitat-44150).
Vertical Coordination: Vertical coordination within UN-Habitat involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the General Assembly, the Economic and Social Council, other UN agencies, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and local authorities. This is achieved through policy guidance, oversight, reporting, and partnership. Multilevel governance of UN-Habitat is structured under the resolution A/RES/56/206, specifically in Article IA (paragraphs 1-8) and Article 1B  (paragraphs 1-4). UN-Habitat is structured in three main bodies: (1) The Governing Council (GC), whose role is to set the major strategic and policy directions for UN-Habitat and approve its programmes and budget. It is composed of 58 member states that are elected by the UN General Assembly's Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC) (https://unhabitat.org/governing-council). The Governing Council meets every two years, (2) The UN-Habitat Secretariat, whose task is to ensure the execution of the Governing Council’s decisions and to translate these into specific strategies, programmes and initiatives. The Secretariat is the executive body of the organization. Headquartered in Nairobi, Kenya, it acts as the focal point for all urban and human settlement matters within the United Nations system (https://unhabitat.org/our-secretariat), and (3) The Committee of Permanent Representatives (CPR), which ensures that the Governing Council’s decisions are enacted by the Secretariat within the set framework. It has a supervising role and represents the Governing Council at the Secretariat to address issues arising between the biennial Governing Council meetings. The CPR is composed of ambassadors or foreign envoys of member states accredited to UN-Habitat (https://unhabitat.org/governance/committee-of-permanent-representatives).The UN-Habitat operates through the Governing Council of 58 members, elected by the Economic and Social Council, and a secretariat headed by an Executive Director, elected by the General Assembly . The UN-Habitat also has the Urban Forum as a non-legislative technical forum (https://unhabitat.org/sites/default/files/2023/02/2300621e.pdf), and the Advisory Committee of Local Authorities as an advisory body to the Executive Director (https://unhabitat.org/network/united-nations-advisory-committee-of-local-authorities-unacla#:~:text=UNACLA%20was%20established%20by%20the,implementation%20of%20the%20Habitat%20Agenda.). The UN-Habitat assists members in the implementation of the Habitat Agenda and the Declaration on Cities and Other Human Settlements in the New Millennium, and provides technical cooperation and assistance upon request (https://unhabitat.org/sites/default/files/2022/11/english_1.pdf). UN-Habitat's work is organised around four domains of change, each overseen by a Director who works closely with the Executive Director to implement strategies and programmes across all levels of the Programme (https://sdgs.un.org/un-system-sdg-implementation/united-nations-human-settlements-programme-un-habitat-24511). Also, a network of regional offices and country offices supports UN-Habitat's work in promoting sustainable urban development and human settlements as an integral part of regional and national development policies (https://unhabitat.org/where-we-are).
Horizontal Coordination: Horizontal coordination within UN-Habitat involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the urban development and human settlements domain, such as national and local governments, civil society, private sector, academia, and other UN agencies to ensure sustainable urbanization. This coordination is presently guided by the UN-Habitat Strategic Plan for 2020-2023 (https://unhabitat.org/sites/default/files/documents/2019-09/strategic_plan_2020-2023.pdf). For example, UN-Habitat works with the housing sector to promote adequate and affordable housing for all (https://unhabitat.org/5-housing-and-slum-upgrading), with the transport sector to enhance urban mobility and accessibility (https://unhabitat.org/topic/mobility-and-transport), with the health sector to support urban health and well-being (https://unhabitat.org/topic/urban-health), or with the environment sector to strengthen climate action and improve urban environment (https://unhabitat.org/climate-action). Horizontal coordination within UN-Habitat can take various forms, such as: (1) Global flagship programmes, which are integrated and multisectoral programmes that aim to achieve impact at scale in the four domains of change of UN-Habitat, namely spatial inequality and poverty, shared prosperity, climate action and urban environment, and urban crisis prevention and response. They are designed and implemented in partnership with other sectors and stakeholders, such as UNDP, UNEP, UNICEF, WHO, World Bank, and others. Examples of global flagship programmes are the Global Public Space Programme (https://unhabitat.org/programme/global-public-space-programme) or the Participatory Slum Upgrading Programme (https://unhabitat.org/programme/the-participatory-slum-upgrading-programme-psup), (2) Interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, which are mechanisms that facilitate coordination, information exchange, and joint action among different sectors and stakeholders on urban issues and policies. UN-Habitat participates in and leads several of these mechanisms, such as the UN Sustainable Development Group (https://unsdg.un.org/about), or the UN Task Team on the New Urban Agenda (https://habitat3.org/the-new-urban-agenda/preparatory-process/united-nations-task-team/), (3) Guidelines, standards, and tools for urban sector engagement through products that provide evidence-based guidance, technical norms, and practical solutions for urban sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the International Guidelines on Urban and Territorial Planning (https://unhabitat.org/international-guidelines-on-urban-and-territorial-planning) or the City Prosperity Initiative (https://unhabitat.org/knowledge/city-prosperity-initiative), and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for urban issues and policies through activities that aim to influence and inform other sectors and stakeholders about the importance and potential of sustainable urbanization and human settlements, such as the World Habitat Day (https://unhabitat.org/world-habitat-day) or the World’s Cities Report (https://unhabitat.org/wcr/).

Spatial Jurisdiction: UNIDO’s jurisdiction is global, encompassing the industrial development of its member states and regions. This includes a focus on developing countries and countries with economies in transition, with authority extending to the promotion and acceleration of industrial cooperation among these states, covering key sectors and technologies (https://www.unido.org/sites/default/files/files/2020-11/19-12162_UNIDO_Constitution_ebook.pdf).
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: UNIDO is responsible for the industrial development of its member states and regions, such as manufacturing, agro-industry, energy, environment, and innovation. This includes supporting industrial policy and strategy, enhancing productivity and competitiveness, fostering inclusive and sustainable industrialisation, and strengthening international cooperation and partnerships. UNIDO also offers technical assistance, capacity building, knowledge sharing, and advocacy for industrial development, as well as contributing to the achievement of the UN’s development agenda and the Sustainable Development Goals (https://www.unido.org/sites/default/files/files/2020-11/19-12162_UNIDO_Constitution_ebook.pdf).
Source of Jurisdiction: UNIDO derives its mandate from its own Constitution, which entered into force in 1985 (https://www.unido.org/sites/default/files/files/2020-11/19-12162_UNIDO_Constitution_ebook.pdf). The Constitution provides the legal basis for UNIDO’s jurisdiction over the industrial development of its member states and regions, as well as the promotion and acceleration of industrial cooperation among these states. Additionally, UNIDO’s jurisdiction is influenced by the 2013 Lima Declaration (https://www.unido.org/sites/default/files/files/2018-12/UNIDO_GC15_Lima_Declaration.pdf) and the 2019 Abu Dhabi Declaration (https://www.unido.org/sites/default/files/files/2019-11/UNIDO_Abu_Dhabi_Declaration_1.pdf), which reaffirm UNIDO’s role as the specialized agency of the UN for inclusive and sustainable industrial development. UNIDO also supports the implementation of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the Sustainable Development Goals, which provide further frameworks for UNIDO’s jurisdiction over specific industrial sectors and issues (https://www.unido.org/sites/default/files/2017-05/IDB.45_12_E_UNIDO_and_the_2030_Agenda_for_Sustainable_Development_V1702655_0.pdf).
Defined Objectives: According to Chapter I of the Constitution of the UNIDO, the Organization's objectives are to promote and accelerate industrial development in the developing countries, with a view to assisting in the establishment of a new international economic order, and to promote industrial development and cooperation on global, regional and national, as well as on sectoral levels (Article 1). To fulfil these objectives, the Organization shall perform various functions, such as encouraging and assisting the developing countries in their industrialization efforts, initiating and coordinating the activities of the United Nations system in the field of industrial development, creating and developing new concepts and approaches for industrial development, providing a forum and an instrument for international cooperation and dialogue on industrial matters, serving as a clearing-house for industrial information, promoting and encouraging the development, transfer and use of industrial technology, organizing and supporting industrial training programmes, assisting in the exploitation, conservation and transformation of natural resources, developing special measures for the least-developed and other disadvantaged developing countries, and assisting in obtaining external financing for industrial projects (Article 2). These functions enable the Organization to play the central role in and be responsible for reviewing and promoting the coordination of all activities of the United Nations system in the field of industrial development, in conformity with the responsibilities of the Economic and Social Council under the Charter of the United Nations and with the applicable relationship agreements (https://www.unido.org/sites/default/files/files/2020-11/19-12162_UNIDO_Constitution_ebook.pdf).
Strategies:
UNIDO executes its objectives via several strategies: firstly, a four-year Medium-Term Programme Framework (MTPF), revised biennially by the Industrial Development Board, which defines the strategic guidance, directions, and priorities of the Organization (https://www.unido.org/sites/default/files/unido-publications/2023-02/2022-2025-MEDIUM-TERM-PROGRAMME-FRAMEWORK-en.pdf). This framework, applicable for 2022-2025, aligns with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the Sustainable Development Goals, detailed in document IDB.48/14 (https://downloads.unido.org/ot/21/32/21329747/PBC.37_14_E_United%20Nations%20Development%20System%20reform_V2101499.pdf?_ga=2.15564982.1264381354.1702429546-1974414734.1702429546). Secondly, a biennial programme and budgets, prepared by the Secretariat and approved by the General Conference, which specify the outputs, indicators, and resources for each focus area of expertise and core function of the Organization. The current programme and budgets for 2022-2023 reflect the needs and expectations of the Member States and the development partners, as outlined in document GC.20/5 (https://downloads.unido.org/ot/20/98/20989988/PBC.37_5_E_Programme%20and%20budgets%202022-2023_V2101337.pdf?_ga=2.83258390.1264381354.1702429546-1974414734.1702429546). It also maintains the Country Programme Frameworks (CPFs) and the Regional Programme Frameworks (RPFs) established under the MTPF, which provide the operational framework for implementing the Organization’s mandate at the country and regional levels (https://www.unido.org/sites/default/files/unido-publications/2023-02/2022-2025-MEDIUM-TERM-PROGRAMME-FRAMEWORK-en.pdf). In addition, UNIDO is operationalising  the Third Industrial Development Decade for Africa
(2016–2025) (IDDA III)  through the Roadmap Implementation of the Third Industrial Development Decade for Africa (https://www.unido.org/sites/default/files/files/2018-09/IDDA3_Roadmap_0.pdf) derived from General Assembly resolution 70/293 (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N16/234/02/PDF/N1623402.pdf?OpenElement), to drive Africa on a path towards inclusive and sustainable industrial development. Likewise, UNIDO maintains various partnerships, platforms, initiatives, and networks that provide the collaborative framework for enhancing the impact and effectiveness of the Organization’s interventions, addressing cross-cutting issues such as gender, youth, innovation, and digitalization (https://www.unido.org/about-us/partnerships).
Inter-Institutional Relationship: UNIDO collaborates with various organizations to achieve its objectives and mandates. It works with 170 Member States and various stakeholders through the General Conference, the Industrial Development Board, and the Programme and Budget Committee, which are the policymaking organs of the Organization, as stipulated in Chapter III of the Constitution of UNIDO (https://www.unido.org/sites/default/files/files/2020-11/19-12162_UNIDO_Constitution_ebook.pdf). As a specialized agency of the UN, UNIDO's relationship with the UN is based on the Agreement between the United Nations and the United Nations Industrial Development Organization, which entered into force in 1985, as detailed in resolution 40/180 of the UN General Assembly (https://www.unido.org/sites/default/files/2010-10/UN-UNIDO%20Relationship%20Agreement_1985_CP-2_0.pdf?OpenElement). It also partners with other UN entities, such as FAO, IAEA, ILO, UNCTAD, UNDP, UNEP, UNESCO, UNFCCC, and WHO (https://www.unido.org/our-focus/cross-cutting-services/partnerships-prosperity/partnerships-international-development-organizations).)  international financial institutions, such as the African Development Bank, the European Investment Bank and the World Bank (https://www.unido.org/sites/default/files/files/2018-03/FDI25_Web_15March.pdf), as well as other intergovernmental organizations, such as the African Union, the European Union, the Organization of American States, and the Organization of Islamic Cooperation, addressing common industrial challenges and opportunities (https://www.unido.org/sites/default/files/files/2021-06/PFC%20Newsletter%2010_31May2021.pdf). Moreover, UNIDO engages with the private sector, civil society, academia, and media, fostering inclusive and sustainable industrialization (https://www.unido.org/search?keys=private+sector+partnership).
Vertical Coordination: Vertical coordination within UNIDO involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other specialized agencies, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and local authorities. This is structured under the Relationship with the United Nations section of the Constitution of UNIDO, specifically in Article 9. UNIDO operates through the General Conference of all the members, the Industrial Development Board of 53 members, and the Secretariat headed by a Director General (Articles 5-8) (https://www.unido.org/sites/default/files/files/2020-11/19-12162_UNIDO_Constitution_ebook.pdf). In various countries and regions, UNIDO operates  30 field officers, 19 Regional Hub, 4  Liaison Offices, 10 Investment and Technology Promotion Offices, and 2 Project Offices (https://www.unido.org/who-we-are/unido-worldwide). UNIDO supports the implementation of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the Sustainable Development Goals, which provide the global framework and targets for addressing development challenges and opportunities (https://www.unido.org/our-focus-advancing-economic-competitiveness/achieving-sdgs). UNIDO also partners with other UN entities, such as FAO, IAEA, ILO, UNCTAD, UNDP, UNEP, UNESCO, UNFCCC, and WHO, as well as other intergovernmental organizations, such as the African Union, the European Union, the Organization of American States, and the Organization of Islamic Cooperation, addressing common industrial challenges and opportunities (https://www.unido.org/our-focus/cross-cutting-services/partnerships-prosperity/partnerships-international-development-organizations).
Horizontal Coordination: Horizontal coordination within UNIDO involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the industrial development domain, such as governments, private sector, civil society, academia, and other UN agencies. This coordination is structured under the Objectives and Functions section of the UNIDO Constitution, specifically in Articles 1-2 (https://www.unido.org/sites/default/files/files/2020-11/19-12162_UNIDO_Constitution_ebook.pdf). The UNIDO promotes and accelerates inclusive and sustainable industrial development in developing countries and economies in transition, with a view to assisting in the establishment of a new international economic order (https://sdgs.un.org/sites/default/files/publications/2021Introduction%20to%20UNIDO-%20Inclusive%20and%20Sustainable%20Industrial%20Development.pdf). The UNIDO also initiates, coordinates and follows up the activities of the UN system in the field of industrial development, and acts as a forum and instrument for industrial cooperation and partnership (https://sdgs.un.org/sites/default/files/publications/2021Introduction%20to%20UNIDO-%20Inclusive%20and%20Sustainable%20Industrial%20Development.pdf). The UNIDO provides technical assistance, policy advice, and capacity-building services to its Member States, and supports the development, transfer and adaptation of industrial technology. The UNIDO gives due regard to the specific needs and priorities of the least developed countries, as well as to the principle of equitable geographical distribution (https://www.unido.org/sites/default/files/files/2019-09/Upscaling%20TC_Sept%202019.pdf).

Institution: United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR)
Spatial Jurisdiction: UNDRR's jurisdiction is global, covering all regions and countries that are exposed to disaster risk and losses (https://www.undrr.org/about-undrr/where-we-work). This includes a focus on least developed countries and small island developing states, with authority reaching up to the low water mark of these states, covering key coastal and inland areas and communities (https://www.undrr.org/disaster-risk-reduction-least-developed-countries).
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: The UNDRR Secretariat is responsible for preventing new, and reducing existing disaster risk (https://www.undrr.org/our-work/our-impact). This includes addressing disaster risk reduction issues, such as governance, resilience, preparedness, recovery, and financing (https://www.undrr.org/our-work). UNDRR also provides technical support, guidance and training, knowledge management, advocacy and communication, and partnership development for disaster risk reduction, as well as supporting the monitoring and review of the Sendai Framework and the Sustainable Development Goals (https://www.undrr.org/media/87504/download?startDownload=true).
Source of Jurisdiction: UNDRR derives its mandate from the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), establishing it as the focal point for disaster risk reduction within the United Nations system. Specifically, Resolution 56/195 of the UNGA provides the legal basis for UNDRR's jurisdiction over the coordination and guidance of disaster risk reduction activities and the implementation of the International Strategy for Disaster Reduction  (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N01/492/61/PDF/N0149261.pdf?OpenElement). Additionally, UNDRR's jurisdiction is influenced by the Hyogo Framework for Action 2005-2015 (https://www.unisdr.org/files/1037_hyogoframeworkforactionenglish.pdf) and the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015-2030 (https://www.preventionweb.net/files/43291_sendaiframeworkfordrren.pdf?_gl=1*449ih*_ga*Nzc0NjIwODE4LjE3MDM1ODgxNDM.*_ga_D8G5WXP6YM*MTcwMzU4ODE1Mi4xLjEuMTcwMzU5MDU3My4wLjAuMA..). UNDRR also supports the implementation of other relevant international agreements and frameworks, such as the Paris Agreement on climate change and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://www.undrr.org/media/47679/download?startDownload=true), which provide further legal frameworks for UNDRR's jurisdiction over specific disaster risk reduction issues and goals (https://www.undrr.org/our-work).
Defined Objectives: According to the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015-2030, the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) has been mandated to fulfil several objectives (https://www.preventionweb.net/files/43291_sendaiframeworkfordrren.pdf?_gl=1*2d1si0*_ga*Nzc0NjIwODE4LjE3MDM1ODgxNDM.*_ga_D8G5WXP6YM*MTcwMzU4ODE1Mi4xLjEuMTcwMzU5MTQ1NC4wLjAuMA..), such as: supporting the implementation, follow-up and review of the Framework, including through the development of coherent and actionable guidance for its implementation (paragraph 48 a); supporting the coordination of disaster risk reduction in the United Nations system (paragraph 48 b); supporting the coherence of the disaster risk reduction and climate change agendas (paragraph 48 c); convening the Global Platform for Disaster Risk Reduction and supporting the organization of regional platforms for disaster risk reduction (paragraph 48 d); supporting the development of national and local disaster risk reduction strategies and plans, and facilitating their integration into relevant development and sectoral plans and policies (paragraph 48 e); supporting the development and strengthening of national and local mechanisms and capacities for monitoring and reviewing progress and levels of implementation of the Framework (paragraph 48 f); and supporting the development of indicators and methodologies for the assessment of disaster risk and disaster risk reduction (paragraph 48 g). These objectives enable the UNDRR to fulfil its role as the focal point in the United Nations system for the coordination of disaster risk reduction and the implementation of the Framework (https://www.un.org/en/development/desa/population/migration/generalassembly/docs/globalcompact/A_RES_69_283.pdf).
Strategies: The UNDRR executes its objectives via several strategies: firstly, a four-year Strategic Framework, revised annually by the General Assembly, which establishes the UNDRR's vision, mission, strategic objectives, expected accomplishments, and indicators of achievement (https://www.undrr.org/media/49267/download?startDownload=true). This framework, applicable for 2022-2025, aligns with the Sendai Framework and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, detailed in document A/76/6 (Sect. 23) (https://undocs.org/en/A/76/6(Sect.23)). Secondly, a biennial programme plan and budget, devised by the secretariat and approved by the General Assembly, detail activities, outputs, resources, and performance information corresponding to each strategic objective. The current programme plan and budget for 2022-2023 are tailored to the Member States' needs and stakeholders' priorities, as outlined in document A/76/6/Add.1 (https://undocs.org/en/A/76/6/Add.1). It also maintains the Sendai Framework Monitor, a key tool for the monitoring and review of the Sendai Framework and the disaster risk reduction-related Sustainable Development Goals (https://sendaimonitor.undrr.org/). Finally, various agreements, mechanisms, platforms, and initiatives provide an operational framework for coordinating and guiding disaster risk reduction across the United Nations system and beyond, addressing governance, resilience, preparedness, recovery, and financing, with key instruments listed here (https://www.undrr.org/what-we-do)." Through the revised United Nations plan of action on disaster risk reduction for resilience, the UNDRR executes its commitments to the implementation of the Sendai Framework and integrated approach to the achievement of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://www.preventionweb.net/files/49076_unplanofaction.pdf).
Inter-Institutional Relationship: UNDRR collaborates with various organizations to implement the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015-2030 (https://www.undrr.org/implementing-sendai-framework/partners-and-stakeholders/multistakeholder-initiatives-and-partnershipsf). It works with the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), and the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) to provide technical support and guidance to Member States and other stakeholders on disaster risk reduction, as stated in paragraph 48 (a) of the Sendai Framework (https://www.preventionweb.net/files/43291_sendaiframeworkfordrren.pdf?_gl=1*2d1si0*_ga*Nzc0NjIwODE4LjE3MDM1ODgxNDM.*_ga_D8G5WXP6YM*MTcwMzU4ODE1Mi4xLjEuMTcwMzU5MTQ1NC4wLjAuMA..). It also coordinates with the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD), and the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) to ensure coherence and synergies among the relevant instruments and frameworks, as stated in paragraph 48 (b) of the Sendai Framework (https://www.preventionweb.net/files/43291_sendaiframeworkfordrren.pdf?_gl=1*2d1si0*_ga*Nzc0NjIwODE4LjE3MDM1ODgxNDM.*_ga_D8G5WXP6YM*MTcwMzU4ODE1Mi4xLjEuMTcwMzU5MTQ1NC4wLjAuMA..). Additionally, UNDRR engages with the scientific and technological community, the private sector, civil society, and other relevant actors to foster partnerships and innovation for disaster risk reduction, as stated in paragraph 48 (c) and (d) of the Sendai Framework (https://www.preventionweb.net/files/43291_sendaiframeworkfordrren.pdf?_gl=1*2d1si0*_ga*Nzc0NjIwODE4LjE3MDM1ODgxNDM.*_ga_D8G5WXP6YM*MTcwMzU4ODE1Mi4xLjEuMTcwMzU5MTQ1NC4wLjAuMA..). Moreover, UNDRR supports the Global Platform for Disaster Risk Reduction, the regional and subregional platforms for disaster risk reduction, and the thematic platforms, as well as the United Nations Scientific and Technical Advisory Group, to facilitate dialogue, cooperation, and knowledge-sharing on disaster risk reduction, as stated in paragraph 48 of the Sendai Framework (https://www.un.org/en/development/desa/population/migration/generalassembly/docs/globalcompact/A_RES_69_283.pdf).
Vertical Coordination: Vertical coordination within UNDRR involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other specialized agencies, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and local authorities (https://www.undrr.org/implementing-sendai-framework/partners-and-stakeholders/un-system). This is achieved through coordination, guidance, and support. This is structured under the Institutional Arrangements section of the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015-2030, specifically in paragraphs 48-48 (https://www.preventionweb.net/files/43291_sendaiframeworkfordrren.pdf?_gl=1*2d1si0*_ga*Nzc0NjIwODE4LjE3MDM1ODgxNDM.*_ga_D8G5WXP6YM*MTcwMzU4ODE1Mi4xLjEuMTcwMzU5MTQ1NC4wLjAuMA..). The UNDRR operates through the General Assembly of all the members, the Economic and Social Council, and a secretariat headed by a Special Representative of the Secretary-General (paragraph 48). The UNDRR also has regional and sub-regional offices, thematic platforms, and a Scientific and Technical Advisory Group (paragraph 48). The UNDRR assists members in the development and implementation of national and local disaster risk reduction strategies and plans, and provides technical support and guidance upon request (paragraph 48 e and f). UNDRR's work is organized around five regions, each overseen by a Regional Director who works closely with the Special Representative of the Secretary-General to implement strategies and programmes across all levels of the Organization (https://www.undrr.org/about-undrr/where-we-work). There are also the Regional Platforms, multi-stakeholder forums that reflect the commitment of governments to improve coordination and implementation of disaster risk reduction activities while linking to international and national efforts (https://www.undrr.org/implementing-sendai-framework/regional-platforms), and National Platforms, serving as mechanisms for coordination and policy guidance on disaster risk reduction that are multisectoral and interdisciplinary in nature, with public, private and civil society participation involving all concerned entities within a country (https://www.undrr.org/terminology/national-platform-disaster-risk-reduction). A  "UNDRR Stakeholder Engagement Mechanism" (UNDRR-SEM) has been setup to  leverage the convening and advocacy powers of the  Major Groups and other stakeholders (MGoS) and server as the main interloculator betwwen the UNDRR and other stakeholder groups for the integration of disaster risk reduction into the broader 2030 Agenda (https://www.undrr.org/implementing-sendai-framework/partners-and-stakeholders/stakeholder-engagement-mechanism). Likewise, UNDRR coordinates two mechanisms related to the UN Plan of Action: the high-level UN Senior Leadership Group on Disaster Risk Reduction for Resilience and the UN Disaster Risk Reduction Focal Points Group at the working level (https://www.undrr.org/implementing-sendai-framework/partners-and-stakeholders/un-system). Also, a network of country offices and technical experts supports the UNDRR's work in coordinating and guiding disaster risk reduction as an integral part of regional and national development policies (https://www.undrr.org/where-we-work). Additionally, UNDRR operates the Global Education and Training Institute in Incheon, Republic of Korea, and the Kobe Office in Japan (https://www.undrr.org/who-we-are). Besides the Special Representative of the Secretary-General, at the UNDRR headquarters, there is a clear line of duty within the leadership team comprising of a Deputy Special Representative of the Secretary-General and 7 Directors with portfolios focusing on different aspects in accordance with the UNDRR's mandate (https://www.undrr.org/who-we-are). In addition, UNDRR coordinates with the European Union and its agencies and is the host organization and partner of the Making Cities Resilient 2030 initiative (https://www.undrr.org/news/making-cities-resilient-campaign-2030).
Horizontal Coordination: Horizontal coordination within UNDRR involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the disaster risk reduction domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, scientific community, and other UN agencies to ensure that disaster risk reduction is integrated in all policies and that disaster risk reduction policies are coherent with other sectoral policies (https://www.undrr.org/media/91259/download?startDownload=true). This coordination is guided by the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015-2030 (https://www.preventionweb.net/files/43291_sendaiframeworkfordrren.pdf?_gl=1*2d1si0*_ga*Nzc0NjIwODE4LjE3MDM1ODgxNDM.*_ga_D8G5WXP6YM*MTcwMzU4ODE1Mi4xLjEuMTcwMzU5MTQ1NC4wLjAuMA..). For example, UNDRR works with the education sector to promote disaster risk education and school safety (https://www.preventionweb.net/risk/education), with the finance sector to promote disaster risk financing and insurance (https://www.undrr.org/implementing-sendai-framework/catalyze-investment-in-resilience), or with the environment sector to promote ecosystem-based approaches for disaster risk reduction (https://www.undrr.org/media/48333/download?startDownload=true). Horizontal coordination within UNDRR can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Making Cities Resilient 2030 initiative with UCLG, ICLEI, UN-Habitat and other partners (https://mcr2030.undrr.org/), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the UN Disaster Risk Reduction Focal Points Network (https://undrr.org/sites/default/files/inline-files/UN%20DRR%20Focal%20Points%20Group%20-%20Terms%20of%20Referencce%202016.pdf) or the Global Platform for Disaster Risk Reduction (https://globalplatform.undrr.org/2022/language/bahasa-indonesia.html), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for disaster risk reduction sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Words into Action Guidelines (https://www.undrr.org/publications/words-into-action) or the Disaster Risk Reduction Capacity Analysis Tool (https://www.preventionweb.net/publications/view/76069), (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for disaster risk reduction issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the International Day for Disaster Risk Reduction (https://iddrr.undrr.org/) or the Global Assessment Report on Disaster Risk Reduction (https://www.undrr.org/gar). The UNDRR provides leadership and coordination on disaster risk reduction within the UN system and supports the implementation, monitoring and review of the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015-2030 (https://sdgs.un.org/un-system-sdg-implementation/un-office-disaster-risk-reduction-unisdr-34594). UNDRR facilitates the participation of various actors in the disaster risk reduction sector and enhances cooperation and coordination within the UN system on disaster risk reduction matters (https://www.undrr.org/media/87329/download?startDownload=true).

Institution: United Nations Office for Outer Space Affairs (UNOOSA)
Spatial Jurisdiction: UNOOSA's jurisdiction is focused on the exploration and use of outer space, including the moon and other celestial bodies, for peaceful purposes. This covers all activities of states parties to the Outer Space Treaty, whether carried out by governmental or non-governmental entities, within the framework of international law (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/treaties/outerspacetreaty.html). UNOOSA does not have any authority over the oceans and maritime zones of the Earth, as these are governed by other treaties and principles.
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: UNOOSA is responsible for promoting and facilitating peaceful international cooperation in outer space, including the exploration and use of the moon and other celestial bodies, for the benefit of all countries, especially developing ones (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/aboutus/roles-responsibilities.html). This includes addressing space-related issues such as space law, space applications, space debris, near-Earth objects, and global navigation satellite systems (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/aboutus/roles-responsibilities.html). UNOOSA also provides capacity-building, technical assistance, education and awareness-raising, as well as opportunities for countries to access and leverage space technologies and data for sustainable development (https://www.unoosa.org/). UNOOSA supports the implementation of the Space2030 Agenda and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/outreach/events/2018/spacetrust.html).
Source of Jurisdiction: UNOOSA derives its mandate from the UN General Assembly resolution 1472 (XIV) of 12 December 1959, which established the Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space (COPUOS) and its secretariat, later renamed as UNOOSA (https://www.unoosa.org/pdf/gares/ARES_14_1472E.pdf). Specifically, paragraph 1 of the resolution defines the objectives and functions of COPUOS. Additionally, UNOOSA's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and principles, such as the five treaties and five declarations on outer space, which provide the legal framework for UNOOSA's jurisdiction over the exploration and use of outer space for peaceful purposes (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/treaties.html). The five treaties on outer space are: (1) The Outer Space Treaty (1967) on the Principles Governing the Activities of States in the Exploration and Use of Outer Space, including the Moon and Other Celestial Bodies (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/treaties/introouterspacetreaty.html), (2) The Rescue Agreement (1968) on the Rescue of Astronauts, the Return of Astronauts and the Return of Objects Launched into Outer Space (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/treaties/introrescueagreement.html), (3) The Liability Convention (1972) on International Liability for Damage Caused by Space Objects (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/treaties/introliability-convention.html), (4) The Registration Convention (1976) on Registration of Objects Launched into Outer Space (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/treaties/introregistration-convention.html), and (5) The Moon Agreement (1984) governing the Activities of States on the Moon and Other Celestial Bodies (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/treaties/intromoon-agreement.html). UNOOSA's jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by COPUOS and the General Assembly, such as the Space2030 Agenda and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, which provide guidance and direction for UNOOSA's activities and programmes, as well as cooperation and coordination with other organisations and stakeholders (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/resolutions.html).
Defined Objectives: According to Part A, Section III of UNOOSA's working document "The 'Space2030' Agenda: Space as a Driver of Sustainable Development" (https://www.unoosa.org/res/oosadoc/data/documents/2024/stspace/stspace88_0_html/st_space-088E.pdf), the United Nations UNOOSA has been mandated to fulfil the following objectives: Enhance space-derived economic benefits and strengthen the role of the space sector as a major driver of sustainable development (Overarching objective 1); Harness the potential of space to solve everyday challenges and leverage space-related innovation to improve the quality of life (Overarching objective 2); Improve access to space for all and ensure that all countries can benefit socioeconomically from space science and technology applications and space-based data, information and products, thereby supporting the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals (Overarching objective 3); and Build partnerships and strengthen international cooperation in the peaceful uses of outer space and in the global governance of outer space activities (Overarching objective 4). These objectives are structured around the four pillars of space economy, space society, space accessibility and space diplomacy, and are complemented by four core objectives that outline the specific actions to be taken by Member States, UNOOSA and other stakeholders to implement the "Space2030" Agenda (https://www.unoosa.org/res/oosadoc/data/documents/2024/stspace/stspace88_0_html/st_space-088E.pdf).
Strategies: The UNOOSA executes its objectives through certain strategies: firstly, a vision and strategy for UNOOSA 2024-2030, presented by the Director of UNOOSA to the Member States in February 2024 (https://www.unoosa.org/res/oosadoc/data/documents/2024/stspace/stspace88_0_html/st_space-088E.pdf), establishes the Office's vision, mission, strategic objectives, and core functions. This strategy, aligned with the "Space2030" agenda and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, reflects the high expectations and feedback from the Member States and other stakeholders (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/outreach/events/2018/spacetrust.html). Secondly, an annual programme plan and budget, prepared by UNOOSA and approved by the General Assembly. The proposed UNOOSA budget for 2024 (https://www.unoosa.org/res/oosadoc/data/documents/2023/a78/a786_sect_6_0_html/A_78_06_Sect06E.pdf) supports its proposed 2024 programme plan (https://www.unoosa.org/res/oosadoc/data/documents/2023/aac_1052023crp/aac_1052023crp_3_0_html/AC105_C2_2023_CRP03E.pdf), which aims to make the most of the economic opportunities that space offers and to use the space sector as a catalyst for sustainable development; to tap into the potential of space to solve everyday problems and to enhance the quality of life through space innovation; to enable access to space for all and to ensure that all countries can use space applications and data for achieving the Sustainable Development Goals; and to foster partnerships and cooperation in the peaceful uses of outer space and in the global governance of outer space activities. The budget is mainly funded by the regular budget of the United Nations, but also relies on voluntary contributions from Member States and other entities for some of its activities.
Inter-Institutional Relationship: UNOOSA cooperates with various organisations to promote and facilitate peaceful international cooperation in outer space. It works closely with the Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space (COPUOS), providing substantive secretariat services and implementing its decisions and recommendations, as per General Assembly resolution 1472 (XIV) of 12 December 1959 (https://www.unoosa.org/pdf/gares/ARES_14_1472E.pdf). It also maintains a relationship with the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), coordinating on issues related to global navigation satellite systems and space weather, as detailed in document A/AC.105/2019/CRP.14 (https://www.unoosa.org/res/oosadoc/data/documents/2019/aac_1052019crp/aac_1052019crp_14_0_html/AC105_2019_CRP14E.pdf). Additionally, UNOOSA partners with the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), supporting the use of space applications for sustainable development, particularly in developing economies (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/informationfor/media/2022-unis-os-575.html). It also collaborates with the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), contributing to the Global Environmental Outlook and the Eye on Earth initiatives (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/psa/emnrm/index.html). Moreover, UNOOSA engages with other United Nations entities, intergovernmental organisations, non-governmental organisations, academic institutions, and private sector actors, through various agreements, mechanisms, platforms, and initiatives, such as the Inter-Agency Meeting on Outer Space Activities, the International Committee on Global Navigation Satellite Systems, the International Charter on Space and Major Disasters, and the Access to Space for All initiative (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/aboutus/partnerships.html).
Vertical Coordination: Vertical coordination within UNOOSA involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations and other specialised agencies, as well as regional and sub-regional organisations, national governments, and local authorities. This is achieved through providing secretariat services, implementing decisions and recommendations, and facilitating partnerships and dialogue. UNOOSA operates through the Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space (COPUOS) of all the members, the Scientific and Technical Subcommittee and the Legal Subcommittee of 92 members, and a secretariat headed by a Director (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/aboutus/structure.html). It also has working groups, expert groups, and other subsidiary bodies. The Office of the Director oversees and coordinates the strategic direction and operational priorities of UNOOSA (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/aboutus/director.html); The Committee, Policy and Legal Affairs Section (CPLA) provides substantive, secretariat, organisational and administrative support to the Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space (COPUOS), its Scientific and Technical Subcommittee (STSC) and its Legal Subcommittee (LSC); The Space Applications Section (SAS) plans and implements the United Nations Programme on Space Applications to build national capability in the areas of basic sciences; The United Nations Platform for Space-based Information for Disaster Management and Emergency Response (UN-SPIDER) helps all countries access and use space-based information in all phases of the disaster management cycle, including prevention, preparedness, early warning, response and reconstruction; and the International Committee on Global Navigation Satellite Systems (ICG) brings together all global navigation satellite system (GNSS) providers to improve their uses for sustainable development and their compatibility (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/aboutus/structure.html). The Director of UNOOSA is supported by the Senior Advisor on Space Science and Education, who provides expert advice and supports research relating to the activities and programmes carried out by the Office. The Senior Advisor also works closely with the Regional Centres for Space Science and Technology Education, affiliated to the United Nations (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/aboutus/structure.html). UNOOSA also collaborates with space agencies and intergovernmental and non-governmental organisations involved in space-related activities (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/aboutus/partnerships.html). In addition, UNOOSA maintains, on behalf of the United Nations Secretary-General, the Register of Objects Launched into Outer Space (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/spaceobjectregister/index.html) and discharges the responsibilities of the Secretary-General under the UN treaties and principles on outer space.
Horizontal Coordination: Horizontal coordination within UNOOSA involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the space domain, including its Member States, United Nations entities, intergovernmental and non-governmental organizations, and industry and private sector entities, to promote and facilitate the peaceful uses of outer space and the use of space science and technology for sustainable development. This coordination is guided by the resolutions and decisions of the General Assembly and the Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space (COPUOS) (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/documents-and-resolutions/search.jspx?view=documents&f=oosaDocument.doctags.doctag_s%3ACOPUOSRDOCS), as well as the “Space2030” Agenda and implementation plan (https://www.unoosa.org/res/oosadoc/data/documents/2024/stspace/stspace88_0_html/st_space-088E.pdf). For example, UNOOSA works with the disaster management sector to provide access to space-based information and services for disaster risk reduction and emergency response through the UN-SPIDER programme (https://www.un-spider.org/), with the health sector to strengthen space cooperation for global health (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/psa/globalhealth/index.html), with the education sector to enhance capacity-building, education and training in space science and applications, as well as space law and policy, through the regional centres for space science and technology education, affiliated to the United Nations (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/psa/regional-centres/index.html), or with the environment sector to support the implementation of the Paris Agreement and the Sendai Framework by using space-based data and applications (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/topics/space-and-climate-change.html). Horizontal coordination within UNOOSA can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Access to Space for All initiative (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/access2space4all/index.html) or the Space for Women project (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/topics/spaceforwomen/index.html), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the Inter-Agency Meeting on Outer Space Activities (UN-Space) (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/un-space/iam.html) or the International Committee on Global Navigation Satellite Systems (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/icg/icg.html), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for space sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the United Nations treaties and principles on outer space (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/treaties.html) or the guidelines for the long-term sustainability of outer space activities (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/topics/long-term-sustainability-of-outer-space-activities.html), and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for space issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the World Space Week (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/outreach/events/wsw/index.html) or the World Space Forums (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/world-space-forum/WSF-main-page.html). UNOOSA provides leadership and direction on matters related to the peaceful uses of outer space and the use of space science and technology for sustainable development, shapes the space agenda, sets norms and standards, articulates evidence-based policy options, provides technical support to countries, and monitors and assesses space trends (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/aboutus/structure.html).

Institution: United Nations Office for Project Services (UNOPS)
Spatial Jurisdiction: UNOPS's jurisdiction is global, covering all regions and countries where it implements infrastructure and procurement projects for the United Nations System, international financial institutions, governments and other partners (https://www.unops.org/project-locations). UNOPS does not have a specific authority on oceans and maritime zones, but it supports the efforts of its partners to protect the environment and enhance the resilience of communities to climate change.
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: UNOPS is responsible for providing infrastructure, procurement and project management services for a more sustainable world, in alignment with UN values and principles (https://www.unops.org/about). This includes supporting countries in developing their capacity and resource base for the Sustainable Development Goals; helping people in need through effective specialized expertise grounded in international norms and standards; and enabling partners to ‘do more with less’ through efficient project services, delivered locally or as global shared services. UNOPS also works in post-disaster and peace and security settings, developing countries and economies in transition, covering a range of sectors such as health, humanitarian, basic human needs, cash for work, and environment (https://www.unops.org/).
Source of Jurisdiction: UNOPS derives its mandate from the 2010 General Assembly resolution 65/176 (https://documents.un.org/doc/undoc/gen/n10/523/10/pdf/n1052310.pdf?token=YpwFrn88GVoLxo0p9e&fe=true) and Executive Board Decisions (https://www.unops.org/about/governance/executive-board/executive-board-documents) which reaffirmed the role of UNOPS as a central resource for the United Nations system in procurement and contracts management as well as in civil works and physical infrastructure development, including the related capacity development activities. The resolution also recognized the operational capacity of UNOPS to implement projects in support of peacebuilding, humanitarian and development operations. Specifically, paragraph 1 of the resolution defines the vision and mission of UNOPS, and paragraph 2 outlines the core values and principles of UNOPS. Additionally, UNOPS’s financial regulations and rules (https://content.unops.org/documents/libraries/policies-2020/executive-office-directives-and-instructions/financial-regulations-and-rules/en/EOD.ED-Financial-Regulations-and-Rules.pdf), regulation 1.01 on the scope and applicability, states that UNOPS shall operate in accordance with the policies and procedures established by the Executive Director in consultation with the Executive Board. UNOPS’s jurisdiction is also influenced by the decisions and directives adopted by its Executive Board, such as the strategic plan 2022-2025 (https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/3932593/files/DP_OPS_2021_5-EN.pdf?ln=en), the organizational structure (https://content.unops.org/documents/libraries/policies-2020/executive-office-directives-and-instructions/organizational-principles-and-governance-model/en/EOI.ED-Organisational-Structure.pdf), and the anti-bribery and anti-corruption policy (https://content.unops.org/publications/EB-for-docs-not-going-in-library/UNOPS-Anti-Bribery-and-Anti-Corruption-Policy-December-2023.pdf). UNOPS’s mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://sustainabledevelopment.un.org/content/documents/21252030%20Agenda%20for%20Sustainable%20Development%20web.pdf), the Paris Agreement on Climate Change (https://unfccc.int/sites/default/files/english_paris_agreement.pdf), and the New Urban Agenda (https://habitat3.org/wp-content/uploads/NUA-English.pdf), which provide further legal frameworks for UNOPS’s jurisdiction over specific development issues and domains.
Defined Objectives: According to the UNOPS strategic plan, 2022-2025 (https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/3932593/files/DP_OPS_2021_5-EN.pdf?ln=en), the UNOPS objectives are based on three contribution goals which reflect its purpose, vision and mission. These goals aim to (1) Supports countries in developing their capacity and resource base for the Sustainable Development Goals, by applying its technical expertise in quality infrastructure, public procurement, and sustainable investments in infrastructure and innovation (paragraphs 50-80), (2) Help people in need through effective specialized expertise grounded in international norms and standards, by embedding sustainable, resilient and inclusive implementation approaches, and by learning from its operational experience (paragraphs 81-93), and (3) Enable UNOPS's partners to 'do more with less' through efficient project services, delivered locally or as global shared services, by offering flexible and modular service lines, integrated service offerings and specialized delivery modalities, and by pursuing quality and organizational excellence (paragraphs 94-104).
Strategies: The United Nations Office for Project Services (UNOPS) executes its objectives via several strategies: Firstly, a four-year Strategic Plan, revised as needed, establishes the organization's vision, mission, strategic goals, core functions, and targets (https://www.unops.org/about/governance/strategic-plan). This plan, applicable for 2022-2025 (https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/3932593/files/DP_OPS_2021_5-EN.pdf?ln=en), aligns with the Sustainable Development Goals (https://sustainabledevelopment.un.org/content/documents/21252030%20Agenda%20for%20Sustainable%20Development%20web.pdf). It underscores UNOPS commitment to expanding the capacity and resource base for countries to achieve these goals (https://www.unops.org/about/governance/strategic-plan). The plan was agreed in June 2023 following UNOPS management reforms. The budget for the 2022-2025 strategic plan as presented in the document estimates the total delivery of $8.5 billion and the total expenditure of $1.1 billion for the four-year period. Secondly, UNOPS operates in accordance with a strict legislative framework comprised of Directives and Instructions (https://www.unops.org/policies). These are organization-wide policies that govern actions within UNOPS and its external relations. They explain procedures and business processes for the implementation of Directives, as well as United Nations legislation applicable to UNOPS. Futhermore, UNOPS's flagship publication, the Annual Statistical Report on United Nations Procurement keeps track of the combined spending on goods and services of 39 UN organizations, a record number of reporting organizations (https://www.unops.org/news-and-stories/news/what-did-the-united-nations-buy-last-year). Finally, to advance the 2030 Agenda, UNOPS aims to engage in collaborative partnerships with a focus on sharing its expertise in infrastructure, procurement, project management, human resources, and financial services (https://www.unops.org/about/our-story/partnerships). UNOPS works with a variety of partners, from the UN family to governments, non-governmental organizations, academia, and the private sector. The organization also hosts several entities under its agreements, grouped by theme (https://www.unops.org/about).
Inter-Institutional Relationship: UNOPS works with a variety of partners to support sustainable development operations in developing countries and manage portfolios financed by its partners (https://www.unops.org/about/our-story/partnerships). It establishes and develops strategic relationships with key partners, including the UN family, governments, non-governmental organizations, academia and the private sector. It also has global liaison offices in Bangkok, Brussels, Nordics, Geneva, Nairobi, Tokyo and Washington, D.C., to facilitate partnership development with regional and international organizations, such as the Asian Development Bank, the European Union, the World Bank, the Green Climate Fund, the UN Environment Programme, the UN-Habitat and the United States Agency for International Development (https://www.unops.org/about/our-story/partnerships). Furthermore, UNOPS provides meaningful technical expertise to countries in the implementation of the Sustainable Development Goals and the Paris Agreement on Climate Change, supplementing their own capacities, improving efficiency and transparency, reducing risks, boosting cost-effectiveness and ensuring quality. Additionally, UNOPS manages partnerships, trust funds and project portfolios that support people and communities around the world, such as the Global Fund to Fight Aids, Tuberculosis and Malaria, the Stop TB Partnership, the UN-Water Interagency Trust Fund, the Water Supply and Sanitation Collaborative Council, and the Enhanced Integrated Framework (https://www.unops.org/about/our-story/partnerships).
Vertical Coordination: Vertical coordination within UNOPS involves working with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other specialized agencies, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and local authorities. This is achieved through strategic coordination and advice, operational partnerships and collaboration, and service delivery and support. This is structured under the UNOPS Organizational Principles and Governance Model (https://content.unops.org/documents/libraries/policies-2020/executive-office-directives-and-instructions/organizational-principles-and-governance-model/en/EOD.ED-Organizational-Principles-and-Governance-Model.pdf). UNOPS operates under the oversight and guidance of the UNDP/UNFPA/UNOPS Executive Board, which consists of 36 members representing the five regional groups of the United Nations (https://www.unops.org/about/governance/executive-board). The Executive Director of UNOPS is the head of the organization and reports to the Executive Board and the Secretary-General of the United Nations. The Executive Director is supported by a Deputy Executive Director/Chief Operating Officer and a senior management team comprising the leads of four core management groups (Finance, People and Change, Procurement, and Infrastructure and Project Management) and other functional groups (Legal, Corporate Support, Partnerships and Communications, Business Improvement, Ethics, Audit and Investigations). UNOPS also has an Audit Advisory Committee and an Investment Advisory Committee that provide independent advice to the Executive Director on various aspects of the organization's management and performance (https://www.unops.org/about/governance/accountability/coordination-and-advice). UNOPS work is organized around five regions, each headed by a Regional Director who reports to the Executive Director. The regions are: Asia, Africa, Europe and Central Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean, and the Middle East. Each region has a Regional Office that coordinates and supports the delivery of the regional portfolio and implements the corporate improvement agenda. The regions also have Operational Hubs, Operations Centres, Project Centres, and Clusters that manage and deliver services to partners and clients at the country or thematic level (https://www.unops.org/about/our-structure).
Horizontal Coordination: Horizontal coordination within UNOPS involves working with different sectors and partners within the development, humanitarian and peacebuilding domains, such as governments, civil society, private sector, the UN system, and other international organizations to ensure that projects, infrastructure and procurement are delivered in a sustainable and efficient manner. This coordination is currently guided by the UNOPS Strategic Plan 2022-2025 (https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/3932593/files/DP_OPS_2021_5-EN.pdf?ln=en) and the UNOPS sustainability policy (https://www.unops.org/about/our-story/sustainable-development-goals#:~:text=Sustainability%20at%20UNOPS,-We%20are%20committed&text=Working%20closely%20with%20government%20partners,achieve%20long%2Dterm%20sustainable%20development.). For example, UNOPS works with the health sector to support the COVID-19 response and recovery (https://www.unops.org/news-and-stories/news/standing-together-to-tackle-covid-19#:~:text=CORONAVIRUS%20GLOBAL%20HEALTH%20EMERGENCY&text=Last%20year%2C%20UNOPS%20delivered%20around,term%20impacts%20of%20the%20pandemic.), with the transport sector to improve road safety and connectivity (https://www.unops.org/news-and-stories/news/developing-inclusive-transport-infrastructure), with the water sector to enhance access to clean water and sanitation (https://www.unops.org/news-and-stories/stories/sustainable-water-supply-for-towns-in-darfur) or with the environment sector to promote climate action and resilience (https://www.unops.org/news-and-stories/stories/advancing-climate-action-building-resilience). Horizontal coordination within UNOPS can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint delivery and implementation of projects and programmes with other sectors and partners, such as the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria (https://www.theglobalfund.org/en/) or the European Union (https://www.unops.org/about/our-story/partnerships), (2) Participation in intersectoral and multi-stakeholder platforms and initiatives, such as the Global Infrastructure Hub (https://content.unops.org/publications/Infrastructure_underpining_sustainable_development_EN.pdf) or the UN Road Safety Fund (https://roadsafetyfund.un.org/), (3) Development and application of standards and tools for sustainable project management, infrastructure and procurement, such as the Infrastructure Sustainability Rating Tool (https://sustainable.unops.org/), and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilize support for sustainable development goals and policies among other sectors and partners, such as the UNOPS Possibilities Portal (https://www.unops.org/business-opportunities/unops-possibilities/unops-possibilities-portal) or the UNOPS Annual Report (https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/3971697/files/DP_OPS_2022_5-EN.pdf?ln=en).

Institution: United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC)
Spatial Jurisdiction: UNODC's jurisdiction is not limited to a specific geographical area, but rather to the offences established in accordance with the Organized Crime Convention and other relevant treaties. This means that UNODC can assist states in preventing and combating transnational organized crime, corruption, terrorism, drug trafficking, money laundering, cybercrime, and other related issues, regardless of where they occur (https://www.unodc.org/e4j/en/organized-crime/module-8/key-issues/jurisdictions.html). However, UNODC respects the sovereignty and jurisdiction of each state party, and encourages cooperation and coordination among states to avoid jurisdictional gaps or conflicts (https://www.unodc.org/e4j/en/cybercrime/module-7/key-issues/sovereignty-and-jurisdiction.html). UNODC also has field offices in various regions and countries, which provide technical assistance and support to the local authorities (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/corruption/country-profile/index.html). UNODC does not have a specific jurisdiction over ocean spaces and maritime zones, but rather works with states and other international organizations to address various crimes and threats that occur at sea, in accordance with the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea³ and other relevant treaties (https://www.un.org/Depts/los/general_assembly/contributions_2019/UNODC.pdf).
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: UNODC is a global leader in the fight against illicit drugs and international crime and is mandated to assist member states in their struggle against illicit drugs, crime, and terrorism. In the area of criminal justice, UNODC’s work covers the entire criminal justice chain (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/justice-and-prison-reform/cpcj-home.html). This includes comprehensive crime prevention strategies, legal and institutional reforms, improving crime investigation capacities, promoting humane prison management systems, facilitating international cooperation in legal matters, and addressing specific issues of human trafficking, money laundering, organized crime, cybercrime, and corruption (https://www.unodc.org/documents/Advocacy-Section/UNODC-at-a-glance_PRINT.pdf). In terms of drug prevention, treatment, and care, UNODC supports countries to develop and implement comprehensive drug demand reduction interventions based on scientific evidence (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/drug-prevention-and-treatment/index.html). This includes addressing drug use disorders as any other health disorder, and ensuring access to health-based drug prevention, treatment, care, and rehabilitation services (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/drug-prevention-and-treatment/index.html). Furthermore, UNODC plays a crucial role in addressing HIV/AIDS, particularly in vulnerable populations such as people who use drugs and those in prisons (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/hiv-aids/new/Our_HIV_work.html). It promotes comprehensive, evidence-informed interventions that reduce the risk of HIV, including harm reduction services like needle and syringe programs and opioid substitution therapy (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/hiv-aids/new/Our_HIV_work.html).
Source of Jurisdiction: UNODC derives its jurisdiction from several legal, conventional, and executive bases. The major conventions that underpin its defined objectives, operations, and strategic frameworks include the United Nations Convention against Transnational Organized Crime and the Protocols Thereto, 2000 (https://www.unodc.org/documents/treaties/UNTOC/Publications/TOC%20Convention/TOCebook-e.pdf); the United Nations Convention against Corruption, 2003 (https://www.unodc.org/documents/treaties/UNCAC/Publications/Convention/08-50026_E.pdf); the Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs, 1961 as amended by the 1972 Protocol (https://www.unodc.org/pdf/convention_1961_en.pdf); the Convention on Psychotropic Substances, 1971 (https://www.unodc.org/pdf/convention_1971_en.pdf); the United Nations Convention against Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances, 1988 (https://www.unodc.org/pdf/convention_1988_en.pdf); and  several ant-terrorism conventions (https://sherloc.unodc.org/cld/v3/sherloc/treaties/search.jspx#?mv=treaties&c=%7B%22filters%22:%5B%7B%22fieldName%22:%22treaty.type_s1%22,%22value%22:%22International%22%7D,%7B%22fieldName%22:%22treaty.topics.topic_s%22,%22value%22:%22Terrorism%22%7D%5D,%22match%22:%22%22,%22startAt%22:20,%22sortings%22:%22%22%7D). UNODC’s jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by the Conference of the Parties (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/treaties/CTOC/resolutions-and-decisions-conference-of-the-parties-to-the-united-nations-convention-against-transnational-organized-crime.html#COP11), as well as by the Commission on Narcotic Drugs and the Commission on Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice, which are the policy-making bodies of UNODC (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/commissions/Secretariat/index.html). These resolutions and decisions provide guidance and direction for UNODC’s activities and programmes, as well as cooperation and coordination with other organisations and stakeholders. UNODC’s mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as several international drug control conventions (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/commissions/CND/Mandate_Functions/Scheduling.html), and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/sustainable-development-goals/index.html), which provide further legal frameworks for UNODC’s jurisdiction over specific issues and domains related to drugs, crime, corruption, terrorism, and justice.
Defined Objectives: According to the Secretary-General's bulletin ST/SGB/2004/6 (https://www.unodc.org/pdf/sgb_2004_6_unodc.pdf), UNODC has been mandated to fulfil the following objectives: Implementing the Organization's drug programme and crime programme in an integrated manner, addressing the interrelated issues of drug control, crime prevention and international terrorism in the context of sustainable development and human security (Section 2.1); Serving as the central drug control entity with exclusive responsibility for coordinating and providing effective leadership for all United Nations drug control activities and serving as the repository of technical expertise in international drug control for the Secretariat of the United Nations, including the regional commissions, and other United Nations organs, as well as Member States (Section 2.2 a); Acting on behalf of the Secretary-General in fulfilling his or her responsibilities under the terms of international treaties and resolutions of United Nations organs relating to international drug control (Section 2.2 b); Providing substantive services to the General Assembly, the Economic and Social Council and committees and conferences dealing with drug control matters (Section 2.2 c); Carrying out activities in the field of international crime prevention and control; strengthening regional and international cooperation in preventing and combating transnational crime, in particular organized and economic crime, money-laundering, illicit trafficking in women and children, financial crimes and terrorism in all its forms; and promoting effective and fair administration of justice, with due respect for the rights of all those affected by crime or involved in the criminal justice system (Section 2.3 a); Promoting adherence to the international treaties on drug control, crime prevention and terrorism and their effective implementation by States (Section 6.2 f); and Providing assistance to Member States in the implementation of relevant General Assembly resolutions and declarations related to action against terrorism (Section 6.2 g).
Strategies: UNODC executes its objectives and mandates by having Strategic Plans and work programs supported by annual or biennial integrated budgets. it's most recent five-year Strategic Plan, applicable for 2021-2025, guides its vision, mission, values, and expected accomplishments, and is aligned with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the United Nations reform agenda (https://www.unodc.org/documents/Advocacy-Section/UNODC-Strategy-WEB.pdf). The plan focuses on five thematic areas: world drug problem, organized crime, corruption and economic crime, terrorism, and criminal prevention and criminal justice (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/strategy/index.html). In addition, a proposed annual programme plan and budget, applicable for 2024, specifies the activities, outputs, indicators, and resources for each strategic objective, based on the results and lessons learned from the 2022 budget perfomance evaluation, as well as the priorities and needs of Member States (https://www.unodc.org/documents/commissions/CND/CND_Sessions/CND_65Reconvened/ECN72022_CRP16_ECN152022_CRP9_2221350A.pdf). The international conventions and protocols on drug control, crime prevention and terrorism also provide UNODC with the legal frameworks for its jurisdiction and mandate, and which UNODC serves as the guardian and the secretariat, supporting their implementation by Member States (https://www.unodc.org/pdf/convention_1961_en.pdf). In addition, UNODC work programmes and budgets are influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by its governing bodies, such as the Commission on Narcotic Drugs, the Commission on Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice, and the Economic and Social Council, which also provide guidance and direction for UNODC's cooperation and coordination with other organisations and stakeholders (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/treaties/CTOC/resolutions-and-decisions-conference-of-the-parties-to-the-united-nations-convention-against-transnational-organized-crime.html#COP11). UNODC is funded mainly by voluntary contributions from various sources, but faces challenges in securing predictable and adequate funding to address the growing demands of Member States and to support the 2030 Agenda.
