UNODC aims to diversify its funding sources by expanding its partnership base, exploring new donors and engaging with the private sector and foundations. UNODC also seeks to increase the availability of non-earmarked resources to enhance its programme and results-based management, research, policy guidance and strategic direction (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/donors/index.html).
Inter-Institutional Relationship: UNODC collaborates with various institutions to implement its goals and objectives. It works with the Asian Development Bank on anti-money-laundering and sustainable livelihoods (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/donors/partnership/external.html). It also cooperates with the OPEC Fund for International Development on HIV/AIDS prevention and treatment, and the NATO-Russian Council on issues related to Afghanistan (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/donors/partnership/external.html). UNODC has also established Judicial Regional Platforms in the regions of the Sahel and the Indian Ocean (https://www.unodc.org/documents/treaties/organized_crime/internationalcooperation/Platforms_on_UNODc_site.pdf). It also partners with UN-Habitat, UN Women, UNEP, United Nations Development Programme, United Cities and Local Governments (UCLG), European Forum on Urban Security (EFUS), NGO Alliance on Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice, Peace in Our Cities, UNCAC Coalition, Vienna NGO Committee on Drugs, and others (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/urban-safety/unodcity-partnerships.html).
Vertical Coordination: Vertical coordination within UNODC involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other specialized agencies, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and local authorities. UNODC operates through the Office of the Executive Director (OED), Division for Operations (DO), Division for Treaty Affairs (DTA), Independent Evaluation Section (IES), and Division for Policy Analysis and Public Affairs (DPA), among others. The UNODC also has various regional sections and field offices (https://www.unodc.org/documents/evaluation/UNODC_OrganizationalChart.pdf). UNODC's work is organized around five thematic focus areas identified alongside a streamlining of processes designed to build a more agile, fit-for-purpose organization . The Commission on Narcotic Drugs (CND) and the Commission on Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice (CCPCJ) are policymaking bodies within the United Nations system and act as governing bodies to UNODC, guiding its international action against drugs and crime. The CND is responsible for deciding the scope of control of substances under the international drug control conventions, while the CCPCJ acts as a preparatory and implementing body for the United Nations Congress on Crime prevention and Criminal Justice (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/commissions/index.html).There is also the International Narcotics Control Board (INCB) which is an independent and quasi-judicial monitoring body for the implementation of the United Nations international drug control conventions (https://www.incb.org/).  In addition, UNODC's field offices supports UNODC's work in promoting peace and security, human rights, and development by making the world safer from drugs, crime, corruption, and terrorism (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/field-offices.html). UNODC's operational systems are based on the UNODC Strategy 2021-2025, which aims to equip UNODC to deliver effectively, efficiently, and with accountability, elevating support to Member States to build just, inclusive, and resilient societies. The operational systems are also guided by the UN standards and norms in crime prevention and criminal justice, which promote human rights (https://www.unodc.org/documents/Advocacy-Section/UNODC-Strategy-WEB.pdf).
Horizontal Coordination: Horizontal coordination within UNODC involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the drug, crime, corruption and terrorism domains, such as governments, civil society, private sector, academia, and other UN entities to ensure that the world is safer from these threats and that human rights, development and the rule of law are upheld in all activities and policies. This coordination is guided by the UNODC Strategy 2021-2025 (https://www.unodc.org/documents/Advocacy-Section/UNODC-Strategy-WEB.pdf). For example, UNODC works with the health sector to address the world drug problem and provide prevention and treatment services (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/drug-prevention-and-treatment/index.html), with the justice sector to prevent and counter organized crime and terrorism and strengthen criminal justice systems (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/organized-crime/index.html, https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/terrorism/index.html, https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/justice-and-prison-reform/index.html), with the environment sector to combat crimes that affect the environment and biodiversity (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/wildlife-and-forest-crime/index.html), or with the education sector to promote a culture of lawfulness and prevent violence and crime among youth (https://www.unodc.org/e4j/). Horizontal coordination within UNODC can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Global Programme for Combating Wildlife and Forest Crime (https://www.unodc.org/documents/Wildlife/Annual_Report_GPWLFC2021.pdf) or the Global Maritime Crime Programme (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/piracy/index.html), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the Inter-Agency Coordination Group against Trafficking in Persons (https://icat.un.org/) or the United Nations Global Counter-Terrorism Coordination Compact (https://www.un.org/counterterrorism/global-ct-compact), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for drug, crime, corruption and terrorism sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the International Standards for the Treatment of Drug Use Disorders (https://www.unodc.org/documents/drug-prevention-and-treatment/UNODC-WHO_International_Standards_Treatment_Drug_Use_Disorders_April_2020.pdf) or the Global Judicial Integrity Network (https://www.unodc.org/ji/en/index.html), and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for drug, crime, corruption and terrorism issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the World Drug Report (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/data-and-analysis/world-drug-report-2023.html) or the Education for Justice initiative (https://www.unodc.org/e4j/en/index.html).

Spatial Jurisdiction: UNU's jurisdiction is not limited to any specific geographical area, but rather covers the entire world as a global academic institution and think tank of the United Nations. This includes a network of campuses, programmes, and affiliated institutes spanning 12 countries, as well as partnerships with other academic institutions and policymakers around the world (https://unu.edu/). UNU does not have any authority over oceans and maritime zones, as it is not a State or an intergovernmental organization, but rather an organ of the United Nations General Assembly.
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: UNU is responsible for advancing global sustainability through research and education, in collaboration with the UN and other academic and policy partners (https://unu.edu/learning). UNU focuses on three thematic areas: peace and security; social change and economic development; and environment, climate, and energy (https://unu.edu/about). This includes addressing sustainability issues like climate change, biodiversity, water, urbanization, governance, security, human rights, and health and well-being (https://unu.edu/). UNU also provides postgraduate programmes, fellowships, and capacity development activities for students and professionals from diverse backgrounds and regions, as well as disseminating knowledge and policy recommendations through publications, events, and media outreach (https://unu.edu/ias). UNU contributes to the UN's efforts to achieve the 2030 Agenda and the Sustainable Development Goals (https://unu.edu/).
Source of Jurisdiction: UNU derives its mandate from the Charter of the United Nations University, which established UNU as an international community of scholars and a think tank of the United Nations (https://unu.edu/sites/default/files/2022-12/UNU-Charter-2014.pdf). Specifically, Article I of the Charter defines the purposes and structure of UNU, and Article II affirms its academic freedom and autonomy. Additionally, the Charter outlines the organization (Article III), personnel (Article VIII), finance and budget (Article IX), location (Article X), and the status and authority (Article XI) of UNU. UNU's jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by its governing board, the Council of UNU, which is composed of 12 members appointed by the Secretary-General of the United Nations with the concurrence of the Director-General of UNESCO (https://unu.edu/about/unu-council). These resolutions and decisions provide guidance and direction for UNU's research, postgraduate training, and dissemination of knowledge, as well as cooperation and coordination with other academic institutions and policymakers around the world (Article IV, Paragraph 4). UNU's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the 2030 Agenda and the Sustainable Development Goals, which provide further thematic frameworks for UNU's jurisdiction over specific sustainability issues and domains (https://unu.edu/topics/sdg-partnerships).
Defined Objectives: According to the Charter of the United Nations University (https://unu.edu/sites/default/files/2022-12/UNU-Charter-2014.pdf), the University's objectives are as follows: (1) To contribute, through collaborative research and education, to efforts to resolve the pressing global problems of human survival, development, and welfare that are the concern of the United Nations, its Peoples, and Member States (Article I, paragraph 1); (2) To disseminate the knowledge gained in its activities to the United Nations and its agencies, to scholars and to the public, in order to increase dynamic interaction in the worldwide community of learning and research (Article I, paragraph 4), (3) To assist in the development of vigorous academic and scientific communities everywhere and particularly in the developing countries, devoted to their vital needs in the fields of learning and research within the framework of the aims assigned to those centres and programmes in the present Charter (Article I, paragraph 6); and (4) To grant and confer master’s degrees and doctorates, diplomas, certificates and other academic distinctions under conditions laid down for that purpose in the statutes by the Council of the University (Article I, paragraph 8). These objectives reflect the University's mission as an international community of scholars, engaged in research, postgraduate training and dissemination of knowledge in furtherance of the purposes and principles of the Charter of the United Nations (Article I, paragraph 1).
Strategies: The United Nations University (UNU) implements its objectives and mandates through a variety of strategies: (1) The UNU has a strategic plan that guides the development and implementation of the institute’s research, policy development, teaching, and capacity-building initiatives. The current strategic plan spans from 2020 to 2024 (https://i.unu.edu/media/unu.edu/attachment/100694/UNU-Strategic-Plan-2020-2024.pdf). This plan is closely aligned with the overall strategic direction of the UNU (https://unu.edu/ias/about-unu-ias/strategic-plan). It was produced through an inclusive process of internal stocktaking and dialogue, reflecting the outcomes of a comprehensive external evaluation of UNU-IAS conducted in 2020 (https://unu.edu/ias/about-unu-ias/strategic-plan), (2) The UNU Council is responsible for considering and approving the UNU budget and work programme. The Work Program and budget estimate for the biennium 2022-2023 is designed to support the United Nations University’s (UNU) vision of promoting sustainable human development and its mission to contribute, through research and capacity building, to efforts to resolve the pressing global problems that are the concern of the United Nations, its Peoples and Member States. The budget of USD 124.8 million, a 10.9% increase from the previous biennium, is funded through various sources including project fundraising, institutional fundraising, income from the endowment fund, cumulative surplus carried forward, and other income (https://unu.edu/sites/default/files/2023-01/Approved-UNU-Work-Programme-and-Budget-Estimates-for-the-2022-2023-Biennium.pdf), (3) The UNU has established the UNU SDG–Universities Platform through the UNU-IAS in 2020, which provides opportunities for Japanese universities to proactively collaborate with different stakeholders to promote research and educational activities advancing the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) (https://unu.edu/ias/unu-sdg-universities-platform), and (5) The UNU Council devises the principles and policies that govern the University’s operations. The Council holds two regular sessions per year (https://unu.edu/about/unu-council). Finally, the UNU has 13 institutes located in 12 countries around the world, each contributing to the mission of the UNU through their specific programmes of work. The global UNU system is coordinated by UNU Headquarters in Tokyo (https://unu.edu/unu-system).
Inter-Institutional Relationship: The UNU collaborates with various institutions to advance its research and training objectives. It functions under the joint sponsorship of the UN and UNESCO, through a central body and a network of centres and programmes, as per Article I, paragraph 1 of its Charter (https://unu.edu/sites/default/files/2022-12/UNU-Charter-2014.pdf). It also coordinates its activities with the UN and its agencies, such as UNITAR (Article VI, paragraph 1 f), UNIDO, as well as as as well as regional and national bodies, such as the European Union, the African Development Bank, and the Japanese Government. It may receive voluntary contributions and assistance from governments, organizations, and individuals, and mobilizes resources from various donors and funding agencies, such as the German Government, the World Bank, and the International Climate Initiative, to support its academic projects and core operations (Article IX, paragraphs 1-2). Additionally, the UNU designates certain institutions and centres, particularly in developing countries, as associated institutions of the UNU, on terms and conditions decided by the Council (https://unu.edu/unu-system). Moreover, UNU partners with academic institutions and networks around the world, such as Maastricht University, the University of Tokyo, and the International Partnership for the Satoyama Initiative, to conduct joint research, education, and training programmes (https://unu.edu/about).
Vertical Coordination: Vertical coordination within UNU involves collaboration with affiliated institutions, such as the UN General Assembly and UNESCO. This is achieved through reporting, approving, devising, and implementing the principles, policies, budget, and work programme of the University as structured in Articles III-IX of the UNU Charter (https://unu.edu/sites/default/files/2022-12/UNU-Charter-2014.pdf). The UNU operates through the UNU Council of 12 appointed members, the UNU Rector, and three ex officio members (the UN Secretary-General, the UNESCO Director-General and the UNITAR Executive Director) (Articles III-VI). The UNU Council is responsible for devising the principles and policies that govern the University’s operations, and for considering and approving the UNU budget and work programme (Article IV). The UNU Council reports annually to the UN General Assembly, the UN Economic and Social Council, and the Executive Board of UNESCO (Article IV). The UNU Rector is the chief academic and administrative officer of the University and is appointed by the Secretary-General of the United Nations in consultation with the Director-General of UNESCO (Article V). The UNU Rector exercises the powers delegated to him or her by the UNU Council and is accountable to the UNU Council for the discharge of his or her functions (Article V). The UNU institutes and programmes are the operational units of the University and are established by the UNU Council in accordance with the principles and policies laid down by the Council (Article VII). The UNU institutes and programmes are headed by directors who are appointed by the UNU Rector in consultation with the UNU Council and are responsible to the UNU Rector for the academic and administrative management of their respective units (Article VII, paragraph 2). The UNU institutes and programmes carry out research, teaching, training, and capacity development activities in line with the UNU strategic plan and the UNU Council-approved work programme and budget (Article IX).
Horizontal Coordination: Horizontal coordination within the United Nations University (UNU) involves collaboration with different academic and research institutions, UN agencies, governments, civil society, and other stakeholders to address the pressing global problems of human survival, development and welfare. This coordination is guided by Article I of the UNU Charter, (https://unu.edu/sites/default/files/2022-12/UNU-Charter-2014.pdf), as well as by the UNU 2020-2024 Strategic Plan (https://i.unu.edu/media/unu.edu/attachment/100694/UNU-Strategic-Plan-2020-2024.pdf). For example, UNU consults with the education sector to provide topical, timely and relevant postgraduate training and degree programmes (https://unu.edu/learning), with the social sector to promote human rights and peace (https://unu.edu/topics/human-rights), with the economic sector to foster innovation and sustainable development (https://unu.edu/topics/innovation), and with the environmental sector to protect the environment and natural resources (https://unu.edu/topics/natural-resources). Horizontal coordination within UNU can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint research and training projects and programmes with other academic and research institutions, UN agencies, and other stakeholders, such as the UNU Institute for Integrated Management of Material Fluxes and of Resources (https://flores.unu.edu/en) or the UNU Institute for the Advanced Study of Sustainability (https://ias.unu.edu/en), (2) Participation in academic and policy networks, platforms, and partnerships, such as the Academic Council on the United Nations System (https://acuns.org) or the Sustainable Development Solutions Network (https://www.unsdsn.org), (3) Development and dissemination of publications, reports, and policy briefs for academic and policy audiences, such as the UNU Policy Brief Series (https://unu.edu/ias/unu-ias-policy-brief-series#:~:text=Our%20policy%20briefs%20present%20analysis,global%2C%20national%20and%20local%20levels.) or the UNU World Institute for Development Economics Research Working Paper Series (WIDER) (https://www.wider.unu.edu/publications), and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for the UNU's vision, mission, and activities among academic and policy communities, such as the UNU Conversation Series (https://unu.edu/events/unu-conversation-series) or the UNU Annual Report (https://unu.edu/about/annual-reports).

Spatial Jurisdiction: The WBG does not have specific authority over maritime zones or territorial waters but rather covers economic and political regions such as Africa, East Asia and Pacific, Europe and Central Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean, Middle East and North Africa, and South Asia with activities and presence in more than 189 member countries (https://www.worldbank.org/en/where-we-work). The WBG's regional presence is determined by its borrowing and non-borrowing member countries, and by its strategic priorities for development in each region and sector (https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/896931468189267370/pdf/The-World-Bank-Group-A-to-Z-2016.pdf).
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: The WBG provides loans, grants, and technical assistance to developing countries for various projects of reconstruction and development (https://www.worldbank.org/en/who-we-are/ibrd). Its interests include promoting economic growth, reducing poverty, enhancing regional cooperation, and addressing global challenges such as climate change and pandemics (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/annual-report/working-achieve-development-goals). The WBG also plays a role in mediating international disputes, conducting economic surveys, and offering development advisory services (https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/922161468339057329/pdf/384810ADR1Manu1l1Mediation01PUBLIC1.pdf). Likewise, It works in association with its affiliates, which have different roles and policies in relation to investment in the developing countries (https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/e3804a75-62f2-5348-8d04-6f8ec14212fb/content).
Source of Jurisdiction:
The WBG derives its mandate from the Articles of Agreement, Conventions, or equivalent governance documents of its five constituent institutions: the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD), the International Development Association (IDA), the International Finance Corporation (IFC), the Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA), and the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes (ICSID) (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/articles-of-agreement). These documents outline the conditions of membership, the general principles of organization, management, and operations, and the status, immunities, and privileges of each organization ((https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/articles-of-agreement). The IBRD Articles of Agreement (https://pubdocs.worldbank.org/en/722361541184234501/IBRDArticlesOfAgreement-English.pdf), which came into effect on December 27, 1945, define the purposes and functions of the IBRD, the capital stock and voting power of the members, the loans and guarantees of the IBRD, the operations and transactions of the IBRD, the withdrawal and suspension of membership, and the status, immunities, and privileges of the IBRD. Similarly, the IDA Articles of Agreement (https://ida.worldbank.org/sites/default/files/pdfs/ida-articlesofagreement.pdf), which came into effect on September 24, 1960, define the purposes and functions of the IDA, the resources and management of the IDA, the terms and conditions of financing by the IDA, the operations and transactions of the IDA, the withdrawal and suspension of membership, and the status, immunities, and privileges of the IDA. The IFC Articles of Agreement (https://thedocs.worldbank.org/en/doc/6a4a091b83577eb35e881dbf9016c5c3-0330032020/original/IFCArticlesOfAgreement.pdf), which came into effect on July 20, 1956, define the purposes and functions of the IFC, the capital stock and voting power of the members, the loans, guarantees, and other operations of the IFC, the operations and transactions of the IFC, the withdrawal and suspension of membership, and the status, immunities, and privileges of the IFC. The MIGA Convention (https://www.miga.org/sites/default/files/archive/Documents/miga_convention_november_2010.pdf), which came into force on April 12, 1988, defines the purposes and functions of the MIGA, the membership and capital of the MIGA, the guarantees and other operations of the MIGA, the relations with other international organizations, the withdrawal and suspension of membership, and the status, immunities, and privileges of the MIGA. Lastly, the ICSID Convention (https://icsid.worldbank.org/sites/default/files/ICSID%20Convention%20English.pdf), which entered into force on October 14, 1966, defines the purposes and functions of the ICSID, the jurisdiction of the ICSID, the recognition and enforcement of awards, the administrative and financial provisions of the ICSID, the amendment and interpretation of the ICSID Convention, and the final provisions of the ICSID Convention.
The WBG’s jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by its governing bodies, such as the Boards of Governors, the Boards of Executive Directors, and the Council of Governors (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/leadership). These resolutions and decisions provide guidance and direction for the WBG’s activities and programs, as well as cooperation and coordination with other organizations and stakeholders. The WBG’s mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the Sustainable Development Goals (https://pubdocs.worldbank.org/en/259801562965232326/2030Agenda-2019-final-web.pdf), the Paris Agreement on Climate Change ((https://unfccc.int/sites/default/files/english_paris_agreement.pdf), and the Addis Ababa Action Agenda on Financing for Development (https://sustainabledevelopment.un.org/frameworks/addisababaactionagenda), which provide further legal frameworks for the WBG’s jurisdiction over specific development issues and domains.
Defined Objectives: The objectives of the WBG are established in the Articles of Agreement and Conventions of its constituent institutions (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/articles-of-agreement). The IBRD Articles of Agreement (https://pubdocs.worldbank.org/en/722361541184234501/IBRDArticlesOfAgreement-English.pdf) state that the WBG through IBRD aims to assist in the reconstruction and development of territories of members by facilitating the investment of capital for productive purposes, promoting private foreign investment by means of guarantees or participations in loans and other investments, and supplementing private investment by providing finance for productive purposes out of its own capital, funds raised by it and its other resources (Article I, Section 1). As specified in the IDA Articles of Agreement (https://ida.worldbank.org/sites/default/files/pdfs/ida-articlesofagreement.pdf), the WBG through IDA aims to promote economic development, increase productivity and thus raise standards of living in the less-developed areas of the world by providing finance to projects and programs that contribute to the economic or social development of the members whose per capita income is low, and to those members in the opinion of the Association are not able to borrow from the IBRD on suitable terms (Article I, Section 1). The WBG through the IFC Articles of Agreement (https://thedocs.worldbank.org/en/doc/6a4a091b83577eb35e881dbf9016c5c3-0330032020/original/IFCArticlesOfAgreement.pdf) aims to further economic development by encouraging the growth of productive private enterprise in member countries, particularly in the less-developed areas, by assisting in financing the establishment, improvement and expansion of private productive enterprises, and by stimulating and helping to create conditions conducive to the flow of private capital, domestic and foreign, into productive investment in member countries (Article I, Section 1). According to the MIGA Convention (https://www.miga.org/sites/default/files/archive/Documents/miga_convention_november_2010.pdf), the WBG through MIGA aims to encourage the flow of investments for productive purposes among member countries, and in particular to developing member countries, by providing guarantees against non-commercial risks in respect of investments in member countries, by establishing and operating a trust fund to provide technical assistance to member countries in connection with the promotion of foreign investment, and by exercising such other incidental powers as shall be necessary or desirable in the furtherance of its objective (Article 2, Section 1). Lastly, the WBG through the ICSID Convention (https://icsid.worldbank.org/sites/default/files/ICSID%20Convention%20English.pdf) aims to provide facilities for conciliation and arbitration of investment disputes between contracting states and nationals of other contracting states, and to bring together parties who have agreed to use such facilities, in order to facilitate the settlement of such disputes and to contribute to the development of international law on investments (Article 1, Section 2).
Strategies: The World Bank Group executes its objectives via several strategies: firstly, a World Bank Group Strategy adopted in 2013, based on the principles of country ownership, evidence-based solutions, and global and regional integration (https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/bitstream/handle/10986/16093/32824_ebook.pdf?sequence=4&isAllowed=y). Secondly, a World Bank Group Evolution Roadmap that outlines the key actions and reforms to implement the WBG Strategy and enhance the WBG's effectiveness and efficiency (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/evolution-roadmap). This roadmap, endorsed by the Board of Governors in 2020, focuses on four pillars: (i) strengthening country platforms and partnerships, (ii) enhancing the WBG's financial and operational capacity, (iii) improving the WBG's business model and internal processes, and (iv) fostering a culture of innovation and learning. Thirdly, a set of thematic and sector strategies that provide the strategic framework and guidance for the WBG's engagement in specific areas of development, such as gender, climate change, fragility and conflict, human capital, infrastructure, and private sector development. These strategies are aligned with the WBG Strategy and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, and are informed by global knowledge and evidence (https://www.worldbank.org/en/programs/sdgs-2030-agenda). In addition, the WBG prepares Country Partnership Frameworks (CPFs) and Regional Partnership Frameworks (RPFs) that define the WBG's support to individual countries and regions, based on their development priorities, challenges, and opportunities. These frameworks are developed in consultation with the governments, civil society, and other stakeholders, and are aligned with the WBG Strategy and the country's own development strategy (https://www.worldbank.org/en/projects-operations/country-strategies). The WBG also maintains various initiatives, platforms, and funds that provide the operational and financial instruments for addressing specific development challenges and opportunities (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/what-we-do/brief/initiatives-platforms-and-funds) while engaging in partnerships, coalitions, and networks that provide the collaborative framework for enhancing the impact and effectiveness of the WBG's interventions, leveraging the comparative advantages and resources of different actors, and addressing cross-cutting issues such as governance, data, and innovation (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/partners).
Inter-Institutional Relationship: The WBG collaborates with a wide range of partners and stakeholders, working closely with its five constituent instututions to achieve its defined objectives (https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/896931468189267370/pdf/The-World-Bank-Group-A-to-Z-2016.pdf). The WBG also engages with the International Monetary Fund (IMF), which shares the same premises and some common services, and cooperates on various policy and operational issues (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/history/the-world-bank-group-and-the-imf). Furthermore, it partners with other multilateral and bilateral development agencies, civil society organizations, private sector entities, foundations, and academic institutions, to leverage knowledge, resources, and expertise for development solutions (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/partners). The WBG participates in various global initiatives and platforms, such as the Global Environment Facility (GEF) (https://fiftrustee.worldbank.org/en/about/unit/dfi/fiftrustee/fund-detail/gef), the Global Partnership for Education (GPE) (https://www.worldbank.org/en/topic/education/brief/the-global-partnership-for-education-and-the-world-bank-group-the-facts), the Global Financing Facility (GFF) (https://www.globalfinancingfacility.org/), and the Global Infrastructure Facility (GIF) (https://fiftrustee.worldbank.org/en/about/unit/dfi/fiftrustee/fund-detail/gif), to address specific development challenges and opportunities (https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/729441468325246298/pdf/271450REVISED010WB0Revised01PUBLIC1.pdf).
Vertical Coordination:
Vertical coordination within the WBG involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other international organizations, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and local authorities. This is achieved through consultation, cooperation, and partnership (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/annual-report/collaboration-engagement) and structured under the Articles of Agreement and Conventions of the World Bank’s constituent institutions: IBRD, IDA, IFC, MIGA, and ICSID (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/articles-of-agreement). The WBG operates through the Board of Governors, the Board of Executive Directors, and the President and staff. The Board of Governors consists of one governor and one alternate governor appointed by each member country (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/leadership/governors). The Board of Executive Directors consists of 25 executive directors who represent the member countries or groups of countries. The President is the chief of the operating staff of the WBG and conducts its ordinary business under the direction of the Board of Executive Directors (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/leadership/directors).
The WBG also has committees, commissions, and other subsidiary bodies that assist in its work. The Development Committee advises the Board of Governors on development issues and the transfer of resources to developing countries (https://www.devcommittee.org/en/devcommittee/home); the Inspection Panel investigates complaints from people who believe they have been harmed by a World Bank-funded project (https://www.inspectionpanel.org/); and the Independent Evaluation Group assesses the performance and impact of the World Bank Group’s activities (https://ieg.worldbankgroup.org/evaluations). The WBG’s work is organized around six regions, each overseen by a Vice President who works closely with the President and the Board of Executive Directors to implement the World Bank Group’s agenda across all levels of the organization (https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/922161468339057329/pdf/384810ADR1Manu1l1Mediation01PUBLIC1.pdf). There is also the Global Practices and Cross-Cutting Solutions Areas, which provide technical expertise and knowledge on various sectors and themes; and the International Finance Corporation (IFC), the Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA), and the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes (ICSID), which are separate legal entities within the World Bank Group that focus on private sector development, investment guarantees, and dispute resolution, respectively (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/annual-report/our-organization). With 189 member countries and staff from more than 170 countries, the WBG operates offices and technical centers in more than 130 countries, where it works with governments, civil society, and other partners to support its mission of ending extreme poverty and promoting shared prosperity (https://www.worldbank.org/en/who-we-are). In addition, the WBG coordinates with other international organizations and agencies, such as the United Nations, the International Monetary Fund, the World Trade Organization, and the regional development banks, to enhance global cooperation and effectiveness in addressing development challenges (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/partners).
Horizontal Coordination: Horizontal coordination within the World Bank Group (WBG) involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the development domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, the academic community, and other multilateral institutions to help countries end extreme poverty and promote shared prosperity in a sustainable manner. This coordination is guided by the World Bank Group Strategy (https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/e3804a75-62f2-5348-8d04-6f8ec14212fb/content), which outlines how the WBG will work in partnership to fulfill its mandate. For example, the WBG works with the health sector to improve health outcomes and strengthen health systems (https://www.worldbank.org/en/topic/health), with the education sector to ensure quality and inclusive learning for all (https://www.worldbank.org/en/topic/education), with the energy sector to increase access to affordable, reliable, and sustainable energy (https://www.worldbank.org/en/topic/energy), or with the environment sector to address climate change and environmental challenges (https://www.worldbank.org/en/topic/environment). Horizontal coordination within the WBG can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Global Practice Groups (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/annual-report/collaboration-engagement#global-practice-groups) or the Country Partnership Frameworks (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/annual-report/collaboration-engagement#country-partnership-frameworks), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the G-20 (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/annual-report/collaboration-engagement#g20), the UN Development System (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/annual-report/collaboration-engagement#un-development-system), or the Multilateral Development Banks (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/annual-report/collaboration-engagement#multilateral-development-banks), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for development sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the World bank group evaluation Principles (https://ieg.worldbankgroup.org/sites/default/files/Data/reports/WorldBankEvaluationPrinciples.pdf) or the Business Ready (B-READY) platform (https://www.worldbank.org/en/businessready), and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for development issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Human Capital Project (https://www.worldbank.org/en/publication/human-capital) or the World Development Report (https://www.worldbank.org/en/publication/wdr/wdr-archive).

Spatial Jurisdiction: The World Food Programme (WFP) is a global organization that operates in over 120 countries and territories. However, it doesn't have jurisdiction over specific geographical areas such as oceans or maritime zones, but rather operates wherever there is a need to provide food assistance in emergencies and support sustainable livelihoods to achieve zero hunger, irrespective of political or economic zones (https://www.wfp.org/who-we-are).
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: The World Food Programme (WFP) is responsible for delivering food assistance in emergencies and working with communities to improve nutrition and build resilience (https://www.wfp.org/overview). It focuses on emergency assistance, relief and rehabilitation, development aid, and special operations (https://www.wfp.org/overview). WFP also works to eliminate the root causes of hunger through food assistance, in collaboration with the other two Rome-based UN agencies, Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and the International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD) (https://www.wfp.org/un-agencies-and-international-institutions).
Source of Jurisdiction: The World Food Programme (WFP) derives its mandate from the General Assembly Resolution 2095 (XX) of 20 December 1965 (http://undocs.org/en/A/RES/2095(XX)), which extended the WFP on a continuing basis for as long as multilateral food aid is feasible and desirable, Resolution 1714 (XVI) of 19 December 1961 (http://undocs.org/en/A/RES/1714(XVI)), which established WFP as an experimental programme, and Resolution 3404 (XXX) of 28 November 1975 (http://undocs.org/en/A/RES/3404(XXX)), which named Committee on Food Aid Policies and Programmes oversight of WFP. In addition, pursuant to Resolution 50/8 of 1 November 1995 (https://documents.un.org/doc/resolution/gen/n95/257/30/img/n9525730.pdf?token=lBOUzh2cYTpOtGNhBZ&fe=true), the Committee on Food Aid Policies and Programmes (CFA) was reconstituted as the WFP Executive Board with effect from 1 Jan. 1996. The General Assembly Resolutions 1714 (XVI) and 2095 (XX) define the objectives and scope of WFP, and Resolution 50/8 outlines the structure and membership of the United Nations/FAO Intergovernmental Committee of the WFP, which is the governing body of the programme. Specifically, Article II of the General Regulations and Rules of the WFP (https://executiveboard.wfp.org/document_download/WFP-0000141150) defines the purposes and functions of WFP; Article III outlines the cooperation of WFP with the United Nations and FAO and with other relevant agencies and organizations, and the modalities of such cooperation; Article IV specifies the location of the headquarters of WFP in Rome, Italy; Article V lists the organs of WFP, which are the Executive Board and the Secretariat, and their composition and functions; Article VI details the powers and functions of the Board; Article VII establishes the WFP Secretariat, headed by an Executive Director, and its organization and functions; Article VIII grants WFP legal capacity, drawing on the legal personality of the United Nations and FAO; Article IX sets the eligibility criteria for assistance from WFP, which include being a member of the United Nations or any specialized agency or the IAEA, or being a recipient of emergency food aid requested by the Secretary-General; and Article XIII governs the contributions to WFP, which shall be on a voluntary basis and may be in the form of commodities, cash, or acceptable services. WFP's jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by its governing bodies, such as the Intergovernmental Committee, the FAO Council, and the Economic and Social Council, which provide guidance and direction for WFP's activities and programmes, as well as cooperation and coordination with other organisations and stakeholders (https://executiveboard.wfp.org/about-board). WFP's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the Rome Declaration on World Food Security (https://www.fao.org/3/w3548e/w3548e00.htm#adopt05), the Sustainable Development Goals (https://www.wfp.org/sdgs), and the Agenda for Humanity (https://agendaforhumanity.org/stakeholder/291.html), which provide further legal frameworks for WFP's jurisdiction over specific food security and humanitarian issues and domains.
Defined Objectives: According to Article II of the General Regulations of the WFP (https://executiveboard.wfp.org/document_download/WFP-0000141150), the purposes and functions of WFP encompass several key aspects including using food aid to support economic and social development, concentrating its efforts and resources on the neediest people and countries (Paragraph 1 a); meeting refugee and other emergency and protracted relief food needs, using this assistance to the extent possible to serve both relief and development purposes (Paragraph 1 b); promoting world food security in accordance with the recommendations of the United Nations and FAO (Paragraph 1 c); providing services to bilateral donors, United Nations agencies and non-governmental organizations for operations which are consistent with the purposes of WFP and which complement WFP’s operations (Paragraph 2 d); and implementing food aid programmes, projects and activities, on request, in cooperation and coordination with the United Nations, FAO and other relevant agencies and organizations (Paragraph 2).
Strategies: The World Food Programme (WFP) executes its objectives via several strategies. Firstly, a four-year Strategic Plan establishes the organization’s vision, mission, strategic goals, core functions, and targets. This plan, applicable for 2022-2025 (https://executiveboard.wfp.org/document_download/WFP-0000132205), outlines the many ways for WFP, working in synergy with others, to most efficiently and effectively save and change lives. It is grounded within renewed global commitment to the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and its associated Sustainable Development Goals 9https://www.wfp.org/publications/wfp-strategic-plan-2022-25). Secondly, a biennial Management Plan, presented to the Executive Board, details the projected operational needs, the provisional global implementation plan, the programme support and business operations budget, and the use of reserves and general fund. The current Management Plan for 2024-2026 (https://executiveboard.wfp.org/document_download/WFP-0000151658) highlights the corporate budget required to implement WFP’s programme of work, based on the funding forecasts and prioritization criteria. It also outlines WFP’s key drivers of hunger, such as conflict, climate change, and economic shocks, and how WFP responds to them through various programmes, operations, and platforms (https://www.wfp.org/publications/wfp-management-plan-2024-2026). Thirdly, the Corporate Results Framework (CRF) 2022-2025 (https://executiveboard.wfp.org/document_download/WFP-0000136871) guides the planning, implementation, monitoring, and reporting of WFP’s programmes towards the objectives identified in the 2022-2025 Strategic Plan. The CRF, supplemented by the policy on country strategic plans (CSPs) (https://www.wfp.org/publications/policy-country-strategic-plans), provides a performance and accountability framework that enables WFP to measure and demonstrate its response to humanitarian needs. In addition, the WFP has over 32 policies in effect under the 2022-2025 Strategic Plan. An update of the portfolio of policies is submitted annually and can be found as the “Compendium of Policies” on the Executive Board website (https://executiveboard.wfp.org/document_download/WFP-0000151657). Finally, various policies, frameworks, agreements, and initiatives provide an operational framework for implementing the WFP Strategic Plan, addressing food security, nutrition, resilience, capacity strengthening, social protection, and innovation (https://executiveboard.wfp.org/document_download/WFP-0000132607).
Inter-Institutional Relationship: WFP cooperates with various institutions to achieve its goals and objectives of eradicating hunger and malnutrition. It works closely with other UN agencies and international organizations, as stated in Article III of the General Regulations of the WFP (https://executiveboard.wfp.org/document_download/WFP-0000141150). It has a special relationship with the other two Rome-based UN agencies – FAO and IFAD – with which it shares a common vision of promoting food security. It also has a strong operational partnership with UNHCR for providing food assistance to refugees and internally displaced people. Moreover, WFP collaborates with UNDP and other development partners to support countries' self-defined priorities and accelerate climate action, as part of the UN Development Assistance Framework. Furthermore, WFP engages with other international and regional organizations, such as ECHO, OAS and ICRC, to deliver humanitarian aid and enhance resilience. Additionally, WFP partners with UNV and Online Volunteers to support its work to achieve Zero Hunger (https://www.unv.org/Success-stories/un-volunteers-wfp-road-zero-hunger).
Vertical Coordination: Vertical coordination within WFP involves cooperation with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, FAO, other specialized agencies, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and local authorities. This is achieved through consultation, guidance, supervision, and direction of the activities of WFP in accordance with the overall policy guidance of the United Nations and FAO as structured under Article III-VIII of the General Regulations of WFP (https://executiveboard.wfp.org/document_download/WFP-0000141150), which establish that WFP shall consult with and seek advice and cooperation from the United Nations and FAO, and coordinate and operate in close liaison with appropriate United Nations agencies and operating programmes, bilateral assistance programmes, and other relevant organizations. WFP operates through the Executive Board of 36 members, jointly established by the United Nations and FAO, and a secretariat headed by an Executive Director (Article V, paragraph 1). The Executive Board is responsible for providing intergovernmental support and specific policy direction to and supervision of the activities of WFP, and ensuring that WFP is responsive to the needs and priorities of recipient countries (Article VI, paragraph 1). The Executive Director is responsible and accountable to the Board for the administration of WFP and for the implementation of WFP programmes, projects and other activities (Article VII, paragraph 1). The Executive Director also represents WFP and performs functions conferred by the agreements concluded by the United Nations and FAO on behalf of WFP with States or intergovernmental organizations (Article VIII, paragraph 1). WFP's work is organised around five regions, each overseen by a Regional Director who works closely with the Executive Director to implement strategies and programmes across all levels of the Organization. There is also the Senior Management Group (consisting of the Executive Director, Deputy Executive Directors, Assistant Executive Directors, Regional Directors, Chief of Staff, Inspector General and Director of Legal Services) providing strategic and operational guidance to the Executive Director on matters related to the programmatic and managerial work of WFP; and ensuring coherence and alignment between the three levels of the Organization and the governing bodies (https://www.wfp.org/governance-and-leadership). Additionally, a network of country offices and technical experts supports WFP's work in providing food assistance and enhancing food security and nutrition as an integral part of regional and national development policies. Besides the Executive Director, at the WFP headquarters, there is a clear line of duty within the leadership team comprising of Deputy Executive Directors and Assistant Executive Directors with portfolios focusing on different aspects of WFP's mandate. In addition, WFP coordinates with the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) and other humanitarian partners through the Inter-Agency Standing Committee (IASC) and the cluster system to ensure effective and principled humanitarian action (https://executiveboard.wfp.org/document_download/WFP-0000138085). WFP also collaborates with the Committee on World Food Security (CFS) (https://www.fao.org/sustainable-development-goals-helpdesk/champion/article-detail/committee-on-world-food-security/en#:~:text=The%20Committee%20on%20World%20Food,security%20and%20nutrition%20for%20all.), the Global Network Against Food Crises (GNAFC) (https://www.fightfoodcrises.net/#:~:text=The%20Global%20Network%20Against%20Food,based%20responses%20and%20collective%20efforts), the Scaling Up Nutrition (SUN) Movement 9https://sunbusinessnetwork.org/about-us/#:~:text=The%20Scaling%20Up%20Nutrition%20(SUN,to%20scaling%20up%20nutrition%20action.), and other platforms and initiatives to promote global food security and nutrition.
Horizontal Coordination: Horizontal coordination within WFP involves working with different actors and sectors within the food security and nutrition domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, the scientific community, and other UN agencies to ensure that food assistance is delivered effectively and efficiently to the people in need and that food systems are transformed to support the achievement of zero hunger. This coordination is guided by Article III of the General Regulations of WFP (https://executiveboard.wfp.org/document_download/WFP-0000141150). For example, WFP works with the health sector to address malnutrition and micronutrient deficiencies (https://www.wfp.org/nutrition), with the education sector to provide school feeding and improve learning outcomes (https://www.wfp.org/school-meals), with the social protection sector to strengthen national safety nets and resilience (https://www.wfp.org/social-protection), or with the climate change sector to reduce the risks and impacts of climate shocks on food security (https://www.wfp.org/climate-action). Horizontal coordination within WFP can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and activities with other actors and sectors, such as the Country Strategic Plans (https://www.wfp.org/country-strategic-planning) or the Emergency Response Preparedness Plan (https://www.wfp.org/emergency-preparedness-and-response#:~:text=Emergency%20preparedness%20and%20response%20is,and%20timely%20when%20crises%20erupt.) with OCHA, UNICEF and WHO; (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral mechanisms and platforms, such as the Food Security Cluster (https://www.wfp.org/food-security-cluster) or the Scaling Up Nutrition Movement (https://scalingupnutrition.org/); (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for food security and nutrition sector engagement with other actors and sectors, such as the Food Security and Nutrition Analysis (https://www.wfp.org/food-security-analysis) or the Fill the Nutrient Gap (https://www.wfp.org/publications/fill-nutrient-gap); and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for food security and nutrition issues and policies among other actors and sectors, such as the State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World (https://www.wfp.org/publications/2021-state-food-security-and-nutrition-world-report-and-inbrief) or the Global Report on Food Crises (https://www.wfp.org/publications/global-report-food-crises-2023).

Spatial Jurisdiction: WHO’s jurisdiction is global, encompassing the land and sea areas of its member states. This includes a focus on countries and regions within the six WHO regions, with authority extending to the whole territory of these states, covering key health issues and challenges (https://www.who.int/about/who-we-are/regional-offices).
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: The WHO is responsible for directing and coordinating international health within the United Nations system. This includes providing leadership on global health matters, shaping the health research agenda, setting norms and standards, articulating evidence-based policy options, providing technical support to countries, and monitoring and assessing health trends (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Treaties/1948/04/19480407%2010-51%20PM/Ch_IX_01p.pdf). The WHO also addresses health issues such as communicable and non-communicable diseases, environmental health, health systems, health promotion, and emergency preparedness and response. (https://www.who.int/health-topics). The WHO also works with partners and stakeholders to achieve the health-related targets of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://sdg.iisd.org/news/who-undp-to-cooperate-on-2030-agenda-health-related-targets/)
Source of Jurisdiction: WHO derives its mandate from the Constitution of the World Health Organization, which was adopted by the International Health Conference in 1946 and entered into force in 1948 (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Treaties/1948/04/19480407%2010-51%20PM/Ch_IX_01p.pdf). The Constitution defines the objective, functions, and principles of WHO, as well as the rights and obligations of its member states (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Treaties/1948/04/19480407%2010-51%20PM/Ch_IX_01p.pdf) Additionally, WHO's jurisdiction is influenced by the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (https://www.un.org/sites/un2.un.org/files/2021/03/udhr.pdf) and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Treaties/1976/01/19760103%2009-57%20PM/Ch_IV_03.pdf), which recognize the right to health as a fundamental human right. WHO also supports the implementation of various health-related conventions and treaties, such as the Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (https://iris.who.int/bitstream/handle/10665/42811/9241591013.pdf?sequence=1) and the International Health Regulations (https://iris.who.int/bitstream/handle/10665/246107/9789241580496-eng.pdf?sequence=1), which provide further legal frameworks for WHO's jurisdiction over specific health issues and situations.
Defined Objectives: WHO's objective, as per its Constitution (Chapter I, Article 1), is the attainment of the highest possible health level for all peoples. Its functions include acting as the authority on international health work (Article 2 a), establishing collaboration with the UN, specialized agencies, and health administrations (Article 2 b), assisting governments in strengthening health services (Article 2 c and d), conducting health research and establishing standards (Article 2 n, s, and t), improving teaching and training standards in health-related professions (Article 2 o), studying and reporting on public health techniques (Article 2 p), providing health information and assistance (Article 2 q and r), proposing health-related conventions and recommendations (Article 2 k), and taking actions to further its objectives (Article 2 v). These roles position WHO as a specialized agency within the United Nations system, primarily responsible for international health matters and public health (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Treaties/1948/04/19480407%2010-51%20PM/Ch_IX_01p.pdf)
Strategies: The WHO executes its objectives via several strategies: firstly, a five-year General Programme of Work, approved by the World Health Assembly, which sets the strategic direction, priorities, and budget of the organization (https://apps.who.int/gb/ebwha/pdf_files/EB152/B152_28-en.pdf). This plan, applicable for 2019-2025, aligns with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the triple billion targets of achieving universal health coverage, addressing health emergencies, and promoting healthier populations. (https://www.who.int/data/triple-billion-dashboard) Secondly, a biennial Programme Budget, proposed by the Director-General and adopted by the World Health Assembly, which details the expected results, indicators, and resources for each strategic priority and programme area (https://iris.who.int/bitstream/handle/10665/346071/9789240036109-eng.pdf?sequence=1&isAllowed=y). The current budget for 2022-2023 is based on the Thirteenth General Programme of Work and reflects the needs and priorities of member states and partners (https://iris.who.int/bitstream/handle/10665/346071/9789240036109-eng.pdf?sequence=1&isAllowed=y). Thirdly, various global health sector strategies, developed in consultation with member states and stakeholders, which provide a comprehensive and coherent approach to address specific health issues, such as HIV, viral hepatitis, and sexually transmitted infections. These strategies, applicable for 2022-2030, propose a common vision, goals, and strategic directions for ending epidemics and advancing universal health coverage, primary health care, and health security (https://iris.who.int/bitstream/handle/10665/360348/9789240053779-eng.pdf?sequence=1). Finally, various resolutions, decisions, and recommendations, adopted by the World Health Assembly and the Executive Board, which provide policy guidance and oversight for the implementation of the WHO's objectives and mandates. These include addressing health emergencies, communicable and non-communicable diseases, health systems, health promotion, and health governance, with key instruments listed here (https://www.who.int/teams/integrated-health-services/patient-safety/policy/resolutions).
Inter-Institutional Relationship: WHO collaborates with various organizations to achieve its objectives. It works with 194 Member States and various stakeholders through the World Health Assembly (WHA), established in 1948 by the Constitution of the WHO, serving as the supreme decision-making body for health (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Treaties/1948/04/19480407%2010-51%20PM/Ch_IX_01p.pdf). As a specialized agency within the UN system, WHO's relationship with the UN is based on the Agreement between the United Nations and the World Health Organization, effective since 10 July 1948, which defines the respective responsibilities and cooperation of the two organizations (https://apps.who.int/gb/bd/pdf_files/BD_49th-en.pdf). Additionally, WHO supports various health-related conventions and treaties, providing legal and normative frameworks for specific health issues and situations, such as the Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (https://iris.who.int/bitstream/handle/10665/42811/9241591013.pdf?sequence=1) and the International Health Regulations (https://iris.who.int/bitstream/handle/10665/246107/9789241580496-eng.pdf?sequence=1). It also collaborates with other UN agencies and partners, such as Gavi, The GFF, the Global Fund, UNAIDS, UNDP, UNFPA, UNICEF, UNITAID, UN Women, World Bank Group and WFP and WHO, addressing common health challenges (https://www.who.int/news/item/24-09-2019-multilateral-agencies-launch-a-joint-plan-to-boost-global-health-goals#:~:text=The%2012%20signatory%20agencies%20to,Bank%20Group%2C%20WFP%20and%20WHO.&text=Quotes%20from%20the%2012%20Principals%20are%20available%20below.). Moreover, WHO participates in the Inter-Agency Standing Committee (IASC), contributing to the coordination and delivery of humanitarian assistance, as endorsed by resolution 46/182 of the UN General Assembly (https://ngocoordination.org/system/files/documents/resources/ga-resolution-46-182.pdf).
Vertical Coordination: Vertical coordination within WHO involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other specialized agencies, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and local authorities.  This is achieved through delegation of authority, directing, and controlling. This is structured under the Relationship with the United Nations and Other International Organizations section of the WHO Constitution, specifically in Articles 69-70 (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Treaties/1948/04/19480407%2010-51%20PM/Ch_IX_01p.pdf). The WHO operates through the World Health Assembly of all the members, the Executive Board of 34 members, and a secretariat headed by a Director-General (Articles 18-26) (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Treaties/1948/04/19480407%2010-51%20PM/Ch_IX_01p.pdf). The WHO also has committees, commissions, and other subsidiary bodies (Articles 27-28). The WHO assists members in the implementation of its standards, policies, and programmes, and provides technical cooperation and assistance upon request (Articles 23-24) (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Treaties/1948/04/19480407%2010-51%20PM/Ch_IX_01p.pdf). WHO's work is organized around six regions, each overseen by a Regional Director who works closely with the Director-General to implement strategies and programmes across all levels of the Organization (https://www.who.int/about/who-we-are). There is also the Global Policy Group (consisting of the Director-General, Deputy Director-General, Regional Directors and the Executive Director of the WHO Emergencies Programme) providing strategic and internal policy advice to the Director-General on matters related to the programmatic and managerial work of WHO; and ensuring coherence and alignment between the three levels of the Organization and the governing bodies (https://www.who.int/director-general/global-policy-group). Also, a network of country offices and technical experts supports the WHO's work in promoting health and well-being as an integral part of regional and national development policies (https://www.who.int/countries/en/). Additionally, WHO operates 7 technical centres and in-country offices in 30 Member States (https://www.who.int/europe/about-us/about-who-europe/technical-centres). Besides the director General,  at the WHO headquarters, there is a clear line of duty within the leadership team comprising of an Executive Director and 9 Assistant Director-GeneraI with portfolios focusing on different aspects in accordance with the WHO's mandate (https://www.who.int/director-general/who-headquarters-leadership-team). In addition, WHO/Europe coordinates with the European Union and its agencies and is the host organisation and partner of the European Observatory on Health Systems and Policies (https://www.who.int/europe/about-us/about-who-europe/technical-centres).
Horizontal Coordination:
Horizontal coordination within WHO involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the health domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, scientific community, and other UN agencies to ensure that health is considered in all policies and that health policies are aligned with other sectoral policies. This coordination is guided by Article 2 of the Constitution of the World Health Organization (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Treaties/1948/04/19480407%2010-51%20PM/Ch_IX_01p.pdf). For example, WHO works with the education sector to promote health literacy and school health programmes (https://www.who.int/teams/health-promotion/enhanced-wellbeing/ninth-global-conference/health-literacy), with the transport sector to reduce road traffic injuries and air pollution (https://www.who.int/teams/environment-climate-change-and-health/healthy-urban-environments/transport), or with the ocean sector to enhance the health in coastal areas particularly during natural disasters (https://www.who.int/health-topics/tropical-cyclones#tab=tab_1). Horizontal coordination within WHO can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the One Health Joint Plan of Action (2022 - 2026) with FAO, UNEP and WOAH (https://wedocs.unep.org/bitstream/handle/20.500.11822/40843/one_health.pdf?sequence=1&isAllowed=y),
(2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the Inter-Agency Standing Committee or the UN Interagency Task Force on the Prevention and Control of Noncommunicable Diseases (https://uniatf.who.int/about-us/what-we-do), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for health sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Health in All Policies Framework for Country Action (https://www.afro.who.int/sites/default/files/2017-06/140120HPRHiAPFramework.pdf) or the Health Impact Assessment Toolkit (https://www.who.int/tools/health-impact-assessments), (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for health issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the World Health Day (https://www.who.int/campaigns/world-health-day) or the World Health SStatisticsReport (https://www.who.int/data/gho/publications/world-health-statistics). The WHO provides leadership and direction on matters critical to health, shapes the health research agenda, sets norms and standards, articulates evidence-based policy options, provides technical support to countries, and monitors and assesses health trends (https://www.who.int/about/what-we-do). WHO facilitates the participation of various actors in the health sector and enhances cooperation and coordination within the UN system on health matters (https://apps.who.int/gb/ebwha/pdf_files/WHA75/A75_39-en.pdf).

Spatial Jurisdiction: WIPO does not have a specific authority over oceans and maritime zones, although its jurisdiction is global, encompassing its 193 member states that span all continents and regions (https://www.wipo.int/members/en/). This includes a focus on developing countries and least developed countries, with assistance in building their Intellectual Property (IP) capacity and infrastructure.
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: The WIPO Secretariat is responsible for administering the intellectual property (IP) system, which covers creations of the mind, such as inventions, literary and artistic works, designs, and symbols, names and images used in commerce (https://www.wipo.int/about-ip/en/). This includes addressing IP issues like patents, trademarks, copyright, industrial designs, geographical indications, and trade secrets. WIPO also provides education, training, and skills-building for its member states, especially developing countries and least developed countries, with assistance in building their IP capacity and infrastructure (https://www.wipo.int/academy/en/). In addition, WIPO supports the protection of traditional knowledge and genetic resources, which may be derived from marine biodiversity (https://www.wipo.int/edocs/pubdocs/en/tk/769/wipo_pub_769.pdf). WIPO also administers treaties that cover IP rights in relation to marine resources, such as the Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT) and the Budapest Treaty on the International Recognition of the Deposit of Microorganisms for the Purposes of Patent Procedure (https://www.wipo.int/edocs/pubdocs/en/wipo_pub_277.pdf).
Source of Jurisdiction: WIPO derives its mandate from the Convention Establishing the World Intellectual Property Organization (https://www.wipo.int/wipolex/en/text/283833), which established WIPO as a specialized agency of the United Nations. Specifically, Article 3 of the Convention states the objectives of the Organization; Article 4 lists the functions of the Organization; Article 5 specifies the conditions for membership in the Organization, which are open to any State that is a member of any of the Unions, or a member of the United Nations or related agencies, or invited by the General Assembly; Article 6 defines the composition, functions, voting, and procedures of the General Assembly, which is the supreme organ of the Organization consisting of the States party to this Convention that are members of any of the Unions; Article 8 defines the composition, functions, voting, and procedures of the Coordination Committee, which is an organ of the Organization consisting of the States party to this Convention that are members of the Executive Committees of the Paris Union and the Berne Union, or both; Article 11 outlines the sources and management of the finances of the Organization; Article 12 grants the Organization the legal capacity necessary for the fulfillment of its objectives and the exercise of its functions; and Artice 13 authorizes the Organization to establish working relations and cooperate with other intergovernmental organizations, and to make suitable arrangements for consultation and cooperation with international and national non-governmental organizations, in matters within its competence. WIPO's jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by its governing bodies, such as the General Assembly, the Coordination Committee (https://www.wipo.int/meetings/en/topic.jsp?group_id=104), and the Assemblies of the Unions (https://www.wipo.int/about-wipo/en/assemblies/#:~:text=Assemblies%20of%20WIPO%20%E2%80%93%202024,July%209%20to%2017%2C%202024.). These resolutions and decisions provide guidance and direction for WIPO's activities and programs, as well as cooperation and coordination with other organizations and stakeholders. WIPO's mandate is also supported by the administration of various international treaties and agreements, such as the Paris Convention for the Protection of Industrial Property (https://www.wipo.int/wipolex/en/text/287556), the Berne Convention for the Protection of Literary and Artistic Works (https://www.wipo.int/wipolex/en/text/283693), and the Marrakesh Treaty to Facilitate Access to Published Works for Persons Who Are Blind, Visually Impaired or Otherwise Print Disabled (https://www.wipo.int/wipolex/en/text/301019), which provide further legal frameworks for WIPO's jurisdiction over specific intellectual property issues and domains.
Defined Objectives: According to the Convention Establishing the World Intellectual Property Organization (https://www.wipo.int/wipolex/en/text/283833), WIPO's objectives encompass two main aspects: promoting the protection of intellectual property throughout the world (Article 3(i)) and ensuring administrative cooperation among the Unions (Article 3(ii)). To achieve these objectives, the Organization, through its appropriate organs, has several functions, such as: developing measures to facilitate the efficient protection of intellectual property and to harmonize national legislation in this field (Article 4(i)); performing the administrative tasks of the Paris Union, the Berne Union, and other international agreements related to intellectual property (Article 4(ii)); encouraging the conclusion of international agreements to promote the protection of intellectual property; offering legal-technical assistance to States requesting it (Article 4(iv)); assembling and disseminating information concerning the protection of intellectual property (Article 4(vi)); maintaining services facilitating the international protection of intellectual property (Article 4(vii)); and taking all other appropriate action in relation to the stated objectives (Article 4(viii)). These objectives and functions enable WIPO to contribute to better understanding and cooperation among States for their mutual benefit on the basis of respect for their sovereignty and equality, and to encourage creative activity in the industrial, scientific, literary or artistic fields (Preamble).
Strategies: The WIPO executes its objectives via several strategies. Firstly, a five-year Medium-Term Strategic Plan (MTSP), prepared by the Secretariat and noted by the Assemblies of WIPO, provides high-level strategic guidance for the corresponding Program and Budgets covered by the MTSP. This plan, applicable for 2022-2026 (https://www.wipo.int/edocs/mdocs/govbody/en/wo_pbc_32/wo_pbc_32_3.pdf), outlines WIPO's vision, mission, strategic pillars, and foundation. Secondly, a biennial Program of Work and Budget, approved by the Assemblies of WIPO, details the expected results, performance indicators, and resources for each program and strategic goal. The current Program of Work and Budget for 2022-2023 (https://www.wipo.int/edocs/pubdocs/en/wipo_pub_360_pb22_23.pdf) is based on the MTSP and reflects the priorities and needs of the Member States and stakeholders (https://www.wipo.int/edocs/mdocs/govbody/en/wo_pbc_32/wo_pbc_32_3.pdf). It also supports the implementation of the WIPO Development Agenda, which consists of 45 recommendations to enhance the development dimension of WIPO's activities (https://www.wipo.int/export/sites/www/ip-development/en/agenda/docs/recommendations.pdf). Finally, various initiatives, platforms, and projects provide an operational framework for delivering WIPO's services and advancing its goals, such as WIPO Re:Search (https://www.wipo.int/edocs/pubdocs/en/wipo_pub_gc_18.pdf), which facilitates research and development for neglected tropical diseases, malaria, and tuberculosis; WIPO IP and Gender Action Plan (https://www.wipo.int/edocs/pubdocs/en/wipo-pub-rn2023-1-en-wipo-intellectual-property-ip-and-gender-action-plan-the-role-of-ip-in-support-of-women-and-girls.pdf), which aims to promote gender equality and women's empowerment in the IP ecosystem; and WIPO GREEN (https://www3.wipo.int/wipogreen/en/), which connects providers and seekers of green technologies and fosters innovation and diffusion of environmentally sound solutions.
Inter-Institutional Relationship: WIPO cooperates with various organisations to promote and protect intellectual property rights. It works closely with the World Trade Organization (WTO), implementing the Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS) (https://www.wipo.int/wipolex/en/text/500864), which sets minimum standards for IP protection and enforcement, as per the WIPO-WTO Cooperation Agreement of 1995 (https://www.wipo.int/edocs/mdocs/govbody/en/wo_ga_24/wo_ga_24_5_rev-annex1.doc#:~:text=The%20WIPO%2DWTO%20Agreement%20of,technical%20assistance%20to%20developing%20countries.). Similarly, WIPO maintains a relationship with the United Nations (UN) and its specialised agencies, such as the UN Development Programme (UNDP), the UN Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), and the UN Environment Programme (UNEP), to align its strategies and objectives with the UN's 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, as per the WIPO General Assembly Resolution of 2016 (https://www.wipo.int/wipolex/en/text/305623). Additionally, WIPO supports the WIPO Intergovernmental Committee on Intellectual Property and Genetic Resources, Traditional Knowledge and Folklore (IGC) (https://www.wipo.int/edocs/pubdocs/en/wipo-pub-rn2023-5-2-en-the-wipo-intergovernmental-committee-on-intellectual-property-and-genetic-resources-traditional-knowledge-and-folklore.pdf), which aims to reach an agreement on the protection of these forms of IP, with its mandate and work program detailed in Item 20 of the WIPO General Assembly Decision of 2019 (https://www.wipo.int/export/sites/www/about-wipo/ja/assemblies/pdf/2019_decisions.pdf). It also services the WIPO Standing Committee on the Law of Trademarks, Industrial Designs and Geographical Indications (SCT) (https://www.wipo.int/policy/en/sct/#:~:text=The%20SCT%20was%20created%20in,of%20national%20laws%20and%20procedures.), which deals with the development of international norms and standards in these areas.
Vertical Coordination: Vertical coordination within WIPO involves cooperation with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other specialized agencies, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and non-governmental organizations. This is achieved through working relations, consultation, and collaboration. This is structured under the Relations with Other Organizations section of the WIPO Convention (https://www.wipo.int/wipolex/en/text/283833), specifically in Article 8 (Coordination Committee), Article 9 (International Bureau), and Article 13 (Relations with Other Organizations). The WIPO operates through the General Assembly of all the members, the Conference of all the parties to the Convention, the Coordination Committee of the members of the Executive Committees of the Paris and Berne Unions, and a secretariat headed by a Director General. The WIPO also has permanent committees, standing committees, and other subsidiary bodies. WIPO assists members in the protection of intellectual property throughout the world and provides legal-technical assistance upon request. WIPO's work is organized around six sectors, each overseen by a Deputy Director General who works closely with the Director General to implement strategies and programs across all levels of the Organization (https://www.wipo.int/edocs/mdocs/govbody/en/a_32/a_32_inf_2-main1.doc).
