There is also the Senior Management Team (consisting of the Director General, Deputy Directors General, Assistant Directors General, and the Legal Counsel) providing strategic direction and oversight to the Organization and ensuring coherence and alignment between the different sectors and the governing bodies (https://www.wipo.int/edocs/mdocs/govbody/en/a_32/a_32_inf_2-main1.doc). Additionally, WIPO operates external offices in 7 countries (https://www.wipo.int/about-wipo/en/offices/).
Horizontal Coordination: Horizontal coordination within WIPO involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the intellectual property domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, the scientific community, and other UN agencies to promote and protect intellectual property rights and foster innovation and creativity. This coordination is guided by Article 13 of the WIPO Convention (https://www.wipo.int/wipolex/en/text/283833). For example, WIPO works with the culture sector to safeguard the diversity of cultural expressions and support the creative industries (https://www.wipo.int/edocs/pubdocs/en/tk/913/wipo_pub_913.pdf), with the health sector to facilitate access to medicines and medical technologies (https://tind.wipo.int/record/28688/files/wipo_pub_628.pdf), the education sector to enhance the quality and availability of educational resources (https://welc.wipo.int/) or with the environment sector to address climate change and biodiversity issues (https://www.wipo.int/policy/en/climate_change/). Horizontal coordination within WIPO can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programs and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the WIPO Development Agenda (https://www.wipo.int/ip-development/en/agenda/), the WIPO Re:Search initiative with WHO and BIO Ventures for Global Health (https://www.wipo.int/research/en/), or the WIPO GREEN platform with UNEP and other partners (https://www3.wipo.int/wipogreen/en/), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the UN Inter-Agency Task Force on Financing for Development (https://financing.desa.un.org/iatf/home/) or the Accessible Books Consortium (https://www.accessiblebooksconsortium.org/en/web/abc/about/index), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for intellectual property sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the WIPO Standards (https://www.wipo.int/standards/en/) or the WIPO IP Portal (https://ipportal.wipo.int/), and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilize support for intellectual property issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the World Intellectual Property Day (https://www.wipo.int/ip-outreach/en/ipday/) or the WIPO Magazine (https://www.wipo.int/wipo_magazine/en/).

Spatial Jurisdiction: WMO's jurisdiction is global, encompassing the weather, climate, and water resources of its member states and territories. WMO's authority covers the atmospheric, oceanic, and terrestrial domains, as well as the interfaces between them, with the aim of providing scientific information and services to protect life and property (https://wmo.int/about-wmo/overview).
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: The WMO Secretariat works to facilitate worldwide cooperation in the design and delivery of meteorological services, foster the rapid exchange of meteorological information, advance the standardization of meteorological data, build cooperation between meteorological and hydrological services, encourage research and training in meteorology, and expand the use of meteorology to benefit other sectors such as aviation, shipping, agriculture and water management (https://wmo.int/about-wmo/our-mandate). This includes addressing meteorological issues, such as disaster risk reduction, climate change adaptation, air quality, aviation, marine affairs, and agriculture (https://public.wmo.int/en/our-mandate/focus-areas). WMO also provides technical assistance, research and innovation, data exchange, and capacity development for its member states and territories, as well as supporting the implementation of the UN's development agenda and the Sustainable Development Goals (https://public.wmo.int/en/our-mandate/what-we-do).
Source of Jurisdiction: WMO derives its mandate from the Convention of the World Meteorological Organization, which established WMO as a specialized agency of the United Nations (https://library.wmo.int/viewer/48992/download?file=15_2021_en.pdf&type=pdf&navigator=1). Specifically, Article 2 of the Convention defines the purposes and functions of WMO, and Article 3 outlines the structure and membership of WMO (https://library.wmo.int/viewer/48992/download?file=15_2021_en.pdf&type=pdf&navigator=1). Additionally, WMO's general regulations, regulation 154 on the general function of the WMO secretariat, states that the secretariat shall execute the decisions of the constituent bodies and provide them with the necessary services (https://library.wmo.int/viewer/48992/download?file=15_2021_en.pdf&type=pdf&navigator=1). WMO's jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by its constituent bodies, such as the World Meteorological Congress, the Executive Council, and the regional associations (https://library.wmo.int/viewer/35722/download?file=48-I_en.pdf&type=pdf&navigator=1). These resolutions and decisions provide guidance and direction for WMO's activities and programmes, as well as the cooperation and coordination with other organizations and stakeholders. WMO's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the Framework Convention on Climate Change, the Vienna Convention on the Protection of the Ozone Layer, and the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction, which provide further legal frameworks for WMO's jurisdiction over specific meteorological issues and domains.
Defined Objectives: According to Part II, Article 2 of the Convention of the World Meteorological Organization (https://library.wmo.int/viewer/48992/download?file=15_2021_en.pdf&type=pdf&navigator=1). The objectives encompass six main purposes: facilitating worldwide cooperation in the establishment and maintenance of networks of stations and centres for meteorological, hydrological and related observations and services (Article 2 a); promoting the establishment and maintenance of systems for the rapid exchange of meteorological and related information (Article 2 b); promoting standardization of meteorological and related observations and ensuring the uniform publication of observations and statistics (Article 2 c); furthering the application of meteorology to aviation, shipping, water problems, agriculture and other human activities (Article 2 d); promoting activities in operational hydrology and furthering close cooperation between Meteorological and Hydrological Services (Article 2 e); and encouraging research and training in meteorology and, as appropriate, in related fields and assisting in coordinating the international aspects of such research and training (Article 2 f). These purposes enable the WMO to fulfil its role as the specialized agency of the United Nations for meteorology, operational hydrology and related geophysical sciences (https://library.wmo.int/doc_num.php?explnum_id=11187).
Strategies:
The WMO Secretariat executes its objectives via several strategies: firstly, a Strategic Plan, revised every four years by the World Meteorological Congress, which establishes the secretariat's vision, mission, strategic goals, core functions, and targets (https://community.wmo.int/en/planning-and-monitoring/strategic-planning#:~:text=The%20process&text=The%20WMO%20Strategic%20Plan%20articulates,the%202020%2D2023%20financial%20period). The current plan, applicable for 2024-2027, aligns with the WMO's mandate to advance meteorological, climatological, hydrological, and related environmental services (https://library.wmo.int/viewer/68578/download?file=1336_WMO-Strategic-Plan-2024-2027_en.pdf&type=pdf&navigator=1). Secondly, a  Results-based Budget, devised by the secretariat and ratified by the World Meteorological Congress, detail resources for implementation of the Strategic Plan, including the functioning of constituent bodies and the Secretariat (https://library.wmo.int/viewer/56690?medianame=1236_en_#page=33&viewer=picture&o=bookmark&n=0&q=).  
Finally, various agreements, mechanisms, platforms, and initiatives provide an operational framework for implementing the WMO's mandate, addressing meteorology, hydrology, climatology, and related environmental disciplines (https://library.wmo.int/viewer/55618/download?file=1196_en.pdf&type=pdf&navigator=1). These regulatory provisions make it possible to operate the 24/7/365 global systems for observations, data exchange and management, forecasting and provision of authoritative scientific assessments and standardized service products to a variety of users in each WMO Member State and Member Territory (https://library.wmo.int/viewer/55618/download?file=EC-69_Progress_report_en.pdf&type=pdf&navigator=1). 
The WMO also has a Competency Framework that helps Members design their services for effective delivery, assist in staffing decisions, guide the performance assessment of staff members, and offer recommended learning outcomes to use in planning training programmes (https://library.wmo.int/viewer/56877/download?file=1209_en.pdf&type=pdf&navigator=1).  In addition to these, the WMO has Resolutions, Decisions and Recommendations adopted by the Congress, Executive Council, Regional Associations and Technical Commissions in force (https://tools.wmo.int/wmo-resolutions/). These resolutions and decisions guide the overall progress towards achieving departmental targets and organizational objectives and goals.
Inter-Institutional Relationship:
The WMO collaborates with key organizations to fulfill its objectives. It engages with 193 Member States and various stakeholders through the World Meteorological Congress, serving as the highest-level meteorological decision-making body (https://wmo.int/about-wmo/overview). As the primary meteorological authority within the UN system, WMO's relationship with the UN is grounded in Part XII, Article 25 of the Convention of the World Meteorological Organization (https://library.wmo.int/viewer/48992/download?file=15_2021_en.pdf&type=pdf&navigator=1), pursuant to Article 57 of the Charter of the United Nations (https://www.un.org/en/about-us/un-charter/full-text). 
Additionally, WMO supports National Meteorological and Hydrological Services (NMHSs) and advances the application of meteorology and hydrology in many societal and economic areas (https://wmo.int/about-wmo/overview). Pursuant to Part XIII, Article 26 of its convention, WMO collaborates with UN specialized agencies, multilateral development banks, climate funds and others, addressing shared meteorological concerns (https://library.wmo.int/viewer/48992/download?file=15_2021_en.pdf&type=pdf&navigator=1). 
Moreover, WMO contributes to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction, and the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (https://wmo.int/about-wmo/partnerships).
Furthermore, WMO maintains a relationship with the public, private, and academic sectors operating in the global weather arena through its Public-Private Engagement (PPE) initiative (https://community.wmo.int/en/activity-areas/public-private-partnerships). This initiative encourages and enables Members to pursue mutually beneficial partnerships and engagement with all sectors and stakeholders in order to enhance weather, climate, and water services for businesses, individuals, and society as a whole (https://community.wmo.int/en/activity-areas/public-private-partnerships). 
Finally, WMO facilitates the Voluntary Cooperation Programme (VCP), which focuses on meeting urgent needs of Members through direct financing, small grants and transfer of expertise and technology (https://old.wmo.int/extranet/pages/prog/dra/vcp_en.php).
Vertical Coordination:
Vertical coordination within the WMO involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other specialized agencies, regional and intergovernmental organizations, national governments, and local authorities⁵. This is achieved through reporting, cooperation, and assistance⁶. This is structured under the Convention of the World Meteorological Organization⁵. The WMO operates through the World Meteorological Congress, the supreme body of the Organization, which determines policy (https://public-old.wmo.int/en/about-us/governance#:~:text=The%20World%20Meteorological%20Congress%20is,activities%20within%20their%20respective%20Regions.). Each member state and territory is represented by a Permanent Representative with WMO when Congress meets every four years (https://wmo.int/about-wmo/governance). The Executive Council (EC) implements Congress decisions⁴. The Secretariat is an eight-department organization with a staff of 200 headed by a Secretary-General, who can serve a maximum of two four-year terms (https://wmo.int/about-wmo/governance).  Six regional associations are responsible for the coordination of meteorological, hydrological and related activities within their respective Regions, while technical commissions consisting of technical experts study technical matters and make recommendations to Congress and the Executive Council (https://wmo.int/about-wmo/governance). 
The Officers of WMO are a President and three Vice-Presidents, who are also chair and vice-chairs of Congress and the Executive Council (https://wmo.int/about-wmo/governance). The Secretary-General oversees the functioning of the Secretariat, headquartered in Geneva (https://wmo.int/about-wmo/governance). There is also The Bureau (the Bureau consists of the President, the three Vice-Presidents and the Secretary-General), an informal consultative mechanism to advise the President and facilitate the discharge of his mandate and coordinate the work of Congress and the Executive Council. WMO, in addition to constituent bodies (Executive Council, regional associations and technical commissions), establishes additional bodies to advise on specific subjects. Currently, these include: Research Board on Weather, Climate, Water and the Environment (Research Board), acting as the primary conduit to engage the international research community in the work of WMO; Scientific Advisory Panel (SAP), advising on WMO research strategies and the optimal scientific directions to support the evolution of its mandate in weather, climate, water and related environmental and social sciences; Joint WMO-IOC Collaborative Board (JCB), an interagency body with the Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission of UNESCO to coordinate on ocean matters of common interest; Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), created in 1988 by WMO and UNEP, is the United Nations body for assessing the science related to climate change; the  Financial Advisory Committee (FINAC) provides advice from WMO Members on financial matters and the affordability, sustainability and implementation of the results-based budget to Congress and the Executive Council.
The WMO assists members in the implementation of its standards, policies, and programmes, and provides technical cooperation and assistance upon request (https://wmo.int/about-us/governance/technical-commissions/standards-and-recommended-practices).  Also the WMO Liaison Offices represent the scientific and technical work and priorities of WMO Members in international processes at their location and the wider region (https://wmo.int/about-us/liaison-offices). WMO currently has some 38 institutions acting as 26 Regional Training Centres (RTC), offering short and long-term training to staff of WMO Member National Hydrological and Meteorological Services (https://public-old.wmo.int/en/resources/meteoworld/wmo-regional-training-centres). Additionally, the WMO operates the Education and Training Programme (ETRP) that aims at ensuring the National Meteorological and hydrological Services (NMHSs) and their associated institutions are competent to deliver required services and play other relevant roles in national socioeconomic development, by making available the necessary policy, guidance, resources and training (https://wmo.int/activities/education-and-training-programme).
Horizontal Coordination: Horizontal coordination within WMO involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the meteorological domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, scientific community, and other UN agencies to ensure that meteorological considerations are integrated into all policies and that meteorological policies are aligned with other sectoral policies (https://community.wmo.int/en/activity-areas/public-private-partnerships). This coordination is guided by the WMO Unified Data Policy (https://wmo.int/wmo-unified-data-policy-resolution-res1#:~:text=The%20WMO%20Unified%20Policy%20for,States%20and%20Territories%20of%20WMO.). For example, WMO works with the disaster risk reduction sector to support humanitarian activities (https://community.wmo.int/en/activity-areas/wmo-coordination-mechanism-wcm), with the climate sector to provide weather, water, and climate information (https://wmo.int/news/media-centre/climate-change-bad-health-climate-services-save-lives), or with the ocean sector to enhance the meteorological services in coastal areas (https://community.wmo.int/en/activity-areas/Marine/JCOMM/Overview). Horizontal coordination within WMO can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the WMO Coordination Mechanism (WCM) to support humanitarian activities (https://community.wmo.int/en/activity-areas/wmo-coordination-mechanism-wcm), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the Inter-Agency Standing Committee (https://meetings.wmo.int/EC-76/English/2.%20PROVISIONAL%20REPORT%20%28Approved%20documents%29/EC-76-d03-1%2813%29-WMO-COORDINATION-MECHANISM-IMPLEMENTATION-PLAN-approved_en.docx), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for meteorological sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the WMO Technical Regulations (https://wmo.int/about-us/governance/technical-commissions/standards-and-recommended-practices#:~:text=WMO%20Technical%20Regulations%2C%20an%20international,universal%20application%20by%20all%20Members.) or the WMO Unified Data Policy (https://wmo.int/wmo-unified-data-policy-resolution-res1#:~:text=The%20WMO%20Unified%20Policy%20for,States%20and%20Territories%20of%20WMO.), (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for meteorological issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, as documented in the WMO Strategic Plan 2024-2027 (https://library.wmo.int/viewer/68578/download?file=1336_WMO-Strategic-Plan-2024-2027_en.pdf&type=pdf&navigator=1). The WMO provides leadership and direction on matters critical to meteorology, shapes the meteorological research agenda, sets norms and standards, articulates evidence-based policy options, provides technical support to countries, and monitors and assesses meteorological trends (https://wmo.int/about-wmo/our-mandate). WMO facilitates the participation of various actors in the meteorological sector and enhances cooperation and coordination within the UN system on meteorological matters (https://wmo.int/about-wmo/our-mandate).

Spatial Jurisdiction: UNWTO's jurisdiction is global, encompassing its 160 member states and six associate members from all regions of the world. This includes a focus on developing countries and small island developing states (SIDS) within the oceans, with authority to promote sustainable tourism practices and policies (https://www.unwto.org/about-us#:~:text=Members%3A%20An%20intergovernmental%20organization%2C%20UN,supreme%20organ%20of%20the%20Organization.). However, UN Tourism does not have direct control over the maritime zones or ocean space of its members, as these are subject to national sovereignty and international law.
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: The UNWTO is responsible for promoting responsible, sustainable, and universally accessible tourism (https://www.unwto.org/about-us). It fosters tourism education and training, generates market knowledge, and promotes competitive and sustainable tourism policies (https://www.unwto.org/who-we-are). UNWTO also works to make tourism an effective tool for development through technical assistance projects in over 100 countries. It encourages the implementation of the Global Code of Ethics for Tourism, aiming to maximize tourism's socio-economic contribution while minimizing its possible negative impacts (https://www.unwto.org/who-we-are).
Source of Jurisdiction: UNWTO derives its mandate from the Statutes of the World Tourism Organization (https://webunwto.s3-eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/imported_images/51970/unwtostatuteseng.pdf), which established UNWTO as a specialized agency of the United Nations. Specifically, Article 3 of the Statutes defines the aims and objectives of UNWTO, Articles 4-7 outlines the provisions for membership of the UNWTO, Article 8-24 define organizational structure and governance, and Articles 25-26 describe budgets and expenditures. Additionally, the General Rules of Procedure of UNWTO ((https://webunwto.s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2019-11/130718basicdocumentsenweb.pdf) also govern the functioning and decision-making of UNWTO's governing bodies, namely the General Assembly, the Executive Council, and the regional commissions. The rules of procedure specify the composition, powers, duties, sessions, agenda, voting, languages, and other aspects of these bodies, as well as the role and responsibilities of the UNWTO secretariat. The rules of procedure are based on the Statutes of UNWTO, and can be amended by the General Assembly or the Executive Council, as appropriate. The rules of procedure also provide for the participation of other UNWTO members, such as associate members and affiliate members, as well as observers and guests, in the meetings and activities of UNWTO. UNWTO's jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by its governing bodies, such as the General Assembly, the Executive Council, and the regional commissions (https://www.unwto.org/unwto-general-assembly). These resolutions and decisions provide guidance and direction for UNWTO's policies and programmes, as well as cooperation and coordination with other organisations and stakeholders. UNWTO's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the Global Code of Ethics for Tourism (https://webunwto.s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2019-10/gcetpassportglobalcodeen.pdf), the Convention on the Protection of Tourists (https://webunwto.s3-eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/imported_images/47266/6_report_on_the_convention_of_tourists_en_0.pdf), and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://www.unwto.org/tourism-in-2030-agenda), which provide further legal frameworks for UNWTO's jurisdiction over specific tourism issues and domains.
Defined Objectives: According to Article 3 of the Statutes of the UNWTO, the UNWTO's objectives are defined as (1) To promote and develop tourism as a significant means of fostering international peace and understanding, economic development and international trade (Article 3, paragraph 1), (2) To pay particular attention to the interests of the developing countries in the field of tourism (Article 3, paragraph 2), and (3) To establish and maintain effective collaboration with the appropriate organs of the United Nations and its specialized agencies (Article 3, paragraph 3). Other important aims of the UNWTO include to provide leadership and support to the tourism sector in advancing knowledge and tourism policies worldwide; to encourage the implementation of the Global Code of Ethics for Tourism, to maximize tourism's socio-economic contribution while minimizing its possible negative impacts; to prepare and recommend international agreements on any question that falls within the competence of the Organization; and to make tourism an effective tool for development through technical assistance projects in over 100 countries around the world (https://www.unwto.org/our-focus).
Strategies: The United Nations World Tourism Organization (UNWTO) executes its objectives via several strategies. Firstly, the UNWTO has a strategic plan that is directed towards governments of UNWTO Member States and aims to support and strengthen the capacity of National, regional, and local tourism Administrations (https://www.unwto.org/UNWTO-strategy). This strategic plan involves a sectorial analysis of tourism education and training, identifying weaknesses in the system as well as gaps between the educational offering and the real needs of the sector. The final product of this action is a strategic document containing plans and programmes in education and training at the national or regional level (https://www.unwto.org/UNWTO-strategy). Secondly, the UNWTO has a Programme of Work for 2024-2025, which is a wide-reaching plan built around clear priorities, including key pillars and landmarks (https://webunwto.s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2023-10/A25_4_c_Draft_Programme_Work_2024_2025_rev1_En.pdf?VersionId=f87QHlfdEF31lDDrbrms82gFO2NCQZu5). This plan is aimed at restoring tourist confidence by developing and harmonizing minimum international standards, and providing sufficient guarantees for the protection of international tourists in the post COVID-19 world (https://www.unwto.org/international-code-for-the-protection-of-tourists). Thirdly, the UNWTO has established policy frameworks to effectively support the tourism sector at different levels: national, regional, and local (https://www.unwto.org/policy-destination-management). These policies focus on tourism policy and strategic planning, governance and vertical cooperation, and public-private partnerships. Finally, the UNWTO has instituted several collaborative initiatives. For example, it has signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with the African Civil Aviation Commission (AFCAC) to promote sustainable tourism and the implementation of the Single African Air Transport Market (SAATM) (https://www.unwto.org/news/unwto-and-afcac-partner-around-air-connectivity-in-africa). It also has a partnership with Google to lead global tourism’s recovery through innovation, education, and market intelligence (https://www.unwto.org/news/unwto-and-google-launch-global-partnership-to-lead-tourism-recovery). The UNWTO's strategic plans and initiatives are typically aligned with global agendas such as the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, indicating a long-term perspective (https://www.unwto.org/reports/from-crisis-to-transformation/agenda-2030.html). The UNWTO also works with its members and partners on an ongoing basis to achieve its objectives (https://www.unwto.org/europe/partnerships).
Inter-Institutional Relationship: UNWTO cooperates with various institutions to promote sustainable and responsible tourism (https://www.unwto.org/sustainable-development). It partners with the European Union (EU), implementing a framework agreement signed in Brussels on 28 February 2018, (https://www.unwto.org/europe/press-release/2018-02-28/unwto-deepens-tourism-cooperation-european-union). Likewise, UNWTO maintains a relationship with the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), collaborating on projects related to rural development and food security, based on a memorandum of understanding signed in 2020 (https://www.unwto.org/news/unwto-and-fao-to-work-together-on-developing-tourism-for-rural-development). Furthermore, UNWTO supports the World Trade Organization (WTO), contributing to the trade and development agenda and the Aid for Trade initiative (https://www.unwto.org/global/news/2019-07-15/tourism-world-trade-organization-wto-aid-trade-global-review-2019). It also engages with the UN system, participating in the UN System Chief Executives Board for Coordination (UNCEB) (https://www.unwto.org/archive/global/press-release/2013-04-04/unwto-hosts-meeting-un-chief-executives-board) and the UN Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) (https://www.unwto.org/archive/africa/press-release/2017-07-07/unwto-hosts-presentation-unctad-report-tourism-driver-transformative-and-in), preparing joint reports and recommendations. Additionally, UNWTO facilitates the Partnerships in Education (https://www.unwto.org/partnerships-in-education) to enhance education and training capabilities in tourism, involving certified programmes and affiliate members.
Vertical Coordination: Vertical coordination within UNWTO involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other specialized agencies, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and local authorities. This is achieved through policy and governance models, strategic leadership, effective implementation, and efficient governance. This is structured under the Statutes of the World Tourism Organization (https://webunwto.s3-eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/imported_images/51970/unwtostatuteseng.pdf) under the Sections Headquarters (Article 2), Organs (Article 8), General Assembly (Articles 9-13), Executive Council (Articles 14-20), Secretariat (Articles 21-24), Budget and Expenditure (Articles 25-26), Quorum (Article 27), Voting (Articles 28-30), Legal Personality, Privileges and Immunities (Articles 31-32), and Amendments (Article 33). The UNWTO operates through the General Assembly of all the Full Members, the Executive Council of elected Full Members, and a Secretariat headed by a Secretary-General. The UNWTO also has technical or regional bodies that may be established by the Assembly and assists Members in the development and management of tourism destinations, the promotion and development of tourism, and the implementation of its standards, policies, and programmes. UNWTO's work is organised around five regions, each overseen by a Regional Director who works closely with the Secretary-General to implement strategies and programmes across all levels of the Organization (https://www.unwto.org/regional-departments). There is also the Global Tourism Crisis Committee, composed of the Secretary-General, the Regional Directors, the Chairs of the Executive Council and the Committee of Affiliate Members, and representatives of the United Nations and other international organizations, which provides guidance and recommendations on the response of the tourism sector to the COVID-19 crisis and the recovery measures (https://www.unwto.org/news/global-tourism-crisis-committee-meets-again-to-explore-safe-travel-in-age-of-vaccines). In addition, the Affiliate Members of UNWTO are a network of over 500 entities from the private sector, including companies, educational and research institutions, destinations, and NGOs. They collaborate with UNWTO and its Member States to promote sustainable tourism development. By joining the Affiliate Members, entities gain benefits such as global visibility, competitiveness, innovation, and access to UNWTO resources and events. The Affiliate Members have an exclusive online platform, AMConnected+, where they can communicate, share information, and build relationships within the network and with UNWTO. The strategic direction and activities of the Affiliate Members are overseen by the Board of Affiliate Members, which is composed of 12 elected representatives and liaises with UNWTO (https://www.unwto.org/affiliate-members).
Horizontal Coordination: Horizontal coordination within UNWTO involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the tourism domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, the academic community, and other UN agencies to ensure that tourism is a driver of economic growth, social inclusion, environmental sustainability, and cultural diversity (https://www.unwto.org/news/unwto-at-fitur-2024-investments-sustainable-tourism-and-collaboration). For example, UNWTO works with the health sector to support the safe and responsible recovery of tourism from the COVID-19 pandemic (https://www.unwto.org/covid-19-oneplanet-responsible-recovery), with the education sector to enhance the quality and relevance of tourism education and training (https://www.unwto.org/un-tourism-academy), with the culture sector to foster the preservation and promotion of cultural heritage and diversity (https://www.unwto.org/tourism-and-culture), or with the environment sector to advance the transition to a low-carbon and circular economy in tourism (https://www.unwto.org/sustainable-development/one-planet). Horizontal coordination within UNWTO can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Technical Cooperation Programme (https://www.unwto.org/technical-cooperation) or the Global Tourism Plastics Initiative with UNEP and the Ellen MacArthur Foundation (https://www.unwto.org/sustainable-development/global-tourism-plastics-initiative), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the Committee on Tourism and Competitiveness (https://www.unwto.org/competitiveness-commitee-ctc#:~:text=The%20Committee%20on%20Tourism%20and%20Competitiveness%20(CTC)%20is%20one%20of,DEC%2F7(XCV).) or the UN Inter-Agency Task Force on Social and Solidarity Economy (https://unsse.org/), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for tourism sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the International Recommendations for Tourism Statistics (https://unstats.un.org/unsd/publication/Seriesm/SeriesM_83rev1e.pdf) or the Tourism Satellite Account (https://unstats.un.org/unsd/publication/Seriesf/SeriesF_80rev1e.pdf), and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for tourism issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the World Tourism Day (https://www.unwto.org/world-tourism-day) or the Tourism for SDGs Platform (https://tourism4sdgs.org/).

Spatial Jurisdiction: The World Trade Organization (WTO)'s jurisdiction is not limited to a specific geographical area, ocean space, territory, or maritime zones. Instead, as an intergovernmental organization that regulates and facilitates international trade it has a global reach, with 164 member states representing over 98% of global trade and global GDP (https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/whatis_e/tif_e/org6_e.htm). The WTO's authority extends to the trade practices within these member states, irrespective of their location or the extent of their territorial waters and exclusive economic zones. It does not exercise jurisdiction in the same way a state does as its main purpose is to reduce tariffs and other barriers to trade.
Subject Matter Jurisdiction: The WTO is an international body that oversees global trade rules. It acts as a forum for negotiating trade agreements, handling trade disputes, and monitoring trade policies. The WTO's areas of responsibility extend to goods and services, as well as intellectual property¹. It also cooperates with other international organizations and provides technical assistance and training for developing economies. However, it does not have specific authority over marine affairs, fisheries, or environmental protection (https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/whatis_e/inbrief_e/inbr_e.htm).
Source of Jurisdiction: The WTO derives its mandate from the Marrakesh Agreement Establishing the World Trade Organization (https://www.wto.org/english/docs_e/legal_e/04-wto.pdf), which entered into force on 1 January 1995 and established the WTO as the successor to the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) (https://www.wto.org/english/res_e/booksp_e/agrmntseries2_gatt_e.pdf). Specifically, Articles II and III of the Marrakesh Agreement define the scope and functions of the WTO, and Article IV outlines the structure and decision-making of the WTO. Additionally, the WTO's Dispute Settlement Understanding (DSU), which is annexed to the Marrakesh Agreement, sets out the rules and procedures for the settlement of disputes between WTO members (https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/dispu_e/dsu_e.htm). The DSU establishes the jurisdiction of the WTO panels and the Appellate Body, which are the adjudicating bodies of the WTO dispute settlement system. The DSU also provides for the implementation and enforcement of the rulings and recommendations of the panels and the Appellate Body. The WTO's jurisdiction is also influenced by the other agreements and arrangements that are annexed to the Marrakesh Agreement, which are collectively known as the "covered agreements" of the WTO (https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/whatis_e/tif_e/utw_chap2_e.pdf). These agreements and arrangements cover various aspects of trade in goods, services, intellectual property, and trade policy reviews, and they contain specific rights and obligations for WTO members (https://www.wto.org/english/docs_e/legal_e/legal_e.htm). The covered agreements also provide for the application of the DSU to disputes arising under them, unless otherwise specified (https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/dispu_e/dsu_e.htm). The covered agreements are an integral part of the WTO legal framework and constitute the primary source of law for the WTO dispute settlement system. The WTO's mandate is also supported by the participation of the WTO in various international agreements and frameworks, such as the Agreement on Trade Facilitation, the Trade and Environment Committee, and the Trade and Development Committee, which provide further legal frameworks for the WTO's jurisdiction over specific trade-related issues and domains (https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/whatis_e/tif_e/agrm1_e.htm). These agreements and frameworks also aim to enhance the cooperation and coordination between the WTO and other international organisations and stakeholders.
Defined Objectives: According to Article III of the Marrakesh Agreement Establishing the World Trade Organization (https://www.wto.org/english/docs_e/legal_e/04-wto.pdf), the WTO's objectives encompass several key functions: facilitating the implementation, administration and operation of the WTO agreements and providing a framework for their further negotiation (paragraph 1); providing a forum for trade negotiations and a framework for their implementation (paragraph 2); administering the dispute settlement mechanism and ensuring the prompt and effective resolution of trade disputes (paragraph 3); administering the trade policy review mechanism and enhancing the transparency of trade policies (paragraph 4); cooperating with other international organizations and ensuring greater coherence in global economic policy-making (paragraph 5); and helping developing countries, especially the least-developed ones, to benefit from the multilateral trading system and to achieve their trade and development objectives. These functions enable the WTO to fulfil its role as the common institutional framework for the conduct of trade relations among its members in matters related to the WTO agreements (Article II, paragraph 1).
Strategies: The WTO has a comprehensive strategy in place to achieve its objectives and mandates in ensuring that trade flows as smoothly, predictably, and freely as possible. It operates a non-discriminatory trading system that spells out the rights and obligations of its members (https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/whatis_e/inbrief_e/inbr_e.htm). The WTO agreements, which are the result of negotiations, cover a wide range of activities including agriculture, textiles and clothing, banking, telecommunications, government purchases, industrial standards and product safety, food sanitation regulations, intellectual property, and more (https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/whatis_e/tif_e/fact2_e.htm). The WTO’s strategic plans are largely the outcome of negotiations between the members. The current round of trade negotiations, known as the Doha Development Agenda, was launched in 2001 (https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/dda_e/dda_e.htm) to succeed the Uruguay Round negotiations (1986–94) (https://www.wto.org/gatt_docs/english/sulpdf/92160001.pdf). The WTO has expanded its scope to include cooperation with the UN system, the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), and other international partners on a wide range of issues (https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/coher_e/mdg_e/global_partnership_e.htm). The WTO’s annual budget is contributed by its members based on their proportion of international trade (https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/secre_e/budget_e.htm). The current budget proposal for the WTO Secretariat for the biennium 2024-2025 (https://docs.wto.org/dol2fe/Pages/SS/directdoc.aspx?filename=q:/WT/BFA/W643.pdf&Open=True) requests a modest increase of 7.4% in 2024 and 0.9% in 2025, amounting to CHF 211.76 million and CHF 213.7 million respectively. The WTO’s regulatory mechanisms are based on a number of simple, fundamental principles that run throughout all of its documents. These principles include trade without discrimination, national treatment (treating foreigners and locals equally), and the commitment to lowering trade barriers (https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/whatis_e/tif_e/utw_chap1_e.pdf).
Inter-Institutional Relationship: The WTO cooperates with various institutions to promote trade and development. It works with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank, based on the coherence mandate in the Marrakesh Decision of 1994 (https://www.wto.org/english/docs_e/legal_e/marrakesh_decl_e.htm), to ensure consistency and complementarity of global economic policies (https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/coher_e/coher_e.htm). Likewise, the WTO collaborates with the United Nations (UN) and its specialized agencies, such as the UN Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), the World Health Organization (WHO), and the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO), under the arrangements for effective cooperation signed in 1995, to address the linkages between trade and other policy areas, as specified in Article V of the WTO Agreement (https://www.wto.org/english/docs_e/legal_e/04-wto.pdf). Furthermore, the WTO partners with the International Trade Centre (ITC), a joint agency of the WTO and the UN, to provide trade-related technical assistance and capacity building for developing countries, as stated in the Doha Ministerial Declaration of 2001 (https://www.wto.org/english/res_e/booksp_e/ddec_e.pdf). It also engages with the Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU), an international organization of national parliaments, to enhance the parliamentary dimension of the WTO and foster dialogue and accountability on trade issues, as agreed in the Memorandum of Understanding of 2018 (https://www.wto.org/english/forums_e/parliamentarians_e/parliamentarians_conf_e.htm). Additionally, the WTO participates in various collaborative initiatives with like-minded groups of members and other stakeholders, such as the Joint Statement Initiative on E-commerce (https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/ecom_e/joint_statement_e.htm), the Joint Statement on Investment Facilitation (https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/minist_e/mc12_e/briefing_notes_e/bfinvfac_e.htm#:~:text=Originally%20launched%20by%20a%20group,of%20the%20economy%20(goods%20and), and the COVAX Facility on COVID-19 vaccines (https://www.wto.org/english/news_e/roadmap_igo_01jun21_e.htm), to advance discussions and actions on emerging and pressing trade challenges.
Vertical Coordination: Vertical coordination connected to the WTO involves downward coordination into subsidiary bodies of WTO and receipt of governance input from member states.  This is structured under the Organization section of the WTO Agreement (https://www.wto.org/english/docs_e/legal_e/04-wto.pdf), specifically in Articles IV-IX. The WTO operates through the Ministerial Conference of all the members, the General Council of representatives from all members, and a secretariat headed by a Director-General. It also has councils, committees, and other subsidiary bodies (Article IV, paragraph 2) (https://www.wto.org/english/docs_e/legal_e/04-wto.pdf). In addition, the WTO assists members in the implementation of its agreements, policies, and programmes and provides technical cooperation and training upon request (https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/devel_e/teccop_e/tct_e.htm). WTO's work is organised around three main areas: trade negotiations, trade disputes, and trade policy reviews. Each area is overseen by a specific council or body that works closely with the Director-General to implement strategies and programmes across all levels of the Organization (https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/whatis_e/tif_e/org1_e.htm). There is also the Trade Negotiations Committee (consisting of the Director-General and representatives from all members) that supervises the conduct of the multilateral trade negotiations and reports to the Ministerial Conference (https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/dda_e/negotiating_groups_e.htm). Additionally, WTO operates six regional offices and liaison offices in 12 Member States (https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/whatis_e/tif_e/org3_e.htm). Besides the Director-General, at the WTO headquarters, there is a clear line of duty within the leadership team comprising of four Deputy Directors-General and 16 Directors with portfolios focusing on different aspects of the WTO's mandate (https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/dg_e/senior_management_e.htm). In addition, WTO/Europe coordinates with the European Union and its institutions and is the host organisation and partner of the European Trade Policy Forum (https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/countries_e/european_communities_e.htm).
Horizontal Coordination: Horizontal coordination within the WTO involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the trade domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, the academic community, and other international organizations to ensure that trade flows smoothly, predictably and freely as possible and that trade policies are consistent with the multilateral trading system. This coordination is guided by Article V of the WTO Agreement (https://www.wto.org/english/docs_e/legal_e/04-wto.pdf). For example, the WTO works with the agriculture sector to reduce trade barriers and distortions in agricultural markets (https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/agric_e/agric_e.htm), with the services sector to facilitate the expansion and liberalization of trade in services (https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/serv_e/serv_e.htm), the environment sector to address the linkages between trade and environmental policies (https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/envir_e/envir_e.htm) or with the development sector to assist developing and least-developed countries to benefit from the global trading system (https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/devel_e/devel_e.htm). Horizontal coordination within the WTO can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Aid for Trade initiative (https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/devel_e/a4t_e/aid4trade_e.htm) or the Trade Facilitation Agreement Facility (https://www.tfafacility.org/), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the Committee on Trade and Environment (https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/envir_e/cte00_e.htm) or the Enhanced Integrated Framework (https://www.enhancedif.org/en), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for trade sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Trade Policy Review Mechanism (https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/tpr_e/tpr_e.htm) or the Trade Monitoring Database (https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/tpr_e/trade_monitoring_e.htm), and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for trade issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Public Forum (https://www.wto.org/english/forums_e/public_forum_e/public_forum_e.htm) or the World Trade Report (https://www.wto.org/english/res_e/publications_e/world_trade_report_e.htm).
